metadata.title: The Stable Rank of Diagonal ASH Algebras and Crossed Products by Minimal Homeomorphisms

extraction_notes.note: Parts of these proofs argue from matrix-region pictures (\includegraphics); the figure content is not in the source, and the Section 3.1 lemma dependency diagram is omitted.
Remark 2.5 retyped as definition: it introduces the closure notation used later; could stay a remark.
Section 3.1 outline is a proof sketch of Theorem 3.26: the sketch rule asks for rigor semi_formal on the proof node, while the rigor rule excludes proofs; followed the sketch rule.
Enumerated lists inside proofs restate an applied lemma's conclusions; since every list item is an author label, each item became a child step of the step applying the lemma.
The inline claim 'Let us show how to define tau_i and D^{(i+1)}' was extended over the next two paragraphs, which carry out that construction, instead of stopping at the paragraph break.
Roadmap and motivation paragraphs, the 'Simply put' display of C_i notation (not used later) and the acknowledgement were left out.

nodes.name: Stable rank
nodes.statement: The \textit{stable rank} of a unital $\mathrm{C}^{*}$-algebra $A$ is the least natural number $n$ for which the set of all $n$-tuples of $A$ that generate $A$ as a left ideal is dense in $A^{n}$; if no such integer exists, the stable rank is said to be $\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Stable rank of a unital C*-algebra: least n such that left-generating n-tuples are dense in A^n.

nodes.name: Rieffel's characterization of stable rank one
nodes.statement: In \cite{rie}, Proposition 3.1, it is shown that a unital $\mathrm{C}^{*}$-algebra has stable rank one if and only if the set of invertible elements is dense within the algebra.
assumptions: a unital $\mathrm{C}^{*}$-algebra
conclusions: a unital $\mathrm{C}^{*}$-algebra has stable rank one if and only if the set of invertible elements is dense within the algebra
equivalent_conditions: the set of invertible elements is dense within the algebra

nodes.name: Rørdam's UHF stable rank one theorem
nodes.statement: He showed that the tensor product of a simple unital stably finite $\mathrm{C}^{*}$-algebra and a UHF algebra has stable rank one.
conclusions: the tensor product of a simple unital stably finite $\mathrm{C}^{*}$-algebra and a UHF algebra has stable rank one

nodes.name: Dădărlat–Nagy–Némethi–Pasnicu stable rank one theorem
nodes.statement: This was followed by a result of D\u{a}d\u{a}rlat, Nagy, N{\'{e}}methi, and Pasnicu, who proved in \cite{4Rom} that a simple unital inductive limit of full matrix algebras (those of the form $C(X,M_{n}(\mathbb{C}))$ for a compact Hausdorff space $X$) always has stable rank one assuming there is a uniform upper bound on the dimensions of the base spaces in the finite stage algebras.
assumptions: assuming there is a uniform upper bound on the dimensions of the base spaces in the finite stage algebras
conclusions: a simple unital inductive limit of full matrix algebras (those of the form $C(X,M_{n}(\mathbb{C}))$ for a compact Hausdorff space $X$) always has stable rank one

nodes.name: Rørdam's Z-stable stable rank one theorem
nodes.statement: Later, in \cite{Ror2}, R\o{}rdam also showed that every simple unital finite $\mathrm{C}^{*}$-algebra that absorbs the Jiang--Su algebra, $\mathcal{Z}$, tensorially has stable rank one.
conclusions: every simple unital finite $\mathrm{C}^{*}$-algebra that absorbs the Jiang--Su algebra, $\mathcal{Z}$, tensorially has stable rank one

nodes.name: Villadsen's counterexample to the converse
nodes.statement: Villadsen proved in \cite{vil1} that the converse to the result in \cite{4Rom} does not hold by constructing a unital simple limit of full matrix algebras, whose base space dimensions were not uniformly bounded above, yet which nonetheless still had stable rank one.
conclusions: the converse to the result in \cite{4Rom} does not hold

nodes.name: Villadsen's AH algebras of arbitrary stable rank
nodes.statement: He went on, in \cite{vil2}, to construct a class of simple unital AH algebras---inductive limits of homogeneous $\mathrm{C}^{*}$-algebras (those whose irreducible representations all have the same dimension)---of arbitrary stable rank, thereby affirming the subtleties present in the problem of stable rank.
conclusions: to construct a class of simple unital AH algebras

nodes.name: Diagonal map between full matrix algebras
nodes.statement: Given compact metric spaces $X$ and $Z$, together with continuous functions $\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{k}\colon Z\to X$, there is a naturally induced $^*$-homomorphism from $C(X,M_{n}(\mathbb{C}))$ to $C(Z,M_{nk}(\mathbb{C}))$ given by $$ f\mapsto\operatorname{diag}(f\circ\lambda_{1},\ldots,f\circ\lambda_{k}). $$ These induced maps between full matrix algebras are referred to as \textit{diagonal}.
nodes.statement_short: The *-homomorphism C(X,M_n)->C(Z,M_nk) f -> diag(f o lambda_1,...,f o lambda_k) induced by maps lambda_i: Z->X is called diagonal.

nodes.name: Elliott–Ho–Toms stable rank one theorem
nodes.statement: Just over a decade ago, another stable rank one result was obtained by Elliott, Ho, and Toms in \cite{EHT}. Their paper, which stemmed from Ho's work in \cite{Ho}, showed that the condition of bounded dimension in \cite{4Rom} could be replaced with the assumption that all of the bonding maps in the inductive limit are diagonal.
conclusions: the condition of bounded dimension in \cite{4Rom} could be replaced with the assumption that all of the bonding maps in the inductive limit are diagonal
nodes.statement_short: Simple unital AH limits with diagonal bonding maps have stable rank one (no bounded dimension needed).

nodes.name: Approximately subhomogeneous (ASH) algebra
nodes.statement: In this present paper, we extend the AH stable rank one result of Elliott, Ho, and Toms in \cite{EHT} to a suitable class of approximately subhomogeneous (ASH) algebras---inductive limits of subhomogeneous $\mathrm{C}^{*}$-algebras (those whose irreducible representations all have dimension at most some fixed integer).

nodes.name: Archey–Niu–Phillips conjecture
nodes.statement: Using our stable rank one theorem for inductive limits and results of Archey and Phillips developed in \cite{arcphil}, we are able to prove a conjecture of Archey, Niu, and Phillips stated in the same paper (Conjecture 7.2); namely, that for an infinite compact metric space $T$ and a minimal homeomorphism $h\colon T\to T$, the dynamical crossed product $\mathrm{C^*}(\mathbb{Z},T,h)$ has stable rank one (see \autoref{main2}).
assumptions: for an infinite compact metric space $T$ and a minimal homeomorphism $h\colon T\to T$
conclusions: the dynamical crossed product $\mathrm{C^*}(\mathbb{Z},T,h)$ has stable rank one
nodes.statement_short: Crossed products C*(Z,T,h) by minimal homeomorphisms of infinite compact metric spaces have stable rank one.

nodes.name: Notation for positive integers and inclusion
nodes.statement: Throughout the paper, we use $\mathbb{N}$ to denote the set of strictly positive integers and the symbol $\subset$ to denote non-strict set inclusion.

nodes.name: Spectrum of a C*-algebra
nodes.statement: Given a $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra $A$, we let $\hat{A}$ denote the set of equivalence classes of non-zero irreducible representations of $A$ equipped with the hull-kernel topology.

nodes.name: Unit notation
nodes.statement: If $A$ is unital, we use $1_{A}$ to denote the unit of $A$.

nodes.name: Matrix algebra shorthand
nodes.statement: For $n\in\mathbb{N}$, we use the shorthand $M_{n}$ to refer to the matrix algebra $M_{n}(\mathbb{C})$.

nodes.name: Matrix entry and identity notation
nodes.statement: When speaking about a matrix $D\in M_{n}$, we denote the $(i,j)$-entry of $D$ by $D_{i,j}$, and we let $1_{n}$ denote the identity matrix in $M_{n}$.

nodes.name: Phillips: homogeneous algebras are recursive subhomogeneous
nodes.statement: In Corollary 1.8 of \cite{phil}, Phillips shows that every unital homogeneous $\mathrm{C}^{*}$-algebra (regardless of its Dixmier--Douady class) has a recursive subhomogeneous decomposition.
conclusions: every unital homogeneous $\mathrm{C}^{*}$-algebra (regardless of its Dixmier--Douady class) has a recursive subhomogeneous decomposition

nodes.name: Recursive subhomogeneous algebra
nodes.statement: A \textit{recursive subhomogeneous algebra} is a $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra given by the following recursive definition. \begin{enumerate} \item If $X$ is a compact metric space and $n\geq 1$, then $C(X,M_{n})$ is a recursive subhomogeneous algebra. \item If $A$ is a recursive subhomogeneous algebra, $X$ is a compact metric space, $Y\subset X$ is closed, $\varphi\colon A\to C(Y, M_{n})$ is any unital $^*$-homomorphism, and $\rho\colon C(X,M_{n})\to C(Y, M_{n})$ is the restriction $^*$-homomorphism, then the pullback $$ A\oplus_{C(Y, M_{n})}C(X,M_{n}):=\{(a,f)\in A\oplus C(X,M_{n}):\varphi(a)=\rho(f)\} $$ is a recursive subhomogeneous algebra. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Smallest class containing C(X,M_n) and closed under pullbacks along unital maps into C(Y,M_n) with Y closed in X.

nodes.name: Recursive subhomogeneous decomposition
nodes.statement: Therefore, if $A$ is a recursive subhomogeneous algebra, there are compact metric spaces $X_{1},\ldots, X_{ l}$ (the \textit{base spaces} of $A$), closed subspaces $Y_{1}:=\varnothing$, $Y_{2}\subset X_{2},\ldots, Y_{ l}\subset X_{ l}$, positive integers $n_{1},\ldots, n_{ l}$, $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebras $A^{(i)}\subset\bigoplus_{j=1}^{i}C(X_{j},M_{n_{j}})$ for $1\leq i\leq l$, and unital $^*$-homomorphisms $\varphi_{i}\colon A^{(i)}\to C(Y_{i+1},M_{n_{i+1}})$ for $1\leq i\leq l-1$ such that: \begin{enumerate} \item $A^{(1)}=C(X_{1},M_{n_{1}})$; \item for all $1\leq i\leq l-1$ $$ A^{(i+1)}=\{(a,f)\in A^{(i)}\oplus C(X_{i+1},M_{n_{i+1}}):\varphi_{i}(a)=f|_{Y_{i+1}}\}; $$ \item $A=A^{( l)}$.
nodes.statement_short: A recursive subhomogeneous algebra is an iterated pullback A^(i+1) of A^(i) and C(X_{i+1},M_{n_{i+1}}) along phi_i over Y_{i+1}.

nodes.name: Length of a recursive subhomogeneous algebra
nodes.statement: In particular, we refer to the number $ l$ above as the \textit{length of $A$}.

nodes.name: Coordinate notation for elements
nodes.statement: Since for all $1\leq i\leq l$, we have $A^{(i)}\subset\bigoplus_{j=1}^{i}C(X_{j},M_{n_{j}})$, we can view each element $f\in A^{(i)}$ as $(f_{1},\ldots,f_{i})$, where $f_{j}\in C(X_{j},M_{n_{j}})$ for all $1\leq j\leq i$.

nodes.name: Evaluation map
nodes.statement: For $1\leq i\leq l$ and $x\in X_{i}$, we have the usual \textit{evaluation map} $\operatorname{ev}_{x}\colon A\to M_{n_{i}}$ given by $\operatorname{ev}_{x}(f):=f_{i}(x)$ for all $f\in A$.

nodes.name: Minimal and maximal matrix sizes
nodes.statement: We let $\mathfrak{s}(A):=\min\{n_{1},\ldots,n_{ l}\}$ and $\mathfrak{S}(A):=\max\{n_{1},\ldots,n_{ l}\}$.

nodes.name: Diagonal subhomogeneous (DSH) algebra
nodes.statement: A $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra $A$ is a \textit{diagonal subhomogeneous (DSH) algebra} (of length $ l$) provided that it is a recursive subhomogeneous algebra (of length $ l$) (with a decomposition as described above), and for all $1\leq i\leq l-1$ and $y\in Y_{i+1}$, there is a list of points $x_{1}\in X_{i_{1}}\setminus Y_{i_{1}},\ldots, x_{t}\in X_{i_{t}}\setminus Y_{i_{t}}$ such that for all $f\in A^{(i)}$, $$ \varphi_{i}(f)(y)=\operatorname{diag}(f_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots,f_{i_{t}}(x_{t})). $$ We say $y$ \textit{decomposes into} $x_{1},\ldots,x_{t}$, that each $x_{j}$ is a point \textit{in the decomposition of $y$}, and that $x_{j}$ \textit{begins at index $1+n_{i_{1}}+\cdots+n_{i_{j-1}}$ down the diagonal of $y$}. Given $1\leq j\leq i$ and $y'\in Y_{j}$, we say that $y'$ is \textit{in the decomposition of $y$} if there exists a $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$ with the property that for all $f\in A^{(i)}$ there are matrices $P\in M_{k-1}$ and $Q\in M_{n_{i}-n_{j}-(k-1)}$ such that $f_{i}(y)=\operatorname{diag}(P,f_{j}(y'),Q)$.
differentia: for all $1\leq i\leq l-1$ and $y\in Y_{i+1}$, there is a list of points $x_{1}\in X_{i_{1}}\setminus Y_{i_{1}},\ldots, x_{t}\in X_{i_{t}}\setminus Y_{i_{t}}$ such that for all $f\in A^{(i)}$
nodes.statement_short: A recursive subhomogeneous algebra whose pullback maps are diagonal: phi_i(f)(y)=diag(f_{i_1}(x_1),...,f_{i_t}(x_t)); also defines 'decomposes into'.
nodes.label: DSH def

nodes.name: Diagonal map between DSH algebras
nodes.statement: Given two DSH algebras $A_{1}$ and $A_{2}$ of lengths $ l_{1}$ and $ l_{2}$ and with base spaces $X_{1}^{1},\ldots,X_{ l_{1}}^{1}$ and $X_{1}^{2},\ldots,X_{ l_{2}}^{2}$, respectively, we say that a $^*$-homomorphism $\psi\colon A_{1}\to A_{2}$ is \textit{diagonal} provided that for all $1\leq i\leq l_{2}$ and $x\in X_{i}^{2}$, there are points $x_{1},\ldots,x_{t}$ with $x_{j}\in X_{i_{j}}^{1}$ such that for all $f\in A_{1}$, $$ \psi(f)_{i}(x)=\operatorname{diag}(f_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots,f_{i_{t}}(x_{t})). $$ We say that $x$ \textit{decomposes into} $x_{1},\ldots,x_{t}$.
nodes.statement_short: psi: A_1->A_2 is diagonal if each psi(f)_i(x) is diag(f_{i_1}(x_1),...,f_{i_t}(x_t)) for points x_j of A_1's base spaces.
nodes.label: diagonal map

nodes.name: Equivalent definition of diagonal maps via X_i minus Y_i
nodes.statement: Note that if $Y_{1}^{1}\subset X_{1}^{1},\ldots ,Y_{ l_{1}}^{1}\subset X_{ l_{1}}^{1}$ and $Y_{1}^{2}\subset X_{1}^{2},\ldots ,Y_{ l_{2}}^{2}\subset X_{ l_{2}}^{2}$ are the corresponding closed subsets of the base spaces in \autoref{diagonal map}, then, owing to the decomposition structure of $A_{1}$ and $A_{2}$, we get an equivalent definition by replacing $X_{i}^{2}$ and $X_{i_{j}}^{1}$ above with $X_{i}^{2}\setminus Y_{i}^{2}$ and $X_{i_{j}}^{1}\setminus Y_{i_{j}}^{1}$, respectively.

nodes.name: Diagonal maps are unital
nodes.statement: Note, too, that by definition diagonal maps are automatically unital.

nodes.name: Standing assumption: A is a DSH algebra (Section 2.1)
nodes.statement: For the remainder of \cref{sub: intro}, let us assume that $A$ is a DSH algebra of length $ l$.

nodes.name: Spectrum of a recursive subhomogeneous algebra
nodes.statement: The map $x\mapsto [\operatorname{ev}_{x}]$ defines a continuous bijection $$ \bigsqcup_{i=1}^{\ell}(X_{i}\setminus Y_{i})\to \hat{A}, $$ (where, recall, $Y_{1}:=\varnothing$) whose restriction to each $X_{i}\setminus Y_{i}$ is a homeomorphism onto its image. In particular every irreducible representation of $A$ is unitarily equivalent to $\operatorname{ev}_{x}$ for some $x\in \bigsqcup_{i=1}^{\ell}(X_{i}\setminus Y_{i})$.
assumptions: let us assume that $A$ is a DSH algebra of length $ l$
conclusions: The map $x\mapsto [\operatorname{ev}_{x}]$ defines a continuous bijection
whose restriction to each $X_{i}\setminus Y_{i}$ is a homeomorphism onto its image
every irreducible representation of $A$ is unitarily equivalent to $\operatorname{ev}_{x}$ for some $x\in \bigsqcup_{i=1}^{\ell}(X_{i}\setminus Y_{i})$
nodes.statement_short: Points of the X_i minus Y_i biject continuously onto the spectrum of A, homeomorphically on each piece.
nodes.label: DSH spectrum

nodes.name: Points identified with irreducible representations
nodes.statement: We often tacitly refer to a given irreducible representation $\operatorname{ev}_{x}$ simply as $x$, since we view such an element both as an irreducible representation and as a point in $X_{i}$.

nodes.name: Closure notation in a base space
nodes.statement: A subset $D\subset X_{i}\setminus Y_{i}$ can be viewed as a subset both of $X_{i}$ and of $\hat{A}$. We denote by $\overline{D}^{X_{i}}$ the closure of $D$ with respect to the topology on $X_{i}$. With one or two exceptions, when speaking about open and closed subsets of $X_{i}$ in this paper, we mean with respect to the topology on $X_{i}$; such subsets could, in general, include points in $Y_{i}$, in which case they would not even be a subset of the spectrum. In any case, for subsets of $X_{i}\setminus Y_{i}$, the topology is always made explicit.
nodes.statement_short: For D in X_i minus Y_i, the closure of D in X_i is written with superscript X_i; topology on X_i is the default.

nodes.name: Uniqueness of the decomposition of a point
nodes.statement: Suppose $2\leq i\leq l$ and $y\in Y_{i}$. If $y$ decomposes into $x_{1},\ldots,x_{t}$ and $z_{1},\ldots,z_{s}$, then $s=t$ and for $1\leq j\leq s$, $x_{j}=z_{j}$.
assumptions: $2\leq i\leq l$ and $y\in Y_{i}$
$y$ decomposes into $x_{1},\ldots,x_{t}$ and $z_{1},\ldots,z_{s}$
conclusions: $s=t$ and for $1\leq j\leq s$, $x_{j}=z_{j}$
also_stated_at: the decomposition of $y$ is unique up to the re-indexing of identical points; that is, if $y$ decomposes into $x_{1},\ldots,x_{t}$ and $z_{1},\ldots,z_{s}$, then $s=t$ and, for $1\leq j\leq s$, $x_{j}=z_{j}$
nodes.label: unique

nodes.name: Proof of uniqueness of decompositions
nodes.statement: By \autoref{DSH spectrum}, $A$ is liminary and $x_{1}=z_{1}$ if and only if $\operatorname{ev}_{x_{1}}=\operatorname{ev}_{z_{1}}$. Hence, if $x_{1}\not=z_{1}$, Proposition 4.2.5 of \cite{dix} furnishes a function $f\in A$ such that $\operatorname{ev}_{x_{1}}(f)$ and $\operatorname{ev}_{z_{1}}(f)$ are the $0$ and identity matrix of appropriate sizes, respectively. This contradicts the assumption that \begin{equation} \operatorname{diag}(\operatorname{ev}_{x_{1}}(f),\ldots,\operatorname{ev}_{x_{t}}(f))=f_{i}(y)=\operatorname{diag}(\operatorname{ev}_{z_{1}}(f),\ldots,\operatorname{ev}_{z_{s}}(f)). \end{equation} Therefore, $x_{1}=z_{1}$. Continuing inductively, we see that if $s<t$, $s>t$, or $x_{j}\not=z_{j}$ for some $j$, then \autoref{2 decomps} is violated. Hence, \autoref{unique} follows.
nodes.statement_short: Separate distinct points by a function (Dixmier 4.2.5) to contradict the two diagonal forms of f_i(y); then induct along the list.

nodes.name: First points coincide
nodes.statement: By \autoref{DSH spectrum}, $A$ is liminary and $x_{1}=z_{1}$ if and only if $\operatorname{ev}_{x_{1}}=\operatorname{ev}_{z_{1}}$. Hence, if $x_{1}\not=z_{1}$, Proposition 4.2.5 of \cite{dix} furnishes a function $f\in A$ such that $\operatorname{ev}_{x_{1}}(f)$ and $\operatorname{ev}_{z_{1}}(f)$ are the $0$ and identity matrix of appropriate sizes, respectively. This contradicts the assumption that \begin{equation} \operatorname{diag}(\operatorname{ev}_{x_{1}}(f),\ldots,\operatorname{ev}_{x_{t}}(f))=f_{i}(y)=\operatorname{diag}(\operatorname{ev}_{z_{1}}(f),\ldots,\operatorname{ev}_{z_{s}}(f)). \end{equation} Therefore, $x_{1}=z_{1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Separate distinct x_1, z_1 by a function to contradict the two diagonal forms; so x_1 = z_1

nodes.name: Induct along the list
nodes.statement: Continuing inductively, we see that if $s<t$, $s>t$, or $x_{j}\not=z_{j}$ for some $j$, then \autoref{2 decomps} is violated. Hence, \autoref{unique} follows.
nodes.statement_short: Repeat the argument along the list to get s=t and x_j=z_j

nodes.name: Two diagonal decompositions of f_i(y)
nodes.statement: \operatorname{diag}(\operatorname{ev}_{x_{1}}(f),\ldots,\operatorname{ev}_{x_{t}}(f))=f_{i}(y)=\operatorname{diag}(\operatorname{ev}_{z_{1}}(f),\ldots,\operatorname{ev}_{z_{s}}(f)).
nodes.label: 2 decomps

nodes.name: Evaluation at a point of Y_i splits into irreducibles
nodes.statement: By \autoref{DSH spectrum} and \autoref{DSH def}, given $y\in \bigsqcup_{i=1}^{ l}X_{i}$, either $\operatorname{ev}_{y}$ is an irreducible representation of $A$ or, if $y$ is in some $Y_{i}$, $\operatorname{ev}_{y}$ splits up into irreducible representations of $A$.

nodes.name: The sets B_{i,k}
nodes.statement: Given $1\leq i\leq l$ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$, we define $B_{i,k}$ to be the set of points in $X_{i}$ that have an irreducible representation beginning at index $k$ down their diagonal. For $k\leq 0$, we set $B_{i,k}:=\varnothing$.
nodes.statement_short: B_{i,k}: points of X_i having an irreducible representation that begins at index k down their diagonal.
nodes.label: Bik def

nodes.name: Basic properties of the sets B_{i,k}
nodes.statement: \mbox{} \begin{enumerate} \item $B_{i,1}=X_{i}$ for all $1\leq i\leq l$. \item If $1\leq i\leq l$ and $k>1$, then $B_{i,k}\subset Y_{i}$. In particular, $B_{1,k}=\varnothing$ for $k>1$. \item If $2\leq i\leq l$ and $y\in Y_{i}$ decomposes into $x_{1}\in X_{i_{1}}\setminus Y_{i_{1}},\ldots,x_{t}\in X_{i_{t}}\setminus Y_{i_{t}}$, then $y\in B_{i,k}$ if and only if $k=1+n_{i_{1}}+\cdots+n_{i_{j-1}}$ for some $1\leq j\leq t$. In particular, $B_{i,k}=\varnothing$ for all $n_{i}-(\mathfrak{s}(A)-1)< k\leq n_{i}$, where, recall, $\mathfrak{s}(A):=\min\{n_{j}:1\leq j\leq l\}$. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: $1\leq i\leq l$ and $k>1$
$2\leq i\leq l$ and $y\in Y_{i}$ decomposes into $x_{1}\in X_{i_{1}}\setminus Y_{i_{1}},\ldots,x_{t}\in X_{i_{t}}\setminus Y_{i_{t}}$
conclusions: $B_{i,1}=X_{i}$ for all $1\leq i\leq l$
$B_{i,k}\subset Y_{i}$
$y\in B_{i,k}$ if and only if $k=1+n_{i_{1}}+\cdots+n_{i_{j-1}}$ for some $1\leq j\leq t$
$B_{i,1}=X_{i}$ for all $1\leq i\leq l$

assumptions: $1\leq i\leq l$ and $k>1$
conclusions: $B_{i,k}\subset Y_{i}$

assumptions: $2\leq i\leq l$ and $y\in Y_{i}$ decomposes into $x_{1}\in X_{i_{1}}\setminus Y_{i_{1}},\ldots,x_{t}\in X_{i_{t}}\setminus Y_{i_{t}}$
conclusions: $y\in B_{i,k}$ if and only if $k=1+n_{i_{1}}+\cdots+n_{i_{j-1}}$ for some $1\leq j\leq t$

nodes.statement_short: B_{i,1}=X_i; B_{i,k} lies in Y_i for k>1; y is in B_{i,k} exactly at the starting indices of its decomposition blocks.
nodes.label: Bik

nodes.name: Proof of the properties of B_{i,k}
nodes.statement: Fix $1\leq i\leq l$ and suppose $y\in X_{i}$. If $y$ belongs to $Y_{i}$ and decomposes into $x_{1},\ldots,x_{t}$, then by \autoref{DSH def}, $x_{1}$ begins at index $1$ down the diagonal of $y$, and so $y\in B_{i,1}$. If $y\notin Y_{i}$, then by \autoref{DSH spectrum}, $y$ is irreducible and trivially begins at index $1$ down its diagonal, and, moreover, cannot have any irreducible representation beginning at any index $k\geq 2$. This proves \textit{(1)} and \textit{(2)}. To prove \textit{(3)}, suppose $y$ belongs to $Y_{i}$ and decomposes into $x_{1}\in X_{i_{1}}\setminus Y_{i_{1}},\ldots,x_{t}\in X_{i_{t}}\setminus Y_{i_{t}}$. By \autoref{DSH def}, $y\in B_{i,k}$ if $k=1+n_{i_{1}}+\cdots+n_{i_{j-1}}$ for some $1\leq j\leq t$. Since \autoref{unique} shows that the decomposition of $y$ is unique, it follows that $y$ cannot belong to any other $B_{i,k}$, which establishes \textit{(3)}.
nodes.statement_short: Case split on whether y lies in Y_i, using the DSH definition, the spectrum lemma and uniqueness of decompositions.

nodes.name: Case y in Y_i
nodes.statement: Fix $1\leq i\leq l$ and suppose $y\in X_{i}$. If $y$ belongs to $Y_{i}$ and decomposes into $x_{1},\ldots,x_{t}$, then by \autoref{DSH def}, $x_{1}$ begins at index $1$ down the diagonal of $y$, and so $y\in B_{i,1}$.
nodes.statement_short: If y is in Y_i its first decomposition point starts at index 1

nodes.name: Case y not in Y_i
nodes.statement: If $y\notin Y_{i}$, then by \autoref{DSH spectrum}, $y$ is irreducible and trivially begins at index $1$ down its diagonal, and, moreover, cannot have any irreducible representation beginning at any index $k\geq 2$. This proves \textit{(1)} and \textit{(2)}.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise y is irreducible, starting only at index 1; proves (1) and (2)

nodes.name: Part (3)
nodes.statement: To prove \textit{(3)}, suppose $y$ belongs to $Y_{i}$ and decomposes into $x_{1}\in X_{i_{1}}\setminus Y_{i_{1}},\ldots,x_{t}\in X_{i_{t}}\setminus Y_{i_{t}}$. By \autoref{DSH def}, $y\in B_{i,k}$ if $k=1+n_{i_{1}}+\cdots+n_{i_{j-1}}$ for some $1\leq j\leq t$. Since \autoref{unique} shows that the decomposition of $y$ is unique, it follows that $y$ cannot belong to any other $B_{i,k}$, which establishes \textit{(3)}.
nodes.statement_short: Starting indices of the blocks give (3), by uniqueness of the decomposition

nodes.name: Y_i may be assumed to have empty interior
nodes.statement: For each $2\leq i\leq l$, we may assume $\operatorname{int}(Y_{i})=\varnothing$.
assumptions: For each $2\leq i\leq l$
conclusions: we may assume $\operatorname{int}(Y_{i})=\varnothing$
nodes.label: empty interior

nodes.name: Proof that int(Y_i) may be taken empty
nodes.statement: Fix $1\leq i\leq l-1$. Let $Y_{i+1}':=Y_{i+1}\setminus\operatorname{int}(Y_{i+1})$ and $X_{i+1}':=X_{i+1}\setminus\operatorname{int}(Y_{i+1})$. We have the following commutative diagram of restriction $^*$-homomorphisms: $$ \begin{tikzcd} C(X_{i+1},M_{n_{i+1}}) \arrow{r}{\rho} \arrow[swap]{d}{\lambda} & C(Y_{i+1},M_{n_{i+1}}) \arrow{d}{\tau} \\ C(X_{i+1}',M_{n_{i+1}}) \arrow{r}{\rho'} & C(Y_{i+1}',M_{n_{i+1}}) \end{tikzcd} $$ Let $B^{(i+1)}:= A^{(i)}\oplus_{C(Y_{i+1}',M_{n_{i+1}})}C(X_{i+1}',M_{n_{i+1}})$, where the connecting $^*$-homomorphism is $\varphi_{i}':=\tau\circ\varphi_{i}\colon A^{(i)}\to C(Y_{i+1}',M_{n_{i+1}})$. Let us show that $A^{(i+1)}$ is isomorphic to $B^{(i+1)}$. Given $a\in A^{(i)}$ and $f\in C(X_{i+1},M_{n_{i+1}})$ with $(a,f)\in A^{(i+1)}$, define $\Gamma\colon A^{(i+1)}\to B^{(i+1)}$ by $\Gamma((a,f)):=(a,\lambda(f))$. Note that $\varphi_{i}'(a)=\tau(\varphi_{i}(a))=\tau(\rho(f))=\rho'(\lambda(f))$, so that $\Gamma$ is well defined. It is easy to see that $\Gamma$ is a $^*$-homomorphism. To see that $\Gamma$ is injective, suppose $(a,f)\in A^{(i+1)}$ with $(a,\lambda(f))=\Gamma((a,f))=(0,0)$. Then $a=0$ and so $f|_{Y_{i+1}}=\varphi_{i}(a)=0$, which, together with the fact that $\lambda(f)=0$, yields that $f=0$. For surjectivity suppose $a\in A^{(i)}$ and $g\in C(X_{i+1}',M_{n_{i+1}})$ with $(a,g)\in B^{(i+1)}$. Then $\varphi_{i}(a)|_{Y_{i+1}'}=g|_{Y_{i+1}'}$, so that the function $h\colon X_{i+1}\to M_{n_{i+1}}$ defined to be $\varphi_{i}(a)(x)$ for $x\in Y_{i+1}$ and $g(x)$ for $x\in X_{i+1}'$ is well defined and continuous. Moreover, $\varphi_{i}(a)=h|_{Y_{i+1}}$, which implies $(a,h)\in A^{(i+1)}$ and $\Gamma((a,h))=(a,\lambda(h))=(a,g)$, proving surjectivity.
nodes.statement_short: Remove int(Y_{i+1}) from X_{i+1} and Y_{i+1}; show the restricted pullback is isomorphic to A^{(i+1)} via Gamma(a,f)=(a,f|).

nodes.name: Remove the interior of Y_{i+1}
nodes.statement: Fix $1\leq i\leq l-1$. Let $Y_{i+1}':=Y_{i+1}\setminus\operatorname{int}(Y_{i+1})$ and $X_{i+1}':=X_{i+1}\setminus\operatorname{int}(Y_{i+1})$. We have the following commutative diagram of restriction $^*$-homomorphisms: $$ \begin{tikzcd} C(X_{i+1},M_{n_{i+1}}) \arrow{r}{\rho} \arrow[swap]{d}{\lambda} & C(Y_{i+1},M_{n_{i+1}}) \arrow{d}{\tau} \\ C(X_{i+1}',M_{n_{i+1}}) \arrow{r}{\rho'} & C(Y_{i+1}',M_{n_{i+1}}) \end{tikzcd} $$ Let $B^{(i+1)}:= A^{(i)}\oplus_{C(Y_{i+1}',M_{n_{i+1}})}C(X_{i+1}',M_{n_{i+1}})$, where the connecting $^*$-homomorphism is $\varphi_{i}':=\tau\circ\varphi_{i}\colon A^{(i)}\to C(Y_{i+1}',M_{n_{i+1}})$.
nodes.statement_short: Define Y', X' and the restricted pullback B^{(i+1)}

nodes.name: Claim: A^{(i+1)} is isomorphic to B^{(i+1)}
nodes.statement: Let us show that $A^{(i+1)}$ is isomorphic to $B^{(i+1)}$. Given $a\in A^{(i)}$ and $f\in C(X_{i+1},M_{n_{i+1}})$ with $(a,f)\in A^{(i+1)}$, define $\Gamma\colon A^{(i+1)}\to B^{(i+1)}$ by $\Gamma((a,f)):=(a,\lambda(f))$. Note that $\varphi_{i}'(a)=\tau(\varphi_{i}(a))=\tau(\rho(f))=\rho'(\lambda(f))$, so that $\Gamma$ is well defined. It is easy to see that $\Gamma$ is a $^*$-homomorphism. To see that $\Gamma$ is injective, suppose $(a,f)\in A^{(i+1)}$ with $(a,\lambda(f))=\Gamma((a,f))=(0,0)$. Then $a=0$ and so $f|_{Y_{i+1}}=\varphi_{i}(a)=0$, which, together with the fact that $\lambda(f)=0$, yields that $f=0$. For surjectivity suppose $a\in A^{(i)}$ and $g\in C(X_{i+1}',M_{n_{i+1}})$ with $(a,g)\in B^{(i+1)}$. Then $\varphi_{i}(a)|_{Y_{i+1}'}=g|_{Y_{i+1}'}$, so that the function $h\colon X_{i+1}\to M_{n_{i+1}}$ defined to be $\varphi_{i}(a)(x)$ for $x\in Y_{i+1}$ and $g(x)$ for $x\in X_{i+1}'$ is well defined and continuous. Moreover, $\varphi_{i}(a)=h|_{Y_{i+1}}$, which implies $(a,h)\in A^{(i+1)}$ and $\Gamma((a,h))=(a,\lambda(h))=(a,g)$, proving surjectivity.
nodes.statement_short: Show the restriction map Gamma is a *-isomorphism

nodes.name: Define Gamma
nodes.statement: Given $a\in A^{(i)}$ and $f\in C(X_{i+1},M_{n_{i+1}})$ with $(a,f)\in A^{(i+1)}$, define $\Gamma\colon A^{(i+1)}\to B^{(i+1)}$ by $\Gamma((a,f)):=(a,\lambda(f))$. Note that $\varphi_{i}'(a)=\tau(\varphi_{i}(a))=\tau(\rho(f))=\rho'(\lambda(f))$, so that $\Gamma$ is well defined. It is easy to see that $\Gamma$ is a $^*$-homomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Define Gamma(a,f)=(a,lambda(f)) and check it is a well-defined *-homomorphism

nodes.name: Injectivity
nodes.statement: To see that $\Gamma$ is injective, suppose $(a,f)\in A^{(i+1)}$ with $(a,\lambda(f))=\Gamma((a,f))=(0,0)$. Then $a=0$ and so $f|_{Y_{i+1}}=\varphi_{i}(a)=0$, which, together with the fact that $\lambda(f)=0$, yields that $f=0$.
nodes.statement_short: a=0 forces f to vanish on Y and on X', hence f=0

nodes.name: Surjectivity
nodes.statement: For surjectivity suppose $a\in A^{(i)}$ and $g\in C(X_{i+1}',M_{n_{i+1}})$ with $(a,g)\in B^{(i+1)}$. Then $\varphi_{i}(a)|_{Y_{i+1}'}=g|_{Y_{i+1}'}$, so that the function $h\colon X_{i+1}\to M_{n_{i+1}}$ defined to be $\varphi_{i}(a)(x)$ for $x\in Y_{i+1}$ and $g(x)$ for $x\in X_{i+1}'$ is well defined and continuous. Moreover, $\varphi_{i}(a)=h|_{Y_{i+1}}$, which implies $(a,h)\in A^{(i+1)}$ and $\Gamma((a,h))=(a,\lambda(h))=(a,g)$, proving surjectivity.
nodes.statement_short: Glue phi_i(a) on Y with g on X' to get a preimage

nodes.name: Pointwise invertibility implies invertibility
nodes.statement: Suppose $f\in A$ and that for all $1\leq i\leq l$ and $x\in X_{i}\setminus Y_{i}$, the matrix $f_{i}(x)$ is invertible in $M_{n_{i}}$. Then $f$ is invertible in $A$.
assumptions: $f\in A$ and that for all $1\leq i\leq l$ and $x\in X_{i}\setminus Y_{i}$, the matrix $f_{i}(x)$ is invertible in $M_{n_{i}}$
conclusions: $f$ is invertible in $A$
nodes.label: non-invertible at point

nodes.name: Proof of pointwise invertibility criterion
nodes.statement: Owing to the diagonal decomposition at points in $Y_{i}$, we may assume that $f_{i}(x)$ is an invertible matrix for all $1\leq i\leq l$ and $x\in X_{i}$. Define $g\in\bigoplus_{i=1}^{ l }C(X_{i},M_{n_{i}})$ to be $(g_{1},\ldots,g_{ l })$, where for $1\leq i\leq l $ and $z\in X_{i}$, $g_{i}(z):=f_{i}(z)^{-1}$. Since $g$ is the inverse of $f$ in $\bigoplus_{i=1}^{ l }C(X_{i},M_{n_{i}})$, to prove the lemma, we need only to verify that $g\in A$. Suppose $1\leq i\leq l -1$ and that $y\in Y_{i+1}$ decomposes into $x_{1}\in X_{i_{1}}\setminus Y_{i_{1}},\ldots,x_{t}\in X_{i_{t}}\setminus Y_{i_{t}}$. Then, $$ \begin{aligned} g_{i+1}(y)&=f_{i+1}(y)^{-1}\\ &=\operatorname{diag}((f_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots,f_{i_{t}}(x_{t}))^{-1}\\ &=\operatorname{diag}((f_{i_{1}}(x_{1})^{-1},\ldots,f_{i_{t}}(x_{t})^{-1})\\ &=\operatorname{diag}(g_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots,g_{i_{t}}(x_{t})), \end{aligned} $$ so that $g\in A$.
nodes.statement_short: Invert f pointwise in the direct sum and check the inverse respects the diagonal decomposition at points of Y_i.

nodes.name: Reduce to all points
nodes.statement: Owing to the diagonal decomposition at points in $Y_{i}$, we may assume that $f_{i}(x)$ is an invertible matrix for all $1\leq i\leq l$ and $x\in X_{i}$.
nodes.statement_short: By the diagonal decomposition f_i(x) is invertible at every point

nodes.name: Pointwise inverse
nodes.statement: Define $g\in\bigoplus_{i=1}^{ l }C(X_{i},M_{n_{i}})$ to be $(g_{1},\ldots,g_{ l })$, where for $1\leq i\leq l $ and $z\in X_{i}$, $g_{i}(z):=f_{i}(z)^{-1}$. Since $g$ is the inverse of $f$ in $\bigoplus_{i=1}^{ l }C(X_{i},M_{n_{i}})$, to prove the lemma, we need only to verify that $g\in A$.
nodes.statement_short: Define g as the pointwise inverse; it remains to show g lies in A

nodes.name: g respects the decomposition
nodes.statement: Suppose $1\leq i\leq l -1$ and that $y\in Y_{i+1}$ decomposes into $x_{1}\in X_{i_{1}}\setminus Y_{i_{1}},\ldots,x_{t}\in X_{i_{t}}\setminus Y_{i_{t}}$. Then, $$ \begin{aligned} g_{i+1}(y)&=f_{i+1}(y)^{-1}\\ &=\operatorname{diag}((f_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots,f_{i_{t}}(x_{t}))^{-1}\\ &=\operatorname{diag}((f_{i_{1}}(x_{1})^{-1},\ldots,f_{i_{t}}(x_{t})^{-1})\\ &=\operatorname{diag}(g_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots,g_{i_{t}}(x_{t})), \end{aligned} $$ so that $g\in A$.
nodes.statement_short: Inverse of a block-diagonal matrix is block-diagonal, so g is in A

nodes.name: Open sets of a base space that are open in the spectrum
nodes.statement: Suppose $1\leq i\leq \ell$. If $U\subset X_{i}\setminus Y_{i}$ is open with respect to the topology on $X_{i}$ and has the property that no point in $U$ appears in the decomposition of any point in $Y_{j}$ for any $j>i$, then $U$ is open with respect to the hull-kernel topology on $\hat{A}$.
assumptions: $1\leq i\leq \ell$
$U\subset X_{i}\setminus Y_{i}$ is open with respect to the topology on $X_{i}$ and has the property that no point in $U$ appears in the decomposition of any point in $Y_{j}$ for any $j>i$
conclusions: $U$ is open with respect to the hull-kernel topology on $\hat{A}$
nodes.label: open in spectrum

nodes.name: Proof that U is open in the spectrum
nodes.statement: Let $x\in U$ be arbitrary. Put $g_{j}\equiv0$ for $j<i$ and define $g_{i}\in C(X_{i},M_{n_{i}})$ to be any function such that $g_{i}(x)\not=0$ and $g_{i}|_{X_{i}\setminus U}\equiv 0$. Since $Y_{i}\subset X_{i}\setminus U$, $g_{i}$ vanishes on $Y_{i}$, so that $\varphi_{i-1}((g_{1},\ldots,g_{i-1}))=0=g_{i}|_{Y_{i}}$; thus, $(g_{1},\ldots,g_{i})\in A^{(i)}$. For $j>i$, set $g_{j}\equiv 0$. Since no point in $U$ is in the decomposition of any point in $Y_{j}$ for any $j>i$, it follows inductively that $g:=(g_{1},\ldots,g_{\ell})\in A$. This proves that $U$ is open in $\hat{A}$.
nodes.statement_short: For each x in U build g in A supported in U with g_i(x) nonzero, so U is open in the hull-kernel topology.

nodes.name: Bump function at x
nodes.statement: Let $x\in U$ be arbitrary. Put $g_{j}\equiv0$ for $j<i$ and define $g_{i}\in C(X_{i},M_{n_{i}})$ to be any function such that $g_{i}(x)\not=0$ and $g_{i}|_{X_{i}\setminus U}\equiv 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose g_i nonzero at x and vanishing off U

nodes.name: g lies in A^{(i)}
nodes.statement: Since $Y_{i}\subset X_{i}\setminus U$, $g_{i}$ vanishes on $Y_{i}$, so that $\varphi_{i-1}((g_{1},\ldots,g_{i-1}))=0=g_{i}|_{Y_{i}}$; thus, $(g_{1},\ldots,g_{i})\in A^{(i)}$.
nodes.statement_short: g_i vanishes on Y_i so (g_1,...,g_i) is in A^{(i)}

nodes.name: Extend by zero
nodes.statement: For $j>i$, set $g_{j}\equiv 0$. Since no point in $U$ is in the decomposition of any point in $Y_{j}$ for any $j>i$, it follows inductively that $g:=(g_{1},\ldots,g_{\ell})\in A$. This proves that $U$ is open in $\hat{A}$.
nodes.statement_short: Extending by zero stays in A since U meets no later decomposition, so U is open

nodes.name: Points in decompositions form a closed set
nodes.statement: Suppose $1\leq i < j \leq\ell$ and let $F\subset X_{i}$ denote the set of points that are in the decomposition of a point in $Y_{j}$. Then, $F$ is closed in $X_{i}$.
assumptions: $1\leq i < j \leq\ell$ and let $F\subset X_{i}$ denote the set of points that are in the decomposition of a point in $Y_{j}$
conclusions: $F$ is closed in $X_{i}$
nodes.label: not decomposition

nodes.name: Proof that F is closed
nodes.statement: Suppose $(z_{n})_{n}$ is a sequence of points in $F$ converging to $x\in X_{i}$. For each $n\in\mathbb{N}$, there is a $y_{n}\in Y_{j}$ with the property that $z_{n}$ is in the decomposition of $y_{n}$. Since $Y_{j}$ is compact, we may pass to a subsequence to conclude that there is a $y\in Y_{j}$ such that $y_{n}\to y$. Passing to a further subsequence, we may assume that there is a $1\leq k\leq n_{j}$ such that for all $n\in \mathbb{N}$, the representation $\operatorname{ev}_{z_{n}}$ begins at index $k$ down the diagonal of $\operatorname{ev}_{y_{n}}$. Suppose $y$ decomposes into $x_{1}\in X_{i_{1}}\setminus Y_{i_{1}},\ldots,x_{t}\in X_{i_{t}}\setminus Y_{i_{t}}$. Let us show that $x\in F$ by proving it is in the decomposition of $y$. Let $f\in A$ be arbitrary. For each $n\in\mathbb{N}$, there are matrices $P_{n}\in M_{k-1}$ and $Q_{n}\in M_{n_{j}-n_{i}-(k-1)}$ such that $f_{j}(y_{n})=\operatorname{diag}(P_{n},f_{i}(z_{n}),Q_{n})$. Since $\lim_{n\to\infty}f_{j}(y_{n})=f_{j}(y)$, there are matrices $P\in M_{k-1}$ and $Q\in M_{n_{j}-n_{i}-(k-1)}$ such that \begin{equation} f_{j}(y)=\operatorname{diag}(P,f_{i}(x),Q). \end{equation} If $x\in Y_{i}$, it follows by definition that $x$ is in the decomposition of $y$. If $x\in X_{i}\setminus Y_{i}$ and $x$ is not in the decomposition of $y$, then we may use Proposition 4.2.5 of \cite{dix} to find a function $g\in A$ that is non-zero at $x$, but vanishes at all points in the decomposition of $y$, which implies that $g_{j}(y)=0$ and contradicts \autoref{decomp equation}. Thus, $x$ is in the decomposition of $y$ and, hence, $x\in F$.
nodes.statement_short: Take z_n in F converging to x; by compactness pass to y_n -> y with fixed index k, then show x is in the decomposition of y.

nodes.name: Sequences and limits
nodes.statement: Suppose $(z_{n})_{n}$ is a sequence of points in $F$ converging to $x\in X_{i}$. For each $n\in\mathbb{N}$, there is a $y_{n}\in Y_{j}$ with the property that $z_{n}$ is in the decomposition of $y_{n}$. Since $Y_{j}$ is compact, we may pass to a subsequence to conclude that there is a $y\in Y_{j}$ such that $y_{n}\to y$. Passing to a further subsequence, we may assume that there is a $1\leq k\leq n_{j}$ such that for all $n\in \mathbb{N}$, the representation $\operatorname{ev}_{z_{n}}$ begins at index $k$ down the diagonal of $\operatorname{ev}_{y_{n}}$. Suppose $y$ decomposes into $x_{1}\in X_{i_{1}}\setminus Y_{i_{1}},\ldots,x_{t}\in X_{i_{t}}\setminus Y_{i_{t}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Take z_n -> x in F, y_n -> y in Y_j, and a common starting index k

nodes.name: Claim: x is in the decomposition of y
nodes.statement: Let us show that $x\in F$ by proving it is in the decomposition of $y$. Let $f\in A$ be arbitrary. For each $n\in\mathbb{N}$, there are matrices $P_{n}\in M_{k-1}$ and $Q_{n}\in M_{n_{j}-n_{i}-(k-1)}$ such that $f_{j}(y_{n})=\operatorname{diag}(P_{n},f_{i}(z_{n}),Q_{n})$. Since $\lim_{n\to\infty}f_{j}(y_{n})=f_{j}(y)$, there are matrices $P\in M_{k-1}$ and $Q\in M_{n_{j}-n_{i}-(k-1)}$ such that \begin{equation} f_{j}(y)=\operatorname{diag}(P,f_{i}(x),Q). \end{equation} If $x\in Y_{i}$, it follows by definition that $x$ is in the decomposition of $y$. If $x\in X_{i}\setminus Y_{i}$ and $x$ is not in the decomposition of $y$, then we may use Proposition 4.2.5 of \cite{dix} to find a function $g\in A$ that is non-zero at $x$, but vanishes at all points in the decomposition of $y$, which implies that $g_{j}(y)=0$ and contradicts \autoref{decomp equation}. Thus, $x$ is in the decomposition of $y$ and, hence, $x\in F$.
nodes.statement_short: Show x is in the decomposition of y

nodes.name: Limit block form
nodes.statement: Let $f\in A$ be arbitrary. For each $n\in\mathbb{N}$, there are matrices $P_{n}\in M_{k-1}$ and $Q_{n}\in M_{n_{j}-n_{i}-(k-1)}$ such that $f_{j}(y_{n})=\operatorname{diag}(P_{n},f_{i}(z_{n}),Q_{n})$. Since $\lim_{n\to\infty}f_{j}(y_{n})=f_{j}(y)$, there are matrices $P\in M_{k-1}$ and $Q\in M_{n_{j}-n_{i}-(k-1)}$ such that \begin{equation} f_{j}(y)=\operatorname{diag}(P,f_{i}(x),Q). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Pass to the limit in the block forms to get f_j(y)=diag(P,f_i(x),Q)

nodes.name: Case x in Y_i
nodes.statement: If $x\in Y_{i}$, it follows by definition that $x$ is in the decomposition of $y$.
nodes.statement_short: Then x is in the decomposition of y by definition

nodes.name: Case x not in Y_i
nodes.statement: If $x\in X_{i}\setminus Y_{i}$ and $x$ is not in the decomposition of $y$, then we may use Proposition 4.2.5 of \cite{dix} to find a function $g\in A$ that is non-zero at $x$, but vanishes at all points in the decomposition of $y$, which implies that $g_{j}(y)=0$ and contradicts \autoref{decomp equation}. Thus, $x$ is in the decomposition of $y$ and, hence, $x\in F$.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise a separating function contradicts the block form; so x is in F

nodes.name: Block form of f_j(y) at the limit point
nodes.statement: f_{j}(y)=\operatorname{diag}(P,f_{i}(x),Q).
nodes.label: decomp equation

nodes.name: Phillips: quotients of recursive subhomogeneous algebras
nodes.statement: In Proposition 3.1 of \cite{phil}, Phillips shows that the class of (separable) recursive subhomogeneous algebras is closed under the taking of quotients.
conclusions: the class of (separable) recursive subhomogeneous algebras is closed under the taking of quotients

nodes.name: Standing assumption: quotient B of a DSH algebra A (Section 2.2)
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a DSH algebra of length $ l$. Suppose we have a non-zero $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra $B$ and a surjective $^*$-homomorphism $\rho\colon A\to B$.

nodes.name: Induced map on spectra
nodes.statement: This yields an injective single-valued map $\hat{\rho}\colon\hat{B}\to\hat{A}$ given by $\hat{\rho}([\pi]):=[\pi\circ \rho]$.

nodes.name: Base spaces X_i' and Y_i' of the quotient
nodes.statement: For $1\leq i\leq l$, define $X_{i}':=\overline{X_{i}\cap \hat{\rho}(\hat{B})}^{X_{i}}$ and $Y_{i}':=X_{i}'\cap Y_{i}$. Recall that these definitions make sense by \autoref{DSH spectrum}.

nodes.name: Image of the quotient spectrum is closed
nodes.statement: $\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})$ is closed in $\hat{A}$.
assumptions: Suppose we have a non-zero $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra $B$ and a surjective $^*$-homomorphism $\rho\colon A\to B$
conclusions: $\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})$ is closed in $\hat{A}$
nodes.label: image closed

nodes.name: Proof that the image of the quotient spectrum is closed
nodes.statement: Suppose $[\pi]\in\overline{\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})}$. Then $$ \ker\pi\supset\bigcap_{[\sigma]\in\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})}\ker\sigma=\bigcap_{[\tau]\in \hat{B}} \ker\hat{\rho}([\tau])=\bigcap_{[\tau]\in\hat{B}}\ker(\tau\circ\rho). $$ Note that $a\in\bigcap_{[\tau]\in\hat{B}}\ker(\tau\circ\rho)$ if and only if $\rho(a)\in\bigcap_{[\tau]\in\hat{B}}\ker\tau$ if and only if $\rho(a)=0$. Hence, $\ker\pi\supset\ker\rho$. Thus, the irreducible representation $\tau$ of $B$ given by $\tau(b):=\pi(a)$, where $a$ is any lift of $b$ under $\rho$ is well defined. Therefore, $[\pi]=[\tau\circ\rho]=\hat{\rho}([\tau])\in\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})$, so that $\overline{\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})}\subset\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})$.
nodes.statement_short: A point in the closure has kernel containing ker(rho), so it factors through B and lies in the image.

nodes.name: Kernel inclusion
nodes.statement: Suppose $[\pi]\in\overline{\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})}$. Then $$ \ker\pi\supset\bigcap_{[\sigma]\in\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})}\ker\sigma=\bigcap_{[\tau]\in \hat{B}} \ker\hat{\rho}([\tau])=\bigcap_{[\tau]\in\hat{B}}\ker(\tau\circ\rho). $$
nodes.statement_short: A point of the closure has kernel containing the intersection of the kernels

nodes.name: Kernel contains ker rho
nodes.statement: Note that $a\in\bigcap_{[\tau]\in\hat{B}}\ker(\tau\circ\rho)$ if and only if $\rho(a)\in\bigcap_{[\tau]\in\hat{B}}\ker\tau$ if and only if $\rho(a)=0$. Hence, $\ker\pi\supset\ker\rho$.
nodes.statement_short: That intersection is ker rho

nodes.name: Factor through B
nodes.statement: Thus, the irreducible representation $\tau$ of $B$ given by $\tau(b):=\pi(a)$, where $a$ is any lift of $b$ under $\rho$ is well defined. Therefore, $[\pi]=[\tau\circ\rho]=\hat{\rho}([\tau])\in\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})$, so that $\overline{\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})}\subset\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})$.
nodes.statement_short: pi factors through B, so [pi] is in the image

nodes.name: Decomposition points of Y_i' lie in the quotient spectrum
nodes.statement: Suppose $1\leq i\leq l$ and $y\in Y_{i}'$. If $1\leq j<i$ and $x\in X_{j}\setminus Y_{j}$ is in the decomposition of $y$, then $x\in X_{j}\cap\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})\subset X_{j}'$.
assumptions: $1\leq i\leq l$ and $y\in Y_{i}'$
$1\leq j<i$ and $x\in X_{j}\setminus Y_{j}$ is in the decomposition of $y$
conclusions: $x\in X_{j}\cap\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})\subset X_{j}'$
nodes.label: quotient decomp

nodes.name: Proof that decomposition points lie in the quotient spectrum
nodes.statement: Since $y\in Y_{i}'$, we have $y\in X_{i}'=\overline{X_{i}\cap\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})}^{X_{i}}$. Choose a sequence $(z_{n})_{n}$ in $X_{i}\cap\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})$ such that $z_{n}\to y$ with respect to the topology on $X_{i}$. Let us show that $(\operatorname{ev}_{z_{n}})_{n}\to \operatorname{ev}_{x}$, with respect to the hull-kernel topology on $\hat{A}$. Suppose $U$ is an open set in $\hat{A}$ containing $\operatorname{ev}_{x}$. Then there is a function $f\in A$ that is non-zero at $x$, but vanishes at each point in $\hat{A}\setminus U$. Since $x$ is in the decomposition of $y$, this implies that $f_{i}(y)\not=0$. Since $z_{n}\to y$ in $X_{i}$ and since $f_{i}$ is continuous, there is an $n_{0}$ such that for all $n\geq n_{0}$, $f_{i}(z_{n})\not=0$. In particular, this means that for all $n\geq n_{0}$, $\operatorname{ev}_{z_{n}}\in U$. Therefore, $\operatorname{ev}_{z_{n}}\to \operatorname{ev}_{x}$ in $\hat{A}$. Now, by \autoref{image closed}, $\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})$ is closed and, hence, what we've shown implies that $\operatorname{ev}_{x}\in\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})$. Therefore, $x\in X_{j}\cap\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})\subset X_{j}'$.
nodes.statement_short: Approximate y by points z_n of the image; show ev_{z_n} converges to ev_x in the spectrum and use closedness of the image.

nodes.name: Approximating sequence
nodes.statement: Since $y\in Y_{i}'$, we have $y\in X_{i}'=\overline{X_{i}\cap\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})}^{X_{i}}$. Choose a sequence $(z_{n})_{n}$ in $X_{i}\cap\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})$ such that $z_{n}\to y$ with respect to the topology on $X_{i}$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose z_n in the image converging to y in X_i

nodes.name: Claim: ev_{z_n} converges to ev_x
nodes.statement: Let us show that $(\operatorname{ev}_{z_{n}})_{n}\to \operatorname{ev}_{x}$, with respect to the hull-kernel topology on $\hat{A}$. Suppose $U$ is an open set in $\hat{A}$ containing $\operatorname{ev}_{x}$. Then there is a function $f\in A$ that is non-zero at $x$, but vanishes at each point in $\hat{A}\setminus U$. Since $x$ is in the decomposition of $y$, this implies that $f_{i}(y)\not=0$. Since $z_{n}\to y$ in $X_{i}$ and since $f_{i}$ is continuous, there is an $n_{0}$ such that for all $n\geq n_{0}$, $f_{i}(z_{n})\not=0$. In particular, this means that for all $n\geq n_{0}$, $\operatorname{ev}_{z_{n}}\in U$. Therefore, $\operatorname{ev}_{z_{n}}\to \operatorname{ev}_{x}$ in $\hat{A}$.
nodes.statement_short: Show ev_{z_n} -> ev_x in the hull-kernel topology

nodes.name: Function detecting U
nodes.statement: Suppose $U$ is an open set in $\hat{A}$ containing $\operatorname{ev}_{x}$. Then there is a function $f\in A$ that is non-zero at $x$, but vanishes at each point in $\hat{A}\setminus U$. Since $x$ is in the decomposition of $y$, this implies that $f_{i}(y)\not=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose f nonzero at x vanishing off U; then f_i(y) is nonzero

nodes.name: Eventually in U
nodes.statement: Since $z_{n}\to y$ in $X_{i}$ and since $f_{i}$ is continuous, there is an $n_{0}$ such that for all $n\geq n_{0}$, $f_{i}(z_{n})\not=0$. In particular, this means that for all $n\geq n_{0}$, $\operatorname{ev}_{z_{n}}\in U$. Therefore, $\operatorname{ev}_{z_{n}}\to \operatorname{ev}_{x}$ in $\hat{A}$.
nodes.statement_short: By continuity f_i(z_n) is eventually nonzero, so ev_{z_n} enters U

nodes.name: Use closedness
nodes.statement: Now, by \autoref{image closed}, $\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})$ is closed and, hence, what we've shown implies that $\operatorname{ev}_{x}\in\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})$. Therefore, $x\in X_{j}\cap\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})\subset X_{j}'$.
nodes.statement_short: The image is closed, so ev_x lies in it

nodes.name: Canonical DSH algebra D over the quotient base spaces
nodes.statement: There is a DSH algebra $D$ of length $ l$ with the following properties: \begin{enumerate} \item $D^{(1)}=C(X_{1}',M_{n_{1}})$; \item for all $1\leq i\leq l$, $D^{(i)}\subset\bigoplus_{j=1}^{i}C(X_{j}',M_{n_{j}})$; \item for all $1\leq i < l$, the pullback map $\tau_{i}\colon D^{(i)}\to C(Y_{i+1}',M_{n_{i+1}})$ is given by $\tau_{i}(f)(y):=\operatorname{diag}(f_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots,f_{i_{t}}(x_{t}))$, where $x_{1},\ldots,x_{t}$ are the points in the decomposition of $y$ coming from the definition of $A$; \item for $1\leq i< l$, $D^{(i+1)}=D^{(i)}\oplus_{C(Y_{i+1}',M_{n_{i+1}})}C(X_{i+1}',M_{n_{i+1}})$ with pullback map $\tau_{i}$; \item for all $1\leq i\leq l$, if $(f_{1},\ldots,f_{i})\in D^{(i)}$, there is a $(g_{1},\ldots,g_{i})\in A^{(i)}$ such that for all $1\leq j\leq i$, $g_{j}|_{X_{j}'}=f_{j}$. \end{enumerate}
conclusions: There is a DSH algebra $D$ of length $ l$ with the following properties
nodes.statement_short: A DSH algebra D over the base spaces X_i' whose pullback maps restrict those of A, and whose elements extend to elements of A.
nodes.label: isomorphic quotient

nodes.name: Inductive construction of D
nodes.statement: Let us proceed by induction on $i$. Define $D^{(1)}:=C(X_{1}',M_{n_{1}})$ so that \textit{(1)} holds. Since $X_{1}'$ is closed in $X_{1}$, we may extend a function in $D^{(1)}$ to a function in $A^{(1)}=C(X_{1},M_{n_{1}})$, so that \textit{(5)} holds when $i=1$. Now, fix $1\leq i\leq l-1$ and assume that we have defined $D^{(1)},\ldots,D^{(i)}$ and $\tau_{1},\ldots,\tau_{i-1}$ satisfying conditions \textit{(1)} to \textit{(5)}. Let us show how to define $\tau_{i}$ and $D^{(i+1)}$. Given $(f_{1},\ldots, f_{i})\in D^{(i)}$, use \textit{(5)} to get $(g_{1},\ldots,g_{i})\in A^{(i)}$ such that $g_{j}|_{X_{j}'}=f_{j}$ for $1\leq j\leq i$. Define $\tau_{i}\colon D^{(i)}\to C(Y_{i+1}',M_{n_{i+1}})$ by $\tau_{i}((f_{1},\ldots,f_{i})):=\varphi_{i}((g_{1},\ldots,g_{i}))|_{Y_{i+1}'}$. To see that $\tau_{i}$ is a well-defined $^*$-homomorphism satisfying \textit{(3)}, suppose $(h_{1},\ldots,h_{i})\in A^{(i)}$ also restricts coordinate-wise to $(f_{1},\ldots,f_{i})$. If $y\in Y_{i+1}'$ decomposes into $x_{1}\in X_{i_{1}}\setminus Y_{i_{1}},\ldots,x_{t}\in X_{i_{t}}\setminus Y_{i_{t}}$, then by \autoref{quotient decomp}, we have $x_{1}\in X_{i_{1}}',\ldots,x_{t}\in X_{i_{t}}'$. Hence, $$ \begin{aligned} \varphi_{i}((g_{1},\ldots,g_{i}))(y)&=\operatorname{diag}(g_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots,g_{i_{t}}(x_{t}))\\ &=\operatorname{diag}(f_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots,f_{i_{t}}(x_{t}))\\ &=\operatorname{diag}(h_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots,h_{i_{t}}(x_{t}))\\ &=\varphi_{i}((h_{1},\ldots,h_{i}))(y). \end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $\tau_{i}$ satisfies \textit{(3)} and is independent of the choice of extension used. Moreover, $\tau_{i}((f_{1},\ldots,f_{i}))$ is continuous, being the restriction of a continuous function. Thus, $\tau_{i}$ is well defined and it is clearly a $^*$-homomorphism since $\varphi_{i}$ is. Next, define $D^{(i+1)}:=D^{(i)}\oplus_{C(Y_{i+1}',M_{n_{i+1}})}C(X_{i+1}',M_{n_{i+1}})$, using $\tau_{i}$ as the pullback map. This ensures that \textit{(2)} and \textit{(4)} hold, and so we just need to verify \textit{(5)}. Suppose $(d,f)\in D^{(i+1)}$, where $d\in D^{(i)}$ and $f\in C(X'_{i+1},M_{n_{i+1}})$. By the inductive hypothesis, we may apply \textit{(5)} to $d$ to obtain a $b\in A^{(i)}$ such that $b_{j}|_{X_{j}'}=d_{j}$ for all $1\leq j\leq i$. Let $g:=\varphi_{i}(b)\in C(Y_{i+1},M_{n_{i+1}})$. If $y\in X_{i+1}'\cap Y_{i+1}=Y_{i+1}'$, then $g(y)=\varphi_{i}(b)(y)=\tau_{i}(d)(y)=f(y)$. Thus, since $X_{i+1}'$ and $Y_{i+1}$ are both closed in $X_{i+1}$ and since $f$ and $g$ agree on their intersection, they have a common extension $h\in C(X_{i+1},M_{n_{i+1}})$. Since $\varphi_{i}(b)=g=h|_{Y_{i+1}}$, we have $(b,h)\in A^{(i+1)}$, and since $h|_{X_{j+1}'}=f$, it follows that \textit{(5)} holds.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on i: define tau_i by extending to A^{(i)} and restricting phi_i; check well-definedness and the extension property (5).

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: Let us proceed by induction on $i$. Define $D^{(1)}:=C(X_{1}',M_{n_{1}})$ so that \textit{(1)} holds. Since $X_{1}'$ is closed in $X_{1}$, we may extend a function in $D^{(1)}$ to a function in $A^{(1)}=C(X_{1},M_{n_{1}})$, so that \textit{(5)} holds when $i=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Define D^{(1)}=C(X_1',M_{n_1}); (1) and (5) hold by Tietze extension

nodes.name: Inductive hypothesis
nodes.statement: Now, fix $1\leq i\leq l-1$ and assume that we have defined $D^{(1)},\ldots,D^{(i)}$ and $\tau_{1},\ldots,\tau_{i-1}$ satisfying conditions \textit{(1)} to \textit{(5)}.
nodes.statement_short: Assume D^{(1..i)} and tau_{1..i-1} satisfy (1)-(5)

nodes.name: Claim: define tau_i and D^{(i+1)}
nodes.statement: Let us show how to define $\tau_{i}$ and $D^{(i+1)}$. Given $(f_{1},\ldots, f_{i})\in D^{(i)}$, use \textit{(5)} to get $(g_{1},\ldots,g_{i})\in A^{(i)}$ such that $g_{j}|_{X_{j}'}=f_{j}$ for $1\leq j\leq i$. Define $\tau_{i}\colon D^{(i)}\to C(Y_{i+1}',M_{n_{i+1}})$ by $\tau_{i}((f_{1},\ldots,f_{i})):=\varphi_{i}((g_{1},\ldots,g_{i}))|_{Y_{i+1}'}$. To see that $\tau_{i}$ is a well-defined $^*$-homomorphism satisfying \textit{(3)}, suppose $(h_{1},\ldots,h_{i})\in A^{(i)}$ also restricts coordinate-wise to $(f_{1},\ldots,f_{i})$. If $y\in Y_{i+1}'$ decomposes into $x_{1}\in X_{i_{1}}\setminus Y_{i_{1}},\ldots,x_{t}\in X_{i_{t}}\setminus Y_{i_{t}}$, then by \autoref{quotient decomp}, we have $x_{1}\in X_{i_{1}}',\ldots,x_{t}\in X_{i_{t}}'$. Hence, $$ \begin{aligned} \varphi_{i}((g_{1},\ldots,g_{i}))(y)&=\operatorname{diag}(g_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots,g_{i_{t}}(x_{t}))\\ &=\operatorname{diag}(f_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots,f_{i_{t}}(x_{t}))\\ &=\operatorname{diag}(h_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots,h_{i_{t}}(x_{t}))\\ &=\varphi_{i}((h_{1},\ldots,h_{i}))(y). \end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $\tau_{i}$ satisfies \textit{(3)} and is independent of the choice of extension used. Moreover, $\tau_{i}((f_{1},\ldots,f_{i}))$ is continuous, being the restriction of a continuous function. Thus, $\tau_{i}$ is well defined and it is clearly a $^*$-homomorphism since $\varphi_{i}$ is. Next, define $D^{(i+1)}:=D^{(i)}\oplus_{C(Y_{i+1}',M_{n_{i+1}})}C(X_{i+1}',M_{n_{i+1}})$, using $\tau_{i}$ as the pullback map. This ensures that \textit{(2)} and \textit{(4)} hold, and so we just need to verify \textit{(5)}. Suppose $(d,f)\in D^{(i+1)}$, where $d\in D^{(i)}$ and $f\in C(X'_{i+1},M_{n_{i+1}})$. By the inductive hypothesis, we may apply \textit{(5)} to $d$ to obtain a $b\in A^{(i)}$ such that $b_{j}|_{X_{j}'}=d_{j}$ for all $1\leq j\leq i$. Let $g:=\varphi_{i}(b)\in C(Y_{i+1},M_{n_{i+1}})$. If $y\in X_{i+1}'\cap Y_{i+1}=Y_{i+1}'$, then $g(y)=\varphi_{i}(b)(y)=\tau_{i}(d)(y)=f(y)$. Thus, since $X_{i+1}'$ and $Y_{i+1}$ are both closed in $X_{i+1}$ and since $f$ and $g$ agree on their intersection, they have a common extension $h\in C(X_{i+1},M_{n_{i+1}})$. Since $\varphi_{i}(b)=g=h|_{Y_{i+1}}$, we have $(b,h)\in A^{(i+1)}$, and since $h|_{X_{j+1}'}=f$, it follows that \textit{(5)} holds.
nodes.statement_short: Construct tau_i and D^{(i+1)} and check (1)-(5)

nodes.name: Define tau_i
nodes.statement: Given $(f_{1},\ldots, f_{i})\in D^{(i)}$, use \textit{(5)} to get $(g_{1},\ldots,g_{i})\in A^{(i)}$ such that $g_{j}|_{X_{j}'}=f_{j}$ for $1\leq j\leq i$. Define $\tau_{i}\colon D^{(i)}\to C(Y_{i+1}',M_{n_{i+1}})$ by $\tau_{i}((f_{1},\ldots,f_{i})):=\varphi_{i}((g_{1},\ldots,g_{i}))|_{Y_{i+1}'}$.
nodes.statement_short: Extend to A^{(i)} by (5) and restrict phi_i to Y'_{i+1}

nodes.name: tau_i well defined
nodes.statement: To see that $\tau_{i}$ is a well-defined $^*$-homomorphism satisfying \textit{(3)}, suppose $(h_{1},\ldots,h_{i})\in A^{(i)}$ also restricts coordinate-wise to $(f_{1},\ldots,f_{i})$. If $y\in Y_{i+1}'$ decomposes into $x_{1}\in X_{i_{1}}\setminus Y_{i_{1}},\ldots,x_{t}\in X_{i_{t}}\setminus Y_{i_{t}}$, then by \autoref{quotient decomp}, we have $x_{1}\in X_{i_{1}}',\ldots,x_{t}\in X_{i_{t}}'$. Hence, $$ \begin{aligned} \varphi_{i}((g_{1},\ldots,g_{i}))(y)&=\operatorname{diag}(g_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots,g_{i_{t}}(x_{t}))\\ &=\operatorname{diag}(f_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots,f_{i_{t}}(x_{t}))\\ &=\operatorname{diag}(h_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots,h_{i_{t}}(x_{t}))\\ &=\varphi_{i}((h_{1},\ldots,h_{i}))(y). \end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $\tau_{i}$ satisfies \textit{(3)} and is independent of the choice of extension used. Moreover, $\tau_{i}((f_{1},\ldots,f_{i}))$ is continuous, being the restriction of a continuous function. Thus, $\tau_{i}$ is well defined and it is clearly a $^*$-homomorphism since $\varphi_{i}$ is.
nodes.statement_short: Decomposition points lie in the X_j' (previous lemma), so tau_i is independent of the extension

nodes.name: Define D^{(i+1)} and verify (5)
nodes.statement: Next, define $D^{(i+1)}:=D^{(i)}\oplus_{C(Y_{i+1}',M_{n_{i+1}})}C(X_{i+1}',M_{n_{i+1}})$, using $\tau_{i}$ as the pullback map. This ensures that \textit{(2)} and \textit{(4)} hold, and so we just need to verify \textit{(5)}. Suppose $(d,f)\in D^{(i+1)}$, where $d\in D^{(i)}$ and $f\in C(X'_{i+1},M_{n_{i+1}})$. By the inductive hypothesis, we may apply \textit{(5)} to $d$ to obtain a $b\in A^{(i)}$ such that $b_{j}|_{X_{j}'}=d_{j}$ for all $1\leq j\leq i$. Let $g:=\varphi_{i}(b)\in C(Y_{i+1},M_{n_{i+1}})$. If $y\in X_{i+1}'\cap Y_{i+1}=Y_{i+1}'$, then $g(y)=\varphi_{i}(b)(y)=\tau_{i}(d)(y)=f(y)$. Thus, since $X_{i+1}'$ and $Y_{i+1}$ are both closed in $X_{i+1}$ and since $f$ and $g$ agree on their intersection, they have a common extension $h\in C(X_{i+1},M_{n_{i+1}})$. Since $\varphi_{i}(b)=g=h|_{Y_{i+1}}$, we have $(b,h)\in A^{(i+1)}$, and since $h|_{X_{j+1}'}=f$, it follows that \textit{(5)} holds.
nodes.statement_short: Take the pullback along tau_i and extend elements by gluing on X'_{i+1} and Y_{i+1}

nodes.name: Quotients of DSH algebras are DSH
nodes.statement: Let $D=D^{( l)}$ be the DSH algebra constructed in \autoref{isomorphic quotient}. There is a $^*$-isomorphism $\Gamma\colon B\to D$ given coordinate-wise by $\Gamma(b)_{i}:=a_{i}|_{X_{i}'}$ for $1\leq i\leq l$, where $a\in A$ is any lift of $b$ under $\rho$. In particular, the quotient $B$ is a DSH algebra.
assumptions: Let $D=D^{( l)}$ be the DSH algebra constructed in \autoref{isomorphic quotient}
conclusions: There is a $^*$-isomorphism $\Gamma\colon B\to D$ given coordinate-wise by $\Gamma(b)_{i}:=a_{i}|_{X_{i}'}$ for $1\leq i\leq l$, where $a\in A$ is any lift of $b$ under $\rho$
the quotient $B$ is a DSH algebra
nodes.statement_short: Restriction of lifts to the X_i' gives a *-isomorphism from the quotient B onto D, so B is DSH.
nodes.label: quotient DSH

nodes.name: Proof that B is isomorphic to D
nodes.statement: Let us first show that $\Gamma(b)$ is independent of the choice of lift. Fix $1\leq i\leq l$ and suppose $g,h\in A$ satisfy $\rho(g)=\rho(h)$. We must show that $g_{i}|_{X_{i}'}=h_{i}|_{X_{i}'}$. Note that $\overline{X_{i}'\setminus Y_{i}'}^{X_{i}}=X_{i}'$. Indeed, $X_{i}'$ is closed with respect to the topology on $X_{i}$, and so the fact that $\overline{X_{i}'\setminus Y_{i}'}^{X_{i}}$ is a subset of $X_{i}'$ is clear; for the reverse inclusion, if $z\in X_{i}'$, there is a sequence $(z_{n})_{n}\subset \hat{\rho}(\hat{B})\cap X_{i}\subset X_{i}'\setminus Y_{i}\subset X_{i}'\setminus Y_{i}'$ that converges to $z$ in $X_{i}$. Hence, by continuity, it suffices to show that $g_{i}|_{X_{i}'\setminus Y_{i}'}=h_{i}|_{X_{i}'\setminus Y_{i}'}$. To this end, suppose $x\in X_{i}'\setminus Y_{i}'$. Then $x\in \overline{X_{i}\cap\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})}^{X_{i}}=\overline{(X_{i}\setminus Y_{i})\cap\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})}^{X_{i}}$ and $x\notin Y_{i}$. By \autoref{image closed} and \autoref{DSH spectrum}, $(X_{i}\setminus Y_{i})\cap \hat{\rho}(\hat{B})$ is closed in $X_{i}\setminus Y_{i}$ in the subspace topology coming from $X_{i}$. Thus, $$ \begin{aligned} x\in \overline{(X_{i}\setminus Y_{i})\cap\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})}^{X_{i}}\cap (X_{i}\setminus Y_{i}) =\overline{(X_{i}\setminus Y_{i})\cap\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})}^{X_{i}\setminus Y_{i}} =(X_{i}\setminus Y_{i})\cap\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})\subset\hat{\rho}(\hat{B}). \end{aligned} $$ Therefore, there is a $[\pi]\in \hat{B}$ such that $[\pi\circ\rho]=\hat{\rho}([\pi])=[\operatorname{ev}_{x}]$. But this implies that $g-h\in\ker \operatorname{ev}_{x}$ since $g-h\in \ker\rho$. Hence, $g_{i}(x)=h_{i}(x)$, as desired. Moreover, $\Gamma(b)_{i}$ belongs to $C(X_{i}',M_{n_{i}})$, being the restriction of a continuous function. To see that $\Gamma(b)$ respects the decomposition structure of $D$, suppose $y\in Y_{i}'$ decomposes into $x_{1}\in X_{i_{1}}'\setminus Y_{i_{1}}', \ldots, x_{t}\in X_{i_{t}}'\setminus Y_{i_{t}}'$. Then, $$ \begin{aligned} \Gamma(b)_{i}(y)=a_{i}(y) =\operatorname{diag}(a_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots, a_{i_{t}}(x_{t})) =\operatorname{diag}(\Gamma(b)_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots,\Gamma(b)_{i_{t}}(x_{t})). \end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $\Gamma$ is well defined and it is straightforward to check that it is a $^*$-homomorphism. We have left only to check that it is a bijection. To see that $\Gamma$ is injective, suppose $b\in B$ and $a\in A$ is such that $\rho(a)=b$. Assume that $\Gamma(b)=0$. Let $\pi$ be an arbitrary irreducible representation of $B$. To show that $b=0$, it suffices to show that $\pi(b)=0$. Note that $[\pi\circ\rho]=\hat{\rho}([\pi])\in\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})$. Thus, for some $1\leq i\leq l$, there is an $x\in (X_{i}\setminus Y_{i})\cap \hat{\rho}(\hat{B})\subset X_{i}'$ such that $[\pi\circ \rho]=[\operatorname{ev}_{x}]$. Since $\operatorname{ev}_{x}(a)=a_{i}(x)=\Gamma(b)_{i}(x)=0$, it follows that $\pi(b)=\pi(\rho(a))=0$. Thus, $\Gamma$ is injective. To see that $\Gamma$ is surjective, suppose $d\in D$. By property \textit{(5)} in \autoref{isomorphic quotient}, there is a $g\in A$ such that $g_{i}|_{X_{i}'}=d_{i}$ for all $1\leq i\leq l$. Let $h=\rho(g)\in B$ and observe that for all $1\leq i\leq l$, we have $\Gamma(h)_{i}=g_{i}|_{X_{i}'}=d_{i}$. Thus, $\Gamma(h)=d$, so $\Gamma$ is surjective. We have shown that $\Gamma$ is a $^*$-isomorphism, from which it follows that $B$ is a DSH algebra.
nodes.statement_short: Check Gamma is independent of the lift (density of X_i' minus Y_i' and closedness of the image), respects decompositions, and is bijective.

nodes.name: Goal: independence of the lift
nodes.statement: Let us first show that $\Gamma(b)$ is independent of the choice of lift. Fix $1\leq i\leq l$ and suppose $g,h\in A$ satisfy $\rho(g)=\rho(h)$. We must show that $g_{i}|_{X_{i}'}=h_{i}|_{X_{i}'}$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to showing g_i=h_i on X_i' when rho(g)=rho(h)

nodes.name: Density reduction
nodes.statement: Note that $\overline{X_{i}'\setminus Y_{i}'}^{X_{i}}=X_{i}'$. Indeed, $X_{i}'$ is closed with respect to the topology on $X_{i}$, and so the fact that $\overline{X_{i}'\setminus Y_{i}'}^{X_{i}}$ is a subset of $X_{i}'$ is clear; for the reverse inclusion, if $z\in X_{i}'$, there is a sequence $(z_{n})_{n}\subset \hat{\rho}(\hat{B})\cap X_{i}\subset X_{i}'\setminus Y_{i}\subset X_{i}'\setminus Y_{i}'$ that converges to $z$ in $X_{i}$. Hence, by continuity, it suffices to show that $g_{i}|_{X_{i}'\setminus Y_{i}'}=h_{i}|_{X_{i}'\setminus Y_{i}'}$.
nodes.statement_short: X_i' minus Y_i' is dense in X_i', so it suffices to check there

nodes.name: Points of X_i' minus Y_i' lie in the image
nodes.statement: To this end, suppose $x\in X_{i}'\setminus Y_{i}'$. Then $x\in \overline{X_{i}\cap\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})}^{X_{i}}=\overline{(X_{i}\setminus Y_{i})\cap\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})}^{X_{i}}$ and $x\notin Y_{i}$. By \autoref{image closed} and \autoref{DSH spectrum}, $(X_{i}\setminus Y_{i})\cap \hat{\rho}(\hat{B})$ is closed in $X_{i}\setminus Y_{i}$ in the subspace topology coming from $X_{i}$. Thus, $$ \begin{aligned} x\in \overline{(X_{i}\setminus Y_{i})\cap\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})}^{X_{i}}\cap (X_{i}\setminus Y_{i}) =\overline{(X_{i}\setminus Y_{i})\cap\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})}^{X_{i}\setminus Y_{i}} =(X_{i}\setminus Y_{i})\cap\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})\subset\hat{\rho}(\hat{B}). \end{aligned} $$ Therefore, there is a $[\pi]\in \hat{B}$ such that $[\pi\circ\rho]=\hat{\rho}([\pi])=[\operatorname{ev}_{x}]$. But this implies that $g-h\in\ker \operatorname{ev}_{x}$ since $g-h\in \ker\rho$. Hence, $g_{i}(x)=h_{i}(x)$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Such x lie in the image of the quotient spectrum, so g-h vanishes at x

nodes.name: Gamma respects decompositions
nodes.statement: Moreover, $\Gamma(b)_{i}$ belongs to $C(X_{i}',M_{n_{i}})$, being the restriction of a continuous function. To see that $\Gamma(b)$ respects the decomposition structure of $D$, suppose $y\in Y_{i}'$ decomposes into $x_{1}\in X_{i_{1}}'\setminus Y_{i_{1}}', \ldots, x_{t}\in X_{i_{t}}'\setminus Y_{i_{t}}'$. Then, $$ \begin{aligned} \Gamma(b)_{i}(y)=a_{i}(y) =\operatorname{diag}(a_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots, a_{i_{t}}(x_{t})) =\operatorname{diag}(\Gamma(b)_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots,\Gamma(b)_{i_{t}}(x_{t})). \end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $\Gamma$ is well defined and it is straightforward to check that it is a $^*$-homomorphism. We have left only to check that it is a bijection.
nodes.statement_short: Gamma(b) is continuous and diagonal at points of Y_i', so Gamma is a well-defined *-homomorphism

nodes.name: Injectivity
nodes.statement: To see that $\Gamma$ is injective, suppose $b\in B$ and $a\in A$ is such that $\rho(a)=b$. Assume that $\Gamma(b)=0$. Let $\pi$ be an arbitrary irreducible representation of $B$. To show that $b=0$, it suffices to show that $\pi(b)=0$. Note that $[\pi\circ\rho]=\hat{\rho}([\pi])\in\hat{\rho}(\hat{B})$. Thus, for some $1\leq i\leq l$, there is an $x\in (X_{i}\setminus Y_{i})\cap \hat{\rho}(\hat{B})\subset X_{i}'$ such that $[\pi\circ \rho]=[\operatorname{ev}_{x}]$. Since $\operatorname{ev}_{x}(a)=a_{i}(x)=\Gamma(b)_{i}(x)=0$, it follows that $\pi(b)=\pi(\rho(a))=0$. Thus, $\Gamma$ is injective.
nodes.statement_short: Every irreducible representation of B is some ev_x with x in X_i', so Gamma(b)=0 forces b=0

nodes.name: Surjectivity
nodes.statement: To see that $\Gamma$ is surjective, suppose $d\in D$. By property \textit{(5)} in \autoref{isomorphic quotient}, there is a $g\in A$ such that $g_{i}|_{X_{i}'}=d_{i}$ for all $1\leq i\leq l$. Let $h=\rho(g)\in B$ and observe that for all $1\leq i\leq l$, we have $\Gamma(h)_{i}=g_{i}|_{X_{i}'}=d_{i}$. Thus, $\Gamma(h)=d$, so $\Gamma$ is surjective.
nodes.statement_short: Extend d to g in A by property (5) and take rho(g)

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: We have shown that $\Gamma$ is a $^*$-isomorphism, from which it follows that $B$ is a DSH algebra.
nodes.statement_short: Gamma is a *-isomorphism, so B is DSH

nodes.name: Bonding maps may be assumed injective
nodes.statement: Given an inductive limit $$ A_{1}\overset{\psi_{1}}{\longrightarrow} A_{2}\overset{\psi_{2}}{\longrightarrow} A_{3}\overset{\psi_{3}}{\longrightarrow}\cdots\longrightarrow A:=\varinjlim A_{i} $$ of DSH algebras with diagonal maps, there exist DSH algebras $D_{1},D_{2},\ldots$ and injective diagonal maps $\psi_{i}'\colon D_{i}\to D_{i+1}$ such that $$ D_{1}\overset{\psi_{1}'}{\longrightarrow} D_{2}\overset{\psi_{2}'}{\longrightarrow} D_{3}\overset{\psi_{3}'}{\longrightarrow}\cdots\longrightarrow A. $$
assumptions: of DSH algebras with diagonal maps
conclusions: there exist DSH algebras $D_{1},D_{2},\ldots$ and injective diagonal maps $\psi_{i}'\colon D_{i}\to D_{i+1}$ such that
nodes.statement_short: Any inductive limit of DSH algebras with diagonal maps is also a limit of DSH algebras with injective diagonal maps.
nodes.label: injective

nodes.name: Proof that bonding maps may be taken injective
nodes.statement:
For $n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $\mu_{n}\colon A_{n}	o A$ denote the map in the construction of the inductive limit and consider the surjective map $\kappa_{n}\colon A_{n}	o A_{n}/\ker\mu_{n}=:B_{n}$. The induced map $
u_{n}\colon B_{n}	o B_{n+1}$ given by $
u_{n}(\kappa_{n}(a)):=\kappa_{n+1}(\psi_{n}(a))$ for all $a\in A_{n}$ is well defined and injective. Furthermore, $\varinjlim(B_{n},\{
u_{n}\}_{n})=A$. Let $X_{1}^{n},\ldots,X_{ l(n)}^{n}$ denote the base spaces of $A_{n}$ and let $Y_{1}^{n},\ldots,Y_{ l(n)}^{n}$ denote the corresponding closed subsets. Let $D_{n}$ denote the DSH algebra given by \autoref{isomorphic quotient} and isomorphic to $B_{n}$ (with base spaces $\overline{X_{i}^{n}\cap\hat{\kappa}_{n}(\hat{B_{n}})}^{X_{i}^{n}}=:Z_{i}^{n}$ and corresponding closed subsets $Z_{i}^{n}\cap Y_{i}^{n}=:W_{i}^{n}$ for $1\leq i\leq l(n)$). By \autoref{quotient DSH}, the injective map $
u_{n}$ drops down to an injective map $\psi_{n}'\colon D_{n}	o D_{n+1}$ given by $\psi_{n}'(d)_{i}:=\psi_{n}(a)_{i}|_{Z_{i}^{n+1}}$ for all $1\leq i\leq l(n+1)$, where $a\in A_{n}$ is any coordinate-wise extension of $d$. Moreover, $\varinjlim(D_{n},\{\psi'_{n}\}_{n})=A$. We need to check that $\psi'_{n}$ is diagonal. Fix $1\leq i\leq l(n+1)$ and suppose $x\in Z_{i}^{n+1}\setminus W_{i}^{n+1}\subset X^{n+1}_{i}\setminus Y_{i}^{n+1}$ decomposes into $x_{1}\in X_{i_{1}}^{n}\setminus Y_{i_{1}}^{n},\ldots,x_{t}\in X_{i_{t}}^{n}\setminus Y_{i_{t}}^{n}$ under the diagonal map $\psi_{n}$. We need to show that $x_{j}\in Z_{i_{j}}^{n}\setminus W_{i_{j}}^{n}$ for all $1\leq j\leq t$. Since $\operatorname{ev}_{x}\circ\psi_{n}'$ is a $^*$-representation of $D_{n}$, it is unitarily equivalent to a finite direct sum of irreducible representations $\operatorname{ev}_{z_{1}},\ldots,\operatorname{ev}_{z_{k}}\in igsqcup_{s=1}^{ l(n)}(Z_{s}^{n}\setminus W_{s}^{n})\subset \hat{A}_{n}$. Fix $1\leq j\leq t$. If $x_{j}
otin\{z_{1},\ldots,z_{k}\}$, then by Proposition 4.2.5 of \cite{dix}, there is a function $a\in A_{n}$ such that $\operatorname{ev}_{z_{s}}(a)=0$ for all $1\leq s\leq k$, but $\operatorname{ev}_{x_{j}}(a)
ot=0$. Since $x_{j}$ is in the decomposition of $x$ under $\psi_{n}$, this implies that $\operatorname{ev}_{x}(\psi_{n}(a))$ is both zero and non-zero simultaneously. Therefore, it must be that $x_{j}\in \{z_{1},\ldots,z_{k}\}$ and, thus, that $x_{j}\in Z_{i_{j}}^{n}\setminus W_{i_{j}}^{n}$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Pass to quotients A_n/ker(mu_n), identified with DSH algebras D_n; separate points with Dixmier 4.2.5 to show the induced maps stay diagonal.

nodes.name: Quotient system
nodes.statement:
For $n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $\mu_{n}\colon A_{n}	o A$ denote the map in the construction of the inductive limit and consider the surjective map $\kappa_{n}\colon A_{n}	o A_{n}/\ker\mu_{n}=:B_{n}$. The induced map $
u_{n}\colon B_{n}	o B_{n+1}$ given by $
u_{n}(\kappa_{n}(a)):=\kappa_{n+1}(\psi_{n}(a))$ for all $a\in A_{n}$ is well defined and injective. Furthermore, $\varinjlim(B_{n},\{
u_{n}\}_{n})=A$.
nodes.statement_short: Replace A_n by B_n=A_n/ker(mu_n) with injective induced maps nu_n

nodes.name: Identify B_n with DSH algebras D_n
nodes.statement: Let $X_{1}^{n},\ldots,X_{ l(n)}^{n}$ denote the base spaces of $A_{n}$ and let $Y_{1}^{n},\ldots,Y_{ l(n)}^{n}$ denote the corresponding closed subsets. Let $D_{n}$ denote the DSH algebra given by \autoref{isomorphic quotient} and isomorphic to $B_{n}$ (with base spaces $\overline{X_{i}^{n}\cap\hat{\kappa}_{n}(\hat{B_{n}})}^{X_{i}^{n}}=:Z_{i}^{n}$ and corresponding closed subsets $Z_{i}^{n}\cap Y_{i}^{n}=:W_{i}^{n}$ for $1\leq i\leq l(n)$). By \autoref{quotient DSH}, the injective map $\nu_{n}$ drops down to an injective map $\psi_{n}'\colon D_{n}\to D_{n+1}$ given by $\psi_{n}'(d)_{i}:=\psi_{n}(a)_{i}|_{Z_{i}^{n+1}}$ for all $1\leq i\leq l(n+1)$, where $a\in A_{n}$ is any coordinate-wise extension of $d$. Moreover, $\varinjlim(D_{n},\{\psi'_{n}\}_{n})=A$.
nodes.statement_short: Use the quotient propositions to get D_n and injective maps psi_n' with the same limit

nodes.name: Goal: psi_n' is diagonal
nodes.statement: We need to check that $\psi'_{n}$ is diagonal. Fix $1\leq i\leq l(n+1)$ and suppose $x\in Z_{i}^{n+1}\setminus W_{i}^{n+1}\subset X^{n+1}_{i}\setminus Y_{i}^{n+1}$ decomposes into $x_{1}\in X_{i_{1}}^{n}\setminus Y_{i_{1}}^{n},\ldots,x_{t}\in X_{i_{t}}^{n}\setminus Y_{i_{t}}^{n}$ under the diagonal map $\psi_{n}$. We need to show that $x_{j}\in Z_{i_{j}}^{n}\setminus W_{i_{j}}^{n}$ for all $1\leq j\leq t$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to showing decomposition points x_j lie in Z minus W

nodes.name: Separation argument
nodes.statement: Since $\operatorname{ev}_{x}\circ\psi_{n}'$ is a $^*$-representation of $D_{n}$, it is unitarily equivalent to a finite direct sum of irreducible representations $\operatorname{ev}_{z_{1}},\ldots,\operatorname{ev}_{z_{k}}\in\bigsqcup_{s=1}^{ l(n)}(Z_{s}^{n}\setminus W_{s}^{n})\subset \hat{A}_{n}$. Fix $1\leq j\leq t$. If $x_{j}\notin\{z_{1},\ldots,z_{k}\}$, then by Proposition 4.2.5 of \cite{dix}, there is a function $a\in A_{n}$ such that $\operatorname{ev}_{z_{s}}(a)=0$ for all $1\leq s\leq k$, but $\operatorname{ev}_{x_{j}}(a)\not=0$. Since $x_{j}$ is in the decomposition of $x$ under $\psi_{n}$, this implies that $\operatorname{ev}_{x}(\psi_{n}(a))$ is both zero and non-zero simultaneously. Therefore, it must be that $x_{j}\in \{z_{1},\ldots,z_{k}\}$ and, thus, that $x_{j}\in Z_{i_{j}}^{n}\setminus W_{i_{j}}^{n}$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: If x_j were not among the irreducible summands, a separating function gives a contradiction

nodes.name: Homogeneous DSH pullbacks are full matrix algebras
nodes.statement: Let $X_{1},X_{2}$ be compact metric spaces. Let $Y_{2}$ be a closed subset of $X_{2}$. Let $\varphi\colon C(X_{1},M_{n})\to C(Y_{2},M_{n})$ be a unital $^*$-homomorphism and suppose the associated pullback $C(X_{1},M_{n})\oplus_{C(Y_{2},M_{n})}C(X_{2},M_{n})$ is a DSH algebra. Then, there is a compact metric space $Z^{*}$ such that $C(X_{1},M_{n})\oplus_{C(Y_{2},M_{n})}C(X_{2},M_{n})$ is isomorphic to $C(Z^{*},M_{n})$.
assumptions: $X_{1},X_{2}$ be compact metric spaces
$Y_{2}$ be a closed subset of $X_{2}$
$\varphi\colon C(X_{1},M_{n})\to C(Y_{2},M_{n})$ be a unital $^*$-homomorphism and suppose the associated pullback $C(X_{1},M_{n})\oplus_{C(Y_{2},M_{n})}C(X_{2},M_{n})$ is a DSH algebra
conclusions: there is a compact metric space $Z^{*}$ such that $C(X_{1},M_{n})\oplus_{C(Y_{2},M_{n})}C(X_{2},M_{n})$ is isomorphic to $C(Z^{*},M_{n})$
nodes.label: homcomb

nodes.name: Proof that a homogeneous DSH pullback is a full matrix algebra
nodes.statement_short: Glue X_1 and X_2 along the continuous closed map tau: Y_2 -> X_1 into a quotient space Z*, show it is Hausdorff (hence metrizable), and identify the pullback with C(Z*,M_n).

nodes.name: Define tau
nodes.statement: For a given $y\in Y_{2}$, we know by \autoref{unique} that the point it decomposes into is unique; alternatively, note that if there were two distinct points in the decomposition of $y$ under $\varphi$, then these two points could not be separated by any function in $C(X_{1},M_{n})$. Denote this unique point by $\tau(y)$.
nodes.statement_short: Each y in Y_2 decomposes into a unique point tau(y) of X_1

nodes.name: Claim: tau is closed and continuous
nodes.statement: \begin{claim} $\tau\colon Y_{2}\to X_{1}$ is a closed and continuous map. \end{claim} \begin{proof}[Proof of \autoref{closed and continuous}] Suppose first that $(y_{n})_{n}$ is a sequence in $Y_{2}$ converging to a point $y$ and let $f\in C(X_{1},M_{n_{1}})$ be arbitrary. As $\varphi(f)$ is continuous, $$ \lim_{n}f(\tau(y_{n}))=\lim_{n}\varphi(f)(y_{n})=\varphi(f)(y)=f(\tau(y)), $$ which proves that $(\tau(y_{n}))_{n}$ converges to $\tau(y)$, since functions in $C(X_{1},M_{n_{1}})$ separate points. Thus, $\tau$ is continuous. To see that $\tau$ is closed, fix a closed subset $F$ of $Y_{2}$, and suppose that $(x_{n})_{n}$ is a sequence in $\tau(F)$ converging to a point $x\in X_{1}$. Choose, for each $n$, a point $y_{n}\in F$ with $\tau(y_{n})=x_{n}$. Since $F$ is compact, we may assume (by passing to a subsequence) that $(y_{n})_{n}$ converges to a point $y$ in $F$. Letting $f\in C(X_{1},M_{n_{1}})$ be arbitrary, it follows that $$ f(x)=\lim_{n}f(x_{n})=\lim_{n}f(\tau(y_{n}))=\lim_{n}\varphi(f)(y_{n})=\varphi(f)(y)=f(\tau(y)). $$ Since this holds for all $f\in C(X_{1},M_{n_{1}})$, it must be that $x=\tau(y)\in \tau(F)$, which proves that $\tau$ is closed, completing the proof of \autoref{closed and continuous}. \end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: Inner claim with its proof

nodes.name: Quotient space Z*
nodes.statement: Continuing with the proof of \autoref{homcomb}, let $Z:=X_{1}\sqcup X_{2}$. Then $Z$ is a compact metric space. Given $z\in Z$, we define $[z]$ as follows: $$ [z]:= \begin{aligned} \begin{cases} \{z\}&\text{ if }z\in X_{2}\setminus Y_{2}\\ \{z\}\cup\tau^{-1}(z)&\text{ if }z\in X_{1}\\ \{\tau(z)\}\cup\tau^{-1}(\tau(z))&\text{ if }z\in Y_{2}. \end{cases} \end{aligned} $$ Let $Z^{*}:=\{[z]:z\in Z\}$ and let $p\colon Z\to Z^{*}$ denote the canonical surjection $p(z):=[z]$. Then $Z^{*}$ is a collection of sets that partition $Z$. We equip it with the quotient topology induced by $p$; that is, a set $U\subset Z^{*}$ is open in $Z^{*}$ if and only if $p^{-1}(U)$ is open in $Z$. Since $Z$ is compact, so is $Z^{*}$.
nodes.statement_short: Glue X_1 and X_2 into Z* by identifying y with tau(y); Z* is compact

nodes.name: Reduce metrizability to Hausdorff
nodes.statement: To establish that $Z^{*}$ is in fact a metric space, it suffices to ensure that it is Hausdorff. Indeed, letting $w(Y)$ denote the smallest cardinality of a basis for a given topological space $Y$, it follows by Theorem 3.1.22 of \cite{eng} that $w(Z^{*})\leq w(Z)$. Since a compact Hausdorff space is metrizable if and only if it has a countable basis, showing that $Z^{*}$ is Hausdorff would guarantee that it is also metrizable.
nodes.statement_short: By Engelking 3.1.22, Hausdorff suffices for metrizability

nodes.name: Claim: Z* is Hausdorff
nodes.statement_short: Inner claim with its proof

nodes.name: Define Lambda
nodes.statement: Returning to the proof of \autoref{homcomb}, define $\Lambda\colon C(X_{1},M_{n})\oplus_{C(Y_{2},M_{n})}C(X_{2},M_{n})\to C(Z^{*},M_{n})$ by: $$ \Lambda((f,g))([z]):= \begin{aligned} \begin{cases} f(z)&\text{ if }z\in X_{1}\\ g(z)&\text{ if }z\in X_{2}. \end{cases} \end{aligned} $$ To conclude the proof, let us show that $\Lambda$ is a well-defined $^*$-isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Define Lambda((f,g))([z]) by f on X_1 and g on X_2

nodes.name: Lambda well defined and injective
nodes.statement: To see that $\Lambda$ is well defined, suppose $z_{1},z_{2}\in Z$ and that $[z_{1}]=[z_{2}]$. Unless $z_{1}=z_{2}$, this implies that one of the two points is in the decomposition of the other. Assume without loss of generality that $\tau(z_{2})=z_{1}$. Then for all $(f,g)\in C(X_{1},M_{n})\oplus_{C(Y_{2},M_{n})}C(X_{2},M_{n})$, we have $g(z_{2})=\varphi(f)(z_{2})=f(\tau(z_{2}))=f(z_{1})$. This shows that $\Lambda$ is well defined. It is clear that $\Lambda$ is an injective $^*$-homomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Identified points carry equal values by the pullback condition

nodes.name: Lambda surjective
nodes.statement: To see surjectivity, suppose $h\in C(Z^{*},M_{n})$ and define $f:=h\circ p|_{X_{1}}\in C(X_{1},M_{n})$ and $g:=h\circ p|_{X_{2}}\in C(X_{2},M_{n})$. Given $y\in Y_{2}$, we have $$ g(y)=h([y])=h([\tau(y)])=f(\tau(y))=\varphi(f)(y), $$ so that $(f,g)\in C(X_{1},M_{n})\oplus_{C(Y_{2},M_{n})}C(X_{2},M_{n})$. Moreover, $\Lambda((f,g))=h$, proving that $\Lambda$ is surjective. The proof of \autoref{homcomb} is now complete.
nodes.statement_short: Pull back h along p to get (f,g) in the pullback

nodes.name: tau is closed and continuous
nodes.statement: $\tau\colon Y_{2}\to X_{1}$ is a closed and continuous map.
conclusions: $\tau\colon Y_{2}\to X_{1}$ is a closed and continuous map
nodes.label: closed and continuous

nodes.name: Proof that tau is closed and continuous
nodes.statement: Suppose first that $(y_{n})_{n}$ is a sequence in $Y_{2}$ converging to a point $y$ and let $f\in C(X_{1},M_{n_{1}})$ be arbitrary.
