As $\varphi(f)$ is continuous, $$ \lim_{n}f(\tau(y_{n}))=\lim_{n}\varphi(f)(y_{n})=\varphi(f)(y)=f(\tau(y)), $$ which proves that $(\tau(y_{n}))_{n}$ converges to $\tau(y)$, since functions in $C(X_{1},M_{n_{1}})$ separate points. Thus, $\tau$ is continuous. To see that $\tau$ is closed, fix a closed subset $F$ of $Y_{2}$, and suppose that $(x_{n})_{n}$ is a sequence in $\tau(F)$ converging to a point $x\in X_{1}$. Choose, for each $n$, a point $y_{n}\in F$ with $\tau(y_{n})=x_{n}$. Since $F$ is compact, we may assume (by passing to a subsequence) that $(y_{n})_{n}$ converges to a point $y$ in $F$. Letting $f\in C(X_{1},M_{n_{1}})$ be arbitrary, it follows that $$ f(x)=\lim_{n}f(x_{n})=\lim_{n}f(\tau(y_{n}))=\lim_{n}\varphi(f)(y_{n})=\varphi(f)(y)=f(\tau(y)). $$ Since this holds for all $f\in C(X_{1},M_{n_{1}})$, it must be that $x=\tau(y)\in \tau(F)$, which proves that $\tau$ is closed, completing the proof of \autoref{closed and continuous}.
nodes.statement_short: Continuity and closedness via sequences, using that functions in C(X_1,M_n) separate points and compactness of closed F.

nodes.name: Continuity
nodes.statement: Suppose first that $(y_{n})_{n}$ is a sequence in $Y_{2}$ converging to a point $y$ and let $f\in C(X_{1},M_{n_{1}})$ be arbitrary. As $\varphi(f)$ is continuous, $$ \lim_{n}f(\tau(y_{n}))=\lim_{n}\varphi(f)(y_{n})=\varphi(f)(y)=f(\tau(y)), $$ which proves that $(\tau(y_{n}))_{n}$ converges to $\tau(y)$, since functions in $C(X_{1},M_{n_{1}})$ separate points. Thus, $\tau$ is continuous.
nodes.statement_short: Sequential continuity since functions separate points

nodes.name: Closedness
nodes.statement: To see that $\tau$ is closed, fix a closed subset $F$ of $Y_{2}$, and suppose that $(x_{n})_{n}$ is a sequence in $\tau(F)$ converging to a point $x\in X_{1}$. Choose, for each $n$, a point $y_{n}\in F$ with $\tau(y_{n})=x_{n}$. Since $F$ is compact, we may assume (by passing to a subsequence) that $(y_{n})_{n}$ converges to a point $y$ in $F$. Letting $f\in C(X_{1},M_{n_{1}})$ be arbitrary, it follows that $$ f(x)=\lim_{n}f(x_{n})=\lim_{n}f(\tau(y_{n}))=\lim_{n}\varphi(f)(y_{n})=\varphi(f)(y)=f(\tau(y)). $$ Since this holds for all $f\in C(X_{1},M_{n_{1}})$, it must be that $x=\tau(y)\in \tau(F)$, which proves that $\tau$ is closed, completing the proof of \autoref{closed and continuous}.
nodes.statement_short: Limits of tau(y_n) are tau of a limit point by compactness

nodes.name: Z* is Hausdorff
nodes.statement: $Z^{*}$ is Hausdorff.
conclusions: $Z^{*}$ is Hausdorff
nodes.label: hausdorff

nodes.name: Proof that Z* is Hausdorff
nodes.statement_short: Four cases by where z_1, z_2 lie; in the hardest case build saturated disjoint open sets from neighbourhoods in X_1 and their tau-preimages.

nodes.name: Four cases
nodes.statement: Suppose $z_{1},z_{2}\in Z$ with $[z_{1}]\not=[z_{2}]$. Let us show that $[z_{1}]$ and $[z_{2}]$ can be separated by open sets in $Z^{*}$. Without loss of generality, we must be in one of the following four cases.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to four cases for the positions of z_1, z_2

nodes.name: Case one
nodes.statement: Case one: $z_{1},z_{2}\in (X_{2}\setminus Y_{2})\cup (X_{1}\setminus \tau(Y_{2}))$. nodes.name: E_1 and E_2 are open
nodes.statement: It remains to be shown that $\mathcal{E}_{1}$ and $\mathcal{E}_{2}$ are open in $Z^{*}$. Owing to the symmetry of the setup, we only show that $\mathcal{E}_{1}$ is open in $Z^{*}$, and to do this it is sufficient to prove that $p^{-1}(\mathcal{E}_{1})\cap X_{1}=U_{1}$ and $p^{-1}(\mathcal{E}_{1})\cap X_{2}=\mathcal{O}_{1}$. Assume we are given $t\in p^{-1}(\mathcal{E}_{1})\cap X_{1}$. Thus $[t]\in p(\mathcal{O}_{1})\cup p(U_{1})$. If there is an $s\in U_{1}$ such that $[t]=[s]$, then, since both $t$ and $s$ lie in $X_{1}$, it must be that $t=s$. If instead there is an $s\in\mathcal{O}_{1}$ such that $[t]=[s]$, then it follows that $s\in Y_{2}$, and hence, that $\tau(s)\in U_{1}$. Thus, $[t]=[s]=[\tau(s)]$, from which we deduce as before that $t=\tau(s)\in U_{1}$. Therefore, we may conclude that $p^{-1}(\mathcal{E}_{1})\cap X_{1}\subset U_{1}$, and hence, $p^{-1}(\mathcal{E}_{1})\cap X_{1}=U_{1}$. Now, suppose that we are given $t\in p^{-1}(\mathcal{E}_{1})\cap X_{2}$. As before, $[t]\in p(\mathcal{O}_{1})\cup p(U_{1})$. Suppose first that there is an $s\in\mathcal{O}_{1}$ such that $[t]=[s]$. If either $t$ or $s$ is in $X_{2}\setminus Y_{2}$, then $t=s\in \mathcal{O}_{1}$; otherwise, it must be that $s,t\in Y_{2}$ and, in particular, $\tau(t)=\tau(s)\in U_{1}$. Therefore, $t\in V_{1}\cap W_{1}=\mathcal{O}_{1}$. If instead there is an $s\in U_{1}$ such that $[t]=[s]$, then it must be that $t\in Y_{2}$ and $\tau(t)=s\in U_{1}$, which implies (as above) that $t\in\mathcal{O}_{1}$. Thus, $p^{-1}(\mathcal{E}_{1})\cap X_{2}\subset \mathcal{O}_{1}$, and hence, $p^{-1}(\mathcal{E}_{1})\cap X_{2}=\mathcal{O}_{1}$. Therefore, by our analysis, this implies that $\mathcal{E}_{1}$ and $\mathcal{E}_{2}$ are open in $Z^{*}$. This completes the proof of \autoref{hausdorff}.
nodes.statement_short: Preimages of E_1 are U_1 and O_1, which are open

nodes.name: Homogeneous DSH algebras are full matrix algebras
nodes.statement: Every $n$-homogeneous DSH algebra is isomorphic to a full matrix algebra, i.e., isomorphic to $C(X,M_{n})$ for some compact metric space $X$.
assumptions: Every $n$-homogeneous DSH algebra
conclusions: is isomorphic to a full matrix algebra, i.e., isomorphic to $C(X,M_{n})$ for some compact metric space $X$
also_stated_at: such a bonding is possible only if the homogeneous algebra is in fact a full matrix algebra
nodes.label: homogeneous DSH

nodes.name: Outline of the proof of the main theorem
nodes.statement: Our general strategy for proving that a simple inductive limit of DSH algebras with diagonal maps has stable rank one is essentially the one in \cite{EHT}. We start with a given element $f$ in the limit algebra $A$, which may be assumed to lie in some finite-stage building block $A_{j}$. If $f$ is invertible, then there is nothing to prove, and so we may assume that $f$ is not invertible. The goal is then to show that the image $\psi_{j',j}(f)$ of $f$ in a later stage algebra $A_{j'}$ is close to an invertible in $A_{j'}$. If we approximate $\psi_{j',j}(f)$, multiply this approximation by unitaries, approximate again, multiply the new approximation by unitaries, and show that an element thus obtained is close to an invertible, then, upon unpacking the approximations, it follows that $\psi_{j',j}(f)$ is close to an invertible in $A_{j'}$. Finally, as R\o rdam observed in \cite{Ror}, every nilpotent element of a unital $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra is close to an invertible. Therefore, it suffices to show that an element, obtained from $\psi_{j',j}(f)$ as above, is nilpotent. To execute this strategy, we proceed as follows. In \autoref{perturb}, we first use \autoref{non-invertible at point} to show that there is a point in one of the base spaces $X_{i}$ of $A_{j}$ at which $f_{i}$ is a non-invertible matrix. After multiplying by unitary matrices on the left and right we obtain a new matrix whose first row and column contain only zeros (or one that has a \textit{zero cross at index $1$} (see \autoref{zero cross})). We show that after perturbing $f$ slightly, we may multiply this perturbation $f'$ on the left and right by unitaries $w,v\in A_{j}$, so that $wf'v$ has a zero cross at index $1$ not just at one point, but over a whole open subset of the spectrum of $A_{j}$. By \autoref{injective}, we may assume the maps in the given sequence are injective. Hence, in \autoref{far out}, we may apply our simplicity criterion (\autoref{simplicity}) with the open subset of the spectrum obtained above to conclude that in some later stage algebra $A_{j'}$, the diagonal image $\psi_{j',j}(wf'v)$ has ``many'' (see the following paragraphs) zero crosses at every point in each base space of $A_{j'}$; because of simplicity and the fact that the maps in the sequence are diagonal, this ``many'' may be taken (using \autoref{big enough lemma}) to be as large as desired. We are then able to construct unitaries $V,V'\in A_{j'}$ that organize the location of these zero crosses, so that the element $f''=V\psi_{j',j}(f')V'$ has ``many'' zero crosses occurring at tractable locations at each point in every base space of $A_{j'}$. We use \autoref{block on set} to approximate $f''$ by a function $g\in A_{j'}$ that preserves the zero crosses of $f''$ at each point, and, in addition, extends the block-diagonal structure of the algebra to neighbourhoods of the closed subsets of the base spaces (the $Y_{i}$'s in the definition of $A_{j'}$). This allows us, in \autoref{cross shift}, to conjugate $g$ by a unitary $W\in A_{j'}$, so that in the resulting conjugation $g'=WgW^{*}$, the zero crosses of $g$ are grouped together into block zero crosses at every point in each of the base spaces of $A_{j'}$. The unitaries $V,V'$, and $W$ above are constructed in such a way that at every point in each base space the \textit{bandwidth}, which measures how far a non-zero entry can occur from the diagonal in a matrix (see \autoref{bandwidth}), of $g'$ at that point is bounded above by a quantity independent of $j'$. Thus, by ensuring that the ``many'' above is at least as large as this upper bound, we are able to construct a unitary $W'$ in \autoref{lower triangular} that shifts the block zero cross mentioned above so that $g'W'$ is strictly lower triangular at each point. This ensures that $g'W'$ is nilpotent and yields the desired result. The unitaries $V,V',W$, and $W'$ above are all defined using continuous paths of unitaries between permutation matrices (see \autoref{unitaries} and \autoref{transposition prod}). In \autoref{indicatorprep}, we construct certain indicator-function-like elements of DSH algebras, the final versions of which (\autoref{indicators}) help to define $V,V',W$, and $W'$ by allowing us to implement the continuous paths of unitary matrices constructed in \cref{sc: prelim lemmas} in the DSH framework. Their job is to tell the continuous paths used in defining these unitaries which rows and columns to shift around, so as to ensure that they respect the decomposition structure of the algebra and that the zero crosses are achieved in the target locations.
nodes.section: 3.1 Outline of the Proof of the Main Theorem
nodes.statement_short: Proof sketch following Elliott-Ho-Toms: move zero crosses with unitaries until the perturbed element is strictly lower triangular, hence nilpotent and close to an invertible.

nodes.name: Comparison with the Elliott–Ho–Toms proof
nodes.statement: The proof of \autoref{main} shares many similarities with the original AH proof of Elliott, Ho, and Toms found in \cite{EHT}. In particular, in the case that all of the DSH algebras in the context of \autoref{main} are homogeneous (hence, by \autoref{homogeneous DSH}, full matrix algebras), the unitaries $V,V',W$, and $W'$ constructed above essentially reduce the those constructed in \cite{EHT}. For a more in-depth analysis of this, see \S 5.1 of \cite{alb}, where it is also observed that the AH proof does not require the full matrix algebra building blocks in the inductive limit to be separable. In our ASH setting, however, separability is necessary since the indicator-function-like elements constructed in \autoref{indicators}, which are not required in the AH case, rely on the assumption that the base spaces of any given DSH algebra are metrizable.
nodes.section: 3.1 Outline of the Proof of the Main Theorem
nodes.statement_short: In the homogeneous case the unitaries reduce to those of Elliott-Ho-Toms; separability (metrizable base spaces) is needed for the indicator elements.

nodes.name: Zero cross
nodes.statement: Given a matrix $D\in M_{n}$ and $1\leq k\leq n$, we say that $D$ has a \textit{zero cross at index $k$} provided that each entry in the $k$th row and column of $D$ is $0$.
differentia: each entry in the $k$th row and column of $D$ is $0$
nodes.label: zero cross

nodes.name: Bandwidth of a matrix
nodes.statement: Given a matrix $D\in M_{n}$, we let $$ \mathfrak{r}(D):=\min\{m\geq 0:D_{i,j}=0\text{ whenever }|i-j|\geq m\} $$ if it exists, and $\mathfrak{r}(D):= n$ otherwise, and we call this number the \textit{bandwidth} of $D$.
nodes.statement_short: r(D): least m with D_{i,j}=0 whenever |i-j|>=m (n if none).
nodes.label: bandwidth

nodes.name: Permutation unitaries and transposition paths
nodes.statement: Given $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and a permutation $\pi\in S_{n}$, let $U[\pi]$ denote the permutation unitary in $M_{n}$ obtained from the identity matrix by moving the $i$th row to the $\pi(i)$th row. If we are given a transposition $(i \ j) \in S_{n}$, let $u_{(i \ j)}\colon[0,1]\to \mathcal{U}(M_{n})$ denote a continuous path of unitaries with the following properties: \begin{enumerate} \item $u_{(i \ j)}(0)=1_{n}$; \item $u_{(i \ j)}(1)=U[(i \ j)]$; \item for all $0\leq \theta\leq 1$, $u_{(i \ j)}(\theta)$ may only differ from the identity matrix at entries $(i,i)$, $(i,j)$, $(j, i)$, and $(j,j)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: U[pi] is the permutation unitary; u_(i j) is a path of unitaries from 1 to U[(i j)] supported on rows/columns i, j.
nodes.label: unitaries

nodes.name: Conjugation by transposition paths preserves untouched zero crosses
nodes.statement: Let $n,M,l\in\mathbb{N}$ with $l+M-1\leq n$, and let $(\xi_{l},\ldots,\xi_{l+M-1})$ be a vector in $[0,1]^{M}$. Put $$ U:=\prod_{t=1}^{M-1}u_{(l \ l+t)}(\xi_{l+t})\in\mathcal{U}(M_{n}), $$ where each $u_{(l \ l+t)}\colon [0,1]\to M_{n}$ is a connecting path of unitaries as described in \autoref{unitaries}. \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)] \item Suppose $D\in M_{n}$, $\xi\in [0,1]$, and $(l_{1} \ l_{2})\in S_{n}$. If $D$ has a zero cross at index $l\not=l_{1},l_{2}$, then so does $u_{(l_{1} \ l_{2})}(\xi)Du_{(l_{1} \ l_{2})}(\xi)^{*}$. \item Suppose $D\in M_{n}$. If $D$ has a zero cross at index $l'\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus \{l,\ldots,l+M-1\}$, then so does $UDU^{*}$. \item Suppose $D\in M_{n}$ is such that for all $l\leq l'\leq l+M-1$, $D$ has a zero cross at index $l'$ whenever $\xi_{l'}>0$. If at least one of $\xi_{l},\ldots,\xi_{l+M-1}$ is $1$, then $UDU^{*}$ has a zero cross at index $l$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Proof of the untouched-crosses lemma
nodes.statement:
Let us start by proving 	extit{(a)}. Suppose $D$ has a zero cross at index $l
ot=l_{1},l_{2}$. By property (3) of \autoref{unitaries}, the $l_{1}$th and $l_{2}$th columns of $Du_{(l_{1} \ l_{2})}(\xi)^{*}$ are linear combinations of the $l_{1}$th and $l_{2}$th columns of $D$, while every other column is identical to its corresponding column in $D$. Since $l
ot=l_{1},l_{2}$ and since every entry in the $l$th row of $D$ is zero, it follows that $Du_{(l_{1} \ l_{2})}(\xi)^{*}$ has a zero cross at index $l$. A similar analysis involving rows shows that $u_{(l_{1} \ l_{2})}(\xi)Du_{(l_{1} \ l_{2})}(\xi)^{*}$ has a zero cross at index $l$, which proves 	extit{(a)}. Looking at the definition of $U$, we see that 	extit{(b)} follows from $M-1$ applications of 	extit{(a)}. Let us now prove 	extit{(c)}. Suppose that $D$ has a zero cross at index $l'$ whenever $\xi_{l'}>0$ and that at least one of $\xi_{l},\ldots,\xi_{l+M-1}$ is $1$. Let $T:=\{l+1\leq q\leq l+M-1:\xi_{q}>0\}$. If $\xi_{l+t}=0$, we have $u_{(l \ l+t)}(\xi_{l+t})=1_{n}$. Hence, $$ U:=  egin{aligned}  egin{cases} u_{(l \ l_{1})}(\xi_{l_{1}})\cdots u_{(l \ l_{r})}(\xi_{l_{r}}) & 	ext{if }T=\{l_{1}<\cdots<l_{r}\}\ \qquad\qquad\quad1_{n} & 	ext{if }T=\varnothing. \end{cases} \end{aligned} $$ If $T=\varnothing$, then, since at least one of $\xi_{l},\ldots,\xi_{l+M-1}$ is $1$, it must be that $\xi_{l}=1$. Hence, $UDU^{*}=D$ has a zero cross at index $l$ in this case by the assumption in the lemma. Thus, we may assume $T
ot=\varnothing$, so that $D$ has zero crosses at indices $l_{1},\ldots,l_{r}$. We consider two cases. Case one: $\xi_{l_{s}}<1$ for all $1\leq s\leq r$. In this case, as we argued above, it must be that $D$ has a zero cross at index $l$. When conjugating $D$ by $u_{(l \ l_{r})}(\xi_{l_{r}})$, we can see by property (3) of \autoref{unitaries} that $u_{(l \ l_{r})}(\xi_{l_{r}})$ is only acting on two zero crosses (the one at index $l$ and the one at index $l_{r}$) of $D$ and, hence, $$ u_{(l \ l_{r})}(\xi_{l_{r}})Du_{(l \ l_{r})}(\xi_{l_{r}})^{*}=D. $$ From this we can inductively see that $UDU^{*}=D$, which has a zero cross at index $l$. Case two: $\xi_{l_{s}}=1$ for some $1\leq s\leq r$. Let $$ D':=\left(\prod_{p=s+1}^{r}u_{(l \ l_{p})}(\xi_{l_{p}})ight)D\left(\prod_{p=s+1}^{r}u_{(l \ l_{p})}(\xi_{l_{p}})ight)^{*}. $$ Then $r-s$ applications of $(a)$ show that $D'$ has zero crosses at indices $l_{1},\ldots,l_{s}$. Note that $$  egin{aligned} UDU^{*} =\left(\prod_{p=1}^{s}u_{(l \ l_{p})}(\xi_{l_{p}})ight)D'\left(\prod_{p=1}^{s}u_{(l \ l_{p})}(\xi_{l_{p}})ight)^{*} =\left(\prod_{p=1}^{s-1}u_{(l \ l_{p})}(\xi_{l_{p}})ight)E\left(\prod_{p=1}^{s-1}u_{(l \ l_{p})}(\xi_{l_{p}})ight)^{*}, \end{aligned} $$ where $E:=U[(l \ l_{s})]D'U[(l \ l_{s})]^{*}$. Since $D'$ has a zero cross at index $l_{s}$, conjugating it by $U[(l \ l_{s})]$ brings this zero cross to index $l$, so that the matrix $E$ has zero crosses at indices $l,l_{1},\ldots,l_{s-1}$. Hence, as in the argument used in case one, the matrix $E$ is unaltered when conjugated by $\prod_{p=1}^{s-1}u_{(l \ l_{p})}(\xi_{l_{p}})$. Therefore, $UDU^{*}=E$, which has a zero cross at index $l$. This proves 	extit{(c)} and establishes the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: (a) by tracking which rows/columns u_(l1 l2) mixes; (b) iterates (a); (c) by two cases on whether some active parameter equals 1.

nodes.name: Part (a)
nodes.statement: Let us start by proving \textit{(a)}. Suppose $D$ has a zero cross at index $l\not=l_{1},l_{2}$. By property (3) of \autoref{unitaries}, the $l_{1}$th and $l_{2}$th columns of $Du_{(l_{1} \ l_{2})}(\xi)^{*}$ are linear combinations of the $l_{1}$th and $l_{2}$th columns of $D$, while every other column is identical to its corresponding column in $D$. Since $l\not=l_{1},l_{2}$ and since every entry in the $l$th row of $D$ is zero, it follows that $Du_{(l_{1} \ l_{2})}(\xi)^{*}$ has a zero cross at index $l$. A similar analysis involving rows shows that $u_{(l_{1} \ l_{2})}(\xi)Du_{(l_{1} \ l_{2})}(\xi)^{*}$ has a zero cross at index $l$, which proves \textit{(a)}.
nodes.statement_short: Conjugation by u_(l1 l2) only mixes rows/columns l1, l2, so the zero cross at l survives

nodes.name: Part (b)
nodes.statement: Looking at the definition of $U$, we see that \textit{(b)} follows from $M-1$ applications of \textit{(a)}.
nodes.statement_short: (b) follows from M-1 applications of (a)

nodes.name: Setup for (c)
nodes.statement: Let us now prove \textit{(c)}. Suppose that $D$ has a zero cross at index $l'$ whenever $\xi_{l'}>0$ and that at least one of $\xi_{l},\ldots,\xi_{l+M-1}$ is $1$. Let $T:=\{l+1\leq q\leq l+M-1:\xi_{q}>0\}$. If $\xi_{l+t}=0$, we have $u_{(l \ l+t)}(\xi_{l+t})=1_{n}$. Hence, $$ U:= \begin{aligned} \begin{cases} u_{(l \ l_{1})}(\xi_{l_{1}})\cdots u_{(l \ l_{r})}(\xi_{l_{r}}) & \text{if }T=\{l_{1}<\cdots<l_{r}\}\\ \qquad\qquad\quad1_{n} & \text{if }T=\varnothing. \end{cases} \end{aligned} $$ If $T=\varnothing$, then, since at least one of $\xi_{l},\ldots,\xi_{l+M-1}$ is $1$, it must be that $\xi_{l}=1$. Hence, $UDU^{*}=D$ has a zero cross at index $l$ in this case by the assumption in the lemma. Thus, we may assume $T\not=\varnothing$, so that $D$ has zero crosses at indices $l_{1},\ldots,l_{r}$. We consider two cases.
nodes.statement_short: Discard factors with xi=0; reduce to T nonempty and two cases

nodes.name: Case one
nodes.statement: Case one: $\xi_{l_{s}}<1$ for all $1\leq s\leq r$. In this case, as we argued above, it must be that $D$ has a zero cross at index $l$. When conjugating $D$ by $u_{(l \ l_{r})}(\xi_{l_{r}})$, we can see by property (3) of \autoref{unitaries} that $u_{(l \ l_{r})}(\xi_{l_{r}})$ is only acting on two zero crosses (the one at index $l$ and the one at index $l_{r}$) of $D$ and, hence, $$ u_{(l \ l_{r})}(\xi_{l_{r}})Du_{(l \ l_{r})}(\xi_{l_{r}})^{*}=D. $$ From this we can inductively see that $UDU^{*}=D$, which has a zero cross at index $l$.
nodes.statement_short: All active parameters below 1: each factor acts on two zero crosses, so U D U* = D

nodes.name: Case two
nodes.statement: Case two: $\xi_{l_{s}}=1$ for some $1\leq s\leq r$. Let $$ D':=\left(\prod_{p=s+1}^{r}u_{(l \ l_{p})}(\xi_{l_{p}})\right)D\left(\prod_{p=s+1}^{r}u_{(l \ l_{p})}(\xi_{l_{p}})\right)^{*}. $$ Then $r-s$ applications of $(a)$ show that $D'$ has zero crosses at indices $l_{1},\ldots,l_{s}$. Note that $$ \begin{aligned} UDU^{*} =\left(\prod_{p=1}^{s}u_{(l \ l_{p})}(\xi_{l_{p}})\right)D'\left(\prod_{p=1}^{s}u_{(l \ l_{p})}(\xi_{l_{p}})\right)^{*} =\left(\prod_{p=1}^{s-1}u_{(l \ l_{p})}(\xi_{l_{p}})\right)E\left(\prod_{p=1}^{s-1}u_{(l \ l_{p})}(\xi_{l_{p}})\right)^{*}, \end{aligned} $$ where $E:=U[(l \ l_{s})]D'U[(l \ l_{s})]^{*}$. Since $D'$ has a zero cross at index $l_{s}$, conjugating it by $U[(l \ l_{s})]$ brings this zero cross to index $l$, so that the matrix $E$ has zero crosses at indices $l,l_{1},\ldots,l_{s-1}$. Hence, as in the argument used in case one, the matrix $E$ is unaltered when conjugated by $\prod_{p=1}^{s-1}u_{(l \ l_{p})}(\xi_{l_{p}})$. Therefore, $UDU^{*}=E$, which has a zero cross at index $l$. This proves \textit{(c)} and establishes the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Some parameter equals 1: the full transposition brings a zero cross to index l, untouched afterwards

nodes.name: Matrix conjugator paths delta and w
nodes.statement: Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$. For $1\leq i\leq j\leq n$, let $\delta_{j}^{i}\colon[0,1]\to[0,1]$ be given by the following definition: $$ \begin{aligned} \delta_{j}^{i}(\xi):= \begin{cases} 0&\text{ if }0\leq\xi\leq\frac{i-1}{j}\\ \text{linear}&\text{ if }\frac{i-1}{j}\leq\xi\leq\frac{i}{j}\\ 1&\text{ if }\frac{i}{j}\leq\xi\leq 1. \end{cases} \end{aligned} $$ Moreover, for $1\leq i<j\leq n$, let $w_{j}^{i}\in C([0,1],M_{n})$ be the unitary defined by $$ w_{j}^{i}(\xi):=u_{(i \ i+1)}(\delta_{j-i}^{j-i}(\xi)) u_{(i+1 \ i+2)}(\delta_{j-i}^{j-i-1}(\xi))\cdots u_{(j-1 \ j)}(\delta_{j-i}^{1}(\xi)), $$ where the unitaries $u_{(k \ k+1)}\colon [0,1]\to M_{n}$ are those of \autoref{unitaries}, and set $w_{i}^{i}\equiv 1_{n}$. In particular, \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} w_{j}^{i}(1)=u_{(i \ i+1)}(1)\cdots u_{(j-1 \ j)}(1)=U[(i \ \ i+1 \ \cdots \ j)]. \end{aligned} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Piecewise-linear switches delta_j^i and unitary paths w_j^i that successively apply adjacent transpositions, ending at the cycle (i i+1 ... j).
nodes.label: matrix conjugator

nodes.name: Endpoint of w_j^i is a cycle permutation unitary
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} w_{j}^{i}(1)=u_{(i \ i+1)}(1)\cdots u_{(j-1 \ j)}(1)=U[(i \ \ i+1 \ \cdots \ j)]. \end{aligned}
nodes.label: permutation

nodes.name: Bandwidth bound for cycle conjugation
nodes.statement: Suppose $D\in M_{n}$ has a zero cross at index $j$. Then, $\mathfrak{r}(w_{j}^{1}(1)Dw_{j}^{1}(1)^{*})\leq \mathfrak{r}(D)$ and, for $2\leq i\leq j$, $\mathfrak{r}(w_{j}^{i}(1)Dw_{j}^{i}(1)^{*})\leq\mathfrak{r}(D)+1$.
assumptions: $D\in M_{n}$ has a zero cross at index $j$
conclusions: $\mathfrak{r}(w_{j}^{1}(1)Dw_{j}^{1}(1)^{*})\leq \mathfrak{r}(D)$
for $2\leq i\leq j$, $\mathfrak{r}(w_{j}^{i}(1)Dw_{j}^{i}(1)^{*})\leq\mathfrak{r}(D)+1$
nodes.label: matrix1

nodes.name: Proof of the cycle-conjugation bandwidth bound
nodes.statement: By \autoref{permutation}, $w_{j}^{1}(1)=U[(1 \ 2 \ \cdots \ j)]$. Consider the matrix $D$ broken up into the four regions created by the zero cross at $j$, together with the matrix $w_{j}^{1}(1)Dw_{j}^{1}(1)^{*}$: \begin{figure}[H] \begin{minipage}{0.5\textwidth} \centering \includegraphics[scale=1]{matrix1.pdf} \caption{The Matrix $D$} \end{minipage}\hfill \begin{minipage}{.5\textwidth} \centering \includegraphics[scale=1]{matrix1T.pdf} \caption{The Matrix $w_{j}^{1}(1)Dw_{j}^{1}(1)^{*}$} \end{minipage} \end{figure} \noindent Since no non-zero entry gets shifted away from the diagonal, $\mathfrak{r}(w_{j}^{1}(1)Dw_{j}^{1}(1)^{*})\leq\mathfrak{r}(D)$. Suppose now that $2\leq i\leq j$. If $i=j$, then the desired inequality is trivial, so we may assume that $i<j$. By \autoref{permutation}, $w_{j}^{i}(1)=U[(i \ i+1 \ \cdots \ j)]$. Consider the matrix $D$ broken up into the following nine regions created by the zero cross at $j$ and the $i$th row and column, together with the matrix $w_{j}^{i}(1)Dw_{j}^{i}(1)^{*}$: \begin{figure}[H] \begin{minipage}{0.5\textwidth} \centering \includegraphics[scale=1]{matrix2.pdf} \caption{The Matrix $D$} \end{minipage}\hfill \begin{minipage}{.5\textwidth} \centering \includegraphics[scale=1]{matrix2T.pdf} \caption{The Matrix $w_{j}^{i}(1)Dw_{j}^{i}(1)^{*}$} \end{minipage} \end{figure} \noindent With the exception of $D_{2}$ and $D_{4}$, which get shifted one unit away from the diagonal, no entry in the other seven regions is moved away from the diagonal. Therefore, $\mathfrak{r}(w_{j}^{i}(1)Dw_{j}^{i}(1)^{*})\leq \mathfrak{r}(D)+1$, which proves \autoref{matrix1}.
nodes.statement_short: Partition D by the zero cross (and row/column i) into regions and track how the cyclic permutation moves each region relative to the diagonal.

nodes.name: Case i = 1
nodes.statement: By \autoref{permutation}, $w_{j}^{1}(1)=U[(1 \ 2 \ \cdots \ j)]$. Consider the matrix $D$ broken up into the four regions created by the zero cross at $j$, together with the matrix $w_{j}^{1}(1)Dw_{j}^{1}(1)^{*}$: \begin{figure}[H] \begin{minipage}{0.5\textwidth} \centering \includegraphics[scale=1]{matrix1.pdf} \caption{The Matrix $D$} \end{minipage}\hfill \begin{minipage}{.5\textwidth} \centering \includegraphics[scale=1]{matrix1T.pdf} \caption{The Matrix $w_{j}^{1}(1)Dw_{j}^{1}(1)^{*}$} \end{minipage} \end{figure} \noindent Since no non-zero entry gets shifted away from the diagonal, $\mathfrak{r}(w_{j}^{1}(1)Dw_{j}^{1}(1)^{*})\leq\mathfrak{r}(D)$.
nodes.statement_short: The cycle moves no nonzero entry away from the diagonal

nodes.name: Case i >= 2
nodes.statement: Suppose now that $2\leq i\leq j$. If $i=j$, then the desired inequality is trivial, so we may assume that $i<j$. By \autoref{permutation}, $w_{j}^{i}(1)=U[(i \ i+1 \ \cdots \ j)]$. Consider the matrix $D$ broken up into the following nine regions created by the zero cross at $j$ and the $i$th row and column, together with the matrix $w_{j}^{i}(1)Dw_{j}^{i}(1)^{*}$: \begin{figure}[H] \begin{minipage}{0.5\textwidth} \centering \includegraphics[scale=1]{matrix2.pdf} \caption{The Matrix $D$} \end{minipage}\hfill \begin{minipage}{.5\textwidth} \centering \includegraphics[scale=1]{matrix2T.pdf} \caption{The Matrix $w_{j}^{i}(1)Dw_{j}^{i}(1)^{*}$} \end{minipage} \end{figure} \noindent With the exception of $D_{2}$ and $D_{4}$, which get shifted one unit away from the diagonal, no entry in the other seven regions is moved away from the diagonal. Therefore, $\mathfrak{r}(w_{j}^{i}(1)Dw_{j}^{i}(1)^{*})\leq \mathfrak{r}(D)+1$, which proves \autoref{matrix1}.
nodes.statement_short: Only two regions shift one unit away from the diagonal

nodes.name: Bandwidth bound along the conjugator path
nodes.statement: Suppose $D\in M_{n}$ has a zero cross at index $j$. If $1\leq i\leq j$ and $\xi\in [0,1]$, then $\mathfrak{r}(w_{j}^{i}(\xi)D w_{j}^{i}(\xi)^{*})\leq \mathfrak{r}(D)+2$.
assumptions: $D\in M_{n}$ has a zero cross at index $j$
$1\leq i\leq j$ and $\xi\in [0,1]$
conclusions: $\mathfrak{r}(w_{j}^{i}(\xi)D w_{j}^{i}(\xi)^{*})\leq \mathfrak{r}(D)+2$
nodes.label: matrix2

nodes.name: Proof of the path bandwidth bound
nodes.statement:
Fix $1\leq i\leq j$ and $\xi\in[0,1]$. If $\xi=0$ or if $i=j$, then $w_{j}^{i}(\xi)=1_{n}$ and the result is trivial. Hence, we may assume $i<j$ and $\xi\in(0,1]$. Let $1\leq k\leq j-i$ be the unique integer such that $\xi\in\left( rac{k-1}{j-i}, rac{k}{j-i}ight]$. Then,  egin{equation}  egin{aligned} &w_{j}^{i}(\xi)\ =&u_{(i \ i+1)}(0)\cdots u_{(j-k-1\ j-k)}(0)u_{(j-k \ j-k+1)}(\delta_{j-i}^{k}(\xi))u_{(j-k+1 \ j-k+2)}(1)\cdots u_{(j-1 \ j)}(1)\ =&u_{(j-k \ j-k+1)}(\delta_{j-i}^{k}(\xi))w^{j-k+1}_{j}(1). \end{aligned} \end{equation} Let $D':=w^{j-k+1}_{j}(1) D w^{j-k+1}_{j}(1)^{*}$. By \autoref{matrix1}, $\mathfrak{r}(D')\leq \mathfrak{r}(D)+1$. Now, consider the conjugation of $D'$ by $u_{(j-k \ j-k+1)}(\delta_{j-i}^{k}(\xi))$, which we denote by $E$. The entries of $D'$ affected by this conjugation lie in one of the following three regions:  egin{figure}[H]  egin{minipage}{0.333	extwidth} \includegraphics[scale=.81]{regionA1.pdf} \caption{Region A} \end{minipage}\hfill  egin{minipage}{0.333	extwidth} \includegraphics[scale=.81]{regionB1.pdf} \caption{Region B} \end{minipage}\hfill  egin{minipage}{0.333	extwidth} \includegraphics[scale=.81]{regionC1.pdf} \caption{Region C} \end{minipage} \end{figure} We make the following observations:  egin{itemize} \item An entry in $E$ lying in 
ameref{regionA1} will be a linear combination of the two corresponding shaded entries in $D'$ lying in the same row; \item An entry in $E$ lying in 
ameref{regionB1} will be a linear combination of the two corresponding shaded entries in $D'$ lying in the same column; \item An entry in $E$ lying in 
ameref{regionC1} will be a linear combination of the four shaded entries in $D'$ lying in 
ameref{regionC1}. \end{itemize} We see that in all instances, a non-zero entry in $E$ never appears more than one unit further away from the diagonal than a non-zero entry in $D'$. Thus, $$ \mathfrak{r}(u_{(j-k \ j-k+1)}(\delta_{j-i}^{k}(\xi))D'u_{(j-k \ j-k+1)}(\delta_{j-i}^{k}(\xi))^{*})\leq \mathfrak{r}(D')+1\leq\mathfrak{r}(D)+2, $$ which proves \autoref{matrix2}.
nodes.statement_short: Factor w_j^i(xi) as one partial transposition times a completed cycle; apply the previous lemma, then show the partial transposition adds at most one.

nodes.name: Trivial cases
nodes.statement: Fix $1\leq i\leq j$ and $\xi\in[0,1]$. If $\xi=0$ or if $i=j$, then $w_{j}^{i}(\xi)=1_{n}$ and the result is trivial. Hence, we may assume $i<j$ and $\xi\in(0,1]$.
nodes.statement_short: Dispose of xi=0 or i=j

nodes.name: Factor the path
nodes.statement: Let $1\leq k\leq j-i$ be the unique integer such that $\xi\in\left(\frac{k-1}{j-i},\frac{k}{j-i}\right]$. Then, \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} &w_{j}^{i}(\xi)\\ =&u_{(i \ i+1)}(0)\cdots u_{(j-k-1\ j-k)}(0)u_{(j-k \ j-k+1)}(\delta_{j-i}^{k}(\xi))u_{(j-k+1 \ j-k+2)}(1)\cdots u_{(j-1 \ j)}(1)\\ =&u_{(j-k \ j-k+1)}(\delta_{j-i}^{k}(\xi))w^{j-k+1}_{j}(1). \end{aligned} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Write w_j^i(xi) as one partial transposition times a completed cycle

nodes.name: Apply the cycle bound
nodes.statement: Let $D':=w^{j-k+1}_{j}(1) D w^{j-k+1}_{j}(1)^{*}$. By \autoref{matrix1}, $\mathfrak{r}(D')\leq \mathfrak{r}(D)+1$.
nodes.statement_short: The completed cycle raises bandwidth by at most 1

nodes.name: Regions affected
nodes.statement: Now, consider the conjugation of $D'$ by $u_{(j-k \ j-k+1)}(\delta_{j-i}^{k}(\xi))$, which we denote by $E$. The entries of $D'$ affected by this conjugation lie in one of the following three regions: \begin{figure}[H] \begin{minipage}{0.333\textwidth} \includegraphics[scale=.81]{regionA1.pdf} \caption{Region A} \end{minipage}\hfill \begin{minipage}{0.333\textwidth} \includegraphics[scale=.81]{regionB1.pdf} \caption{Region B} \end{minipage}\hfill \begin{minipage}{0.333\textwidth} \includegraphics[scale=.81]{regionC1.pdf} \caption{Region C} \end{minipage} \end{figure} We make the following observations:
nodes.statement_short: Entries changed by the partial transposition lie in three regions

nodes.name: Region A
nodes.statement: An entry in $E$ lying in \nameref{regionA1} will be a linear combination of the two corresponding shaded entries in $D'$ lying in the same row;
nodes.statement_short: Row combinations of two entries

nodes.name: Region B
nodes.statement: An entry in $E$ lying in \nameref{regionB1} will be a linear combination of the two corresponding shaded entries in $D'$ lying in the same column;
nodes.statement_short: Column combinations of two entries

nodes.name: Region C
nodes.statement: An entry in $E$ lying in \nameref{regionC1} will be a linear combination of the four shaded entries in $D'$ lying in \nameref{regionC1}.
nodes.statement_short: Combinations of four entries

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: We see that in all instances, a non-zero entry in $E$ never appears more than one unit further away from the diagonal than a non-zero entry in $D'$. Thus, $$ \mathfrak{r}(u_{(j-k \ j-k+1)}(\delta_{j-i}^{k}(\xi))D'u_{(j-k \ j-k+1)}(\delta_{j-i}^{k}(\xi))^{*})\leq \mathfrak{r}(D')+1\leq\mathfrak{r}(D)+2, $$ which proves \autoref{matrix2}.
nodes.statement_short: Each region moves at most one unit, giving r(D)+2

nodes.name: Unitary path moving zero crosses to the front
nodes.statement: Suppose $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $1\leq z_{1}<z_{2}<\cdots<z_{m}\leq n$. There is a unitary $W\in C([0,1],M_{n})$ with the following properties: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)] \item $W(0)=1_{n}$; \item if $T\in M_{n}$ has zero crosses at indices $z_{1},\ldots,z_{m}$, then $W(1)TW(1)^{*}$ has zero crosses at indices $1,2,\ldots,m$ and $\mathfrak{r}(W(\xi)TW(\xi)^{*})\leq\mathfrak{r}(T)+2$ for all $\xi\in[0,1]$; \item if $b\in\mathbb{N}$, $T\in M_{n\times b}$, and the rows of $T$ at indices $z_{1},\ldots,z_{m}$ consist entirely of zeros, then the first $m$ rows of $W(1)T$ consist entirely of zeros and for all $\xi\in[0,1]$, $$ \mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{n\times n} & W(\xi)T\\ 0_{b\times n} & 0_{b\times b} \end{pmatrix} \right)\leq\mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{n\times n} & T\\ 0_{b\times n} & 0_{b\times b} \end{pmatrix} \right); $$ \item if $b\in\mathbb{N}$, $T\in M_{b\times n}$, and the columns of $T$ at indices $z_{1},\ldots,z_{m}$ consist entirely of zeros, then the first $m$ columns of $TW(1)^{*}$ consist entirely of zeros and for all $\xi\in[0,1]$, $$ \mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{n\times n} & 0_{n\times b}\\ TW(\xi)^{*} & 0_{b\times b} \end{pmatrix} \right)\leq\mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{n\times n} & 0_{n\times b}\\ T & 0_{b\times b} \end{pmatrix} \right). $$ \end{enumerate}
assumptions: $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $1\leq z_{1}<z_{2}<\cdots<z_{m}\leq n$
conclusions: There is a unitary $W\in C([0,1],M_{n})$ with the following properties
nodes.statement_short: A unitary path W from 1 that moves zero crosses at z_1<...<z_m to indices 1..m, increasing bandwidth by at most 2 along the way.
nodes.label: matrix

nodes.name: Proof of the zero-cross moving lemma
nodes.statement: For $1\leq i\leq j\leq n$, let $\delta_{j}^{i}$ and $w_{j}^{i}\in C([0,1],M_{n})$ be given as in \autoref{matrix conjugator}. Define $$ W:=(w_{z_{m}}^{1}\circ\delta_{m}^{m}) \cdots(w_{z_{1}}^{1}\circ\delta_{m}^{1}), $$ which is a unitary in $C([0,1],M_{n})$. By \autoref{unitaries} and \autoref{matrix conjugator}, $W(0)=w_{z_{m}}^{1}(0)\cdots w_{z_{1}}^{1}(0)=1_{n}$, so that \textit{(a)} holds. Since \textit{(d)} follows immediately from \textit{(c)} by taking adjoints, only \textit{(b)} and \textit{(c)} remain to be verified. Let $\sigma$ denote the permutation $$ (1 \ 2 \ \cdots \ z_{m})(1 \ 2 \ \cdots \ z_{m-1})\cdots(1 \ 2 \ \cdots \ z_{1})\in S_{n} $$ and note that $\sigma(z_{k})=m-k+1$ for $1\leq k\leq m$. Hence, if $T$ is any matrix in $M_{n}$ (resp. $M_{n\times b}$) with zero crosses (resp. rows) at indices $z_{1},\ldots,z_{m}$, then $U[\sigma]TU[\sigma]^{*}$ (resp. $U[\sigma]T$) has zero crosses (resp. rows) at indices $1,\ldots,m$. Since $W(1)=U[\sigma]$ by \autoref{permutation}, this proves the first half of \textit{(b)} and \textit{(c)}. Let us now establish the bandwidth approximations in \textit{(b)} and \textit{(c)}. Fix $\xi\in[0,1]$. If $\xi=0$, the results are trivial, and so we may assume $\xi\in(0,1]$. Let $1\leq k\leq m$ be the unique integer such that $\xi\in\left(\frac{k-1}{m},\frac{k}{m}\right]$. Then we may write $$ \begin{aligned} W(\xi)&=w_{z_{m}}^{1}(0)\cdots w_{z_{k+1}}^{1}(0) w_{z_{k}}^{1}(\delta_{m}^{k}(\xi)) w_{z_{k-1}}^{1}(1)\cdots w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)\\ &=w_{z_{k}}^{1}(\delta_{m}^{k}(\xi)) w_{z_{k-1}}^{1}(1)\cdots w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1). \end{aligned} $$ Suppose first that $T\in M_{n}$ has zero crosses at indices $z_{1},\ldots,z_{m}$. Then by \autoref{matrix1}, $\mathfrak{r}(w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)Tw_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)^{*})\leq \mathfrak{r}(T)$ since $T$ has a zero cross at index $z_{1}$. Moreover, $z_{1}-1$ applications of part \textit{(a)} of \autoref{untouched crosses} shows that $w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)Tw_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)^{*}$ has a zero cross at indices $z_{2},\ldots,z_{m}$, since $z_{2},\ldots,z_{m}$ are not among the indices affected by the conjugation. Hence, we may apply \autoref{matrix1} again to conclude that $$ \mathfrak{r}(w_{z_{2}}^{1}(1)w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)Tw_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)^{*}w_{z_{2}}^{1}(1)^{*})\leq\mathfrak{r}(w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)Tw_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)^{*})\leq \mathfrak{r}(T). $$ Continuing inductively in this way, it follows that $\mathfrak{r}(D)\leq\mathfrak{r}(T)$, where $$ D=w_{z_{k-1}}^{1}(1)\cdots w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)Tw_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)^{*}\cdots w_{z_{k-1}}^{1}(1)^{*} $$ and, moreover, $D$ has a zero cross at indices $z_{k},\ldots,z_{m}$. Thus, by \autoref{matrix2}, $$ \mathfrak{r}(W(\xi)TW(\xi)^{*})=\mathfrak{r}(w_{z_{k}}^{1}(\delta_{m}^{k}(\xi))Dw_{z_{k}}^{1}(\delta_{m}^{k}(\xi))^{*})\leq\mathfrak{r}(D)+2\leq \mathfrak{r}(T)+2, $$ which yields the approximation in \textit{(b)}. To complete the proof of \textit{(c)} suppose $T\in M_{n\times b}$ and that the rows of $T$ at indices $z_{1},\ldots,z_{m}$ consist entirely of zeros. Following the lines of the proof of \autoref{matrix1}, we have $$ \mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{n\times n} & w_{z_{k-1}}^{1}(1)\cdots w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)T\\ 0_{b\times n} & 0_{b\times b} \end{pmatrix} \right)\leq\mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{n\times n} & T\\ 0_{b\times n} & 0_{b\times b} \end{pmatrix}\right) $$ by \autoref{permutation} since only rows of zeros are shifted up when multiplying $T$ on the left by $w_{z_{k-1}}^{1}(1)\cdots w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)$, while non-zero entries remain in place or are shifted down towards the diagonal. Similar reasoning to that used when deducing \autoref{wij} shows that there exist $\beta\in[0,1]$ and $1\leq p\leq z_{k}-1$ such that $$ w_{z_{k}}^{1}(\delta_{m}^{k}(\xi))=u_{(z_{k} - p \ z_{k}-p+1)}(\beta) w_{z_{k}}^{z_{k}-p+1}(1). $$ Since the $z_{k}$th row of a given matrix remains unchanged when multiplying on the left by $w_{z_{k-1}}^{1}(1)\cdots w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)$, the $z_{k}$th row of $w_{z_{k-1}}^{1}(1)\cdots w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)T$ contains only zeros. Hence, multiplying this given matrix on the left by $w_{z_{k}}^{z_{k}-p+1}(1)=U[(z_{k}-p+1 \ \cdots \ z_{k})]$ shifts the zero row from index $z_{k}$ to index $z_{k}-p+1$, while shifting the rows $z_{k}-p+1,\ldots,z_{k}-1$ down by one towards the diagonal. Thus, $$ \mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{n\times n} & E\\ 0_{b\times n} & 0_{b\times b} \end{pmatrix} \right)\leq \mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{n\times n} & w_{z_{k-1}}^{1}(1)\cdots w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)T\\ 0_{b\times n} & 0_{b\times b} \end{pmatrix} \right)\leq\mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{n\times n} & T\\ 0_{b\times n} & 0_{b\times b} \end{pmatrix}\right), $$ where $E:=U[(z_{k}-p+1 \ \cdots \ z_{k})]w_{z_{k-1}}^{1}(1)\cdots w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)T$. Now, $E$ and $u_{(z_{k}-p \ z_{k}-p+1)}(\beta)E$ may differ only on rows $z_{k}-p$ and $z_{k}-p+1$, where these two rows of the latter matrix are linear combinations of the same two rows of $E$. From this and the fact that the $z_{k}-p+1$ row of $E$ consists only of zeros, it is clear that for a given column $\lambda$, the $(z_{k}-p,\lambda)$- or $(z_{k}-p+1,\lambda)$-entry of $u_{(z_{k}-p \ z_{k}-p+1)}(\beta)E$ can be non-zero only if the $(z_{k}-p,\lambda)$ entry of $E$ is non-zero. Hence, $$ \mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{n\times n} & u_{(z_{k}-p \ z_{k}-p+1)}(\beta)E\\ 0_{b\times n} & 0_{b\times b} \end{pmatrix} \right)\leq \mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{n\times n} & E\\ 0_{b\times n} & 0_{b\times b} \end{pmatrix} \right)\leq \mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{n\times n} & T\\ 0_{b\times n} & 0_{b\times b} \end{pmatrix}\right). $$ Since $W(\xi)T=u_{(z_{k}-p \ z_{k}-p+1)}(\beta)E$, this establishes the bandwidth approximation in \textit{(c)}, thus completing the proof of the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Define W as a concatenation of the paths w_{z_k}^1; endpoints give the permutation, and bandwidth bounds follow inductively from the two previous lemmas.

nodes.name: Define W
nodes.statement: For $1\leq i\leq j\leq n$, let $\delta_{j}^{i}$ and $w_{j}^{i}\in C([0,1],M_{n})$ be given as in \autoref{matrix conjugator}. Define $$ W:=(w_{z_{m}}^{1}\circ\delta_{m}^{m}) \cdots(w_{z_{1}}^{1}\circ\delta_{m}^{1}), $$ which is a unitary in $C([0,1],M_{n})$.
nodes.statement_short: W is the concatenation of the paths w_{z_k}^1 reparametrized by delta

nodes.name: W(0)=1 and reduction
nodes.statement: By \autoref{unitaries} and \autoref{matrix conjugator}, $W(0)=w_{z_{m}}^{1}(0)\cdots w_{z_{1}}^{1}(0)=1_{n}$, so that \textit{(a)} holds. Since \textit{(d)} follows immediately from \textit{(c)} by taking adjoints, only \textit{(b)} and \textit{(c)} remain to be verified.
nodes.statement_short: (a) holds; (d) follows from (c) by adjoints

nodes.name: Endpoint permutation
nodes.statement: Let $\sigma$ denote the permutation $$ (1 \ 2 \ \cdots \ z_{m})(1 \ 2 \ \cdots \ z_{m-1})\cdots(1 \ 2 \ \cdots \ z_{1})\in S_{n} $$ and note that $\sigma(z_{k})=m-k+1$ for $1\leq k\leq m$. Hence, if $T$ is any matrix in $M_{n}$ (resp. $M_{n\times b}$) with zero crosses (resp. rows) at indices $z_{1},\ldots,z_{m}$, then $U[\sigma]TU[\sigma]^{*}$ (resp. $U[\sigma]T$) has zero crosses (resp. rows) at indices $1,\ldots,m$. Since $W(1)=U[\sigma]$ by \autoref{permutation}, this proves the first half of \textit{(b)} and \textit{(c)}.
nodes.statement_short: W(1)=U[sigma] moves the zero crosses at z_k to 1..m

nodes.name: Bandwidth bound in (b)
nodes.statement: Let us now establish the bandwidth approximations in \textit{(b)} and \textit{(c)}. Fix $\xi\in[0,1]$. If $\xi=0$, the results are trivial, and so we may assume $\xi\in(0,1]$. Let $1\leq k\leq m$ be the unique integer such that $\xi\in\left(\frac{k-1}{m},\frac{k}{m}\right]$. Then we may write $$ \begin{aligned} W(\xi)&=w_{z_{m}}^{1}(0)\cdots w_{z_{k+1}}^{1}(0) w_{z_{k}}^{1}(\delta_{m}^{k}(\xi)) w_{z_{k-1}}^{1}(1)\cdots w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)\\ &=w_{z_{k}}^{1}(\delta_{m}^{k}(\xi)) w_{z_{k-1}}^{1}(1)\cdots w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1). \end{aligned} $$ Suppose first that $T\in M_{n}$ has zero crosses at indices $z_{1},\ldots,z_{m}$. Then by \autoref{matrix1}, $\mathfrak{r}(w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)Tw_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)^{*})\leq \mathfrak{r}(T)$ since $T$ has a zero cross at index $z_{1}$. Moreover, $z_{1}-1$ applications of part \textit{(a)} of \autoref{untouched crosses} shows that $w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)Tw_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)^{*}$ has a zero cross at indices $z_{2},\ldots,z_{m}$, since $z_{2},\ldots,z_{m}$ are not among the indices affected by the conjugation. Hence, we may apply \autoref{matrix1} again to conclude that $$ \mathfrak{r}(w_{z_{2}}^{1}(1)w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)Tw_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)^{*}w_{z_{2}}^{1}(1)^{*})\leq\mathfrak{r}(w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)Tw_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)^{*})\leq \mathfrak{r}(T). $$ Continuing inductively in this way, it follows that $\mathfrak{r}(D)\leq\mathfrak{r}(T)$, where $$ D=w_{z_{k-1}}^{1}(1)\cdots w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)Tw_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)^{*}\cdots w_{z_{k-1}}^{1}(1)^{*} $$ and, moreover, $D$ has a zero cross at indices $z_{k},\ldots,z_{m}$. Thus, by \autoref{matrix2}, $$ \mathfrak{r}(W(\xi)TW(\xi)^{*})=\mathfrak{r}(w_{z_{k}}^{1}(\delta_{m}^{k}(\xi))Dw_{z_{k}}^{1}(\delta_{m}^{k}(\xi))^{*})\leq\mathfrak{r}(D)+2\leq \mathfrak{r}(T)+2, $$ which yields the approximation in \textit{(b)}.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the bandwidth along the path for square T

nodes.name: Locate xi
nodes.statement: Let us now establish the bandwidth approximations in \textit{(b)} and \textit{(c)}. Fix $\xi\in[0,1]$. If $\xi=0$, the results are trivial, and so we may assume $\xi\in(0,1]$. Let $1\leq k\leq m$ be the unique integer such that $\xi\in\left(\frac{k-1}{m},\frac{k}{m}\right]$. Then we may write $$ \begin{aligned} W(\xi)&=w_{z_{m}}^{1}(0)\cdots w_{z_{k+1}}^{1}(0) w_{z_{k}}^{1}(\delta_{m}^{k}(\xi)) w_{z_{k-1}}^{1}(1)\cdots w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)\\ &=w_{z_{k}}^{1}(\delta_{m}^{k}(\xi)) w_{z_{k-1}}^{1}(1)\cdots w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1). \end{aligned} $$
nodes.statement_short: Write W(xi) as one partial path times completed paths

nodes.name: Completed paths
nodes.statement: Suppose first that $T\in M_{n}$ has zero crosses at indices $z_{1},\ldots,z_{m}$. Then by \autoref{matrix1}, $\mathfrak{r}(w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)Tw_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)^{*})\leq \mathfrak{r}(T)$ since $T$ has a zero cross at index $z_{1}$. Moreover, $z_{1}-1$ applications of part \textit{(a)} of \autoref{untouched crosses} shows that $w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)Tw_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)^{*}$ has a zero cross at indices $z_{2},\ldots,z_{m}$, since $z_{2},\ldots,z_{m}$ are not among the indices affected by the conjugation. Hence, we may apply \autoref{matrix1} again to conclude that $$ \mathfrak{r}(w_{z_{2}}^{1}(1)w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)Tw_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)^{*}w_{z_{2}}^{1}(1)^{*})\leq\mathfrak{r}(w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)Tw_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)^{*})\leq \mathfrak{r}(T). $$
nodes.statement_short: Completed cycles do not increase bandwidth and keep later zero crosses

nodes.name: Partial path
nodes.statement: Continuing inductively in this way, it follows that $\mathfrak{r}(D)\leq\mathfrak{r}(T)$, where $$ D=w_{z_{k-1}}^{1}(1)\cdots w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)Tw_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)^{*}\cdots w_{z_{k-1}}^{1}(1)^{*} $$ and, moreover, $D$ has a zero cross at indices $z_{k},\ldots,z_{m}$. Thus, by \autoref{matrix2}, $$ \mathfrak{r}(W(\xi)TW(\xi)^{*})=\mathfrak{r}(w_{z_{k}}^{1}(\delta_{m}^{k}(\xi))Dw_{z_{k}}^{1}(\delta_{m}^{k}(\xi))^{*})\leq\mathfrak{r}(D)+2\leq \mathfrak{r}(T)+2, $$ which yields the approximation in \textit{(b)}.
nodes.statement_short: The partial path adds at most 2 by the path bandwidth lemma

nodes.name: Bandwidth bound in (c)
nodes.statement: To complete the proof of \textit{(c)} suppose $T\in M_{n\times b}$ and that the rows of $T$ at indices $z_{1},\ldots,z_{m}$ consist entirely of zeros. Following the lines of the proof of \autoref{matrix1}, we have $$ \mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{n\times n} & w_{z_{k-1}}^{1}(1)\cdots w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)T\\ 0_{b\times n} & 0_{b\times b} \end{pmatrix} \right)\leq\mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{n\times n} & T\\ 0_{b\times n} & 0_{b\times b} \end{pmatrix}\right) $$ by \autoref{permutation} since only rows of zeros are shifted up when multiplying $T$ on the left by $w_{z_{k-1}}^{1}(1)\cdots w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)$, while non-zero entries remain in place or are shifted down towards the diagonal. Similar reasoning to that used when deducing \autoref{wij} shows that there exist $\beta\in[0,1]$ and $1\leq p\leq z_{k}-1$ such that $$ w_{z_{k}}^{1}(\delta_{m}^{k}(\xi))=u_{(z_{k} - p \ z_{k}-p+1)}(\beta) w_{z_{k}}^{z_{k}-p+1}(1). $$ Since the $z_{k}$th row of a given matrix remains unchanged when multiplying on the left by $w_{z_{k-1}}^{1}(1)\cdots w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)$, the $z_{k}$th row of $w_{z_{k-1}}^{1}(1)\cdots w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)T$ contains only zeros. Hence, multiplying this given matrix on the left by $w_{z_{k}}^{z_{k}-p+1}(1)=U[(z_{k}-p+1 \ \cdots \ z_{k})]$ shifts the zero row from index $z_{k}$ to index $z_{k}-p+1$, while shifting the rows $z_{k}-p+1,\ldots,z_{k}-1$ down by one towards the diagonal. Thus, $$ \mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{n\times n} & E\\ 0_{b\times n} & 0_{b\times b} \end{pmatrix} \right)\leq \mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{n\times n} & w_{z_{k-1}}^{1}(1)\cdots w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)T\\ 0_{b\times n} & 0_{b\times b} \end{pmatrix} \right)\leq\mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{n\times n} & T\\ 0_{b\times n} & 0_{b\times b} \end{pmatrix}\right), $$ where $E:=U[(z_{k}-p+1 \ \cdots \ z_{k})]w_{z_{k-1}}^{1}(1)\cdots w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)T$. Now, $E$ and $u_{(z_{k}-p \ z_{k}-p+1)}(\beta)E$ may differ only on rows $z_{k}-p$ and $z_{k}-p+1$, where these two rows of the latter matrix are linear combinations of the same two rows of $E$. From this and the fact that the $z_{k}-p+1$ row of $E$ consists only of zeros, it is clear that for a given column $\lambda$, the $(z_{k}-p,\lambda)$- or $(z_{k}-p+1,\lambda)$-entry of $u_{(z_{k}-p \ z_{k}-p+1)}(\beta)E$ can be non-zero only if the $(z_{k}-p,\lambda)$ entry of $E$ is non-zero. Hence, $$ \mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{n\times n} & u_{(z_{k}-p \ z_{k}-p+1)}(\beta)E\\ 0_{b\times n} & 0_{b\times b} \end{pmatrix} \right)\leq \mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{n\times n} & E\\ 0_{b\times n} & 0_{b\times b} \end{pmatrix} \right)\leq \mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{n\times n} & T\\ 0_{b\times n} & 0_{b\times b} \end{pmatrix}\right). $$ Since $W(\xi)T=u_{(z_{k}-p \ z_{k}-p+1)}(\beta)E$, this establishes the bandwidth approximation in \textit{(c)}, thus completing the proof of the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the bandwidth for rectangular T with zero rows

nodes.name: Completed paths shift zero rows up
nodes.statement: To complete the proof of \textit{(c)} suppose $T\in M_{n\times b}$ and that the rows of $T$ at indices $z_{1},\ldots,z_{m}$ consist entirely of zeros. Following the lines of the proof of \autoref{matrix1}, we have $$ \mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{n\times n} & w_{z_{k-1}}^{1}(1)\cdots w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)T\\ 0_{b\times n} & 0_{b\times b} \end{pmatrix} \right)\leq\mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{n\times n} & T\\ 0_{b\times n} & 0_{b\times b} \end{pmatrix}\right) $$ by \autoref{permutation} since only rows of zeros are shifted up when multiplying $T$ on the left by $w_{z_{k-1}}^{1}(1)\cdots w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)$, while non-zero entries remain in place or are shifted down towards the diagonal.
nodes.statement_short: Completed cycles only move zero rows up

nodes.name: Factor the partial path
nodes.statement: Similar reasoning to that used when deducing \autoref{wij} shows that there exist $\beta\in[0,1]$ and $1\leq p\leq z_{k}-1$ such that $$ w_{z_{k}}^{1}(\delta_{m}^{k}(\xi))=u_{(z_{k} - p \ z_{k}-p+1)}(\beta) w_{z_{k}}^{z_{k}-p+1}(1). $$ Since the $z_{k}$th row of a given matrix remains unchanged when multiplying on the left by $w_{z_{k-1}}^{1}(1)\cdots w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)$, the $z_{k}$th row of $w_{z_{k-1}}^{1}(1)\cdots w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)T$ contains only zeros. Hence, multiplying this given matrix on the left by $w_{z_{k}}^{z_{k}-p+1}(1)=U[(z_{k}-p+1 \ \cdots \ z_{k})]$ shifts the zero row from index $z_{k}$ to index $z_{k}-p+1$, while shifting the rows $z_{k}-p+1,\ldots,z_{k}-1$ down by one towards the diagonal. Thus, $$ \mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{n\times n} & E\\ 0_{b\times n} & 0_{b\times b} \end{pmatrix} \right)\leq \mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{n\times n} & w_{z_{k-1}}^{1}(1)\cdots w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)T\\ 0_{b\times n} & 0_{b\times b} \end{pmatrix} \right)\leq\mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{n\times n} & T\\ 0_{b\times n} & 0_{b\times b} \end{pmatrix}\right), $$ where $E:=U[(z_{k}-p+1 \ \cdots \ z_{k})]w_{z_{k-1}}^{1}(1)\cdots w_{z_{1}}^{1}(1)T$.
nodes.statement_short: Split the partial path into a cycle and one transposition path

nodes.name: Last transposition
nodes.statement: Now, $E$ and $u_{(z_{k}-p \ z_{k}-p+1)}(\beta)E$ may differ only on rows $z_{k}-p$ and $z_{k}-p+1$, where these two rows of the latter matrix are linear combinations of the same two rows of $E$. From this and the fact that the $z_{k}-p+1$ row of $E$ consists only of zeros, it is clear that for a given column $\lambda$, the $(z_{k}-p,\lambda)$- or $(z_{k}-p+1,\lambda)$-entry of $u_{(z_{k}-p \ z_{k}-p+1)}(\beta)E$ can be non-zero only if the $(z_{k}-p,\lambda)$ entry of $E$ is non-zero. Hence, $$ \mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{n\times n} & u_{(z_{k}-p \ z_{k}-p+1)}(\beta)E\\ 0_{b\times n} & 0_{b\times b} \end{pmatrix} \right)\leq \mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{n\times n} & E\\ 0_{b\times n} & 0_{b\times b} \end{pmatrix} \right)\leq \mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{n\times n} & T\\ 0_{b\times n} & 0_{b\times b} \end{pmatrix}\right). $$ Since $W(\xi)T=u_{(z_{k}-p \ z_{k}-p+1)}(\beta)E$, this establishes the bandwidth approximation in \textit{(c)}, thus completing the proof of the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: The final transposition mixes a zero row, so bandwidth does not grow

nodes.name: Block transposition permutations and paths
nodes.statement: Let $N\in\mathbb{N}$. For $j,k,n\in\mathbb{N}$ satisfying $N\leq j\leq k\leq n$, we define $$ \sigma^{n}_{j,k}:=(j-N+1 \ \ k-N+1)\cdots(j \ k)\in S_{n}. $$ We define $u_{j,k}^{n}\colon[0,1]\to M_{n}$ to be the unitary $$ u^{n}_{j,k}(\xi):=u_{(j-N+1 \ k-N+1)}(\xi)\cdots u_{(j \ k)}(\xi), $$ where $u_{(i \ i')}\colon [0,1]\to M_{n}$ is a continuous path of unitaries defined as in \autoref{unitaries}.
nodes.label: transposition prod

nodes.name: Block transpositions commute
nodes.statement: Note that in the definition above, if $j\leq n-N$, then $\sigma^{n}_{j,n}$ is the permutation in $S_{n}$ that interchanges $j-N+1,\ldots,j$ and $n-N+1,\ldots,n$; moreover, in this case, all of the factors in the definition of $u^{n}_{j,n}(\xi)$ (for any $\xi\in[0,1]$) commute with each other by \autoref{unitaries}.
nodes.label: commuting perms

nodes.name: Conjugation identity for block transposition paths
nodes.statement: Suppose $N,n,k,i\in\mathbb{N}$ satisfy $N\leq k\leq i-N$ and $i\leq n-N$, and that $\xi\in[0,1]$. Then, $$ u^{n}_{k,n}(\xi)=U[\sigma^{n}_{i,n}]u^{n}_{k,i}(\xi)U[\sigma^{n}_{i,n}], $$ where $u^{n}_{k,n}(\xi)$, $u^{n}_{k,i}(\xi)$, and $\sigma^{n}_{i,n}$ are each products of $N$ factors as defined in \autoref{transposition prod}.
assumptions: $N,n,k,i\in\mathbb{N}$ satisfy $N\leq k\leq i-N$ and $i\leq n-N$, and that $\xi\in[0,1]$
conclusions: u^{n}_{k,n}(\xi)=U[\sigma^{n}_{i,n}]u^{n}_{k,i}(\xi)U[\sigma^{n}_{i,n}]
nodes.label: factormain

nodes.name: Proof of the block conjugation identity
nodes.statement: By definition, \begin{equation} U[\sigma^{n}_{i,n}]u^{n}_{k,i}(\xi) =\left(\prod_{j=-(N-1)}^{0}U[(i+j \ \ n+j)]\right)\left(\prod_{j=-(N-1)}^{0}u_{(k+j \ i+j)}(\xi)\right). \end{equation} Note that for any $-(N-1)\leq j,j'\leq 0$, $$ i+j\leq i<n-(N-1)\leq n+j' $$ and $$ k+j\leq i-N+j\leq i-N<i-(N-1)\leq i+j'. $$ Thus, whenever $-(N-1)\leq j,j'\leq 0$ with $j\not=j'$, the permutations $(i +j' \ \ n+j')$ and $(k+j \ \ i+j)$ are disjoint, and hence, $U[(i +j' \ \ n+j')]$ and $u_{(k+j \ \ i+j)}(\xi)$ commute. Hence, \autoref{negprod} can be restated as $$ U[\sigma^{n}_{i,n}]u^{n}_{k,i}(\xi)=\prod_{j=-(N-1)}^{0}U[(i+j \ \ n+j)]u_{(k+j \ i+j)}(\xi). $$ By the same reasoning, $$ \begin{aligned} U[\sigma^{n}_{i,n}]u^{n}_{k,i}(\xi)U[\sigma^{n}_{i,n}] &=\prod_{j=-(N-1)}^{0}U[(i+j \ \ n+j)]u_{(k+j \ i+j)}(\xi)\prod_{j=-(N-1)}^{0}U[(i+j \ \ n+j)]\\ &=\prod_{j=-(N-1)}^{0}U[(i+j \ \ n+j)]u_{(k+j \ i+j)}(\xi)U[(i+j \ \ n+j)]. \end{aligned} $$ It is elementary to see that $U[(a \ b)]u_{(c \ b)}(\zeta)U[(a \ b)]=u_{(c \ a)}(\zeta)$ whenever $c\leq b\leq a$ and $\zeta\in[0,1]$. Hence, $$ U[\sigma^{n}_{i,n}]u^{n}_{k,i}(\xi)U[\sigma^{n}_{i,n}] =\prod_{j=-(N-1)}^{0}u_{(k+j \ n+j)}(\xi)=u^{n}_{k,n}(\xi), $$ which proves the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Commute disjoint transposition factors and conjugate each u_(k+j i+j) by U[(i+j n+j)].

nodes.name: Expand the product
nodes.statement: By definition, \begin{equation} U[\sigma^{n}_{i,n}]u^{n}_{k,i}(\xi) =\left(\prod_{j=-(N-1)}^{0}U[(i+j \ \ n+j)]\right)\left(\prod_{j=-(N-1)}^{0}u_{(k+j \ i+j)}(\xi)\right). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Write U[sigma]u^n_{k,i} as products of factors

nodes.name: Disjoint factors commute
nodes.statement: Note that for any $-(N-1)\leq j,j'\leq 0$, $$ i+j\leq i<n-(N-1)\leq n+j' $$ and $$ k+j\leq i-N+j\leq i-N<i-(N-1)\leq i+j'. $$ Thus, whenever $-(N-1)\leq j,j'\leq 0$ with $j\not=j'$, the permutations $(i +j' \ \ n+j')$ and $(k+j \ \ i+j)$ are disjoint, and hence, $U[(i +j' \ \ n+j')]$ and $u_{(k+j \ \ i+j)}(\xi)$ commute.
nodes.statement_short: Index inequalities show distinct factors are disjoint, hence commute

nodes.name: Regroup
nodes.statement: Hence, \autoref{negprod} can be restated as $$ U[\sigma^{n}_{i,n}]u^{n}_{k,i}(\xi)=\prod_{j=-(N-1)}^{0}U[(i+j \ \ n+j)]u_{(k+j \ i+j)}(\xi). $$ By the same reasoning, $$ \begin{aligned} U[\sigma^{n}_{i,n}]u^{n}_{k,i}(\xi)U[\sigma^{n}_{i,n}] &=\prod_{j=-(N-1)}^{0}U[(i+j \ \ n+j)]u_{(k+j \ i+j)}(\xi)\prod_{j=-(N-1)}^{0}U[(i+j \ \ n+j)]\\ &=\prod_{j=-(N-1)}^{0}U[(i+j \ \ n+j)]u_{(k+j \ i+j)}(\xi)U[(i+j \ \ n+j)]. \end{aligned} $$
nodes.statement_short: Regroup into products of conjugated pairs

nodes.name: Conjugate each factor
nodes.statement: It is elementary to see that $U[(a \ b)]u_{(c \ b)}(\zeta)U[(a \ b)]=u_{(c \ a)}(\zeta)$ whenever $c\leq b\leq a$ and $\zeta\in[0,1]$. Hence, $$ U[\sigma^{n}_{i,n}]u^{n}_{k,i}(\xi)U[\sigma^{n}_{i,n}] =\prod_{j=-(N-1)}^{0}u_{(k+j \ n+j)}(\xi)=u^{n}_{k,n}(\xi), $$ which proves the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: U[(a b)]u_(c b)U[(a b)]=u_(c a) gives the identity

nodes.name: Expanded product U[sigma]u^n_{k,i}
nodes.statement: U[\sigma^{n}_{i,n}]u^{n}_{k,i}(\xi) =\left(\prod_{j=-(N-1)}^{0}U[(i+j \ \ n+j)]\right)\left(\prod_{j=-(N-1)}^{0}u_{(k+j \ i+j)}(\xi)\right).
nodes.label: negprod

nodes.name: Cycle permutations gamma
nodes.statement: For integers $1\leq j\leq k\leq n$, define $$ \gamma^{n}_{j,k}:=(j \ \ j+1 \ \cdots \ k)\in S_{n}. $$

nodes.name: Product identity for shifted block paths
nodes.statement: Let $N,n,t\in\mathbb{N}$ with $1\leq N<t\leq n-N$, and let $(\xi_{N+1},\ldots,\xi_{t-1})$ be a vector in $[0,1]^{t-1-N}$ whose final $N-1$ entries consist only of zeros. Then, $$ \begin{aligned} U[\gamma^{n}_{1,n}]^{N}\left(\prod_{k=N}^{t-2}u^{n}_{k,n}(\xi_{k+1})\right)U[\sigma^{n}_{t-1,n}] =U[\gamma^{n}_{1,t-1}]^{N}\left(\prod_{k=N}^{t-2}u^{n}_{k,t-1}(\xi_{k+1})\right)U[\gamma^{n}_{t,n}]^{N}, \end{aligned} $$ where $u_{k,n}^{n}(\xi_{k+1})$, $u_{k,t-1}^{n}(\xi_{k+1})$, and $\sigma_{t-1,n}^{n}$ are each products of $N$ factors as defined in \autoref{transposition prod}.
assumptions: $N,n,t\in\mathbb{N}$ with $1\leq N<t\leq n-N$
let $(\xi_{N+1},\ldots,\xi_{t-1})$ be a vector in $[0,1]^{t-1-N}$ whose final $N-1$ entries consist only of zeros
conclusions: U[\gamma^{n}_{1,n}]^{N}\left(\prod_{k=N}^{t-2}u^{n}_{k,n}(\xi_{k+1})\right)U[\sigma^{n}_{t-1,n}] =U[\gamma^{n}_{1,t-1}]^{N}\left(\prod_{k=N}^{t-2}u^{n}_{k,t-1}(\xi_{k+1})\right)U[\gamma^{n}_{t,n}]^{N}
nodes.statement_short: Identity splitting a product of block-transposition paths on n indices into paths on the first t-1 indices and a shift on the rest.
nodes.label: calculation

nodes.name: Proof of the product identity
nodes.statement: If $t-1=N$, then the products on either side of the equality above are empty and the equation reduces to \begin{equation} U[\gamma^{n}_{1,n}]^{N}U[\sigma^{n}_{t-1,n}]=U[\gamma^{n}_{1,t-1}]^{N}U[\gamma^{n}_{t,n}]^{N}. \end{equation} By \autoref{commuting perms}, it is elementary to see that \autoref{elementary} holds. Therefore, for the remainder of the proof, we may assume that $t-2\geq N$. For any $N\leq k\leq t-1-N$, we may apply \autoref{factormain} (recalling that $t-1\leq n-N$) to conclude that \begin{equation} u^{n}_{k,n}(\xi_{k+1})=U[\sigma^{n}_{t-1,n}]u^{n}_{k,t-1}(\xi_{k+1})U[\sigma^{n}_{t-1,n}]. \end{equation} In fact, \autoref{factor} holds for all $N\leq k\leq t-2$. Indeed, if $t-N\leq k\leq t-2$, then by the assumption of the lemma, it must be that $\xi_{k+1}=0$. In this case, \autoref{factor} reduces to $1_{n}=U[\sigma^{n}_{t-1,n}]^{2}$, which holds by \autoref{commuting perms}. Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned} \prod_{k=N}^{t-2}u^{n}_{k,n}(\xi_{k+1})&=\prod_{k=N}^{t-2}U[\sigma^{n}_{t-1,n}]u^{n}_{k,t-1}(\xi_{k+1})U[\sigma^{n}_{t-1,n}]\\ &=U[\sigma^{n}_{t-1,n}]\left(\prod_{k=N}^{t-2}u^{n}_{k,t-1}(\xi_{k+1})\right)U[\sigma^{n}_{t-1,n}], \end{aligned} $$ which, together with \autoref{elementary}, yields that \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} U[\gamma^{n}_{1,n}]^{N}\prod_{k=N}^{t-2}u^{n}_{k,n}(\xi_{k+1}) =U[\gamma^{n}_{1,t-1}]^{N}U[\gamma^{n}_{t,n}]^{N}\left(\prod_{k=N}^{t-2}u^{n}_{k,t-1}(\xi_{k+1})\right)U[\sigma^{n}_{t-1,n}]. \end{aligned} \end{equation} Moreover, for each $k=N,\ldots,t-2$, the indices in each transposition-like unitary factor in $u^{n}_{k,t-1}(\xi_{k+1})$ are distinct from $t,\ldots,n$. Hence, $U[\gamma^{n}_{t,n}]^{N}$ and $\prod_{k=N}^{t-2}u^{n}_{k,t-1}(\xi_{k+1})$ commute, and so, using \autoref{penultimate}, it follows that $$ \begin{aligned} U[\gamma^{n}_{1,n}]^{N}\prod_{k=N}^{t-2}u^{n}_{k,n}(\xi_{k+1}) = U[\gamma^{n}_{1,t-1}]^{N}\left(\prod_{k=N}^{t-2}u^{n}_{k,t-1}(\xi_{k+1})\right)U[\gamma^{n}_{t,n}]^{N}U[\sigma^{n}_{t-1,n}]. \end{aligned} $$ \autoref{calculation} then follows by multiplying $U[\sigma^{n}_{t-1,n}]$ on the right of both sides in the above expression.
nodes.statement_short: Handle t-1=N directly, then rewrite each factor via the block conjugation identity and commute disjoint factors.

nodes.name: Case t-1=N
nodes.statement: If $t-1=N$, then the products on either side of the equality above are empty and the equation reduces to \begin{equation} U[\gamma^{n}_{1,n}]^{N}U[\sigma^{n}_{t-1,n}]=U[\gamma^{n}_{1,t-1}]^{N}U[\gamma^{n}_{t,n}]^{N}. \end{equation} By \autoref{commuting perms}, it is elementary to see that \autoref{elementary} holds. Therefore, for the remainder of the proof, we may assume that $t-2\geq N$.
nodes.statement_short: The identity reduces to an elementary permutation identity

nodes.name: Apply the conjugation identity
nodes.statement: For any $N\leq k\leq t-1-N$, we may apply \autoref{factormain} (recalling that $t-1\leq n-N$) to conclude that \begin{equation} u^{n}_{k,n}(\xi_{k+1})=U[\sigma^{n}_{t-1,n}]u^{n}_{k,t-1}(\xi_{k+1})U[\sigma^{n}_{t-1,n}]. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite each factor u^n_{k,n} by conjugation

nodes.name: Extend to all k
nodes.statement: In fact, \autoref{factor} holds for all $N\leq k\leq t-2$. Indeed, if $t-N\leq k\leq t-2$, then by the assumption of the lemma, it must be that $\xi_{k+1}=0$. In this case, \autoref{factor} reduces to $1_{n}=U[\sigma^{n}_{t-1,n}]^{2}$, which holds by \autoref{commuting perms}.
nodes.statement_short: For large k the parameter is zero and the identity is trivial

nodes.name: Combine
nodes.statement: Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned} \prod_{k=N}^{t-2}u^{n}_{k,n}(\xi_{k+1})&=\prod_{k=N}^{t-2}U[\sigma^{n}_{t-1,n}]u^{n}_{k,t-1}(\xi_{k+1})U[\sigma^{n}_{t-1,n}]\\ &=U[\sigma^{n}_{t-1,n}]\left(\prod_{k=N}^{t-2}u^{n}_{k,t-1}(\xi_{k+1})\right)U[\sigma^{n}_{t-1,n}], \end{aligned} $$ which, together with \autoref{elementary}, yields that \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} U[\gamma^{n}_{1,n}]^{N}\prod_{k=N}^{t-2}u^{n}_{k,n}(\xi_{k+1}) =U[\gamma^{n}_{1,t-1}]^{N}U[\gamma^{n}_{t,n}]^{N}\left(\prod_{k=N}^{t-2}u^{n}_{k,t-1}(\xi_{k+1})\right)U[\sigma^{n}_{t-1,n}]. \end{aligned} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Telescoping the conjugations gives the penultimate identity

nodes.name: Commute and finish
nodes.statement: Moreover, for each $k=N,\ldots,t-2$, the indices in each transposition-like unitary factor in $u^{n}_{k,t-1}(\xi_{k+1})$ are distinct from $t,\ldots,n$. Hence, $U[\gamma^{n}_{t,n}]^{N}$ and $\prod_{k=N}^{t-2}u^{n}_{k,t-1}(\xi_{k+1})$ commute, and so, using \autoref{penultimate}, it follows that $$ \begin{aligned} U[\gamma^{n}_{1,n}]^{N}\prod_{k=N}^{t-2}u^{n}_{k,n}(\xi_{k+1}) = U[\gamma^{n}_{1,t-1}]^{N}\left(\prod_{k=N}^{t-2}u^{n}_{k,t-1}(\xi_{k+1})\right)U[\gamma^{n}_{t,n}]^{N}U[\sigma^{n}_{t-1,n}]. \end{aligned} $$ \autoref{calculation} then follows by multiplying $U[\sigma^{n}_{t-1,n}]$ on the right of both sides in the above expression.
nodes.statement_short: Commute disjoint factors and multiply by U[sigma]

nodes.name: Penultimate product identity
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} U[\gamma^{n}_{1,n}]^{N}\prod_{k=N}^{t-2}u^{n}_{k,n}(\xi_{k+1}) =U[\gamma^{n}_{1,t-1}]^{N}U[\gamma^{n}_{t,n}]^{N}\left(\prod_{k=N}^{t-2}u^{n}_{k,t-1}(\xi_{k+1})\right)U[\sigma^{n}_{t-1,n}]. \end{aligned}
nodes.label: penultimate

nodes.name: Unitaries W_n
nodes.statement: Let $N\in\mathbb{N}$. Given $n\in\mathbb{N}$ with $n\geq N$, let $W_{n}\in C([0,1]^{n},M_{n})$ be the unitary \begin{equation} W_{n}(\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{n}):=U[\gamma^{n}_{1,n}]^{N}\left(\prod_{k=N}^{n-1}u^{n}_{k,n}(\xi_{k+1})\right), \end{equation} where $u_{k,n}^{n}$ is the product of $N$ factors as in \autoref{transposition prod}. We adopt the convention that $W_{n}:=1_{n}$ if $n=N$.
nodes.statement_short: W_n(xi) = U[gamma_{1,n}]^N times the product of block-transposition paths u^n_{k,n}(xi_{k+1}).
nodes.label: ltmatrix

nodes.name: Definition of W_n
nodes.statement: W_{n}(\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{n}):=U[\gamma^{n}_{1,n}]^{N}\left(\prod_{k=N}^{n-1}u^{n}_{k,n}(\xi_{k+1})\right),
nodes.label: Wn

nodes.name: Block-diagonal reduction of W_n
nodes.statement: Let $N\in\mathbb{N}$. Suppose $n$ is an integer greater than $N$ and $\vec{\xi}:=(\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{n})$ is a vector in $[0,1]^{n}$ with the property that $\xi_{1}=1$, the final $N$ entries are all zero, and for any consecutive $N$ entries, at most one is non-zero. Suppose $K=\{1=k_{1}<k_{2}<\cdots<k_{m}\}$ is any set of indices, containing $1$, at which $\vec{\xi}$ is $1$; put $k_{m+1}:=n+1$. Then, \begin{equation} W_{n}(\vec{\xi})=\operatorname{diag}\left(W_{k_{2}-k_{1}}(\xi_{k_{1}},\ldots,\xi_{k_{2}-1}),\ldots,W_{k_{m+1}-k_{m}}(\xi_{k_{m}},\ldots,\xi_{k_{m+1}-1})\right), \end{equation} where $N$ is the fixed positive integer being used to define $W_{n},W_{k_{2}-k_{1}},\ldots,W_{k_{m+1}-k_{m}}$ in \autoref{ltmatrix}.
assumptions: $n$ is an integer greater than $N$ and $\vec{\xi}:=(\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{n})$ is a vector in $[0,1]^{n}$ with the property that $\xi_{1}=1$, the final $N$ entries are all zero, and for any consecutive $N$ entries, at most one is non-zero
$K=\{1=k_{1}<k_{2}<\cdots<k_{m}\}$ is any set of indices, containing $1$, at which $\vec{\xi}$ is $1$
conclusions: W_{n}(\vec{\xi})=\operatorname{diag}\left(W_{k_{2}-k_{1}}(\xi_{k_{1}},\ldots,\xi_{k_{2}-1}),\ldots,W_{k_{m+1}-k_{m}}(\xi_{k_{m}},\ldots,\xi_{k_{m+1}-1})\right)
nodes.statement_short: If xi equals 1 at the indices of K, W_n(xi) splits block-diagonally into W's of the consecutive blocks.
nodes.label: Wn reduction

nodes.name: Block-diagonal form of W_n
nodes.statement: W_{n}(\vec{\xi})=\operatorname{diag}\left(W_{k_{2}-k_{1}}(\xi_{k_{1}},\ldots,\xi_{k_{2}-1}),\ldots,W_{k_{m+1}-k_{m}}(\xi_{k_{m}},\ldots,\xi_{k_{m+1}-1})\right),
nodes.label: Wn decomp

nodes.name: Proof of the W_n reduction
nodes.statement: Fix an integer $n>N$, a vector $\vec{\xi}$, and an associated set $K$, satisfying the hypotheses of the lemma. Let us proceed by induction on the size $m$ of $K$. If $m=1$, there is nothing to show. Fix $m\geq 2$ and suppose that \autoref{Wn reduction} holds for every natural number $n'>N$, vector $\zeta$, and associated set $K'$ of size $m-1$, provided they satisfy the required hypotheses. Assume that $|K|=m$. Let us show \autoref{Wn decomp} holds in this case. Note that by assumption $\xi_{k_{2}-(N-1)},\ldots,\xi_{k_{2}-1}=0$ and \begin{equation} N<k_{2}\leq n-N. \end{equation} Therefore, we may apply \autoref{calculation} with $N$, $n$, $k_{2}$, and $(\xi_{N+1},\ldots,\xi_{k_{2}-1})$ to conclude that \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} U[\gamma^{n}_{1,n}]^{N}\left(\prod_{k=N}^{k_{2}-2}u^{n}_{k,n}(\xi_{k+1})\right)U[\sigma^{n}_{k_{2}-1,n}] =U[\gamma^{n}_{1,k_{2}-1}]^{N}\left(\prod_{k=N}^{k_{2}-2}u^{n}_{k,k_{2}-1}(\xi_{k+1})\right)U[\gamma^{n}_{k_{2},n}]^{N}. \end{aligned} \end{equation} By \autoref{Wn} and \autoref{k2upperbound}, $$ \begin{aligned} W_{n}(\vec{\xi})&=U[\gamma^{n}_{1,n}]^{N}\left(\prod_{k=N}^{n-1}u^{n}_{k,n}(\xi_{k+1})\right)\\ &=U[\gamma^{n}_{1,n}]^{N}\left(\prod_{k=N}^{k_{2}-2}u^{n}_{k,n}(\xi_{k+1})\right)u^{n}_{k_{2}-1,n}(\xi_{k_{2}})\left(\prod_{k=k_{2}}^{n-1}u^{n}_{k,n}(\xi_{k+1})\right). \end{aligned} $$ Since $u^{n}_{k_{2}-1,n}(\xi_{k_{2}})=u^{n}_{k_{2}-1,n}(1)=U[\sigma^{n}_{k_{2}-1,n}]$, we may apply \autoref{calculation2} to obtain \begin{equation} W_{n}(\vec{\xi})=U[\gamma^{n}_{1,k_{2}-1}]^{N}\left(\prod_{k=N}^{k_{2}-2}u^{n}_{k,k_{2}-1}(\xi_{k+1})\right)U[\gamma^{n}_{k_{2},n}]^{N}\left(\prod_{k=k_{2}}^{n-1}u^{n}_{k,n}(\xi_{k+1})\right). \end{equation} Let $\vec{\xi'}:=(\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{k_{2}-1})$ and $\vec{\xi''}:=(\xi_{k_{2}},\ldots,\xi_{n})$. By \autoref{k2upperbound}, $|\vec{\xi'}|\geq N$, so that \begin{equation} W_{k_{2}-k_{1}}(\vec{\xi'})=U[\gamma^{k_{2}-1}_{1,k_{2}-1}]^{N}\left(\prod_{k=N}^{(k_{2}-1)-1}u^{k_{2}-1}_{k,k_{2}-1}(\xi_{k+1})\right)\in M_{k_{2}-k_{1}}. \end{equation} Furthermore, $|\vec{\xi''}|>N$, so that \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} W_{n+1-k_{2}}(\vec{\xi''})&=W_{n+1-k_{2}}(\xi_{k_{2}},\ldots,\xi_{n})\\ &=U[\gamma^{n+1-k_{2}}_{1,n+1-k_{2}}]^{N}\left(\prod_{k=N}^{n+1-k_{2}-1}u^{n+1-k_{2}}_{k, n+1-k_{2}}(\xi_{k_{2}+k})\right)\\ &=U[\gamma^{n+1-k_{2}}_{1,n+1-k_{2}}]^{N}\left(\prod_{k=1}^{n-k_{2}}u^{n+1-k_{2}}_{k, n+1-k_{2}}(\xi_{k_{2}+k})\right)\\ &=U[\gamma^{n+1-k_{2}}_{1,n+1-k_{2}}]^{N}\left(\prod_{k=k_{2}}^{n-1}u^{n+1-k_{2}}_{k+1-k_{2}, n+1-k_{2}}(\xi_{k+1})\right)\in M_{n+1-k_{2}}, \end{aligned} \end{equation} where the penultimate equality follows since $\xi_{k_{2}}=1$ and at most one of any $N$ consecutive entries of $\vec{\xi}$ is non-zero. Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned} &\operatorname{diag}(W_{k_{2}-k_{1}}(\vec{\xi'}),W_{n+1-k_{2}}(\vec{\xi''}))\\ =&\operatorname{diag}(W_{k_{2}-k_{1}}(\vec{\xi'}),1_{n+1-k_{2}})\operatorname{diag}(1_{k_{2}-k_{1}},W_{n+1-k_{2}}(\vec{\xi''}))\\ =&U[\gamma^{n}_{1,k_{2}-1}]^{N}\left(\prod_{k=N}^{(k_{2}-1)-1}u^{n}_{k,k_{2}-1}(\xi_{k+1})\right) U[\gamma^{n}_{k_{2},n}]^{N}\left(\prod_{k=k_{2}}^{n-1}u^{n}_{k, n}(\xi_{k+1})\right), \end{aligned} $$ where in the last equality the indices in the $\gamma$'s and $u$'s have been altered appropriately from the ones in \autoref{induction1} and \autoref{induction2} to accommodate for the identity factors in the diagonal. Combining this with \autoref{induction} yields that \begin{equation} W_{n}(\vec{\xi})=\operatorname{diag}(W_{k_{2}-k_{1}}(\vec{\xi'}),W_{n+1-k_{2}}(\vec{\xi''})). \end{equation} We may apply the inductive hypothesis to $n'=|\vec{\xi''}|>N$, vector $\vec{\xi''}$, and associated set $K'=\{k_{2},\ldots,k_{m}\}$ of size $m-1$ to conclude that $$ \begin{aligned} W_{n+1-k_{2}}(\vec{\xi''}) =\operatorname{diag}\left(W_{k_{3}-k_{2}}(\xi_{k_{2}},\ldots,\xi_{k_{3}-1}),\ldots,W_{k_{m+1}-k_{m}}(\xi_{k_{m}},\ldots,\xi_{k_{m+1}-1})\right). \end{aligned} $$ Substituting this into \autoref{breakup} yields that $$ W_{n}(\vec{\xi})=\operatorname{diag}\left(W_{k_{2}-k_{1}}(\xi_{k_{1}},\ldots,\xi_{k_{2}-1}),\ldots,W_{k_{m+1}-k_{m}}(\xi_{k_{m}},\ldots,\xi_{k_{m+1}-1})\right), $$ which proves \autoref{Wn reduction}.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on |K|: use the product identity at k_2 to split off the first block, then apply the hypothesis to the rest.

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: Fix an integer $n>N$, a vector $\vec{\xi}$, and an associated set $K$, satisfying the hypotheses of the lemma. Let us proceed by induction on the size $m$ of $K$. If $m=1$, there is nothing to show.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on m=|K|; m=1 is trivial

nodes.name: Inductive hypothesis
nodes.statement: Fix $m\geq 2$ and suppose that \autoref{Wn reduction} holds for every natural number $n'>N$, vector $\zeta$, and associated set $K'$ of size $m-1$, provided they satisfy the required hypotheses. Assume that $|K|=m$. Let us show \autoref{Wn decomp} holds in this case.
nodes.statement_short: Assume the statement for sets of size m-1

nodes.name: Apply the product identity at k_2
nodes.statement: Note that by assumption $\xi_{k_{2}-(N-1)},\ldots,\xi_{k_{2}-1}=0$ and \begin{equation} N<k_{2}\leq n-N. \end{equation} Therefore, we may apply \autoref{calculation} with $N$, $n$, $k_{2}$, and $(\xi_{N+1},\ldots,\xi_{k_{2}-1})$ to conclude that \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} U[\gamma^{n}_{1,n}]^{N}\left(\prod_{k=N}^{k_{2}-2}u^{n}_{k,n}(\xi_{k+1})\right)U[\sigma^{n}_{k_{2}-1,n}] =U[\gamma^{n}_{1,k_{2}-1}]^{N}\left(\prod_{k=N}^{k_{2}-2}u^{n}_{k,k_{2}-1}(\xi_{k+1})\right)U[\gamma^{n}_{k_{2},n}]^{N}. \end{aligned} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: k_2 is in range, so the product identity applies

nodes.name: First split
nodes.statement: By \autoref{Wn} and \autoref{k2upperbound}, $$ \begin{aligned} W_{n}(\vec{\xi})&=U[\gamma^{n}_{1,n}]^{N}\left(\prod_{k=N}^{n-1}u^{n}_{k,n}(\xi_{k+1})\right)\\ &=U[\gamma^{n}_{1,n}]^{N}\left(\prod_{k=N}^{k_{2}-2}u^{n}_{k,n}(\xi_{k+1})\right)u^{n}_{k_{2}-1,n}(\xi_{k_{2}})\left(\prod_{k=k_{2}}^{n-1}u^{n}_{k,n}(\xi_{k+1})\right). \end{aligned} $$ Since $u^{n}_{k_{2}-1,n}(\xi_{k_{2}})=u^{n}_{k_{2}-1,n}(1)=U[\sigma^{n}_{k_{2}-1,n}]$, we may apply \autoref{calculation2} to obtain \begin{equation} W_{n}(\vec{\xi})=U[\gamma^{n}_{1,k_{2}-1}]^{N}\left(\prod_{k=N}^{k_{2}-2}u^{n}_{k,k_{2}-1}(\xi_{k+1})\right)U[\gamma^{n}_{k_{2},n}]^{N}\left(\prod_{k=k_{2}}^{n-1}u^{n}_{k,n}(\xi_{k+1})\right). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Split W_n at k_2 using u^n_{k_2-1,n}(1)=U[sigma]

nodes.name: Identify the two blocks
nodes.statement: Let $\vec{\xi'}:=(\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{k_{2}-1})$ and $\vec{\xi''}:=(\xi_{k_{2}},\ldots,\xi_{n})$. By \autoref{k2upperbound}, $|\vec{\xi'}|\geq N$, so that \begin{equation} W_{k_{2}-k_{1}}(\vec{\xi'})=U[\gamma^{k_{2}-1}_{1,k_{2}-1}]^{N}\left(\prod_{k=N}^{(k_{2}-1)-1}u^{k_{2}-1}_{k,k_{2}-1}(\xi_{k+1})\right)\in M_{k_{2}-k_{1}}. \end{equation} Furthermore, $|\vec{\xi''}|>N$, so that \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} W_{n+1-k_{2}}(\vec{\xi''})&=W_{n+1-k_{2}}(\xi_{k_{2}},\ldots,\xi_{n})\\ &=U[\gamma^{n+1-k_{2}}_{1,n+1-k_{2}}]^{N}\left(\prod_{k=N}^{n+1-k_{2}-1}u^{n+1-k_{2}}_{k, n+1-k_{2}}(\xi_{k_{2}+k})\right)\\ &=U[\gamma^{n+1-k_{2}}_{1,n+1-k_{2}}]^{N}\left(\prod_{k=1}^{n-k_{2}}u^{n+1-k_{2}}_{k, n+1-k_{2}}(\xi_{k_{2}+k})\right)\\ &=U[\gamma^{n+1-k_{2}}_{1,n+1-k_{2}}]^{N}\left(\prod_{k=k_{2}}^{n-1}u^{n+1-k_{2}}_{k+1-k_{2}, n+1-k_{2}}(\xi_{k+1})\right)\in M_{n+1-k_{2}}, \end{aligned} \end{equation} where the penultimate equality follows since $\xi_{k_{2}}=1$ and at most one of any $N$ consecutive entries of $\vec{\xi}$ is non-zero. Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned} &\operatorname{diag}(W_{k_{2}-k_{1}}(\vec{\xi'}),W_{n+1-k_{2}}(\vec{\xi''}))\\ =&\operatorname{diag}(W_{k_{2}-k_{1}}(\vec{\xi'}),1_{n+1-k_{2}})\operatorname{diag}(1_{k_{2}-k_{1}},W_{n+1-k_{2}}(\vec{\xi''}))\\ =&U[\gamma^{n}_{1,k_{2}-1}]^{N}\left(\prod_{k=N}^{(k_{2}-1)-1}u^{n}_{k,k_{2}-1}(\xi_{k+1})\right) U[\gamma^{n}_{k_{2},n}]^{N}\left(\prod_{k=k_{2}}^{n-1}u^{n}_{k, n}(\xi_{k+1})\right), \end{aligned} $$ where in the last equality the indices in the $\gamma$'s and $u$'s have been altered appropriately from the ones in \autoref{induction1} and \autoref{induction2} to accommodate for the identity factors in the diagonal. Combining this with \autoref{induction} yields that \begin{equation} W_{n}(\vec{\xi})=\operatorname{diag}(W_{k_{2}-k_{1}}(\vec{\xi'}),W_{n+1-k_{2}}(\vec{\xi''})). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Recognize the factors as W of the first block and of the rest

nodes.name: Apply the hypothesis
nodes.statement: We may apply the inductive hypothesis to $n'=|\vec{\xi''}|>N$, vector $\vec{\xi''}$, and associated set $K'=\{k_{2},\ldots,k_{m}\}$ of size $m-1$ to conclude that $$ \begin{aligned} W_{n+1-k_{2}}(\vec{\xi''}) =\operatorname{diag}\left(W_{k_{3}-k_{2}}(\xi_{k_{2}},\ldots,\xi_{k_{3}-1}),\ldots,W_{k_{m+1}-k_{m}}(\xi_{k_{m}},\ldots,\xi_{k_{m+1}-1})\right). \end{aligned} $$ Substituting this into \autoref{breakup} yields that $$ W_{n}(\vec{\xi})=\operatorname{diag}\left(W_{k_{2}-k_{1}}(\xi_{k_{1}},\ldots,\xi_{k_{2}-1}),\ldots,W_{k_{m+1}-k_{m}}(\xi_{k_{m}},\ldots,\xi_{k_{m+1}-1})\right), $$ which proves \autoref{Wn reduction}.
nodes.statement_short: Decompose the remaining block by induction

nodes.name: Bound on k_2
nodes.statement: N<k_{2}\leq n-N.
nodes.label: k2upperbound

nodes.name: Product identity at k_2

nodes.name: Induced map on spectra into finite subsets
nodes.statement: Given unital subhomogeneous $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebras $A$ and $B$ and a unital $^{*}$-homomorphism $\psi\colon A\to B$, an irreducible representation $\pi$ of $B$ yields a representation $\pi\circ\psi$ of $A$. The finite-dimensional representation $\pi\circ\psi$ is unitarily equivalent to a direct sum $\tau_{1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\tau_{s}$ of irreducible representations of $A$. In this way, we get a map $\hat{\psi}\colon\hat{B}\to\mathcal{P}(\hat{A})$ given by $\hat{\psi}([\pi]):=\{[\tau_{1}],\ldots,[\tau_{s}]\}$, where multiplicities are ignored.
nodes.statement_short: psi-hat sends an irreducible representation of B to the set of irreducible summands of its pullback to A.

nodes.name: Simplicity criterion for injective limits of subhomogeneous algebras
nodes.statement: Suppose we have an inductive limit of the form $$ A_{1}\overset{\psi_{1}}{\longrightarrow} A_{2}\overset{\psi_{2}}{\longrightarrow} A_{3}\overset{\psi_{3}}{\longrightarrow}\cdots\longrightarrow A:=\varinjlim A_{i}, $$ where $A$ is unital and for each $i\in \mathbb{N}$, $A_{i}$ is subhomogeneous and $\psi_{i}$ is injective. Let $\psi_{j,i}:=\psi_{j-1}\circ\cdots\circ\psi_{i}$. Then, the following statements are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item $A$ is simple. \item For all $i\in\mathbb{N}$ and all non-empty open $U\subset \hat{A_{i}}$, there is a $j>i$ such that $\hat{\psi}_{j,i}([\pi])\cap U\not=\varnothing$ for all $[\pi]\in \hat{A_{j}}$. \item For all $i\in\mathbb{N}$, if $f\in A_{i}$ is non-zero, then there is a $j > i$ such that $\pi(\psi_{j,i}(f))\not=0$ for every non-zero irreducible representation $\pi$ of $A_{j}$. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: $A$ is unital and for each $i\in \mathbb{N}$, $A_{i}$ is subhomogeneous and $\psi_{i}$ is injective
conclusions: the following statements are equivalent
equivalent_conditions: For all $i\in\mathbb{N}$ and all non-empty open $U\subset \hat{A_{i}}$, there is a $j>i$ such that $\hat{\psi}_{j,i}([\pi])\cap U\not=\varnothing$ for all $[\pi]\in \hat{A_{j}}$.
For all $i\in\mathbb{N}$, if $f\in A_{i}$ is non-zero, then there is a $j > i$ such that $\pi(\psi_{j,i}(f))\not=0$ for every non-zero irreducible representation $\pi$ of $A_{j}$.
nodes.statement_short: An injective unital limit of subhomogeneous algebras is simple iff every open set of a spectrum is eventually hit by every point's image, iff nonzero elements are eventually nonzero in every irreducible representation.
nodes.label: simplicity
