nodes.name: Perturbation to a zero cross on an open set
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a DSH algebra of length $ l $. Let $\epsilon >0$. Suppose that $f\in A$ is not invertible. Then, there is an $f'\in A$ with $\|f-f'\|\leq\epsilon$ and there are unitaries $w,v\in A$ such that for some $1\leq i\leq l $, $(wf'v)_{i}$ has a zero cross at index $1$ everywhere on some non-empty set $U\subset \hat{A}\cap (X_{i}\setminus Y_{i})$, which is open with respect to the hull-kernel topology on $\hat{A}$. Moreover, there is a $\Delta\in A$ such that for every $1\leq j\leq l $ and $x\in X_{j}$, $\Delta_{j}(x)$ is a diagonal matrix with entries in $[0,1]$, where $\Delta_{j}(x)_{k,k}>0$ implies $(wf'v)_{j}(x)$ has a zero cross at index $k$; moreover, $\Delta_{i}(z)_{1,1}=1$ for all $z\in U$.
assumptions: Let $A$ be a DSH algebra of length $ l $
Let $\epsilon >0$
$f\in A$ is not invertible
conclusions: there is an $f'\in A$ with $\|f-f'\|\leq\epsilon$ and there are unitaries $w,v\in A$ such that for some $1\leq i\leq l $, $(wf'v)_{i}$ has a zero cross at index $1$ everywhere on some non-empty set $U\subset \hat{A}\cap (X_{i}\setminus Y_{i})$, which is open with respect to the hull-kernel topology on $\hat{A}$

there is a $\Delta\in A$ such that for every $1\leq j\leq l $ and $x\in X_{j}$, $\Delta_{j}(x)$ is a diagonal matrix with entries in $[0,1]$, where $\Delta_{j}(x)_{k,k}>0$ implies $(wf'v)_{j}(x)$ has a zero cross at index $k$
nodes.statement_short: A non-invertible f can be perturbed and multiplied by unitaries to have a zero cross at index 1 on a spectrum-open set, with a diagonal marker Delta.
nodes.label: perturb

nodes.name: Proof of the perturbation lemma
nodes.statement:
Using \autoref{non-invertible at point}, choose $1\leq i\leq l $ and $x\in X_{i}\setminus Y_{i}$ such that $f_{i}(x)$ is a non-invertible matrix. We break the proof up into two cases. Case one: $x$ is not in the decomposition of any point in $Y_{j}$ for any $j>i$. By \autoref{not decomposition}, there is set $U_{1}\subset X_{i}$ containing $x$, which is open in $X_{i}$ and has the property that no point in it is in the decomposition of any point in $Y_{j}$ for any $j>i$. Since $Y_{i}$ is closed in $X_{i}$, the set $U_{1}\cap(X_{i}\setminus Y_{i})$ is open in $X_{i}$. By shrinking $U_{1}$, we may assume that $\|f_{i}(x)-f_{i}(z)\|\leq\epsilon$ for all $z\in U_{1}$. Choose a set $U_{2}$ that is open in $X_{i}$ and satisfies $x\in U_{2}\subset\overline{U_{2}}^{X_{i}}\subset U_{1}\cap(X_{i}\setminus Y_{i})$. Using Urysohn's Lemma, we can define a function $h\in C(X_{i},M_{n_{i}})$ such that $h|_{\overline{U_{2}}^{X_{i}}}\equiv f_{i}(x)$, $h|_{X_{i}\setminus(U_{1}\cap(X_{i}\setminus Y_{i}))}=f_{i}|_{X_{i}\setminus(U_{1}\cap(X_{i}\setminus Y_{i}))}$, and $\|f_{i}-h\|\leq\epsilon$. Define $f'$ coordinate-wise by $f':=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{i-1},h,f_{i+1},\ldots,f_{ l })$. Since $h|_{Y_{i}}=f_{i}|_{Y_{i}}$, we have $(f_{1},\ldots,f_{i-1},h)\in A^{(i)}$. Since no point in $U_{1}$ is in the decomposition of any point in $Y_{j}$ for any $j>i$, and because $h$ may only differ from $f_{i}$ on $U_{1}\cap (X_{i}\setminus Y_{i})\subset U_{1}$, this perturbation does not violate the diagonal decomposition at any point. Thus, $f'\in A$ since $f\in A$, and $\|f-f'\|\leq\epsilon$ because $\|f_{i}-h\|\leq\epsilon$. Since $f_{i}(x)$ is a non-invertible matrix, there are unitary matrices $W$ and $V$ in $M_{n_{i}}$ with the property that $Wf_{i}(x)V$ has a zero cross at index $1$. Since the unitary group in $M_{n_{i}}$ is connected we may, using the same reasoning as above, define unitaries $w,v\in A$ coordinate-wise with $w_{j}=v_{j}\equiv 1_{n_{j}}$ for all $j
ot=i$ and $w_{i},v_{i}\in C(X_{i},M_{n_{i}})$ satisfying $w_{i}|_{\overline{U_{2}}^{X_{i}}}\equiv W$, $v_{i}|_{\overline{U_{2}}^{X_{i}}}\equiv V$, and $w_{i}|_{X_{i}\setminus(U_{1}\cap(X_{i}\setminus Y_{i}))}=v_{i}|_{X_{i}\setminus(U_{1}\cap(X_{i}\setminus Y_{i}))}\equiv 1_{n_{i}}$. Finally, choose a set $U_{3}$ that is open in $X_{i}$ and satisfies $x\in U_{3}\subset\overline{U_{3}}^{X_{i}}\subset U_{2}$. Define $\Delta\in A$ coordinate-wise as follows: $\Delta_{j}\equiv 0$ for $j
ot=i$; let $g\colon X_{i}	o [0,1]$ be any continuous function such that $g|_{\overline{U_{3}}^{X_{i}}}\equiv 1$ and $g|_{X_{i}\setminus U_{2}}\equiv 0$, and put $\Delta_{i}:=\operatorname{diag}(g,0,\ldots,0)\in C(X_{i},M_{n_{i}})$. As argued above for $f'$, we have $\Delta\in A$. Take $U:=U_{3}$. Applying \autoref{open in spectrum}, we conclude $U$ is open in $\hat{A}$. Since $(wf'v)_{i}$ has a zero cross at index $1$ everywhere on $U_{2}$ and since $\Delta$ vanishes outside $U_{2}$, the lemma holds in this case. Case two: There is a $j>i$ such that $x$ is in the decomposition of some point in $Y_{j}$. In this case, we cannot define $f'$ as above, because we are not guaranteed a neighbourhood around $x$ in which we may freely perturb $f$ while remaining in $A$. Let $i'$ denote the largest integer for which $x$ is in the decomposition of some point in $Y_{i'}$. Choose $y\in Y_{i'}$ such that $x$ is in the decomposition of $y$. Then $f_{i'}(y)$ is a non-invertible matrix. Since $x$ is not in the decomposition of any point in $Y_{j'}$ for any $j'>i'$, neither is $y$. Hence, by \autoref{not decomposition}, there is a set $U_{1}\subset X_{i'}$ containing $y$ that is open in $X_{i'}$ with the property that no point in $U_{1}$ is in the decomposition of any point in $Y_{j'}$ for any $j'>i'$. Hence, as in case one, we are able to perturb $f$ on $U_{1}\cap (X_{i'}\setminus Y_{i'})$, while remaining in $A$. By shrinking $U_{1}$, we may assume that $\|f_{i'}(y)-f_{i'}(z)\|\leq \epsilon$ for all $z\in U_{1}$. By \autoref{empty interior}, we may assume that $Y_{i'}$ has empty interior and, thus, that there is a point $x'\in U_{1}\cap (X_{i'}\setminus Y_{i'})$. Choose a set $U_{2}$ which is open in $X_{i'}$ and satisfies $x'\in U_{2}\subset\overline{U_{2}}^{X_{i'}}\subset U_{1}\cap(X_{i'}\setminus Y_{i'})$. As in case one, we may define $f'\in A$ with $\|f-f'\|\leq \epsilon$, $f_{j'}'=f_{j'}$ for $j'
ot=i'$, $f_{i'}'|_{\overline{U_{2}}^{X_{i'}}}\equiv f_{i'}(y)$, and $f_{i'}'|_{X_{i'}\setminus(U_{1}\cap (X_{i'}\setminus Y_{i'}))}=f_{i'}|_{X_{i'}\setminus(U_{1}\cap (X_{i'}\setminus Y_{i'}))}$. Choose unitary matrices $W,V\in M_{n_{i'}}$ such that $Wf_{i'}(y)V$ has a zero cross at index $1$. Then the rest of the proof proceeds verbatim as the proof of case one with $i'$ in place of $i$ and $x'$ in place of $x$.
nodes.statement_short: Find a point where f is singular; perturb f to be constant near it (moving up to the last Y_{i'} containing it if needed), rotate by unitaries to a zero cross, and build Delta by Urysohn.

nodes.statement: Case one: $x$ is not in the decomposition of any point in $Y_{j}$ for any $j>i$. By \autoref{not decomposition}, there is set $U_{1}\subset X_{i}$ containing $x$, which is open in $X_{i}$ and has the property that no point in it is in the decomposition of any point in $Y_{j}$ for any $j>i$. Since $Y_{i}$ is closed in $X_{i}$, the set $U_{1}\cap(X_{i}\setminus Y_{i})$ is open in $X_{i}$. By shrinking $U_{1}$, we may assume that $\|f_{i}(x)-f_{i}(z)\|\leq\epsilon$ for all $z\in U_{1}$. Choose a set $U_{2}$ that is open in $X_{i}$ and satisfies $x\in U_{2}\subset\overline{U_{2}}^{X_{i}}\subset U_{1}\cap(X_{i}\setminus Y_{i})$.
nodes.statement_short: Find U_1 around x free of later decompositions and U_2 inside it

nodes.name: Perturb f
nodes.statement: Using Urysohn's Lemma, we can define a function $h\in C(X_{i},M_{n_{i}})$ such that $h|_{\overline{U_{2}}^{X_{i}}}\equiv f_{i}(x)$, $h|_{X_{i}\setminus(U_{1}\cap(X_{i}\setminus Y_{i}))}=f_{i}|_{X_{i}\setminus(U_{1}\cap(X_{i}\setminus Y_{i}))}$, and $\|f_{i}-h\|\leq\epsilon$. Define $f'$ coordinate-wise by $f':=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{i-1},h,f_{i+1},\ldots,f_{ l })$. Since $h|_{Y_{i}}=f_{i}|_{Y_{i}}$, we have $(f_{1},\ldots,f_{i-1},h)\in A^{(i)}$. Since no point in $U_{1}$ is in the decomposition of any point in $Y_{j}$ for any $j>i$, and because $h$ may only differ from $f_{i}$ on $U_{1}\cap (X_{i}\setminus Y_{i})\subset U_{1}$, this perturbation does not violate the diagonal decomposition at any point. Thus, $f'\in A$ since $f\in A$, and $\|f-f'\|\leq\epsilon$ because $\|f_{i}-h\|\leq\epsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Make f constant equal to f_i(x) near x, staying in A and epsilon-close

nodes.name: Unitaries w, v
nodes.statement: Since $f_{i}(x)$ is a non-invertible matrix, there are unitary matrices $W$ and $V$ in $M_{n_{i}}$ with the property that $Wf_{i}(x)V$ has a zero cross at index $1$. Since the unitary group in $M_{n_{i}}$ is connected we may, using the same reasoning as above, define unitaries $w,v\in A$ coordinate-wise with $w_{j}=v_{j}\equiv 1_{n_{j}}$ for all $j\not=i$ and $w_{i},v_{i}\in C(X_{i},M_{n_{i}})$ satisfying $w_{i}|_{\overline{U_{2}}^{X_{i}}}\equiv W$, $v_{i}|_{\overline{U_{2}}^{X_{i}}}\equiv V$, and $w_{i}|_{X_{i}\setminus(U_{1}\cap(X_{i}\setminus Y_{i}))}=v_{i}|_{X_{i}\setminus(U_{1}\cap(X_{i}\setminus Y_{i}))}\equiv 1_{n_{i}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Rotate f_i(x) to a zero cross at index 1 with unitaries extended over X_i

nodes.name: Delta and U
nodes.statement: Finally, choose a set $U_{3}$ that is open in $X_{i}$ and satisfies $x\in U_{3}\subset\overline{U_{3}}^{X_{i}}\subset U_{2}$. Define $\Delta\in A$ coordinate-wise as follows: $\Delta_{j}\equiv 0$ for $j\not=i$; let $g\colon X_{i}\to [0,1]$ be any continuous function such that $g|_{\overline{U_{3}}^{X_{i}}}\equiv 1$ and $g|_{X_{i}\setminus U_{2}}\equiv 0$, and put $\Delta_{i}:=\operatorname{diag}(g,0,\ldots,0)\in C(X_{i},M_{n_{i}})$. As argued above for $f'$, we have $\Delta\in A$. Take $U:=U_{3}$. Applying \autoref{open in spectrum}, we conclude $U$ is open in $\hat{A}$. Since $(wf'v)_{i}$ has a zero cross at index $1$ everywhere on $U_{2}$ and since $\Delta$ vanishes outside $U_{2}$, the lemma holds in this case.
nodes.statement_short: Define Delta by a Urysohn function and take U=U_3, open in the spectrum

nodes.name: Case two
nodes.statement: Case two: There is a $j>i$ such that $x$ is in the decomposition of some point in $Y_{j}$. In this case, we cannot define $f'$ as above, because we are not guaranteed a neighbourhood around $x$ in which we may freely perturb $f$ while remaining in $A$. Let $i'$ denote the largest integer for which $x$ is in the decomposition of some point in $Y_{i'}$. Choose $y\in Y_{i'}$ such that $x$ is in the decomposition of $y$. Then $f_{i'}(y)$ is a non-invertible matrix. Since $x$ is not in the decomposition of any point in $Y_{j'}$ for any $j'>i'$, neither is $y$. Hence, by \autoref{not decomposition}, there is a set $U_{1}\subset X_{i'}$ containing $y$ that is open in $X_{i'}$ with the property that no point in $U_{1}$ is in the decomposition of any point in $Y_{j'}$ for any $j'>i'$. Hence, as in case one, we are able to perturb $f$ on $U_{1}\cap (X_{i'}\setminus Y_{i'})$, while remaining in $A$. By shrinking $U_{1}$, we may assume that $\|f_{i'}(y)-f_{i'}(z)\|\leq \epsilon$ for all $z\in U_{1}$. By \autoref{empty interior}, we may assume that $Y_{i'}$ has empty interior and, thus, that there is a point $x'\in U_{1}\cap (X_{i'}\setminus Y_{i'})$. Choose a set $U_{2}$ which is open in $X_{i'}$ and satisfies $x'\in U_{2}\subset\overline{U_{2}}^{X_{i'}}\subset U_{1}\cap(X_{i'}\setminus Y_{i'})$. As in case one, we may define $f'\in A$ with $\|f-f'\|\leq \epsilon$, $f_{j'}'=f_{j'}$ for $j'\not=i'$, $f_{i'}'|_{\overline{U_{2}}^{X_{i'}}}\equiv f_{i'}(y)$, and $f_{i'}'|_{X_{i'}\setminus(U_{1}\cap (X_{i'}\setminus Y_{i'}))}=f_{i'}|_{X_{i'}\setminus(U_{1}\cap (X_{i'}\setminus Y_{i'}))}$. Choose unitary matrices $W,V\in M_{n_{i'}}$ such that $Wf_{i'}(y)V$ has a zero cross at index $1$. Then the rest of the proof proceeds verbatim as the proof of case one with $i'$ in place of $i$ and $x'$ in place of $x$.
nodes.statement_short: x appears in some later decomposition

nodes.name: Move to the last level
nodes.statement: Case two: There is a $j>i$ such that $x$ is in the decomposition of some point in $Y_{j}$. In this case, we cannot define $f'$ as above, because we are not guaranteed a neighbourhood around $x$ in which we may freely perturb $f$ while remaining in $A$. Let $i'$ denote the largest integer for which $x$ is in the decomposition of some point in $Y_{i'}$. Choose $y\in Y_{i'}$ such that $x$ is in the decomposition of $y$. Then $f_{i'}(y)$ is a non-invertible matrix. Since $x$ is not in the decomposition of any point in $Y_{j'}$ for any $j'>i'$, neither is $y$.
nodes.statement_short: Pass to y in Y_{i'} for the largest such i'

nodes.name: Free neighbourhood of y
nodes.statement: Hence, by \autoref{not decomposition}, there is a set $U_{1}\subset X_{i'}$ containing $y$ that is open in $X_{i'}$ with the property that no point in $U_{1}$ is in the decomposition of any point in $Y_{j'}$ for any $j'>i'$. Hence, as in case one, we are able to perturb $f$ on $U_{1}\cap (X_{i'}\setminus Y_{i'})$, while remaining in $A$. By shrinking $U_{1}$, we may assume that $\|f_{i'}(y)-f_{i'}(z)\|\leq \epsilon$ for all $z\in U_{1}$. By \autoref{empty interior}, we may assume that $Y_{i'}$ has empty interior and, thus, that there is a point $x'\in U_{1}\cap (X_{i'}\setminus Y_{i'})$. Choose a set $U_{2}$ which is open in $X_{i'}$ and satisfies $x'\in U_{2}\subset\overline{U_{2}}^{X_{i'}}\subset U_{1}\cap(X_{i'}\setminus Y_{i'})$.
nodes.statement_short: Find U_1 around y and an interior point x' using empty interior of Y_{i'}

nodes.name: Repeat case one
nodes.statement: As in case one, we may define $f'\in A$ with $\|f-f'\|\leq \epsilon$, $f_{j'}'=f_{j'}$ for $j'\not=i'$, $f_{i'}'|_{\overline{U_{2}}^{X_{i'}}}\equiv f_{i'}(y)$, and $f_{i'}'|_{X_{i'}\setminus(U_{1}\cap (X_{i'}\setminus Y_{i'}))}=f_{i'}|_{X_{i'}\setminus(U_{1}\cap (X_{i'}\setminus Y_{i'}))}$. Choose unitary matrices $W,V\in M_{n_{i'}}$ such that $Wf_{i'}(y)V$ has a zero cross at index $1$. Then the rest of the proof proceeds verbatim as the proof of case one with $i'$ in place of $i$ and $x'$ in place of $x$.
nodes.statement_short: Perturb near x' and finish as in case one

nodes.name: Indicator-like diagonal elements (preparatory)
nodes.statement: Suppose $A$ is a DSH algebra of length $ l $. Suppose $M\in\mathbb{N}$ and $K:=\{K_{1}< K_{2}<\cdots<K_{m}\}$ are such that $K_{1}\geq 0$, $K_{m}<\mathfrak{s}(A)-M$, and $K_{t+1}-K_{t}\geq M$ for $1\leq t < m$. Then, there is a function $\Phi\in A$ such that: \begin{enumerate} \item for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $x\in X_{i}$, $\Phi_{i}(x)$ is a diagonal matrix with entries in $[0,1]$ whose final $M$ diagonal entries are all $0$, and such that at most one of every $M$ consecutive diagonal entries is non-zero; \item for all $1\leq i\leq \ell$ and $1\leq j\leq n_{i}$: $\Phi_{i}(x)_{j,j}=1$ if and only if there is a $1\leq t\leq m$ such that $x\in B_{i,j-K_{t}}$. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: $A$ is a DSH algebra of length $ l $
$M\in\mathbb{N}$ and $K:=\{K_{1}< K_{2}<\cdots<K_{m}\}$ are such that $K_{1}\geq 0$, $K_{m}<\mathfrak{s}(A)-M$, and $K_{t+1}-K_{t}\geq M$ for $1\leq t < m$
conclusions: there is a function $\Phi\in A$ such that
nodes.statement_short: A diagonal element Phi in A with sparse entries in [0,1], equal to 1 exactly at indices j with x in some B_{i,j-K_t}.
nodes.label: indicatorprep

nodes.name: Construction of Phi
nodes.statement: We define $\Phi$ coordinate-wise inductively. To start, put $\Phi_{1}\equiv\operatorname{diag}(\chi_{K}(0),\ldots, \chi_{K}(n_{1}-1))$, where $\chi_{K}$ is the indicator function corresponding to the set $K=\{K_{1},\ldots,K_{m}\}$. By the assumption on the set $K$, condition \textit{(1)} holds for $\Phi_{1}$. To see that \textit{(2)} holds, suppose $\Phi_{1}(x)_{j,j}=1$. Then $\chi_{K}(j-1)=1$, so there is a $1\leq t\leq m$ such that $j=K_{t}+1$. By \autoref{Bik}, $x\in X_{1}= B_{1,1}=B_{1,j-K_{t}}$. Conversely, if there is a $1\leq t\leq m$ such that $x\in B_{1,j-K_{t}}$, then by \autoref{Bik}, $j-K_{t}=1$, so that $\Phi_{1}(x)_{j,j}=\chi_{K}(j-1)=1$, which proves \textit{(2)}. Now suppose we have a fixed $1<i\leq l $ and assume we have defined $(\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{i-1})\in A^{(i-1)}$ such that for all $i'<i$ and $x\in X_{i'}$: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\Roman*)] \item the matrix $\Phi_{i'}(x)$ satisfies the properties of conditions \textit{(1)} and \textit{(2)}; \item $\Phi_{i'}(x)_{j,j} = \chi_{K}(j-1)$ for all $1\leq j\leq \mathfrak{s}(A)$. \end{enumerate} Let $\Phi'_{i}:=\varphi_{i-1}((\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{i-1}))\in C(Y_{i},M_{n_{i}})$. Fix $y\in Y_{i}$ and suppose $y$ decomposes into $x_{1}\in X_{i_{1}}\setminus Y_{i_{1}},\ldots,x_{r}\in X_{i_{r}}\setminus Y_{i_{r}}$. Let us first check that conditions \textit{(1)} and \textit{(2)} hold for $\Phi_{i}'(y)=\operatorname{diag}(\Phi_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots,\Phi_{i_{r}}(x_{r}))$. By the inductive hypothesis, $\Phi_{i}(y)$ is a diagonal matrix with entries in $[0,1]$ and the last $M$ diagonal entries of $\Phi_{i}'(y)$ are all $0$. Given $M$ consecutive entries down the diagonal of $\Phi_{i}'(y)$, if they are all contained in one of the diagonal blocks, then by the inductive hypothesis applied to that one block, at most one of these entries is non-zero. If instead the $M$ consecutive entries span two blocks $\Phi_{i_{q}}(x_{q})$ and $\Phi_{i_{q+1}}(x_{q+1})$, then by the inductive hypothesis, the last $M$ diagonal entries of $\Phi_{i_{q}}(x_{q})$ are $0$ and at most $1$ of the first $M$ diagonal entries of $\Phi_{i_{q+1}}(x_{q+1})$ can be non-zero. This shows that \textit{(1)} holds for $\Phi_{i}'(y)$. Let us now show that \textit{(2)} holds for $\Phi_{i}'(y)$. Fix $1\leq j\leq n_{i}$. Let $1\leq q\leq r$ and $1\leq j'\leq n_{i_{q}}$ be such that $\Phi_{i}'(y)_{j,j}=\Phi_{i_{q}}(x_{q})_{j',j'}$. Note that $j=n_{i_{1}}+\cdots+n_{i_{q-1}}+j'$. Given $1\leq t\leq m$, we know by \autoref{Bik} that $y\in B_{i,j-K_{t}}$ if and only if there is a $1\leq p\leq r$ such that \begin{equation} j'-K_{t}+n_{i_{1}}+\cdots +n_{i_{q-1}}=j-K_{t}=1+n_{i_{1}}+\cdots+ n_{i_{p-1}} \end{equation} (the right-hand side is $1$ if $p=1$). We claim that if \autoref{pq} holds, then $p=q$. Indeed, using the upper and lower bounds on $j'$ and $K_{t}$, we have $$ 1-\mathfrak{s}(A)< 1-(\mathfrak{s}(A)-M-1)\leq j'-K_{t}\leq n_{i_{q}}, $$ whence $$ 1+n_{i_{1}}+\cdots+n_{i_{q-1}}-\mathfrak{s}(A)<1+n_{i_{1}}+\cdots +n_{i_{p-1}}\leq n_{i_{1}}+\cdots +n_{i_{q-1}}+n_{i_{q}}. $$ The first inequality and the definition of $\mathfrak{s}(A)$ imply that $q\leq p$, while the second inequality forces $q\geq p$, so that $p=q$. Therefore, since $x_{q}\in X_{i_{q}}\setminus Y_{i_{q}}$, the above and \autoref{Bik} show that $$ y\in B_{i,j-K_{t}}\iff j-K_{t}=1+n_{i_{1}}+\cdots+n_{i_{q-1}}\iff j'-K_{t}=1\iff x_{q}\in B_{i_{q},j'-K_{t}}. $$ Since the matrix $\Phi_{i_{q}}(x_{q})$ satisfies \textit{(2)} by the inductive hypothesis, it follows that there is a $1\leq t\leq m$ with $y\in B_{i,j-K_{t}}$ if and only if $\Phi_{i}'(y)_{j,j}=\Phi_{i_{q}}(x_{q})_{j',j'}=1$, which proves that \textit{(2)} holds for $\Phi_{i}'(y)$. Let us now define $\Phi_{i}\in C(X_{i},M_{n_{i}})$ to be a suitable extension of $\Phi_{i}'$. Write $\Phi_{i}'=\operatorname{diag}(h_{1}',\ldots,h_{n_{i}}')$, where $h'_{j}\in C(Y_{i},[0,1])$ for $1\leq j\leq n_{i}$. We define $\Phi_{i}=\operatorname{diag}(h_{1},\ldots,h_{n_{i}})$ by specifying each $h_{j}$ to be a continuous function $h_{j}\colon X_{i}\to [0,1]$ that extends $h_{j}'$. For $1\leq j\leq \mathfrak{s}(A)$, put $h_{j}\equiv \chi_{K}(j-1)$ to insure that (II) in the inductive hypothesis is verified and set $h_{j}\equiv 0$ for $n_{i}-M+1\leq j\leq n_{i}$ (since (I) and (II) hold for $\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{i-1}$, these $h_{j}$'s do indeed extend the corresponding $h_{j}'$'s). We define $h_{j}$ for $\mathfrak{s}(A)+1\leq j\leq n_{i}-M$ inductively. Fix $\mathfrak{s}(A)+1\leq j\leq n_{i}-M$ and assume we have defined $h_{1},\ldots,h_{j-1}$ so that the following property holds: \begin{itemize} \item[($\clubsuit$)] $\bigcup_{t=1}^{M-1}\overline{\operatorname{supp}(h_{j-t})}\subset X_{i}$ is disjoint from $\operatorname{supp}(h_{j}')\subset Y_{i}$. \end{itemize} Note that $\bigcup_{t=1}^{M-1}\overline{\operatorname{supp}(h_{\mathfrak{s}(A)+1-t})}=\varnothing$, and so ($\clubsuit$) holds for the base case $j=\mathfrak{s}(A)+1$. Since $X_{i}$ is a metric space and, hence, perfectly normal, we may use $(\clubsuit)$ to extend $h_{j}'$ to a function $f_{j}$ in $C(X_{i},[0,1])$ that vanishes on $\bigcup_{t=1}^{M-1}\overline{\operatorname{supp}(h_{j-t})}$ and is strictly less than $1$ on $X_{i}\setminus Y_{i}$. Define $g^{0}_{j}:=h_{j}'-\sum_{t=1}^{M-1}h_{j+t}'\in C(Y_{i})$. Then the range of $g_{j}^{0}$ is contained in $[-1,1]$ since by (I) at most one of $h_{j}',\ldots,h_{j+M-1}'$ is non-zero at any given point in $Y_{i}$. Extend $g_{j}^{0}$ to a function $g_{j}'$ in $C(X_{i},[-1,1])$. Put $g_{j}:=\max(g_{j}',0)$ and note that $g_{j}|_{Y_{i}}=h_{j}'$. Since $h_{j}'(y)=0$ for each $y\in \bigcup_{t=1}^{M-1}\operatorname{supp}(h_{j+t}')$, we may choose an open subset $U\supset \bigcup_{t=1}^{M-1}\operatorname{supp}(h_{j+t}')$ of $X_{i}$ on which $g_{j}'$ is strictly negative, so that $g_{j}|_{U}\equiv 0$. Define $h_{j}:=\min(f_{j},g_{j})\in C(X_{i},[0,1])$ and note that $h_{j}|_{Y_{i}}=h_{j}'$. Since $h_{j}|_{U}\equiv 0$, we have $\operatorname{supp}(h_{j})\cap U=\varnothing$, from which it follows that $\overline{\operatorname{supp}(h_{j})}\cap\left(\bigcup_{t=1}^{M-1}\operatorname{supp}(h_{j+t}')\right)=\varnothing$. This ensures that $(\clubsuit)$ holds with $j+1$ in place of $j$ and, hence, that $\Phi_{i}:=\operatorname{diag}(h_{1},\ldots,h_{n_{i}})$ is well defined. To conclude the proof, let us check that $\Phi_{i}$ satisfies \textit{(1)} and \textit{(2)}. In light of the analysis above, we may restrict ourselves to the diagonal entries $\mathfrak{s}(A)+1\leq j\leq n_{i}-M$. By definition, the range of each $h_{j}$ is contained in $[0,1]$. If $h_{j}(x)>0$ for some $x\in X_{i}$, then $f_{j}(x)>0$ and, hence, by the definition of $f_{j}$, $x\notin \bigcup_{t=1}^{M-1}\overline{\operatorname{supp}(h_{j-t})}$. This proves that at most one of any $M$ consecutive entries down the diagonal of $\Phi_{i}(x)$ is non-zero. Hence, \textit{(1)} is established. To prove \textit{(2)}, suppose $x\in X_{i}$ satisfies $h_{j}(x)=1$. Then $f_{j}(x)=1$, which implies that $x\in Y_{i}$. Thus $h_{j}'(x)=1$ and we already established that $x\in B_{i,j-K_{t}}$ for some $t$ in this case. Conversely, suppose $x\in B_{i,j-K_{t}}$ for some $t$. If $j-K_{t}\not=1$, then by \autoref{Bik}, $x\in Y_{i}$ and we already concluded in this case that $h_{j}(x)=h_{j}'(x)=1$. If instead $j-K_{t}=1$, then it must be that $j< \mathfrak{s}(A)$ and we previously defined $h_{j}\equiv 1$ in this case. Therefore, property \textit{(2)} holds. We verified that both (I) and (II) hold for $\Phi_{i}=\operatorname{diag}(h_{1},\ldots,h_{ l })$, and since $\Phi_{i}|_{Y_{i}}=\Phi_{i}'=\varphi_{i-1}((\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{i-1}))$, it follows that $(\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{i})\in A^{(i)}$. Thus, by induction, we obtain $\Phi:=(\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{ l })\in A$, which satisfies the requirements of the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Define Phi coordinate-wise by induction on i; on Y_i it is forced by the pullback, then extend each diagonal entry carefully using perfect normality of metric spaces. Key step: an extension h_j=min(f_j,g_j) keeping supports of nearby entries disjoint.

nodes.name: Base case Phi_1
nodes.statement: We define $\Phi$ coordinate-wise inductively. To start, put $\Phi_{1}\equiv\operatorname{diag}(\chi_{K}(0),\ldots, \chi_{K}(n_{1}-1))$, where $\chi_{K}$ is the indicator function corresponding to the set $K=\{K_{1},\ldots,K_{m}\}$. By the assumption on the set $K$, condition \textit{(1)} holds for $\Phi_{1}$. To see that \textit{(2)} holds, suppose $\Phi_{1}(x)_{j,j}=1$. Then $\chi_{K}(j-1)=1$, so there is a $1\leq t\leq m$ such that $j=K_{t}+1$. By \autoref{Bik}, $x\in X_{1}= B_{1,1}=B_{1,j-K_{t}}$. Conversely, if there is a $1\leq t\leq m$ such that $x\in B_{1,j-K_{t}}$, then by \autoref{Bik}, $j-K_{t}=1$, so that $\Phi_{1}(x)_{j,j}=\chi_{K}(j-1)=1$, which proves \textit{(2)}.
nodes.statement_short: Phi_1 is the constant indicator of K shifted by one; check (1) and (2)

nodes.name: Pullback level
nodes.statement: Now suppose we have a fixed $1<i\leq l $ and assume we have defined $(\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{i-1})\in A^{(i-1)}$ such that for all $i'<i$ and $x\in X_{i'}$: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\Roman*)] \item the matrix $\Phi_{i'}(x)$ satisfies the properties of conditions \textit{(1)} and \textit{(2)}; \item $\Phi_{i'}(x)_{j,j} = \chi_{K}(j-1)$ for all $1\leq j\leq \mathfrak{s}(A)$. \end{enumerate} Let $\Phi'_{i}:=\varphi_{i-1}((\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{i-1}))\in C(Y_{i},M_{n_{i}})$. Fix $y\in Y_{i}$ and suppose $y$ decomposes into $x_{1}\in X_{i_{1}}\setminus Y_{i_{1}},\ldots,x_{r}\in X_{i_{r}}\setminus Y_{i_{r}}$. Let us first check that conditions \textit{(1)} and \textit{(2)} hold for $\Phi_{i}'(y)=\operatorname{diag}(\Phi_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots,\Phi_{i_{r}}(x_{r}))$. By the inductive hypothesis, $\Phi_{i}(y)$ is a diagonal matrix with entries in $[0,1]$ and the last $M$ diagonal entries of $\Phi_{i}'(y)$ are all $0$. Given $M$ consecutive entries down the diagonal of $\Phi_{i}'(y)$, if they are all contained in one of the diagonal blocks, then by the inductive hypothesis applied to that one block, at most one of these entries is non-zero. If instead the $M$ consecutive entries span two blocks $\Phi_{i_{q}}(x_{q})$ and $\Phi_{i_{q+1}}(x_{q+1})$, then by the inductive hypothesis, the last $M$ diagonal entries of $\Phi_{i_{q}}(x_{q})$ are $0$ and at most $1$ of the first $M$ diagonal entries of $\Phi_{i_{q+1}}(x_{q+1})$ can be non-zero. This shows that \textit{(1)} holds for $\Phi_{i}'(y)$. Let us now show that \textit{(2)} holds for $\Phi_{i}'(y)$. Fix $1\leq j\leq n_{i}$. Let $1\leq q\leq r$ and $1\leq j'\leq n_{i_{q}}$ be such that $\Phi_{i}'(y)_{j,j}=\Phi_{i_{q}}(x_{q})_{j',j'}$. Note that $j=n_{i_{1}}+\cdots+n_{i_{q-1}}+j'$. Given $1\leq t\leq m$, we know by \autoref{Bik} that $y\in B_{i,j-K_{t}}$ if and only if there is a $1\leq p\leq r$ such that \begin{equation} j'-K_{t}+n_{i_{1}}+\cdots +n_{i_{q-1}}=j-K_{t}=1+n_{i_{1}}+\cdots+ n_{i_{p-1}} \end{equation} (the right-hand side is $1$ if $p=1$). We claim that if \autoref{pq} holds, then $p=q$. Indeed, using the upper and lower bounds on $j'$ and $K_{t}$, we have $$ 1-\mathfrak{s}(A)< 1-(\mathfrak{s}(A)-M-1)\leq j'-K_{t}\leq n_{i_{q}}, $$ whence $$ 1+n_{i_{1}}+\cdots+n_{i_{q-1}}-\mathfrak{s}(A)<1+n_{i_{1}}+\cdots +n_{i_{p-1}}\leq n_{i_{1}}+\cdots +n_{i_{q-1}}+n_{i_{q}}. $$ The first inequality and the definition of $\mathfrak{s}(A)$ imply that $q\leq p$, while the second inequality forces $q\geq p$, so that $p=q$. Therefore, since $x_{q}\in X_{i_{q}}\setminus Y_{i_{q}}$, the above and \autoref{Bik} show that $$ y\in B_{i,j-K_{t}}\iff j-K_{t}=1+n_{i_{1}}+\cdots+n_{i_{q-1}}\iff j'-K_{t}=1\iff x_{q}\in B_{i_{q},j'-K_{t}}. $$ Since the matrix $\Phi_{i_{q}}(x_{q})$ satisfies \textit{(2)} by the inductive hypothesis, it follows that there is a $1\leq t\leq m$ with $y\in B_{i,j-K_{t}}$ if and only if $\Phi_{i}'(y)_{j,j}=\Phi_{i_{q}}(x_{q})_{j',j'}=1$, which proves that \textit{(2)} holds for $\Phi_{i}'(y)$.
nodes.statement_short: Check (1) and (2) for the forced values Phi_i' on Y_i

nodes.name: Inductive hypothesis
nodes.statement: Now suppose we have a fixed $1<i\leq l $ and assume we have defined $(\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{i-1})\in A^{(i-1)}$ such that for all $i'<i$ and $x\in X_{i'}$:
nodes.statement_short: Assume Phi_1..Phi_{i-1} satisfy:

nodes.name: Hypothesis (I)
nodes.statement: the matrix $\Phi_{i'}(x)$ satisfies the properties of conditions \textit{(1)} and \textit{(2)};
nodes.statement_short: Conditions (1) and (2) hold at earlier levels

nodes.name: Hypothesis (II)
nodes.statement: $\Phi_{i'}(x)_{j,j} = \chi_{K}(j-1)$ for all $1\leq j\leq \mathfrak{s}(A)$.
nodes.statement_short: The first s(A) entries are the indicator of K

nodes.name: Condition (1) on Y_i
nodes.statement: Let $\Phi'_{i}:=\varphi_{i-1}((\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{i-1}))\in C(Y_{i},M_{n_{i}})$. Fix $y\in Y_{i}$ and suppose $y$ decomposes into $x_{1}\in X_{i_{1}}\setminus Y_{i_{1}},\ldots,x_{r}\in X_{i_{r}}\setminus Y_{i_{r}}$. Let us first check that conditions \textit{(1)} and \textit{(2)} hold for $\Phi_{i}'(y)=\operatorname{diag}(\Phi_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots,\Phi_{i_{r}}(x_{r}))$. By the inductive hypothesis, $\Phi_{i}(y)$ is a diagonal matrix with entries in $[0,1]$ and the last $M$ diagonal entries of $\Phi_{i}'(y)$ are all $0$. Given $M$ consecutive entries down the diagonal of $\Phi_{i}'(y)$, if they are all contained in one of the diagonal blocks, then by the inductive hypothesis applied to that one block, at most one of these entries is non-zero. If instead the $M$ consecutive entries span two blocks $\Phi_{i_{q}}(x_{q})$ and $\Phi_{i_{q+1}}(x_{q+1})$, then by the inductive hypothesis, the last $M$ diagonal entries of $\Phi_{i_{q}}(x_{q})$ are $0$ and at most $1$ of the first $M$ diagonal entries of $\Phi_{i_{q+1}}(x_{q+1})$ can be non-zero. This shows that \textit{(1)} holds for $\Phi_{i}'(y)$.
nodes.statement_short: Blocks of Phi_i'(y) satisfy (1), also across block boundaries

nodes.name: Index bookkeeping for (2)
nodes.statement: Let us now show that \textit{(2)} holds for $\Phi_{i}'(y)$. Fix $1\leq j\leq n_{i}$. Let $1\leq q\leq r$ and $1\leq j'\leq n_{i_{q}}$ be such that $\Phi_{i}'(y)_{j,j}=\Phi_{i_{q}}(x_{q})_{j',j'}$. Note that $j=n_{i_{1}}+\cdots+n_{i_{q-1}}+j'$. Given $1\leq t\leq m$, we know by \autoref{Bik} that $y\in B_{i,j-K_{t}}$ if and only if there is a $1\leq p\leq r$ such that \begin{equation} j'-K_{t}+n_{i_{1}}+\cdots +n_{i_{q-1}}=j-K_{t}=1+n_{i_{1}}+\cdots+ n_{i_{p-1}} \end{equation} (the right-hand side is $1$ if $p=1$).
nodes.statement_short: Express membership in B_{i,j-K_t} by an index equation

nodes.name: Claim: p = q
nodes.statement: We claim that if \autoref{pq} holds, then $p=q$. Indeed, using the upper and lower bounds on $j'$ and $K_{t}$, we have $$ 1-\mathfrak{s}(A)< 1-(\mathfrak{s}(A)-M-1)\leq j'-K_{t}\leq n_{i_{q}}, $$ whence $$ 1+n_{i_{1}}+\cdots+n_{i_{q-1}}-\mathfrak{s}(A)<1+n_{i_{1}}+\cdots +n_{i_{p-1}}\leq n_{i_{1}}+\cdots +n_{i_{q-1}}+n_{i_{q}}. $$ The first inequality and the definition of $\mathfrak{s}(A)$ imply that $q\leq p$, while the second inequality forces $q\geq p$, so that $p=q$.
nodes.statement_short: Bounds on j' and K_t force p = q

nodes.name: Inequalities
nodes.statement: Indeed, using the upper and lower bounds on $j'$ and $K_{t}$, we have $$ 1-\mathfrak{s}(A)< 1-(\mathfrak{s}(A)-M-1)\leq j'-K_{t}\leq n_{i_{q}}, $$ whence $$ 1+n_{i_{1}}+\cdots+n_{i_{q-1}}-\mathfrak{s}(A)<1+n_{i_{1}}+\cdots +n_{i_{p-1}}\leq n_{i_{1}}+\cdots +n_{i_{q-1}}+n_{i_{q}}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Derive two-sided bounds on the block start

nodes.name: Conclude p = q
nodes.statement: The first inequality and the definition of $\mathfrak{s}(A)$ imply that $q\leq p$, while the second inequality forces $q\geq p$, so that $p=q$.
nodes.statement_short: The bounds force q <= p <= q

nodes.name: Condition (2) on Y_i
nodes.statement: Therefore, since $x_{q}\in X_{i_{q}}\setminus Y_{i_{q}}$, the above and \autoref{Bik} show that $$ y\in B_{i,j-K_{t}}\iff j-K_{t}=1+n_{i_{1}}+\cdots+n_{i_{q-1}}\iff j'-K_{t}=1\iff x_{q}\in B_{i_{q},j'-K_{t}}. $$ Since the matrix $\Phi_{i_{q}}(x_{q})$ satisfies \textit{(2)} by the inductive hypothesis, it follows that there is a $1\leq t\leq m$ with $y\in B_{i,j-K_{t}}$ if and only if $\Phi_{i}'(y)_{j,j}=\Phi_{i_{q}}(x_{q})_{j',j'}=1$, which proves that \textit{(2)} holds for $\Phi_{i}'(y)$.
nodes.statement_short: Membership reduces to the block x_q, where (2) holds by induction

nodes.name: Extend Phi_i' to X_i
nodes.statement: Let us now define $\Phi_{i}\in C(X_{i},M_{n_{i}})$ to be a suitable extension of $\Phi_{i}'$. Write $\Phi_{i}'=\operatorname{diag}(h_{1}',\ldots,h_{n_{i}}')$, where $h'_{j}\in C(Y_{i},[0,1])$ for $1\leq j\leq n_{i}$. We define $\Phi_{i}=\operatorname{diag}(h_{1},\ldots,h_{n_{i}})$ by specifying each $h_{j}$ to be a continuous function $h_{j}\colon X_{i}\to [0,1]$ that extends $h_{j}'$. For $1\leq j\leq \mathfrak{s}(A)$, put $h_{j}\equiv \chi_{K}(j-1)$ to insure that (II) in the inductive hypothesis is verified and set $h_{j}\equiv 0$ for $n_{i}-M+1\leq j\leq n_{i}$ (since (I) and (II) hold for $\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{i-1}$, these $h_{j}$'s do indeed extend the corresponding $h_{j}'$'s). We define $h_{j}$ for $\mathfrak{s}(A)+1\leq j\leq n_{i}-M$ inductively. Fix $\mathfrak{s}(A)+1\leq j\leq n_{i}-M$ and assume we have defined $h_{1},\ldots,h_{j-1}$ so that the following property holds: \begin{itemize} \item[($\clubsuit$)] $\bigcup_{t=1}^{M-1}\overline{\operatorname{supp}(h_{j-t})}\subset X_{i}$ is disjoint from $\operatorname{supp}(h_{j}')\subset Y_{i}$. \end{itemize} Note that $\bigcup_{t=1}^{M-1}\overline{\operatorname{supp}(h_{\mathfrak{s}(A)+1-t})}=\varnothing$, and so ($\clubsuit$) holds for the base case $j=\mathfrak{s}(A)+1$. Since $X_{i}$ is a metric space and, hence, perfectly normal, we may use $(\clubsuit)$ to extend $h_{j}'$ to a function $f_{j}$ in $C(X_{i},[0,1])$ that vanishes on $\bigcup_{t=1}^{M-1}\overline{\operatorname{supp}(h_{j-t})}$ and is strictly less than $1$ on $X_{i}\setminus Y_{i}$. Define $g^{0}_{j}:=h_{j}'-\sum_{t=1}^{M-1}h_{j+t}'\in C(Y_{i})$. Then the range of $g_{j}^{0}$ is contained in $[-1,1]$ since by (I) at most one of $h_{j}',\ldots,h_{j+M-1}'$ is non-zero at any given point in $Y_{i}$. Extend $g_{j}^{0}$ to a function $g_{j}'$ in $C(X_{i},[-1,1])$. Put $g_{j}:=\max(g_{j}',0)$ and note that $g_{j}|_{Y_{i}}=h_{j}'$. Since $h_{j}'(y)=0$ for each $y\in \bigcup_{t=1}^{M-1}\operatorname{supp}(h_{j+t}')$, we may choose an open subset $U\supset \bigcup_{t=1}^{M-1}\operatorname{supp}(h_{j+t}')$ of $X_{i}$ on which $g_{j}'$ is strictly negative, so that $g_{j}|_{U}\equiv 0$. Define $h_{j}:=\min(f_{j},g_{j})\in C(X_{i},[0,1])$ and note that $h_{j}|_{Y_{i}}=h_{j}'$. Since $h_{j}|_{U}\equiv 0$, we have $\operatorname{supp}(h_{j})\cap U=\varnothing$, from which it follows that $\overline{\operatorname{supp}(h_{j})}\cap\left(\bigcup_{t=1}^{M-1}\operatorname{supp}(h_{j+t}')\right)=\varnothing$. This ensures that $(\clubsuit)$ holds with $j+1$ in place of $j$ and, hence, that $\Phi_{i}:=\operatorname{diag}(h_{1},\ldots,h_{n_{i}})$ is well defined.
nodes.statement_short: Extend each diagonal entry, inductively in j, keeping supports separated

nodes.name: Fixed entries
nodes.statement: Let us now define $\Phi_{i}\in C(X_{i},M_{n_{i}})$ to be a suitable extension of $\Phi_{i}'$. Write $\Phi_{i}'=\operatorname{diag}(h_{1}',\ldots,h_{n_{i}}')$, where $h'_{j}\in C(Y_{i},[0,1])$ for $1\leq j\leq n_{i}$. We define $\Phi_{i}=\operatorname{diag}(h_{1},\ldots,h_{n_{i}})$ by specifying each $h_{j}$ to be a continuous function $h_{j}\colon X_{i}\to [0,1]$ that extends $h_{j}'$. For $1\leq j\leq \mathfrak{s}(A)$, put $h_{j}\equiv \chi_{K}(j-1)$ to insure that (II) in the inductive hypothesis is verified and set $h_{j}\equiv 0$ for $n_{i}-M+1\leq j\leq n_{i}$ (since (I) and (II) hold for $\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{i-1}$, these $h_{j}$'s do indeed extend the corresponding $h_{j}'$'s). We define $h_{j}$ for $\mathfrak{s}(A)+1\leq j\leq n_{i}-M$ inductively. Fix $\mathfrak{s}(A)+1\leq j\leq n_{i}-M$ and assume we have defined $h_{1},\ldots,h_{j-1}$ so that the following property holds:
nodes.statement_short: Fix the first s(A) and last M entries; extend the rest inductively under:

nodes.name: Support condition (club)
nodes.statement: [($\clubsuit$)] $\bigcup_{t=1}^{M-1}\overline{\operatorname{supp}(h_{j-t})}\subset X_{i}$ is disjoint from $\operatorname{supp}(h_{j}')\subset Y_{i}$.
nodes.statement_short: Earlier supports avoid the support of h_j'

nodes.name: Base of inner induction
nodes.statement: Note that $\bigcup_{t=1}^{M-1}\overline{\operatorname{supp}(h_{\mathfrak{s}(A)+1-t})}=\varnothing$, and so ($\clubsuit$) holds for the base case $j=\mathfrak{s}(A)+1$.
nodes.statement_short: Condition (club) holds at j=s(A)+1

nodes.name: Auxiliary extensions f_j, g_j
nodes.statement: Since $X_{i}$ is a metric space and, hence, perfectly normal, we may use $(\clubsuit)$ to extend $h_{j}'$ to a function $f_{j}$ in $C(X_{i},[0,1])$ that vanishes on $\bigcup_{t=1}^{M-1}\overline{\operatorname{supp}(h_{j-t})}$ and is strictly less than $1$ on $X_{i}\setminus Y_{i}$. Define $g^{0}_{j}:=h_{j}'-\sum_{t=1}^{M-1}h_{j+t}'\in C(Y_{i})$. Then the range of $g_{j}^{0}$ is contained in $[-1,1]$ since by (I) at most one of $h_{j}',\ldots,h_{j+M-1}'$ is non-zero at any given point in $Y_{i}$. Extend $g_{j}^{0}$ to a function $g_{j}'$ in $C(X_{i},[-1,1])$. Put $g_{j}:=\max(g_{j}',0)$ and note that $g_{j}|_{Y_{i}}=h_{j}'$.
nodes.statement_short: Use perfect normality to build f_j and g_j

nodes.name: Define h_j
nodes.statement: Since $h_{j}'(y)=0$ for each $y\in \bigcup_{t=1}^{M-1}\operatorname{supp}(h_{j+t}')$, we may choose an open subset $U\supset \bigcup_{t=1}^{M-1}\operatorname{supp}(h_{j+t}')$ of $X_{i}$ on which $g_{j}'$ is strictly negative, so that $g_{j}|_{U}\equiv 0$. Define $h_{j}:=\min(f_{j},g_{j})\in C(X_{i},[0,1])$ and note that $h_{j}|_{Y_{i}}=h_{j}'$. Since $h_{j}|_{U}\equiv 0$, we have $\operatorname{supp}(h_{j})\cap U=\varnothing$, from which it follows that $\overline{\operatorname{supp}(h_{j})}\cap\left(\bigcup_{t=1}^{M-1}\operatorname{supp}(h_{j+t}')\right)=\varnothing$. This ensures that $(\clubsuit)$ holds with $j+1$ in place of $j$ and, hence, that $\Phi_{i}:=\operatorname{diag}(h_{1},\ldots,h_{n_{i}})$ is well defined.
nodes.statement_short: h_j = min(f_j, g_j) extends h_j' and keeps (club) for j+1

nodes.name: Verify (1) and (2) for Phi_i
nodes.statement: To conclude the proof, let us check that $\Phi_{i}$ satisfies \textit{(1)} and \textit{(2)}. In light of the analysis above, we may restrict ourselves to the diagonal entries $\mathfrak{s}(A)+1\leq j\leq n_{i}-M$. By definition, the range of each $h_{j}$ is contained in $[0,1]$. If $h_{j}(x)>0$ for some $x\in X_{i}$, then $f_{j}(x)>0$ and, hence, by the definition of $f_{j}$, $x\notin \bigcup_{t=1}^{M-1}\overline{\operatorname{supp}(h_{j-t})}$. This proves that at most one of any $M$ consecutive entries down the diagonal of $\Phi_{i}(x)$ is non-zero. Hence, \textit{(1)} is established. To prove \textit{(2)}, suppose $x\in X_{i}$ satisfies $h_{j}(x)=1$. Then $f_{j}(x)=1$, which implies that $x\in Y_{i}$. Thus $h_{j}'(x)=1$ and we already established that $x\in B_{i,j-K_{t}}$ for some $t$ in this case. Conversely, suppose $x\in B_{i,j-K_{t}}$ for some $t$. If $j-K_{t}\not=1$, then by \autoref{Bik}, $x\in Y_{i}$ and we already concluded in this case that $h_{j}(x)=h_{j}'(x)=1$. If instead $j-K_{t}=1$, then it must be that $j< \mathfrak{s}(A)$ and we previously defined $h_{j}\equiv 1$ in this case. Therefore, property \textit{(2)} holds.
nodes.statement_short: Supports give sparsity; h_j(x)=1 only on Y_i where (2) holds

nodes.name: Close the induction
nodes.statement: We verified that both (I) and (II) hold for $\Phi_{i}=\operatorname{diag}(h_{1},\ldots,h_{ l })$, and since $\Phi_{i}|_{Y_{i}}=\Phi_{i}'=\varphi_{i-1}((\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{i-1}))$, it follows that $(\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{i})\in A^{(i)}$. Thus, by induction, we obtain $\Phi:=(\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{ l })\in A$, which satisfies the requirements of the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Phi_i agrees with phi_{i-1} on Y_i, so Phi lies in A

nodes.name: Index condition for membership in B_{i,j-K_t}
nodes.label: pq

nodes.name: Indicator-like diagonal elements
nodes.statement: Suppose $A$ is a DSH algebra of length $ l $. Suppose $M\in\mathbb{N}$ and $K:=\{K_{1}< K_{2}<\cdots<K_{m}\}$ are such that $K_{1}\geq 0$, $K_{m}<\mathfrak{s}(A)-M$, and $K_{t+1}-K_{t}\geq M$ for $1\leq t < m$. Suppose that for each $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq j\leq n_{i}$, we have a set $F_{i,j}\subset X_{i}$ that is closed in $X_{i}$ and disjoint from each set $B_{i,j-K_{t}}$ (see \autoref{Bik def}) for $1\leq t\leq m$. Then, there is a function $\Theta\in A$ such that: \begin{enumerate} \item for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $x\in X_{i}$, $\Theta_{i}(x)$ is a diagonal matrix with entries in $[0,1]$ whose final $M$ diagonal entries are all $0$, and such that at most one of every $M$ consecutive diagonal entries is non-zero; \item for all $1\leq i\leq l $, $1\leq j\leq n_{i}$, and $x\in F_{i,j}$, we have $\Theta_{i}(x)_{j,j}=0$; \item for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq j\leq n_{i}$, there is a (possibly empty) open subset $U_{i,j}\subset X_{i}$ containing $B_{i,j}$ with the property that if $x\in U_{i,j}$, then $\Theta_{i}(x)_{j+K_{t},j+K_{t}}=1$ for all $1\leq t\leq m$. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: $A$ is a DSH algebra of length $ l $
$M\in\mathbb{N}$ and $K:=\{K_{1}< K_{2}<\cdots<K_{m}\}$ are such that $K_{1}\geq 0$, $K_{m}<\mathfrak{s}(A)-M$, and $K_{t+1}-K_{t}\geq M$ for $1\leq t < m$
for each $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq j\leq n_{i}$, we have a set $F_{i,j}\subset X_{i}$ that is closed in $X_{i}$ and disjoint from each set $B_{i,j-K_{t}}$
conclusions: there is a function $\Theta\in A$ such that
nodes.statement_short: A sparse diagonal element Theta vanishing on prescribed closed sets F_{i,j} and equal to 1 near B_{i,j} at the shifted indices j+K_t.
nodes.label: indicators

nodes.name: Construction of Theta
nodes.statement: Using the hypotheses of this lemma, \autoref{indicatorprep} furnishes a function $\Phi\in A$ such that: \begin{enumerate}[font=\itshape, label=(\alph*)] \item for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $x\in X_{i}$, $\Phi_{i}(x)$ is a diagonal matrix with entries in $[0,1]$ whose final $M$ diagonal entries are all $0$, and such that at most one of every $M$ consecutive diagonal entries is non-zero; \item for all $1\leq i\leq \ell$ and $1\leq j\leq n_{i}$: $\Phi_{i}(x)_{j,j}=1$ if and only if there is a $1\leq t\leq m$ such that $x\in B_{i,j-K_{t}}$. \end{enumerate} Let us use $\Phi$ to construct a function $\Theta\in A$ satisfying conditions \textit{(1)} to \textit{(3)}. Given $\delta\in [0,1)$, define $g\colon[0,1]\to[0,1]$ by $$ \begin{aligned} g(x):= \begin{cases} 0& \text{ if } 0\leq x\leq\delta\\ \text{linear} &\text{ if } \delta\leq x\leq\frac{1+\delta}{2}\\ 1&\text{ if } \frac{1+\delta}{2}\leq x\leq 1. \end{cases} \end{aligned} $$ For $1\leq i\leq l $, define $\Theta_{i}\colon X_{i}\to M_{n_{i}}$ by $$ \Theta_{i}(x):=\operatorname{diag}(g(\Phi_{i}(x)_{1,1}),\ldots,g(\Phi_{i}(x)_{n_{i},n_{i}})). $$ Then $\Theta:=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{ l }\Theta_{i}\in\bigoplus_{i=1}^{ l }C(X_{i},M_{n_{i}})$. Since each diagonal entry of $\Phi$ is modified in the same way in the definition of $\Theta$, it is straightforward to check that $\Theta$ is compatible with the diagonal structure of $A$. Hence, $\Theta\in A$. Moreover, since $\Theta_{i}(x)_{j,j}=0$ whenever $\Phi_{i}(x)_{j,j}=0$, it is clear that $\Theta$ satisfies \textit{(1)} since $\Phi$ satisfies \textit{(a)}. To see that $\Theta$ satisfies \textit{(2)}, fix $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq j\leq n_{i}$. Since $F_{i,j}$ is disjoint from each $B_{i,j-K_{t}}$ (for $1\leq t\leq m$), condition \textit{(b)} guarantees that $\Phi_{i}(x)_{j,j}<1$ for all $x\in F_{i,j}$. Since $F_{i,j}$ is compact, there is a $\delta_{i,j}\in [0,1)$ such that $\Phi_{i}(x)_{j,j}\leq \delta_{i,j}$ for all $x\in F_{i,j}$. On choosing $\delta:=\max\{\delta_{i,j}:1\leq i\leq l ,1\leq j\leq n_{i}\}\in [0,1)$ in our definition of $g$ above, it follows that $\Theta_{i}(x)_{j,j}=0$ whenever $1\leq i\leq l $, $1\leq j\leq n_{i}$, and $x\in F_{i,j}$, which proves \textit{(2)}. Finally, to see that $\Theta$ satisfies \textit{(3)}, fix $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq j\leq n_{i}$. If $j>n_{i}-(\mathfrak{s}(A)-1)$, we may take $U_{i,j}=\varnothing$ since $B_{i,j}=\varnothing$ by \autoref{Bik} for such $j$. For $j\leq n_{i}-(\mathfrak{s}(A)-1)$, note that if $x\in B_{i,j}$, then by \textit{(b)}, $\Phi_{i}(x)_{j+K_{t},j+K_{t}}=1$ for all $1\leq t\leq m$. Since $g$ is $1$ in a neighbourhood of $1$, it follows that for each $t$, there is an open set $U_{t}\supset B_{i,j}$ on which the function $\Theta_{i}(\,\cdot\,)_{j+K_{t},j+K_{t}}\colon X_{i}\to [0,1]$ is equal to $1$. Taking $U_{i,j}:=\bigcap_{1\leq t\leq m} U_{t}$ yields \textit{(3)} and proves the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Apply a continuous cutoff g (0 below delta, 1 near 1) entrywise to Phi from the preparatory lemma; compactness of F_{i,j} gives delta<1.

nodes.name: Obtain Phi
nodes.statement: Using the hypotheses of this lemma, \autoref{indicatorprep} furnishes a function $\Phi\in A$ such that: \begin{enumerate}[font=\itshape, label=(\alph*)] \item for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $x\in X_{i}$, $\Phi_{i}(x)$ is a diagonal matrix with entries in $[0,1]$ whose final $M$ diagonal entries are all $0$, and such that at most one of every $M$ consecutive diagonal entries is non-zero; \item for all $1\leq i\leq \ell$ and $1\leq j\leq n_{i}$: $\Phi_{i}(x)_{j,j}=1$ if and only if there is a $1\leq t\leq m$ such that $x\in B_{i,j-K_{t}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the preparatory lemma

nodes.name: Apply the preparatory lemma
nodes.statement: Using the hypotheses of this lemma, \autoref{indicatorprep} furnishes a function $\Phi\in A$ such that:
nodes.statement_short: Get Phi in A such that:

nodes.name: Property (a)
nodes.statement: for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $x\in X_{i}$, $\Phi_{i}(x)$ is a diagonal matrix with entries in $[0,1]$ whose final $M$ diagonal entries are all $0$, and such that at most one of every $M$ consecutive diagonal entries is non-zero;
nodes.statement_short: Sparse diagonal entries in [0,1]

nodes.name: Property (b)
nodes.statement: for all $1\leq i\leq \ell$ and $1\leq j\leq n_{i}$: $\Phi_{i}(x)_{j,j}=1$ if and only if there is a $1\leq t\leq m$ such that $x\in B_{i,j-K_{t}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Entry equals 1 exactly on shifted B-sets

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: Let us use $\Phi$ to construct a function $\Theta\in A$ satisfying conditions \textit{(1)} to \textit{(3)}.
nodes.statement_short: Build Theta from Phi

nodes.name: Cutoff function
nodes.statement: Given $\delta\in [0,1)$, define $g\colon[0,1]\to[0,1]$ by $$ \begin{aligned} g(x):= \begin{cases} 0& \text{ if } 0\leq x\leq\delta\\ \text{linear} &\text{ if } \delta\leq x\leq\frac{1+\delta}{2}\\ 1&\text{ if } \frac{1+\delta}{2}\leq x\leq 1. \end{cases} \end{aligned} $$ For $1\leq i\leq l $, define $\Theta_{i}\colon X_{i}\to M_{n_{i}}$ by $$ \Theta_{i}(x):=\operatorname{diag}(g(\Phi_{i}(x)_{1,1}),\ldots,g(\Phi_{i}(x)_{n_{i},n_{i}})). $$ Then $\Theta:=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{ l }\Theta_{i}\in\bigoplus_{i=1}^{ l }C(X_{i},M_{n_{i}})$. Since each diagonal entry of $\Phi$ is modified in the same way in the definition of $\Theta$, it is straightforward to check that $\Theta$ is compatible with the diagonal structure of $A$. Hence, $\Theta\in A$. Moreover, since $\Theta_{i}(x)_{j,j}=0$ whenever $\Phi_{i}(x)_{j,j}=0$, it is clear that $\Theta$ satisfies \textit{(1)} since $\Phi$ satisfies \textit{(a)}.
nodes.statement_short: Theta = g(Phi) entrywise for a cutoff g; Theta is in A and satisfies (1)

nodes.name: Property (2)
nodes.statement: To see that $\Theta$ satisfies \textit{(2)}, fix $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq j\leq n_{i}$. Since $F_{i,j}$ is disjoint from each $B_{i,j-K_{t}}$ (for $1\leq t\leq m$), condition \textit{(b)} guarantees that $\Phi_{i}(x)_{j,j}<1$ for all $x\in F_{i,j}$. Since $F_{i,j}$ is compact, there is a $\delta_{i,j}\in [0,1)$ such that $\Phi_{i}(x)_{j,j}\leq \delta_{i,j}$ for all $x\in F_{i,j}$. On choosing $\delta:=\max\{\delta_{i,j}:1\leq i\leq l ,1\leq j\leq n_{i}\}\in [0,1)$ in our definition of $g$ above, it follows that $\Theta_{i}(x)_{j,j}=0$ whenever $1\leq i\leq l $, $1\leq j\leq n_{i}$, and $x\in F_{i,j}$, which proves \textit{(2)}.
nodes.statement_short: By compactness Phi is at most delta<1 on F_{i,j}, so Theta vanishes there

nodes.name: Property (3)
nodes.statement: Finally, to see that $\Theta$ satisfies \textit{(3)}, fix $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq j\leq n_{i}$. If $j>n_{i}-(\mathfrak{s}(A)-1)$, we may take $U_{i,j}=\varnothing$ since $B_{i,j}=\varnothing$ by \autoref{Bik} for such $j$. For $j\leq n_{i}-(\mathfrak{s}(A)-1)$, note that if $x\in B_{i,j}$, then by \textit{(b)}, $\Phi_{i}(x)_{j+K_{t},j+K_{t}}=1$ for all $1\leq t\leq m$. Since $g$ is $1$ in a neighbourhood of $1$, it follows that for each $t$, there is an open set $U_{t}\supset B_{i,j}$ on which the function $\Theta_{i}(\,\cdot\,)_{j+K_{t},j+K_{t}}\colon X_{i}\to [0,1]$ is equal to $1$. Taking $U_{i,j}:=\bigcap_{1\leq t\leq m} U_{t}$ yields \textit{(3)} and proves the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Phi equals 1 on B_{i,j} at shifted indices, so Theta is 1 on a neighbourhood

nodes.name: Length notation for a sequence of DSH algebras
nodes.statement: Given a sequence of DSH algebras $A_{1},A_{2},\ldots$, we denote by $ l (j)$ the length of the DSH algebra $A_{j}$.

nodes.name: Base space notation for a sequence of DSH algebras
nodes.statement: We denote the base spaces of $A_{j}$ by $X^{j}_{1},\ldots,X^{j}_{ l (j)}$ and the corresponding closed subspaces by $Y^{j}_{1},\ldots,Y^{j}_{ l (j)}$.

nodes.name: Matrix size notation for a sequence of DSH algebras
nodes.statement: We denote the size of the matrix algebras in the pullback definition of $A_{j}$ by $n^{j}_{1},\ldots,n^{j}_{ l (j)}$.

nodes.name: B-set notation for a sequence of DSH algebras
nodes.statement: Finally, we denote the sets defined in \autoref{Bik def} corresponding to $A_{j}$ by $B^{j}_{i,k}$.

nodes.name: Matrix sizes grow along simple limits
nodes.statement: Suppose $$ A_{1}\overset{\psi_{1}}{\longrightarrow} A_{2}\overset{\psi_{2}}{\longrightarrow} A_{3}\overset{\psi_{3}}{\longrightarrow}\cdots\longrightarrow A:=\varinjlim A_{i} $$ is a simple limit of infinite-dimensional DSH algebras with injective diagonal maps. Then, for all $j,m\in\mathbb{N}$, there is a $j'>j$ such that $\mathfrak{s}(A_{j'})>m$ (where, recall, $\mathfrak{s}(A_{j})=\min\{n^{j}_{t}:1\leq t\leq l (j)\}$).
assumptions: is a simple limit of infinite-dimensional DSH algebras with injective diagonal maps
conclusions: for all $j,m\in\mathbb{N}$, there is a $j'>j$ such that $\mathfrak{s}(A_{j'})>m$
nodes.label: big enough lemma

nodes.name: Proof that matrix sizes grow
nodes.statement: Since $A_{j}$ is infinite-dimensional, at least one of the base spaces must be infinite. Let $1\leq i\leq l (j)$ be the largest integer for which $X_{i}^{j}$ is infinite. By \autoref{empty interior}, $X_{i}^{j}\setminus Y_{i}^{j}$ is also infinite and $Y_{i'}^{j}=\varnothing$ for $i<i'\leq l (j)$. Choose pairwise-disjoint open in $X_{i}^{j}$ sets $\mathcal{O}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{O}_{m+1}\subset X_{i}^{j}\setminus Y_{i}^{j}$. \autoref{open in spectrum} guarantees that $\mathcal{O}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{O}_{m+1}$ are all open with respect to the hull-kernel topology on $\hat{A}_{j}$. By \autoref{simplicity}, there is a $j'>j$ such that for all $x\in \hat{A}_{j'}$, $\hat{\psi}_{j',j}(x)$ contains a point from each of $\mathcal{O}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{O}_{m+1}$. Hence, $n_{i}^{j'}\geq m+1$ for all $1\leq i\leq l (j')$, which proves the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Pick m+1 disjoint spectrum-open sets in an infinite base space; simplicity forces every later point to see all of them, so sizes exceed m.

nodes.name: Infinite base space
nodes.statement: Since $A_{j}$ is infinite-dimensional, at least one of the base spaces must be infinite. Let $1\leq i\leq l (j)$ be the largest integer for which $X_{i}^{j}$ is infinite. By \autoref{empty interior}, $X_{i}^{j}\setminus Y_{i}^{j}$ is also infinite and $Y_{i'}^{j}=\varnothing$ for $i<i'\leq l (j)$.
nodes.statement_short: Take the last infinite base space; it has infinitely many points outside Y

nodes.name: Disjoint open sets
nodes.statement: Choose pairwise-disjoint open in $X_{i}^{j}$ sets $\mathcal{O}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{O}_{m+1}\subset X_{i}^{j}\setminus Y_{i}^{j}$. \autoref{open in spectrum} guarantees that $\mathcal{O}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{O}_{m+1}$ are all open with respect to the hull-kernel topology on $\hat{A}_{j}$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose m+1 disjoint sets, open in the spectrum

nodes.name: Apply simplicity
nodes.statement: By \autoref{simplicity}, there is a $j'>j$ such that for all $x\in \hat{A}_{j'}$, $\hat{\psi}_{j',j}(x)$ contains a point from each of $\mathcal{O}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{O}_{m+1}$. Hence, $n_{i}^{j'}\geq m+1$ for all $1\leq i\leq l (j')$, which proves the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Every later point decomposes through all m+1 sets, so sizes exceed m

nodes.name: Many zero crosses far out in the sequence
nodes.statement: Suppose $$ A_{1}\overset{\psi_{1}}{\longrightarrow} A_{2}\overset{\psi_{2}}{\longrightarrow} A_{3}\overset{\psi_{3}}{\longrightarrow}\cdots\longrightarrow A:=\varinjlim A_{i} $$ is a simple limit of infinite-dimensional DSH algebras with injective diagonal maps. Suppose that $f$ is a non-invertible element belonging to some $A_{j}$ and that $\epsilon > 0$. Then, there exist $f'\in A_{j}$ with $\|f-f'\|\leq \epsilon$ and $M\in\mathbb{N}$ such that for all $N\in\mathbb{N}$ there exist $j'>j$ satisfying $\mathfrak{s}(A_{j'})>NM$ and unitaries $V,V'\in A_{j'}$ with the following properties: \begin{enumerate} \item for any $1\leq i\leq l (j')$ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}^{j'}$, there is a (possibly empty) open subset $U_{i,k}$ of $X^{j'}_{i}$ containing $B_{i,k}^{j'}$ such that for all $x\in U_{i,k}$, $(V\psi_{j',j}(f')V')_{i}(x)$ has zero crosses at indices $k, k+M, k+2M,\ldots,k+(N-1)M$; \item for all $1\leq i\leq l (j')$ and $x\in X^{j'}_{i}$, we have $\mathfrak{r}((V\psi_{j',j}(f')V')_{i}(x))\leq \mathfrak{S}(A_{j})+M-1$ (where, recall, $\mathfrak{S}(A_{j})=\max\{n^{j}_{t}:1\leq t\leq l (j)\}$). \end{enumerate}
assumptions: is a simple limit of infinite-dimensional DSH algebras with injective diagonal maps
$f$ is a non-invertible element belonging to some $A_{j}$ and that $\epsilon > 0$
conclusions: there exist $f'\in A_{j}$ with $\|f-f'\|\leq \epsilon$ and $M\in\mathbb{N}$ such that for all $N\in\mathbb{N}$ there exist $j'>j$ satisfying $\mathfrak{s}(A_{j'})>NM$ and unitaries $V,V'\in A_{j'}$ with the following properties
nodes.statement_short: Far enough out, a perturbation of a non-invertible f can be conjugated by unitaries to have N zero crosses spaced M apart near each B_{i,k}, with bounded bandwidth.
nodes.label: far out

nodes.name: Proof of the far-out lemma
nodes.statement:
Let $f',w,v,\Delta\in A_{j}$ and $U\subset\hat{A}_{j}$ be given as in \autoref{perturb} (when applied to $f$ and $\epsilon$) and set $g:=wf'v$. Then, at every point in $U$, $g$ has a zero cross at index $1$ and the $(1,1)$-entry of $\Delta$ is $1$. By \autoref{simplicity} and \autoref{DSH spectrum}, there is a $j''>j$ such that $\hat{\psi}_{j'',j}([\operatorname{ev}_{x}])$ contains a point in $U$ for all $x\in  igsqcup_{i=1}^{ l (j'')}(X_{i}^{j''}\setminus Y_{i}^{j''})$. Since $\psi_{j'',j}$ is diagonal, this means that for $1\leq i\leq l (j'')$ and $x\in X^{j''}_{i}\setminus Y_{i}^{j''}$, at least one of the points $x$ decomposes into under $\psi_{j'',j}$ lies in $U$, so that the matrices $\psi_{j'',j}(g)_{i}(x)$ and $\psi_{j'',j}(\Delta)_{i}(x)$ have a zero cross and a $1$, respectively, at the same index along their respective diagonal. Owing to the decomposition structure of $A_{j''}$, these two results hold, in fact, for all $1\leq i\leq l (j'')$ and $x\in X_{i}^{j''}$. Take $M:=2\mathfrak{S}(A_{j''})$ and let $N\in\mathbb{N}$ be arbitrary. By \autoref{big enough lemma}, there is a $j'>j''$ such that  egin{equation} \mathfrak{s}(A_{j'})>NM. \end{equation} Let $\Delta':=\psi_{j',j}(\Delta)=\psi_{j',j''}(\psi_{j'',j}(\Delta))$ and $g':=\psi_{j',j}(g)=\psi_{j',j''}(\psi_{j'',j}(g))$. Given $1\leq i\leq l (j')$ and $x\in X^{j'}_{i}$ and regarding $\Delta'$ as a diagonal image under $\psi_{j',j''}$, it follows from the definition of $M$ that any $M$ consecutive entries down the diagonal of $\Delta_{i}'(x)$ must contain a $1$. Moreover, regarding $g'$ and $\Delta'$ as diagonal images under $\psi_{j',j}$ shows that $g'_{i}(x)$ has a zero cross at index $k$ whenever $\Delta'_{i}(x)_{k,k}>0$ (as a consequence of the conclusion of \autoref{perturb}) and that $\mathfrak{r}(g_{i}'(x))\leq \mathfrak{S}(A_{j})$. We now apply \autoref{indicators} with the natural number $M$, with $m=N$, $K_{1}=0, K_{2}=M, \ldots, K_{N}=(N-1)M$, and $F_{i,k}=\varnothing$ for $1\leq i\leq l (j')$ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}^{j'}$ (note that $K_{N}<\mathfrak{s}(A_{j'})-M$ by \autoref{big enough}). This furnishes a function $\Theta\in A_{j'}$ with the following properties:  egin{enumerate}[label=(\Roman*)] \item for all $1\leq i\leq l (j')$ and $x\in X_{i}^{j'}$, $\Theta_{i}(x)$ is a diagonal matrix with entries in $[0,1]$ whose final $M$ diagonal entries are all $0$, and such that at most one of every $M$ consecutive diagonal entries is non-zero; \item for all $1\leq i\leq l (j')$ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}^{j'}$, there is a (possibly empty) open subset $U_{i,k}\subset X_{i}^{j'}$ containing $B_{i,k}^{j'}$ with the property that if $x\in U_{i,k}$, then $\Theta_{i}(x)_{k+aM,k+aM}=1$ for all $0\leq a\leq N-1$. \end{enumerate} Fix $1\leq i\leq l (j')$. Given $x\in X_{i}^{j'}$ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}^{j'}-(M-1)$, let $$ u_{k}^{i}(x):=\prod_{t=1}^{M-1}u^{i}_{(k \ k+t)}\left(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k,k} \Delta_{i}'(x)_{k+t,k+t}ight)\in M_{n_{i}^{j'}}, $$ where each $u^{i}_{(k \ k+t)}\colon [0,1]	o M_{n_{i}^{j'}}$ is a connecting path of unitaries as described in \autoref{unitaries}. Define $W_{i}\in C(X_{i}^{j'}, M_{n_{i}^{j'}})$ to be the unitary $$ W_{i}(x):=\prod_{k=1}^{n_{i}^{j'}-M}u_{k}^{i}(x). $$ Set $W:=(W_{1},\ldots,W_{ l (j')})$ and take $V:=W\psi_{j',j}(w)$ and $V':=\psi_{j',j}(v)W^{*}$. Before showing that $W\in A_{j'}$, let us prove that statements 	extit{(1)} and 	extit{(2)} of \autoref{far out} hold. Fix $x\in X_{i}^{j'}$. Note that if $\Theta_{i}(x)_{k',k'}=0$, then $u_{k'}^{i}(x)=1_{n_{i}^{j'}}$. Let $\{k_{1}<\cdots<k_{s}\}$ denote the set of indices $r$ at which $\Theta_{i}(x)_{r,r}>0$. Then, $W_{i}(x)=u_{k_{1}}^{i}(x)\cdots u_{k_{s}}^{i}(x)$, where, by (I) above, $k_{p+1}-k_{p}\geq M$ for $1\leq p < s$ and $k_{s}\leq n_{i}^{j'}-M$. Note that conjugating any matrix by $u_{k_{p}}^{i}(x)$ only affects the $k_{p},\ldots, k_{p}+(M-1)$ rows and columns of that matrix. Thus, for $p
ot=q$, the indices of the rows and columns affected when conjugating by $u_{k_{p}}^{i}(x)$ do not overlap with the indices of the rows and columns affected when conjugating by $u_{k_{q}}^{i}(x)$. This observation will be used to prove 	extit{(1)} and 	extit{(2)} below. To prove 	extit{(1)}, fix $1\leq k\leq n_{i}^{j'}$ and assume $x\in U_{i,k}$. For $p=s,s-1,\ldots,1$, let $$ D_{p}:=u_{k_{p}}^{i}(x)\cdots u_{k_{s}}^{i}(x)g_{i}'(x)u_{k_{s}}^{i}(x)^{*}\cdots u_{k_{p}}^{i}(x)^{*} $$ (setting $D_{s+1}:=g'_{i}(x)$) and apply part 	extit{(b)} of \autoref{untouched crosses} with $M$, $n=n^{j'}_{i}$, $l=k_{p}$, $\xi_{l+t}=\Theta_{i}(x)_{l,l}\Delta_{i}'(x)_{l+t,l+t}$ for $t=0,1,\ldots M-1$, $D=D_{p+1}$, and $U=u_{k_{p}}^{i}(x)$ to conclude that $D_{p}$ has a zero cross at any index among $\{1,\ldots,n_{i}^{j'}\}\setminus\{k_{p},\ldots,k_{p}+M-1\}$ whenever $D_{p+1}$ does. Now, fix an integer $0\leq a\leq N-1$. Let us show that $W_{i}(x)g_{i}'(x)W_{i}(x)^{*}$ has a zero cross at index $k+aM$. By (II) above, $\Theta_{i}(x)_{k+aM, k+aM}=1$. Let $r$ denote the unique integer such that $k_{r}=k+aM$. Applying the result obtained just above inductively $s-r$ times, it follows that for every $q\in\{k_{r},\ldots,k_{r}+M-1\}$, $D_{r+1}$ has a zero cross at index $q$ whenever $g_{i}'(x)$ does; in particular, for any such $q$, $D_{r+1}$ has a zero cross at index $q$ provided that $\Delta_{i}'(x)_{q,q}>0$. Hence, since any $M$ consecutive entries along the diagonal of $\Delta_{i}'(x)$ must contain a $1$, the assumptions of part 	extit{(c)} of \autoref{untouched crosses} are satisfied with $M$, $n=n^{j'}_{i}$, $l=k+aM$, $\xi_{l+t}=\Theta_{i}(x)_{l,l}\Delta_{i}'(x)_{l+t,l+t}=\Delta_{i}'(x)_{l+t,l+t}$ for $t=0,1,\ldots, M-1$, $D=D_{r+1}$, and $U=u_{k_{r}}^{i}(x)$. Thus, we may apply that part of the lemma to deduce that $D_{r}$ has a zero cross at index $k+aM$. Appealing to the conclusion of the previous paragraph inductively $r-1$ times, it follows that $D_{1}=W_{i}(x)g_{i}'(x)W_{i}(x)^{*}$ has a zero cross at index $k+aM$, since $k+aM=k_{r}$ is not among the indices affected upon conjugation by $u_{k_{1}}^{i}(x)\cdots u_{k_{r-1}}^{i}(x)$. This proves 	extit{(1)}. Next, recall that $g'$ is the diagonal image of $g$, which has bandwidth at most $\mathfrak{S}(A_{j})$ at every point. To prove 	extit{(2)}, therefore, it suffices to show that for any given matrix $D=(D_{q,t})\in M_{n_{i}^{j'}}$, we have $\mathfrak{r}(W_{i}(x)DW_{i}(x)^{*})\leq \mathfrak{r}(D)+M-1$. This is most easily seen by drawing a picture and examining which rows and columns are potentially affected upon conjugation by the $u_{k_{p}}^{i}$'s:  egin{figure}[H]  egin{minipage}{0.5	extwidth} \centering \includegraphics[scale=.9]{matrix3.pdf} \caption{Affected Rows/Columns} \end{minipage}\hfill  egin{minipage}{.5	extwidth} Since the sets $\{k_{p},\ldots,k_{p}+(M-1)\}$ for $1\leq p\leq s$ are disjoint, the block rows and columns are disjoint. Suppose we are given an index $(q,t)$ that lies in the shaded region of the diagram in \autoref{affected rows/columns}, and suppose that $\lambda$ is the number at entry $(q,t)$ of $W_{i}(x)DW_{i}(x)^{*}$. Upon partitioning this shaded region, it follows that the index $(q,t)$ lies in one of the following three shaded subregions in \autoref{regionA} to \autoref{regionC}: \end{minipage} \end{figure}  egin{figure}[H] \centering  egin{minipage}{0.333	extwidth} \centering \includegraphics[scale=.81]{regionA.pdf} \caption{Region A} \end{minipage}\hfill  egin{minipage}{0.333	extwidth} \centering \includegraphics[scale=.81]{regionB.pdf} \caption{Region B} \end{minipage}\hfill  egin{minipage}{0.333	extwidth} \centering \includegraphics[scale=.81]{regionC.pdf} \caption{Region C} \end{minipage} \end{figure} On 
ameref{regionA}, the matrices $W_{i}(x)DW_{i}(x)^{*}$ and $DW_{i}(x)^{*}$ are equal. Hence, if $(q,t)$ lies in 
ameref{regionA} and $p$ is such that $k_{p}\leq t\leq k_{p}+M-1$, then $\lambda$ is a linear combination of $D_{q,k_{p}},\ldots,D_{q,k_{p}+M-1}$. Thus, $\lambda$ can be non-zero only if one of $D_{q,k_{p}},\ldots,D_{q,k_{p}+M-1}$ is non-zero. Hence, no non-zero entry in this region is more than $M-1$ indices away from a non-zero entry in $D$. On 
ameref{regionB}, the matrices $W_{i}(x)DW_{i}(x)^{*}$ and $W_{i}(x)D$ are equal, and so a symmetrical analysis shows that the same is true also for non-zero entries in this region. If $(q,t)$ lies in one of the $s^{2}$ disjoint $M	imes M$ blocks in 
ameref{regionC}, then $\lambda$ is a linear combination of the corresponding entries in $D$ lying in that block. Hence, in this case $\lambda$ is $0$ unless that $M	imes M$ block in $D$ contains a non-zero entry. Thus, no non-zero entry of $W_{i}(x)DW_{i}(x)^{*}$ in 
ameref{regionC} is more than $M-1$ units further away from the diagonal than a non-zero entry of $D$. This analysis proves that $\mathfrak{r}(W_{i}(x)DW_{i}(x)^{*})\leq \mathfrak{r}(D)+M-1$, yielding 	extit{(2)}. To conclude, let us show that $W\in A_{j'}$. Fix $1\leq i\leq l (j')$ and suppose that $y\in Y_{i}^{j'}$ decomposes into $x_{1}\in X_{i_{1}}^{j'}\setminus Y_{i_{1}}^{j'},\ldots,x_{s}\in X_{i_{s}}^{j'}\setminus Y_{i_{s}}^{j'}$. For $1\leq k\leq s$, let $p_{k}:=1+n^{j'}_{i_{1}}+\cdots+n^{j'}_{i_{k-1}}$. Note that by \autoref{big enough}, $p_{s}\leq n_{i}^{j'}-\mathfrak{s}(A_{j'})+1\leq n_{i}^{j'}-M$. Thus, we may write  egin{equation} W_{i}(y)=\prod_{k=1}^{n_{i}^{j'}-M}u_{k}^{i}(y)=\prod_{m=1}^{s-1}\prod_{k=p_{m}}^{p_{m+1}-1}u_{k}^{i}(y)	imes\prod_{k=p_{s}}^{n_{i}^{j'}-M}u_{k}^{i}(y). \end{equation} Fix $1\leq m<s$. Then, $$ \prod_{k=p_{m}}^{p_{m+1}-1}u_{k}^{i}(y)=\prod_{k=p_{m}}^{p_{m+1}-1}\prod_{t=1}^{M-1}u_{(k \ k+t)}^{i}(\Theta_{i}(y)_{k,k}\Delta_{i}'(y)_{k+t,k+t}). $$ By (I), the last $M$ entries of $\Theta_{i_{m}}(x_{m})$ are zero. Hence, on account of the diagonal decomposition of $\Theta_{i}(y)$, the quantity above is equal to $$ \prod_{k=p_{m}}^{(p_{m+1}-1)-M}\prod_{t=1}^{M-1}u_{(k \ k+t)}^{i}(\Theta_{i_{m}}(x_{m})_{k-p_{m}+1,k-p_{m}+1}\Delta_{i_{m}}'(x_{m})_{k-p_{m}+1+t,k-p_{m}+1+t}), $$ which, upon relabelling indices, becomes  egin{equation} \prod_{q=1}^{p_{m+1}-p_{m}-M}\prod_{t=1}^{M-1}u^{i}_{(q+p_{m}-1 \ q+p_{m}-1+t)}(\Theta_{i_{m}}(x_{m})_{q,q}\Delta_{i_{m}}'(x_{m})_{q+t,q+t}). \end{equation} For each $1\leq q\leq p_{m+1}-p_{m}-M$ and $1\leq t\leq M-1$, note that $$ u^{i}_{(q+p_{m}-1 \ q+p_{m}-1+t)}=\operatorname{diag}(1_{p_{m}-1},u_{(q \ q+t)}^{i_{m}},1_{n_{i}^{j'}-p_{m+1}+1}). $$ Hence, we may rewrite \autoref{reindex} as $$  egin{aligned} \operatorname{diag}\left(1_{p_{m}-1},\prod_{q=1}^{p_{m+1}-p_{m}-M}u_{q}^{i_{m}}(x_{m}),1_{n_{i}^{j'}-p_{m+1}+1}ight) =\operatorname{diag}\left(1_{p_{m}-1},W_{i_{m}}(x_{m}),1_{n_{i}^{j'}-p_{m+1}+1}ight). \end{aligned} $$ Therefore, for all $1\leq m <s$, $$ \prod_{k=p_{m}}^{p_{m+1}-1}u_{k}^{i}(y)=\operatorname{diag}\left(1_{p_{m}-1},W_{i_{m}}(x_{m}),1_{n_{i}^{j'}-p_{m+1}+1}ight) $$ and, similarly, $$ \prod_{k=p_{s}}^{n_{i}^{j'}-M}u_{k}^{i}(y)=\operatorname{diag}(1_{p_{s}-1},W_{i_{s}}(x_{s})). $$ Plugging this into \autoref{Wi} shows that $W_{i}(y)=\operatorname{diag}(W_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots,W_{i_{s}}(x_{s}))$, which proves that $W\in A$. The proof of \autoref{far out} is now complete.
nodes.statement_short: Use the perturbation lemma and simplicity to get a zero cross in every M consecutive indices; then conjugate by products of transposition paths driven by indicator elements Theta. Key step: the untouched-crosses lemma moves a zero cross to each index k+aM.

nodes.statement_short: Get Theta in A_{j'} with:

nodes.name: Property (I)
nodes.statement: for all $1\leq i\leq l (j')$ and $x\in X_{i}^{j'}$, $\Theta_{i}(x)$ is a diagonal matrix with entries in $[0,1]$ whose final $M$ diagonal entries are all $0$, and such that at most one of every $M$ consecutive diagonal entries is non-zero;
nodes.statement_short: Sparse diagonal entries

nodes.name: Property (II)
nodes.statement: for all $1\leq i\leq l (j')$ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}^{j'}$, there is a (possibly empty) open subset $U_{i,k}\subset X_{i}^{j'}$ containing $B_{i,k}^{j'}$ with the property that if $x\in U_{i,k}$, then $\Theta_{i}(x)_{k+aM,k+aM}=1$ for all $0\leq a\leq N-1$.
nodes.statement_short: Entries equal 1 near B_{i,k} at k+aM

nodes.name: Define W, V, V'
nodes.statement: Fix $1\leq i\leq l (j')$. Given $x\in X_{i}^{j'}$ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}^{j'}-(M-1)$, let $$ u_{k}^{i}(x):=\prod_{t=1}^{M-1}u^{i}_{(k \ k+t)}\left(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k,k} \Delta_{i}'(x)_{k+t,k+t}\right)\in M_{n_{i}^{j'}}, $$ where each $u^{i}_{(k \ k+t)}\colon [0,1]\to M_{n_{i}^{j'}}$ is a connecting path of unitaries as described in \autoref{unitaries}. Define $W_{i}\in C(X_{i}^{j'}, M_{n_{i}^{j'}})$ to be the unitary $$ W_{i}(x):=\prod_{k=1}^{n_{i}^{j'}-M}u_{k}^{i}(x). $$ Set $W:=(W_{1},\ldots,W_{ l (j')})$ and take $V:=W\psi_{j',j}(w)$ and $V':=\psi_{j',j}(v)W^{*}$. Before showing that $W\in A_{j'}$, let us prove that statements \textit{(1)} and \textit{(2)} of \autoref{far out} hold.
nodes.statement_short: Products u_k^i of transposition paths with parameters Theta*Delta'

nodes.name: Disjoint supports
nodes.statement: Fix $x\in X_{i}^{j'}$. Note that if $\Theta_{i}(x)_{k',k'}=0$, then $u_{k'}^{i}(x)=1_{n_{i}^{j'}}$. Let $\{k_{1}<\cdots<k_{s}\}$ denote the set of indices $r$ at which $\Theta_{i}(x)_{r,r}>0$. Then, $W_{i}(x)=u_{k_{1}}^{i}(x)\cdots u_{k_{s}}^{i}(x)$, where, by (I) above, $k_{p+1}-k_{p}\geq M$ for $1\leq p < s$ and $k_{s}\leq n_{i}^{j'}-M$. Note that conjugating any matrix by $u_{k_{p}}^{i}(x)$ only affects the $k_{p},\ldots, k_{p}+(M-1)$ rows and columns of that matrix. Thus, for $p\not=q$, the indices of the rows and columns affected when conjugating by $u_{k_{p}}^{i}(x)$ do not overlap with the indices of the rows and columns affected when conjugating by $u_{k_{q}}^{i}(x)$. This observation will be used to prove \textit{(1)} and \textit{(2)} below.
nodes.statement_short: Only indices with Theta>0 contribute, and their blocks of M rows/columns are disjoint

nodes.name: Untouched crosses persist
nodes.statement: To prove \textit{(1)}, fix $1\leq k\leq n_{i}^{j'}$ and assume $x\in U_{i,k}$. For $p=s,s-1,\ldots,1$, let $$ D_{p}:=u_{k_{p}}^{i}(x)\cdots u_{k_{s}}^{i}(x)g_{i}'(x)u_{k_{s}}^{i}(x)^{*}\cdots u_{k_{p}}^{i}(x)^{*} $$ (setting $D_{s+1}:=g'_{i}(x)$) and apply part \textit{(b)} of \autoref{untouched crosses} with $M$, $n=n^{j'}_{i}$, $l=k_{p}$, $\xi_{l+t}=\Theta_{i}(x)_{l,l}\Delta_{i}'(x)_{l+t,l+t}$ for $t=0,1,\ldots M-1$, $D=D_{p+1}$, and $U=u_{k_{p}}^{i}(x)$ to conclude that $D_{p}$ has a zero cross at any index among $\{1,\ldots,n_{i}^{j'}\}\setminus\{k_{p},\ldots,k_{p}+M-1\}$ whenever $D_{p+1}$ does.
nodes.statement_short: Untouched-crosses (b): conjugation preserves zero crosses outside each block

nodes.name: Claim: zero cross at k+aM
nodes.statement: Now, fix an integer $0\leq a\leq N-1$. Let us show that $W_{i}(x)g_{i}'(x)W_{i}(x)^{*}$ has a zero cross at index $k+aM$. By (II) above, $\Theta_{i}(x)_{k+aM, k+aM}=1$. Let $r$ denote the unique integer such that $k_{r}=k+aM$. Applying the result obtained just above inductively $s-r$ times, it follows that for every $q\in\{k_{r},\ldots,k_{r}+M-1\}$, $D_{r+1}$ has a zero cross at index $q$ whenever $g_{i}'(x)$ does; in particular, for any such $q$, $D_{r+1}$ has a zero cross at index $q$ provided that $\Delta_{i}'(x)_{q,q}>0$. Hence, since any $M$ consecutive entries along the diagonal of $\Delta_{i}'(x)$ must contain a $1$, the assumptions of part \textit{(c)} of \autoref{untouched crosses} are satisfied with $M$, $n=n^{j'}_{i}$, $l=k+aM$, $\xi_{l+t}=\Theta_{i}(x)_{l,l}\Delta_{i}'(x)_{l+t,l+t}=\Delta_{i}'(x)_{l+t,l+t}$ for $t=0,1,\ldots, M-1$, $D=D_{r+1}$, and $U=u_{k_{r}}^{i}(x)$. Thus, we may apply that part of the lemma to deduce that $D_{r}$ has a zero cross at index $k+aM$. Appealing to the conclusion of the previous paragraph inductively $r-1$ times, it follows that $D_{1}=W_{i}(x)g_{i}'(x)W_{i}(x)^{*}$ has a zero cross at index $k+aM$, since $k+aM=k_{r}$ is not among the indices affected upon conjugation by $u_{k_{1}}^{i}(x)\cdots u_{k_{r-1}}^{i}(x)$. This proves \textit{(1)}.
nodes.statement_short: Show the conjugate has a zero cross at k+aM

nodes.name: Zero crosses before the block
nodes.statement: By (II) above, $\Theta_{i}(x)_{k+aM, k+aM}=1$. Let $r$ denote the unique integer such that $k_{r}=k+aM$. Applying the result obtained just above inductively $s-r$ times, it follows that for every $q\in\{k_{r},\ldots,k_{r}+M-1\}$, $D_{r+1}$ has a zero cross at index $q$ whenever $g_{i}'(x)$ does; in particular, for any such $q$, $D_{r+1}$ has a zero cross at index $q$ provided that $\Delta_{i}'(x)_{q,q}>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Later blocks preserve the needed zero crosses

nodes.name: Untouched crosses (c)
nodes.statement: Hence, since any $M$ consecutive entries along the diagonal of $\Delta_{i}'(x)$ must contain a $1$, the assumptions of part \textit{(c)} of \autoref{untouched crosses} are satisfied with $M$, $n=n^{j'}_{i}$, $l=k+aM$, $\xi_{l+t}=\Theta_{i}(x)_{l,l}\Delta_{i}'(x)_{l+t,l+t}=\Delta_{i}'(x)_{l+t,l+t}$ for $t=0,1,\ldots, M-1$, $D=D_{r+1}$, and $U=u_{k_{r}}^{i}(x)$. Thus, we may apply that part of the lemma to deduce that $D_{r}$ has a zero cross at index $k+aM$.
nodes.statement_short: Part (c) moves a zero cross to index k+aM

nodes.name: Earlier blocks
nodes.statement: Appealing to the conclusion of the previous paragraph inductively $r-1$ times, it follows that $D_{1}=W_{i}(x)g_{i}'(x)W_{i}(x)^{*}$ has a zero cross at index $k+aM$, since $k+aM=k_{r}$ is not among the indices affected upon conjugation by $u_{k_{1}}^{i}(x)\cdots u_{k_{r-1}}^{i}(x)$. This proves \textit{(1)}.
nodes.statement_short: Earlier blocks do not touch k+aM; this proves (1)

nodes.name: Bandwidth estimate (2)
nodes.statement:
Next, recall that $g'$ is the diagonal image of $g$, which has bandwidth at most $\mathfrak{S}(A_{j})$ at every point. To prove 	extit{(2)}, therefore, it suffices to show that for any given matrix $D=(D_{q,t})\in M_{n_{i}^{j'}}$, we have $\mathfrak{r}(W_{i}(x)DW_{i}(x)^{*})\leq \mathfrak{r}(D)+M-1$. This is most easily seen by drawing a picture and examining which rows and columns are potentially affected upon conjugation by the $u_{k_{p}}^{i}$'s:  egin{figure}[H]  egin{minipage}{0.5	extwidth} \centering \includegraphics[scale=.9]{matrix3.pdf} \caption{Affected Rows/Columns} \end{minipage}\hfill  egin{minipage}{.5	extwidth} Since the sets $\{k_{p},\ldots,k_{p}+(M-1)\}$ for $1\leq p\leq s$ are disjoint, the block rows and columns are disjoint. Suppose we are given an index $(q,t)$ that lies in the shaded region of the diagram in \autoref{affected rows/columns}, and suppose that $\lambda$ is the number at entry $(q,t)$ of $W_{i}(x)DW_{i}(x)^{*}$. Upon partitioning this shaded region, it follows that the index $(q,t)$ lies in one of the following three shaded subregions in \autoref{regionA} to \autoref{regionC}: \end{minipage} \end{figure}  egin{figure}[H] \centering  egin{minipage}{0.333	extwidth} \centering \includegraphics[scale=.81]{regionA.pdf} \caption{Region A} \end{minipage}\hfill  egin{minipage}{0.333	extwidth} \centering \includegraphics[scale=.81]{regionB.pdf} \caption{Region B} \end{minipage}\hfill  egin{minipage}{0.333	extwidth} \centering \includegraphics[scale=.81]{regionC.pdf} \caption{Region C} \end{minipage} \end{figure} On 
ameref{regionA}, the matrices $W_{i}(x)DW_{i}(x)^{*}$ and $DW_{i}(x)^{*}$ are equal. Hence, if $(q,t)$ lies in 
ameref{regionA} and $p$ is such that $k_{p}\leq t\leq k_{p}+M-1$, then $\lambda$ is a linear combination of $D_{q,k_{p}},\ldots,D_{q,k_{p}+M-1}$. Thus, $\lambda$ can be non-zero only if one of $D_{q,k_{p}},\ldots,D_{q,k_{p}+M-1}$ is non-zero. Hence, no non-zero entry in this region is more than $M-1$ indices away from a non-zero entry in $D$. On 
ameref{regionB}, the matrices $W_{i}(x)DW_{i}(x)^{*}$ and $W_{i}(x)D$ are equal, and so a symmetrical analysis shows that the same is true also for non-zero entries in this region. If $(q,t)$ lies in one of the $s^{2}$ disjoint $M	imes M$ blocks in 
ameref{regionC}, then $\lambda$ is a linear combination of the corresponding entries in $D$ lying in that block. Hence, in this case $\lambda$ is $0$ unless that $M	imes M$ block in $D$ contains a non-zero entry. Thus, no non-zero entry of $W_{i}(x)DW_{i}(x)^{*}$ in 
ameref{regionC} is more than $M-1$ units further away from the diagonal than a non-zero entry of $D$. This analysis proves that $\mathfrak{r}(W_{i}(x)DW_{i}(x)^{*})\leq \mathfrak{r}(D)+M-1$, yielding 	extit{(2)}.
nodes.statement_short: Conjugation by W_i adds at most M-1 to bandwidth

nodes.name: Reduce to a conjugation bound
nodes.statement: Next, recall that $g'$ is the diagonal image of $g$, which has bandwidth at most $\mathfrak{S}(A_{j})$ at every point. To prove \textit{(2)}, therefore, it suffices to show that for any given matrix $D=(D_{q,t})\in M_{n_{i}^{j'}}$, we have $\mathfrak{r}(W_{i}(x)DW_{i}(x)^{*})\leq \mathfrak{r}(D)+M-1$. This is most easily seen by drawing a picture and examining which rows and columns are potentially affected upon conjugation by the $u_{k_{p}}^{i}$'s: \begin{figure}[H] \begin{minipage}{0.5\textwidth} \centering \includegraphics[scale=.9]{matrix3.pdf} \caption{Affected Rows/Columns} \end{minipage}\hfill \begin{minipage}{.5\textwidth} Since the sets $\{k_{p},\ldots,k_{p}+(M-1)\}$ for $1\leq p\leq s$ are disjoint, the block rows and columns are disjoint. Suppose we are given an index $(q,t)$ that lies in the shaded region of the diagram in \autoref{affected rows/columns}, and suppose that $\lambda$ is the number at entry $(q,t)$ of $W_{i}(x)DW_{i}(x)^{*}$. Upon partitioning this shaded region, it follows that the index $(q,t)$ lies in one of the following three shaded subregions in \autoref{regionA} to \autoref{regionC}: \end{minipage} \end{figure} \begin{figure}[H] \centering \begin{minipage}{0.333\textwidth} \centering \includegraphics[scale=.81]{regionA.pdf} \caption{Region A} \end{minipage}\hfill \begin{minipage}{0.333\textwidth} \centering \includegraphics[scale=.81]{regionB.pdf} \caption{Region B} \end{minipage}\hfill \begin{minipage}{0.333\textwidth} \centering \includegraphics[scale=.81]{regionC.pdf} \caption{Region C} \end{minipage} \end{figure}
nodes.statement_short: Suffices: r(W D W*) <= r(D)+M-1, examined region by region

nodes.name: Regions A, B, C
nodes.statement:
On 
ameref{regionA}, the matrices $W_{i}(x)DW_{i}(x)^{*}$ and $DW_{i}(x)^{*}$ are equal. Hence, if $(q,t)$ lies in 
ameref{regionA} and $p$ is such that $k_{p}\leq t\leq k_{p}+M-1$, then $\lambda$ is a linear combination of $D_{q,k_{p}},\ldots,D_{q,k_{p}+M-1}$. Thus, $\lambda$ can be non-zero only if one of $D_{q,k_{p}},\ldots,D_{q,k_{p}+M-1}$ is non-zero. Hence, no non-zero entry in this region is more than $M-1$ indices away from a non-zero entry in $D$. On 
ameref{regionB}, the matrices $W_{i}(x)DW_{i}(x)^{*}$ and $W_{i}(x)D$ are equal, and so a symmetrical analysis shows that the same is true also for non-zero entries in this region. If $(q,t)$ lies in one of the $s^{2}$ disjoint $M	imes M$ blocks in 
ameref{regionC}, then $\lambda$ is a linear combination of the corresponding entries in $D$ lying in that block. Hence, in this case $\lambda$ is $0$ unless that $M	imes M$ block in $D$ contains a non-zero entry. Thus, no non-zero entry of $W_{i}(x)DW_{i}(x)^{*}$ in 
ameref{regionC} is more than $M-1$ units further away from the diagonal than a non-zero entry of $D$. This analysis proves that $\mathfrak{r}(W_{i}(x)DW_{i}(x)^{*})\leq \mathfrak{r}(D)+M-1$, yielding 	extit{(2)}.
nodes.statement_short: In each region entries combine within one M-block, giving the bound

nodes.name: W lies in A_{j'}
nodes.statement: To conclude, let us show that $W\in A_{j'}$. Fix $1\leq i\leq l (j')$ and suppose that $y\in Y_{i}^{j'}$ decomposes into $x_{1}\in X_{i_{1}}^{j'}\setminus Y_{i_{1}}^{j'},\ldots,x_{s}\in X_{i_{s}}^{j'}\setminus Y_{i_{s}}^{j'}$. For $1\leq k\leq s$, let $p_{k}:=1+n^{j'}_{i_{1}}+\cdots+n^{j'}_{i_{k-1}}$. Note that by \autoref{big enough}, $p_{s}\leq n_{i}^{j'}-\mathfrak{s}(A_{j'})+1\leq n_{i}^{j'}-M$. Thus, we may write \begin{equation} W_{i}(y)=\prod_{k=1}^{n_{i}^{j'}-M}u_{k}^{i}(y)=\prod_{m=1}^{s-1}\prod_{k=p_{m}}^{p_{m+1}-1}u_{k}^{i}(y)\times\prod_{k=p_{s}}^{n_{i}^{j'}-M}u_{k}^{i}(y). \end{equation} Fix $1\leq m<s$. Then, $$ \prod_{k=p_{m}}^{p_{m+1}-1}u_{k}^{i}(y)=\prod_{k=p_{m}}^{p_{m+1}-1}\prod_{t=1}^{M-1}u_{(k \ k+t)}^{i}(\Theta_{i}(y)_{k,k}\Delta_{i}'(y)_{k+t,k+t}). $$ By (I), the last $M$ entries of $\Theta_{i_{m}}(x_{m})$ are zero.
