Hence, on account of the diagonal decomposition of $\Theta_{i}(y)$, the quantity above is equal to $$ \prod_{k=p_{m}}^{(p_{m+1}-1)-M}\prod_{t=1}^{M-1}u_{(k \ k+t)}^{i}(\Theta_{i_{m}}(x_{m})_{k-p_{m}+1,k-p_{m}+1}\Delta_{i_{m}}'(x_{m})_{k-p_{m}+1+t,k-p_{m}+1+t}), $$ which, upon relabelling indices, becomes \begin{equation} \prod_{q=1}^{p_{m+1}-p_{m}-M}\prod_{t=1}^{M-1}u^{i}_{(q+p_{m}-1 \ q+p_{m}-1+t)}(\Theta_{i_{m}}(x_{m})_{q,q}\Delta_{i_{m}}'(x_{m})_{q+t,q+t}). \end{equation} For each $1\leq q\leq p_{m+1}-p_{m}-M$ and $1\leq t\leq M-1$, note that $$ u^{i}_{(q+p_{m}-1 \ q+p_{m}-1+t)}=\operatorname{diag}(1_{p_{m}-1},u_{(q \ q+t)}^{i_{m}},1_{n_{i}^{j'}-p_{m+1}+1}). $$ Hence, we may rewrite \autoref{reindex} as $$ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{diag}\left(1_{p_{m}-1},\prod_{q=1}^{p_{m+1}-p_{m}-M}u_{q}^{i_{m}}(x_{m}),1_{n_{i}^{j'}-p_{m+1}+1}\right) =\operatorname{diag}\left(1_{p_{m}-1},W_{i_{m}}(x_{m}),1_{n_{i}^{j'}-p_{m+1}+1}\right). \end{aligned} $$ Therefore, for all $1\leq m <s$, $$ \prod_{k=p_{m}}^{p_{m+1}-1}u_{k}^{i}(y)=\operatorname{diag}\left(1_{p_{m}-1},W_{i_{m}}(x_{m}),1_{n_{i}^{j'}-p_{m+1}+1}\right) $$ and, similarly, $$ \prod_{k=p_{s}}^{n_{i}^{j'}-M}u_{k}^{i}(y)=\operatorname{diag}(1_{p_{s}-1},W_{i_{s}}(x_{s})). $$ Plugging this into \autoref{Wi} shows that $W_{i}(y)=\operatorname{diag}(W_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots,W_{i_{s}}(x_{s}))$, which proves that $W\in A$. The proof of \autoref{far out} is now complete.
nodes.statement_short: Check the block-diagonal decomposition of W_i at points of Y_i

nodes.name: Split the product
nodes.statement: To conclude, let us show that $W\in A_{j'}$. Fix $1\leq i\leq l (j')$ and suppose that $y\in Y_{i}^{j'}$ decomposes into $x_{1}\in X_{i_{1}}^{j'}\setminus Y_{i_{1}}^{j'},\ldots,x_{s}\in X_{i_{s}}^{j'}\setminus Y_{i_{s}}^{j'}$. For $1\leq k\leq s$, let $p_{k}:=1+n^{j'}_{i_{1}}+\cdots+n^{j'}_{i_{k-1}}$. Note that by \autoref{big enough}, $p_{s}\leq n_{i}^{j'}-\mathfrak{s}(A_{j'})+1\leq n_{i}^{j'}-M$. Thus, we may write \begin{equation} W_{i}(y)=\prod_{k=1}^{n_{i}^{j'}-M}u_{k}^{i}(y)=\prod_{m=1}^{s-1}\prod_{k=p_{m}}^{p_{m+1}-1}u_{k}^{i}(y)\times\prod_{k=p_{s}}^{n_{i}^{j'}-M}u_{k}^{i}(y). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Split the product defining W_i(y) at the block starts p_k

nodes.name: Reindex a block
nodes.statement: Fix $1\leq m<s$. Then, $$ \prod_{k=p_{m}}^{p_{m+1}-1}u_{k}^{i}(y)=\prod_{k=p_{m}}^{p_{m+1}-1}\prod_{t=1}^{M-1}u_{(k \ k+t)}^{i}(\Theta_{i}(y)_{k,k}\Delta_{i}'(y)_{k+t,k+t}). $$ By (I), the last $M$ entries of $\Theta_{i_{m}}(x_{m})$ are zero. Hence, on account of the diagonal decomposition of $\Theta_{i}(y)$, the quantity above is equal to $$ \prod_{k=p_{m}}^{(p_{m+1}-1)-M}\prod_{t=1}^{M-1}u_{(k \ k+t)}^{i}(\Theta_{i_{m}}(x_{m})_{k-p_{m}+1,k-p_{m}+1}\Delta_{i_{m}}'(x_{m})_{k-p_{m}+1+t,k-p_{m}+1+t}), $$ which, upon relabelling indices, becomes \begin{equation} \prod_{q=1}^{p_{m+1}-p_{m}-M}\prod_{t=1}^{M-1}u^{i}_{(q+p_{m}-1 \ q+p_{m}-1+t)}(\Theta_{i_{m}}(x_{m})_{q,q}\Delta_{i_{m}}'(x_{m})_{q+t,q+t}). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Within a block, vanishing last entries of Theta let the product be reindexed

nodes.name: Identify blocks
nodes.statement: For each $1\leq q\leq p_{m+1}-p_{m}-M$ and $1\leq t\leq M-1$, note that $$ u^{i}_{(q+p_{m}-1 \ q+p_{m}-1+t)}=\operatorname{diag}(1_{p_{m}-1},u_{(q \ q+t)}^{i_{m}},1_{n_{i}^{j'}-p_{m+1}+1}). $$ Hence, we may rewrite \autoref{reindex} as $$ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{diag}\left(1_{p_{m}-1},\prod_{q=1}^{p_{m+1}-p_{m}-M}u_{q}^{i_{m}}(x_{m}),1_{n_{i}^{j'}-p_{m+1}+1}\right) =\operatorname{diag}\left(1_{p_{m}-1},W_{i_{m}}(x_{m}),1_{n_{i}^{j'}-p_{m+1}+1}\right). \end{aligned} $$ Therefore, for all $1\leq m <s$, $$ \prod_{k=p_{m}}^{p_{m+1}-1}u_{k}^{i}(y)=\operatorname{diag}\left(1_{p_{m}-1},W_{i_{m}}(x_{m}),1_{n_{i}^{j'}-p_{m+1}+1}\right) $$ and, similarly, $$ \prod_{k=p_{s}}^{n_{i}^{j'}-M}u_{k}^{i}(y)=\operatorname{diag}(1_{p_{s}-1},W_{i_{s}}(x_{s})). $$ Plugging this into \autoref{Wi} shows that $W_{i}(y)=\operatorname{diag}(W_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots,W_{i_{s}}(x_{s}))$, which proves that $W\in A$. The proof of \autoref{far out} is now complete.
nodes.statement_short: Each block product is W_{i_m}(x_m), so W_i(y) is block diagonal

nodes.name: Matrix sizes exceed NM
nodes.statement: \mathfrak{s}(A_{j'})>NM.
nodes.label: big enough

nodes.name: Block point
nodes.statement: Given a matrix $D\in M_{n}$ and $1\leq k\leq n$, we say that $D$ has a \textit{block point at index $k$} provided that $D_{i,j}=0$ if either $i\geq k$ and $j<k$ or $i<k$ and $j\geq k$.
differentia: $D_{i,j}=0$ if either $i\geq k$ and $j<k$ or $i<k$ and $j\geq k$

nodes.name: Approximation with block points near B_{i,k}
nodes.statement: Suppose $A$ is a DSH algebra of length $ l $. Suppose $f\in A$ and $\epsilon>0$. Then there is a $g\in A$ with $\|g-f\|\leq \epsilon$ and with the property that for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$, there are (possible empty) open sets $\mathcal{O}_{i,k}\supset B_{i,k}$ in $X_{i}$ such that $g_{i}(x)$ has a block point at index $k$ whenever $x\in \mathcal{O}_{i,k}$. Moreover, $g$ can be chosen so that for each $1\leq i\leq l $ and $x\in X_{i}$, $g_{i}(x)$ has a zero cross at index $k$ whenever $f_{i}(x)$ does, and $\mathfrak{r}(g_{i}(x))\leq \mathfrak{r}(f_{i}(x))$.
assumptions: $A$ is a DSH algebra of length $ l $
$f\in A$ and $\epsilon>0$
conclusions: there is a $g\in A$ with $\|g-f\|\leq \epsilon$
$g$ can be chosen so that for each $1\leq i\leq l $ and $x\in X_{i}$, $g_{i}(x)$ has a zero cross at index $k$ whenever $f_{i}(x)$ does, and $\mathfrak{r}(g_{i}(x))\leq \mathfrak{r}(f_{i}(x))$
nodes.statement_short: f can be approximated by g that has block points at index k on neighbourhoods of B_{i,k}, keeping zero crosses and bandwidth.
nodes.label: block on set

nodes.name: Proof of the block-point approximation
nodes.statement: Given $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq s,t\leq n_{i}$, let $f_{i}(\, \cdot\,)_{s,t}\in C(X_{i})$ denote the function taking $x$ into $f_{i}(x)_{s,t}$. Let $\delta=\epsilon/\mathfrak{S}(A)^{2}$. Define $h\in C(\mathbb{C})$ by $h(z):=\frac{z}{|z|}\cdot\max(0,|z|-\delta)$, where it is understood that $h(0)=0$. Note that for any $z\in \mathbb{C}$, if $|z|\leq\delta$, then $|h(z)-z|=|z|\leq \delta$, and if $|z|> \delta$, then $|h(z)-z|=\left|\frac{z}{|z|}(|z|-\delta)-z\right|=\left|\frac{z}{|z|}\delta\right|=\delta$. Thus, for all $z\in \mathbb{C}$, $|h(z)-z|\leq\delta$ and, hence, $|f_{i}(x)_{s,t}-h(f_{i}(x)_{s,t})|\leq \delta$ given any $1\leq i\leq l $, $1\leq s,t\leq n_{i}$, and $x\in X_{i}$. Define $g_{i}(x)_{s,t}:=h(f_{i}(x)_{s,t})$ and denote by $g_{i}$ the matrix-valued function in $C(X_{i},M_{n_{i}})$ given by $(g_{i}(\,\cdot\,)_{s,t})_{s,t}$. Set $g:=(g_{1},\ldots,g_{ l })\in\bigoplus_{i=1}^{ l }C(X_{i},M_{n_{i}})$. For $x\in X_{i}$, $$ \|f_{i}(x)-g_{i}(x)\|\leq\sum_{1\leq s,t\leq n_{i}}\|f_{i}(x)_{s,t}-g_{i}(x)_{s,t}\|\leq n_{i}^{2}\delta\leq \epsilon. $$ Hence, $\|f-g\|\leq\epsilon$. To see that $g\in A$, observe that if $y\in Y_{i}$ decomposes into $x_{1}\in X_{i_{1}}\setminus Y_{i_{1}},\ldots,x_{t}\in X_{i_{t}}\setminus Y_{i_{t}}$, then $f_{i}(y)=\operatorname{diag}(f_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots,f_{i_{t}}(x_{t}))$. Applying $h$ to each coordinate yields that $g_{i}(y)=\operatorname{diag}(g_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots,g_{i_{t}}(x_{t}))$. Furthermore, since $h(0)=0$, $g_{i}(x)$ must have a zero cross at any index that $f_{i}(x)$ does, and $\mathfrak{r}(g_{i}(x))\leq \mathfrak{r}(f_{i}(x))$. Lastly, fix $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$. Let us show how to construct $\mathcal{O}_{i,k}$. If $B_{i,k}=\varnothing$, take $\mathcal{O}_{i,k}:=\varnothing$. Otherwise, suppose $x\in B_{i,k}$. Then, $f_{i}(x)$ has a block point at index $k$. Let $I\subset \{1,\ldots,n_{i}\}^{2}$ denote the set of indices $(s,t)$ such that $s\geq k$ and $t<k$ or such that $s<k$ and $t\geq k$. Given $(s,t)\in I$, it follows that $f_{i}(x)_{s,t}=0$, and hence, that $g_{i}( \, \cdot \,)_{s,t}$ is $0$ on an open set $U_{s,t}(x)\subset X_{i}$ containing $x$. Then $U_{s,t}:=\bigcup_{x\in B_{i,k}}U_{s,t}(x)$ is an open set containing $B_{i,k}$ on which $g_{i}( \, \cdot \,)_{s,t}$ vanishes. Take $\mathcal{O}_{i,k}:=\bigcap_{(s,t)\in I}U_{s,t}$. By construction, then, $g_{i}(x)_{s,t}=0$ whenever $x\in \mathcal{O}_{i,k}$ and $(s,t)\in I$. Thus, $g_{i}(x)$ has a block point at index $k$ provided that $x\in \mathcal{O}_{i,k}$, which completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the entrywise shrinking map h(z)=z/|z| max(0,|z|-delta); small entries vanish on open neighbourhoods of B_{i,k}, where f has block points.

nodes.name: Shrink entries
nodes.statement: Given $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq s,t\leq n_{i}$, let $f_{i}(\, \cdot\,)_{s,t}\in C(X_{i})$ denote the function taking $x$ into $f_{i}(x)_{s,t}$. Let $\delta=\epsilon/\mathfrak{S}(A)^{2}$. Define $h\in C(\mathbb{C})$ by $h(z):=\frac{z}{|z|}\cdot\max(0,|z|-\delta)$, where it is understood that $h(0)=0$. Note that for any $z\in \mathbb{C}$, if $|z|\leq\delta$, then $|h(z)-z|=|z|\leq \delta$, and if $|z|> \delta$, then $|h(z)-z|=\left|\frac{z}{|z|}(|z|-\delta)-z\right|=\left|\frac{z}{|z|}\delta\right|=\delta$. Thus, for all $z\in \mathbb{C}$, $|h(z)-z|\leq\delta$ and, hence, $|f_{i}(x)_{s,t}-h(f_{i}(x)_{s,t})|\leq \delta$ given any $1\leq i\leq l $, $1\leq s,t\leq n_{i}$, and $x\in X_{i}$. Define $g_{i}(x)_{s,t}:=h(f_{i}(x)_{s,t})$ and denote by $g_{i}$ the matrix-valued function in $C(X_{i},M_{n_{i}})$ given by $(g_{i}(\,\cdot\,)_{s,t})_{s,t}$. Set $g:=(g_{1},\ldots,g_{ l })\in\bigoplus_{i=1}^{ l }C(X_{i},M_{n_{i}})$. For $x\in X_{i}$, $$ \|f_{i}(x)-g_{i}(x)\|\leq\sum_{1\leq s,t\leq n_{i}}\|f_{i}(x)_{s,t}-g_{i}(x)_{s,t}\|\leq n_{i}^{2}\delta\leq \epsilon. $$ Hence, $\|f-g\|\leq\epsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Define g by applying the shrinking map h entrywise; g is epsilon-close to f

nodes.name: Shrinking map h
nodes.statement: Given $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq s,t\leq n_{i}$, let $f_{i}(\, \cdot\,)_{s,t}\in C(X_{i})$ denote the function taking $x$ into $f_{i}(x)_{s,t}$. Let $\delta=\epsilon/\mathfrak{S}(A)^{2}$. Define $h\in C(\mathbb{C})$ by $h(z):=\frac{z}{|z|}\cdot\max(0,|z|-\delta)$, where it is understood that $h(0)=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Define delta and h(z)=z/|z| max(0,|z|-delta)

nodes.name: h moves points by at most delta
nodes.statement: Note that for any $z\in \mathbb{C}$, if $|z|\leq\delta$, then $|h(z)-z|=|z|\leq \delta$, and if $|z|> \delta$, then $|h(z)-z|=\left|\frac{z}{|z|}(|z|-\delta)-z\right|=\left|\frac{z}{|z|}\delta\right|=\delta$. Thus, for all $z\in \mathbb{C}$, $|h(z)-z|\leq\delta$ and, hence, $|f_{i}(x)_{s,t}-h(f_{i}(x)_{s,t})|\leq \delta$ given any $1\leq i\leq l $, $1\leq s,t\leq n_{i}$, and $x\in X_{i}$.
nodes.statement_short: |h(z)-z| <= delta

nodes.name: Norm estimate
nodes.statement: Define $g_{i}(x)_{s,t}:=h(f_{i}(x)_{s,t})$ and denote by $g_{i}$ the matrix-valued function in $C(X_{i},M_{n_{i}})$ given by $(g_{i}(\,\cdot\,)_{s,t})_{s,t}$. Set $g:=(g_{1},\ldots,g_{ l })\in\bigoplus_{i=1}^{ l }C(X_{i},M_{n_{i}})$. For $x\in X_{i}$, $$ \|f_{i}(x)-g_{i}(x)\|\leq\sum_{1\leq s,t\leq n_{i}}\|f_{i}(x)_{s,t}-g_{i}(x)_{s,t}\|\leq n_{i}^{2}\delta\leq \epsilon. $$ Hence, $\|f-g\|\leq\epsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Entrywise bound gives ||f-g|| <= epsilon

nodes.name: g lies in A
nodes.statement: To see that $g\in A$, observe that if $y\in Y_{i}$ decomposes into $x_{1}\in X_{i_{1}}\setminus Y_{i_{1}},\ldots,x_{t}\in X_{i_{t}}\setminus Y_{i_{t}}$, then $f_{i}(y)=\operatorname{diag}(f_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots,f_{i_{t}}(x_{t}))$. Applying $h$ to each coordinate yields that $g_{i}(y)=\operatorname{diag}(g_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots,g_{i_{t}}(x_{t}))$. Furthermore, since $h(0)=0$, $g_{i}(x)$ must have a zero cross at any index that $f_{i}(x)$ does, and $\mathfrak{r}(g_{i}(x))\leq \mathfrak{r}(f_{i}(x))$.
nodes.statement_short: Entrywise h preserves diagonal decompositions, zero crosses and bandwidth

nodes.name: Claim: construct O_{i,k}
nodes.statement: Lastly, fix $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$. Let us show how to construct $\mathcal{O}_{i,k}$. If $B_{i,k}=\varnothing$, take $\mathcal{O}_{i,k}:=\varnothing$. Otherwise, suppose $x\in B_{i,k}$. Then, $f_{i}(x)$ has a block point at index $k$. Let $I\subset \{1,\ldots,n_{i}\}^{2}$ denote the set of indices $(s,t)$ such that $s\geq k$ and $t<k$ or such that $s<k$ and $t\geq k$. Given $(s,t)\in I$, it follows that $f_{i}(x)_{s,t}=0$, and hence, that $g_{i}( \, \cdot \,)_{s,t}$ is $0$ on an open set $U_{s,t}(x)\subset X_{i}$ containing $x$. Then $U_{s,t}:=\bigcup_{x\in B_{i,k}}U_{s,t}(x)$ is an open set containing $B_{i,k}$ on which $g_{i}( \, \cdot \,)_{s,t}$ vanishes. Take $\mathcal{O}_{i,k}:=\bigcap_{(s,t)\in I}U_{s,t}$. By construction, then, $g_{i}(x)_{s,t}=0$ whenever $x\in \mathcal{O}_{i,k}$ and $(s,t)\in I$. Thus, $g_{i}(x)$ has a block point at index $k$ provided that $x\in \mathcal{O}_{i,k}$, which completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Construct open sets where g has block points

nodes.name: Empty case
nodes.statement: If $B_{i,k}=\varnothing$, take $\mathcal{O}_{i,k}:=\varnothing$.
nodes.statement_short: Take O empty

nodes.name: Nonempty case
nodes.statement: Otherwise, suppose $x\in B_{i,k}$. Then, $f_{i}(x)$ has a block point at index $k$. Let $I\subset \{1,\ldots,n_{i}\}^{2}$ denote the set of indices $(s,t)$ such that $s\geq k$ and $t<k$ or such that $s<k$ and $t\geq k$. Given $(s,t)\in I$, it follows that $f_{i}(x)_{s,t}=0$, and hence, that $g_{i}( \, \cdot \,)_{s,t}$ is $0$ on an open set $U_{s,t}(x)\subset X_{i}$ containing $x$. Then $U_{s,t}:=\bigcup_{x\in B_{i,k}}U_{s,t}(x)$ is an open set containing $B_{i,k}$ on which $g_{i}( \, \cdot \,)_{s,t}$ vanishes.
nodes.statement_short: Off-block entries of f vanish at x, so those of g vanish near x

nodes.name: Intersect
nodes.statement: Take $\mathcal{O}_{i,k}:=\bigcap_{(s,t)\in I}U_{s,t}$. By construction, then, $g_{i}(x)_{s,t}=0$ whenever $x\in \mathcal{O}_{i,k}$ and $(s,t)\in I$. Thus, $g_{i}(x)$ has a block point at index $k$ provided that $x\in \mathcal{O}_{i,k}$, which completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Intersect the finitely many open sets

nodes.name: Grouping zero crosses into consecutive blocks
nodes.statement: Suppose $A$ is a DSH algebra of length $ l $ and that $M,N\in\mathbb{N}$ with $NM<\mathfrak{s}(A)$. Suppose $f$ is an element of $A$ with the property that for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq j\leq n_{i}$, there is a (possibly empty) open set $U_{i,k}\supset B_{i,k}$ in $X_{i}$ such that if $x\in U_{i,k}$, then $f_{i}(x)$ has zero crosses at indices $k,k+M,\ldots,k+(N-1)M$ and a block point at index $k$. Then, there exists a unitary $V\in A$ with the following properties: \begin{enumerate} \item for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$, there are open sets $\mathcal{O}_{i,k}\supset B_{i,k}$ in $X_{i}$ such that $V_{i}(x)f_{i}(x)V_{i}(x)^{*}$ has zero crosses at indices $k,k+1,\ldots,k+N-1$ whenever $x\in \mathcal{O}_{i,k}$; \item$\mathfrak{r}(V_{i}(x)f_{i}(x)V_{i}(x)^{*})\leq \mathfrak{r}(f_{i}(x))+2$ for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $x\in X_{i}$. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: $A$ is a DSH algebra of length $ l $ and that $M,N\in\mathbb{N}$ with $NM<\mathfrak{s}(A)$

$f$ is an element of $A$ with the property that for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq j\leq n_{i}$, there is a (possibly empty) open set $U_{i,k}\supset B_{i,k}$ in $X_{i}$ such that if $x\in U_{i,k}$, then $f_{i}(x)$ has zero crosses at indices $k,k+M,\ldots,k+(N-1)M$ and a block point at index $k$
conclusions: there exists a unitary $V\in A$ with the following properties
nodes.statement_short: Zero crosses spaced M apart near B_{i,k} can be moved by a unitary to N consecutive indices k,...,k+N-1, raising bandwidth by at most 2.
nodes.label: cross shift

nodes.name: Proof of the cross-shift lemma
nodes.statement: Apply \autoref{indicators} with the natural number $NM$, the index set $K=\{0\}$, and closed sets $F_{i,k}:=X_{i}\setminus U_{i,k}$ for $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$ to obtain a function $\Theta\in A$ possessing the following properties: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\Roman*)] \item for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $x\in X_{i}$, $\Theta_{i}(x)$ is a diagonal matrix with entries in $[0,1]$ whose final $NM$ diagonal entries are all $0$ and such that at most one of any $NM$ consecutive diagonal entries is non-zero; \item for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$, if $x\notin U_{i,k}$, then $\Theta_{i}(x)_{k,k}=0$; \item for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$, there is a (possibly empty) open subset $\mathcal{O}_{i,k}\subset X_{i}$ containing $B_{i,k}$ with the property that $\Theta_{i}(x)_{k,k}=1$ whenever $x\in\mathcal{O}_{i,k}$. \end{enumerate} Now, fix $1\leq i\leq l $. For $1\leq k\leq n_{i}-NM$, let $u_{k}\in C(X_{i},M_{n_{i}})$ be the unitary $$ u_{k}(x):=\operatorname{diag}(1_{k-1}, W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k,k}),1_{n_{i}-(NM+k-1)}), $$ where $W$ is the unitary in $C([0,1],M_{NM})$ given by \autoref{matrix} with $z_{1}:=1$, $z_{2}:=1+M$, \ldots, $z_{N}:=1+(N-1)M$. For $n_{i}-NM<k\leq n_{i}$, set $u_{k}\equiv1_{n_{i}}$. Define $V_{i}\in C(X_{i},M_{n_{i}})$ to be the unitary $$ V_{i}:=\prod_{k=1}^{n_{i}}u_{k}. $$ For $x\in X_{i}$, let $K(x):=\{1\leq k\leq n_{i}:\Theta_{i}(x)_{k,k}>0\}$ and write $K(x)=\{k_{1},\ldots,k_{s}\}$, where $k_{1}<\cdots<k_{s}$ and put $k_{s+1}:=n_{i}+1$. Note that $k_{1}=1$ by (III) above since $B_{i,1}=X_{i}$ by \autoref{Bik}, and for $1\leq t\leq s$, $k_{t+1}-k_{t}\geq NM$ by (I) above. If $k\notin K(x)$, then $u_{k}\equiv 1_{n_{i}}$. Hence, we may write \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} V_{i}(x)&=\prod_{t=1}^{s}u_{k_{t}}(x)\\ &=\operatorname{diag}\left(W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{1},k_{1}}),1_{d_{1}},W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{2},k_{2}}),1_{d_{2}},\ldots,W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{s},k_{s}}),1_{d_{s}}\right), \end{aligned} \end{equation} where $d_{t}:=k_{t+1}-(k_{t}+NM)$ for $1\leq t\leq s$. Let $V:=(V_{1},\ldots,V_{ l })$. In order to prove \autoref{cross shift}, let us show that \textit{(1)} holds, then that \textit{(2)} holds, and finally that $V\in A$. To prove \textit{(1)} and \textit{(2)}, fix $1\leq i\leq l $ and $x\in X_{i}$, and let $K(x)=\{k_{1},\ldots,k_{s}\}$ and $k_{s+1}$ be defined as above. For $1\leq t\leq s$, we have $\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}}>0$. Hence, by (II) above, it must be that $x\in U_{i,k_{t}}$ and, thus, $f_{i}(x)$ has a block point at index $k_{t}$ and zero crosses at indices $k_{t},k_{t}+M,\ldots,k_{t}+(N-1)M$ by the assumption of the lemma. Thus, $f_{i}(x)=\operatorname{diag}(Q_{1},Q_{2},\ldots,Q_{s})$, where $Q_{t}$ is a $k_{t+1}-k_{t}$ block for $1\leq t\leq s$ and has zero crosses at $1,1+M,\ldots,1+(N-1)M$. Therefore, in light of the decomposition of $V_{i}(x)$ in \autoref{Vi}, we may view $V_{i}(x)f_{i}(x)V_{i}(x)^{*}$ as a block-diagonal matrix $\operatorname{diag}(B_{1},\ldots,B_{s})$ with $$ B_{t}=\operatorname{diag}(W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}}),1_{d_{t}})\cdot Q_{t}\cdot\operatorname{diag}(W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}}),1_{d_{t}})^{*}. $$ Thus, to prove \textit{(2)}, it suffices to show that $\mathfrak{r}(B_{t})\leq\mathfrak{r}(Q_{t})+2$. Furthermore, if $x\in \mathcal{O}_{i,k}$ for some $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$, then by (III), $\Theta_{i}(x)_{k,k}=1>0$, and so $k=k_{t}$ for some $1\leq t\leq s$. Since the block $B_{t}$ begins at index $k_{t}$ down the diagonal of $V_{i}(x)f_{i}(x)V_{i}(x)^{*}$, to prove \textit{(1)} it suffices to show that $B_{t}$ has zero crosses at indices $1, 2,\ldots,N$ whenever $\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}}=1$. To this end, fix $1\leq t\leq s$ and write $$ Q_{t}= \begin{pmatrix} D_{11} & D_{12}\\ D_{21} & D_{22} \end{pmatrix}, $$ where $D_{11}\in M_{NM}$, $D_{22}\in M_{d_{t}}$, and $D_{12}$ and $D_{21}$ are $NM\times d_{t}$ and $d_{t}\times NM$ matrices, respectively. Note that $D_{11}$ has zero crosses at indices $1,1+M,\ldots,1+(N-1)M$, while the rows of $D_{12}$ and the columns of $D_{21}$ at these same indices consist entirely of zeros. We may write $$\begin{aligned} B_{t}=& \begin{pmatrix} W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}}) & 0_{NM\times d_{t}}\\ 0_{d_{t}\times NM} & 1_{d_{t}} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} D_{11} & D_{12}\\ D_{21} & D_{22} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}})^{*} & 0_{NM\times d_{t}}\\ 0_{d_{t}\times NM} & 1_{d_{t}} \end{pmatrix}\\ =&\begin{pmatrix} W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}})D_{11}W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}})^{*} & W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}})D_{12}\\ D_{21}W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}})^{*} & D_{22} \end{pmatrix}. \end{aligned} $$ If $\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}}=1$, then $$ B_{t}= \begin{pmatrix} W(1)D_{11}W(1)^{*} & W(1)D_{12}\\ D_{21}W(1)^{*} & D_{22} \end{pmatrix}. $$ By our definition of $W$, we may apply \autoref{matrix} to conclude that $W(1)D_{11}W(1)^{*}$ has zero crosses at indices $1,2,\ldots,N$, and that the first $1,2,\ldots, N$ rows of $W(1)D_{12}$ and columns of $D_{21}W(1)^{*}$ consist only of zeros. It follows that $B_{t}$ has zero crosses at indices $1,2,\ldots, N$, which, based on the aforementioned analysis, proves \textit{(1)}. Let us now prove \textit{(2)} by showing that $\mathfrak{r}(B_{t})\leq\mathfrak{r}(Q_{t})+2$. By our definition of $W$, we may apply \autoref{matrix} to obtain the following estimates: \begin{itemize} \item $\mathfrak{r}(W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}})D_{11}W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}})^{*})\leq \mathfrak{r}(D_{11})+2;$ \vspace{5pt} \item $\mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{NM\times NM} & W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}})D_{12}\\ 0_{d_{t}\times NM} & 0_{d_{t}\times d_{t}} \end{pmatrix} \right)\leq\mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{NM\times NM} & D_{12}\\ 0_{d_{t}\times NM} & 0_{d_{t}\times d_{t}} \end{pmatrix} \right);$ \vspace{5pt} \item $\mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{NM\times NM} & 0_{NM\times d_{t}}\\ D_{21}W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}})^{*} & 0_{d_{t}\times d_{t}} \end{pmatrix} \right)\leq\mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{NM\times NM} & 0_{NM\times d_{t}}\\ D_{21} & 0_{d_{t}\times d_{t}} \end{pmatrix} \right).$ \end{itemize} Combining these estimates gives $$ \mathfrak{r}(B_{t})=\mathfrak{r}\left(\begin{pmatrix} W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}})D_{11}W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}})^{*} & W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}})D_{12}\\ D_{21}W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}})^{*} & D_{22} \end{pmatrix}\right) \leq \mathfrak{r}(Q_{t})+2, $$ which proves \textit{(2)}. Finally, let us verify that $V\in A$. Suppose $y\in Y_{i}$ decomposes into $x_{1}\in X_{i_{1}}\setminus Y_{i_{1}},\ldots,x_{r}\in X_{i_{r}}\setminus Y_{i_{r}}$. We need to show that $V_{i}(y)=\operatorname{diag}(V_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots,V_{i_{r}}(x_{r}))$. Let $K(y)=\{1\leq k\leq n_{i}:\Theta_{i}(y)_{k,k}>0\}$, as defined above. Write $K(y)=\{k_{1},\ldots,k_{s}\}$, where $1=k_{1}<\cdots<k_{s}$, and put $k_{s+1}:=n_{i}+1$. As before, let $d_{t}:=k_{t+1}-(k_{t}+NM)$ for $1\leq t\leq s$. Define $B(y):=\{1\leq k\leq n_{i}:y\in B_{i,k}\}$. By (III) above, $B(y)\subset K(y)$. Hence by \autoref{Bik}, for each $1\leq j\leq r$, there is a $t_{j}\in\{1,\ldots,s\}$ such that $1+n_{i_{1}}+\cdots+n_{i_{j-1}}=k_{t_{j}}$ (where $k_{t_{1}}=1=k_{1}$, so that $t_{1}=1$); set $t_{r+1}:=s+1$, so that $k_{t_{r+1}}=k_{s+1}=n_{i}+1$. Now, fix $1\leq j\leq r$ and observe that $\Theta_{i_{j}}(x_{j})_{k,k}=\Theta_{i}(y)_{k_{t_{j}}+k-1, k_{t_{j}}+k-1}$. Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned} K(x_{j})&=\{1\leq k\leq n_{i_{j}}:\Theta_{i_{j}}(x_{j})_{k,k}>0\}\\ &=\{k-k_{t_{j}}+1:k\in K(y)\text{ and }k_{t_{j}}\leq k<k_{t_{j+1}}\}\\ &=\{k_{t}-k_{t_{j}}+1:t_{j}\leq t<t_{j+1}\}. \end{aligned} $$ Moreover, if $t_{j}\leq t<t_{j+1}$, then $(k_{t+1}-k_{t_{j}}+1)-(k_{t}-k_{t_{j}}+1+NM)=d_{t}$. Given matrices $E_{1},\ldots,E_{p}$, let $\bigoplus_{q=1}^{p}E_{q}:=\operatorname{diag}(E_{1},\ldots,E_{p})$. Then, by the computation of $K(x_{j})$ above and \autoref{Vi}, it follows that $$ \begin{aligned} V_{i_{j}}(x_{j}) &=\bigoplus_{t_{j}\leq t<t_{j+1}}\operatorname{diag}\left(W(\Theta_{i_{j}}(x_{j})_{k_{t}-k_{t_{j}}+1,k_{t}-k_{t_{j}}+1}),1_{(k_{t+1}-k_{t_{j}}+1)-(k_{t}-k_{t_{j}}+1+NM)}\right)\\ &=\bigoplus_{t_{j}\leq t<t_{j+1}}\operatorname{diag}\left(W(\Theta_{i}(y)_{k_{t},k_{t}}),1_{d_{t}}\right). \end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{diag}(V_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots,V_{i_{r}}(x_{r}))&=\bigoplus_{1\leq j\leq r}\bigoplus_{t_{j}\leq t<t_{j+1}}\operatorname{diag}\left(W(\Theta_{i}(y)_{k_{t},k_{t}}),1_{d_{t}}\right)\\ &=\bigoplus_{1\leq t\leq s}\operatorname{diag}\left(W(\Theta_{i}(y)_{k_{t},k_{t}}),1_{d_{t}}\right)\\ &=V_{i}(y), \end{aligned} $$ where the last equality follows by \autoref{Vi}. This shows that $V\in A$. The proof of \autoref{cross shift} is now complete.
nodes.statement_short: Build V_i blockwise from the zero-cross moving path W evaluated at an indicator Theta; check the zero crosses, bandwidth and compatibility with the decomposition.

nodes.name: Indicator Theta
nodes.statement: Apply \autoref{indicators} with the natural number $NM$, the index set $K=\{0\}$, and closed sets $F_{i,k}:=X_{i}\setminus U_{i,k}$ for $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$ to obtain a function $\Theta\in A$ possessing the following properties: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\Roman*)] \item for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $x\in X_{i}$, $\Theta_{i}(x)$ is a diagonal matrix with entries in $[0,1]$ whose final $NM$ diagonal entries are all $0$ and such that at most one of any $NM$ consecutive diagonal entries is non-zero; \item for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$, if $x\notin U_{i,k}$, then $\Theta_{i}(x)_{k,k}=0$; \item for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$, there is a (possibly empty) open subset $\mathcal{O}_{i,k}\subset X_{i}$ containing $B_{i,k}$ with the property that $\Theta_{i}(x)_{k,k}=1$ whenever $x\in\mathcal{O}_{i,k}$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the indicator lemma with K={0} and F=X minus U

nodes.name: Apply the indicator lemma
nodes.statement: Apply \autoref{indicators} with the natural number $NM$, the index set $K=\{0\}$, and closed sets $F_{i,k}:=X_{i}\setminus U_{i,k}$ for $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$ to obtain a function $\Theta\in A$ possessing the following properties:
nodes.statement_short: Get Theta in A with:

nodes.name: Property (I)
nodes.statement: for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $x\in X_{i}$, $\Theta_{i}(x)$ is a diagonal matrix with entries in $[0,1]$ whose final $NM$ diagonal entries are all $0$ and such that at most one of any $NM$ consecutive diagonal entries is non-zero;
nodes.statement_short: Sparse diagonal entries

nodes.name: Property (II)
nodes.statement: for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$, if $x\notin U_{i,k}$, then $\Theta_{i}(x)_{k,k}=0$;
nodes.statement_short: Theta vanishes off U_{i,k}

nodes.name: Property (III)
nodes.statement: for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$, there is a (possibly empty) open subset $\mathcal{O}_{i,k}\subset X_{i}$ containing $B_{i,k}$ with the property that $\Theta_{i}(x)_{k,k}=1$ whenever $x\in\mathcal{O}_{i,k}$.
nodes.statement_short: Theta equals 1 near B_{i,k}

nodes.name: Define V_i
nodes.statement: Now, fix $1\leq i\leq l $. For $1\leq k\leq n_{i}-NM$, let $u_{k}\in C(X_{i},M_{n_{i}})$ be the unitary $$ u_{k}(x):=\operatorname{diag}(1_{k-1}, W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k,k}),1_{n_{i}-(NM+k-1)}), $$ where $W$ is the unitary in $C([0,1],M_{NM})$ given by \autoref{matrix} with $z_{1}:=1$, $z_{2}:=1+M$, \ldots, $z_{N}:=1+(N-1)M$. For $n_{i}-NM<k\leq n_{i}$, set $u_{k}\equiv1_{n_{i}}$. Define $V_{i}\in C(X_{i},M_{n_{i}})$ to be the unitary $$ V_{i}:=\prod_{k=1}^{n_{i}}u_{k}. $$
nodes.statement_short: V_i is the product of blocks diag(1, W(Theta_{k,k}), 1)

nodes.name: Block form of V_i
nodes.statement: For $x\in X_{i}$, let $K(x):=\{1\leq k\leq n_{i}:\Theta_{i}(x)_{k,k}>0\}$ and write $K(x)=\{k_{1},\ldots,k_{s}\}$, where $k_{1}<\cdots<k_{s}$ and put $k_{s+1}:=n_{i}+1$. Note that $k_{1}=1$ by (III) above since $B_{i,1}=X_{i}$ by \autoref{Bik}, and for $1\leq t\leq s$, $k_{t+1}-k_{t}\geq NM$ by (I) above. If $k\notin K(x)$, then $u_{k}\equiv 1_{n_{i}}$. Hence, we may write \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} V_{i}(x)&=\prod_{t=1}^{s}u_{k_{t}}(x)\\ &=\operatorname{diag}\left(W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{1},k_{1}}),1_{d_{1}},W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{2},k_{2}}),1_{d_{2}},\ldots,W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{s},k_{s}}),1_{d_{s}}\right), \end{aligned} \end{equation} where $d_{t}:=k_{t+1}-(k_{t}+NM)$ for $1\leq t\leq s$.
nodes.statement_short: V_i(x) is block diagonal along the indices where Theta is positive

nodes.name: Plan
nodes.statement: Let $V:=(V_{1},\ldots,V_{ l })$. In order to prove \autoref{cross shift}, let us show that \textit{(1)} holds, then that \textit{(2)} holds, and finally that $V\in A$.
nodes.statement_short: Prove (1), (2) and V in A

nodes.name: Reduce to blocks
nodes.statement: To prove \textit{(1)} and \textit{(2)}, fix $1\leq i\leq l $ and $x\in X_{i}$, and let $K(x)=\{k_{1},\ldots,k_{s}\}$ and $k_{s+1}$ be defined as above. For $1\leq t\leq s$, we have $\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}}>0$. Hence, by (II) above, it must be that $x\in U_{i,k_{t}}$ and, thus, $f_{i}(x)$ has a block point at index $k_{t}$ and zero crosses at indices $k_{t},k_{t}+M,\ldots,k_{t}+(N-1)M$ by the assumption of the lemma. Thus, $f_{i}(x)=\operatorname{diag}(Q_{1},Q_{2},\ldots,Q_{s})$, where $Q_{t}$ is a $k_{t+1}-k_{t}$ block for $1\leq t\leq s$ and has zero crosses at $1,1+M,\ldots,1+(N-1)M$. Therefore, in light of the decomposition of $V_{i}(x)$ in \autoref{Vi}, we may view $V_{i}(x)f_{i}(x)V_{i}(x)^{*}$ as a block-diagonal matrix $\operatorname{diag}(B_{1},\ldots,B_{s})$ with $$ B_{t}=\operatorname{diag}(W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}}),1_{d_{t}})\cdot Q_{t}\cdot\operatorname{diag}(W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}}),1_{d_{t}})^{*}. $$ Thus, to prove \textit{(2)}, it suffices to show that $\mathfrak{r}(B_{t})\leq\mathfrak{r}(Q_{t})+2$. Furthermore, if $x\in \mathcal{O}_{i,k}$ for some $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$, then by (III), $\Theta_{i}(x)_{k,k}=1>0$, and so $k=k_{t}$ for some $1\leq t\leq s$. Since the block $B_{t}$ begins at index $k_{t}$ down the diagonal of $V_{i}(x)f_{i}(x)V_{i}(x)^{*}$, to prove \textit{(1)} it suffices to show that $B_{t}$ has zero crosses at indices $1, 2,\ldots,N$ whenever $\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}}=1$.
nodes.statement_short: f_i(x) is block diagonal with blocks Q_t; reduce (1), (2) to each block B_t

nodes.name: Zero crosses in each block
nodes.statement: To this end, fix $1\leq t\leq s$ and write $$ Q_{t}= \begin{pmatrix} D_{11} & D_{12}\\ D_{21} & D_{22} \end{pmatrix}, $$ where $D_{11}\in M_{NM}$, $D_{22}\in M_{d_{t}}$, and $D_{12}$ and $D_{21}$ are $NM\times d_{t}$ and $d_{t}\times NM$ matrices, respectively. Note that $D_{11}$ has zero crosses at indices $1,1+M,\ldots,1+(N-1)M$, while the rows of $D_{12}$ and the columns of $D_{21}$ at these same indices consist entirely of zeros. We may write $$\begin{aligned} B_{t}=& \begin{pmatrix} W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}}) & 0_{NM\times d_{t}}\\ 0_{d_{t}\times NM} & 1_{d_{t}} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} D_{11} & D_{12}\\ D_{21} & D_{22} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}})^{*} & 0_{NM\times d_{t}}\\ 0_{d_{t}\times NM} & 1_{d_{t}} \end{pmatrix}\\ =&\begin{pmatrix} W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}})D_{11}W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}})^{*} & W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}})D_{12}\\ D_{21}W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}})^{*} & D_{22} \end{pmatrix}. \end{aligned} $$ If $\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}}=1$, then $$ B_{t}= \begin{pmatrix} W(1)D_{11}W(1)^{*} & W(1)D_{12}\\ D_{21}W(1)^{*} & D_{22} \end{pmatrix}. $$ By our definition of $W$, we may apply \autoref{matrix} to conclude that $W(1)D_{11}W(1)^{*}$ has zero crosses at indices $1,2,\ldots,N$, and that the first $1,2,\ldots, N$ rows of $W(1)D_{12}$ and columns of $D_{21}W(1)^{*}$ consist only of zeros. It follows that $B_{t}$ has zero crosses at indices $1,2,\ldots, N$, which, based on the aforementioned analysis, proves \textit{(1)}.
nodes.statement_short: The zero-cross moving lemma gives zero crosses at 1..N in B_t

nodes.name: Bandwidth in each block
nodes.statement: Let us now prove \textit{(2)} by showing that $\mathfrak{r}(B_{t})\leq\mathfrak{r}(Q_{t})+2$. By our definition of $W$, we may apply \autoref{matrix} to obtain the following estimates: \begin{itemize} \item $\mathfrak{r}(W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}})D_{11}W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}})^{*})\leq \mathfrak{r}(D_{11})+2;$ \vspace{5pt} \item $\mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{NM\times NM} & W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}})D_{12}\\ 0_{d_{t}\times NM} & 0_{d_{t}\times d_{t}} \end{pmatrix} \right)\leq\mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{NM\times NM} & D_{12}\\ 0_{d_{t}\times NM} & 0_{d_{t}\times d_{t}} \end{pmatrix} \right);$ \vspace{5pt} \item $\mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{NM\times NM} & 0_{NM\times d_{t}}\\ D_{21}W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}})^{*} & 0_{d_{t}\times d_{t}} \end{pmatrix} \right)\leq\mathfrak{r}\left( \begin{pmatrix} 0_{NM\times NM} & 0_{NM\times d_{t}}\\ D_{21} & 0_{d_{t}\times d_{t}} \end{pmatrix} \right).$ \end{itemize} Combining these estimates gives $$ \mathfrak{r}(B_{t})=\mathfrak{r}\left(\begin{pmatrix} W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}})D_{11}W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}})^{*} & W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}})D_{12}\\ D_{21}W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{t},k_{t}})^{*} & D_{22} \end{pmatrix}\right) \leq \mathfrak{r}(Q_{t})+2, $$ which proves \textit{(2)}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine the lemma's three estimates to get r(B_t) <= r(Q_t)+2

nodes.name: Index bookkeeping at Y_i
nodes.statement: Finally, let us verify that $V\in A$. Suppose $y\in Y_{i}$ decomposes into $x_{1}\in X_{i_{1}}\setminus Y_{i_{1}},\ldots,x_{r}\in X_{i_{r}}\setminus Y_{i_{r}}$. We need to show that $V_{i}(y)=\operatorname{diag}(V_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots,V_{i_{r}}(x_{r}))$. Let $K(y)=\{1\leq k\leq n_{i}:\Theta_{i}(y)_{k,k}>0\}$, as defined above. Write $K(y)=\{k_{1},\ldots,k_{s}\}$, where $1=k_{1}<\cdots<k_{s}$, and put $k_{s+1}:=n_{i}+1$. As before, let $d_{t}:=k_{t+1}-(k_{t}+NM)$ for $1\leq t\leq s$. Define $B(y):=\{1\leq k\leq n_{i}:y\in B_{i,k}\}$. By (III) above, $B(y)\subset K(y)$. Hence by \autoref{Bik}, for each $1\leq j\leq r$, there is a $t_{j}\in\{1,\ldots,s\}$ such that $1+n_{i_{1}}+\cdots+n_{i_{j-1}}=k_{t_{j}}$ (where $k_{t_{1}}=1=k_{1}$, so that $t_{1}=1$); set $t_{r+1}:=s+1$, so that $k_{t_{r+1}}=k_{s+1}=n_{i}+1$.
nodes.statement_short: Starting indices of the decomposition are among the indices where Theta is positive

nodes.name: V respects decompositions
nodes.statement: Now, fix $1\leq j\leq r$ and observe that $\Theta_{i_{j}}(x_{j})_{k,k}=\Theta_{i}(y)_{k_{t_{j}}+k-1, k_{t_{j}}+k-1}$. Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned} K(x_{j})&=\{1\leq k\leq n_{i_{j}}:\Theta_{i_{j}}(x_{j})_{k,k}>0\}\\ &=\{k-k_{t_{j}}+1:k\in K(y)\text{ and }k_{t_{j}}\leq k<k_{t_{j+1}}\}\\ &=\{k_{t}-k_{t_{j}}+1:t_{j}\leq t<t_{j+1}\}. \end{aligned} $$ Moreover, if $t_{j}\leq t<t_{j+1}$, then $(k_{t+1}-k_{t_{j}}+1)-(k_{t}-k_{t_{j}}+1+NM)=d_{t}$. Given matrices $E_{1},\ldots,E_{p}$, let $\bigoplus_{q=1}^{p}E_{q}:=\operatorname{diag}(E_{1},\ldots,E_{p})$. Then, by the computation of $K(x_{j})$ above and \autoref{Vi}, it follows that $$ \begin{aligned} V_{i_{j}}(x_{j}) &=\bigoplus_{t_{j}\leq t<t_{j+1}}\operatorname{diag}\left(W(\Theta_{i_{j}}(x_{j})_{k_{t}-k_{t_{j}}+1,k_{t}-k_{t_{j}}+1}),1_{(k_{t+1}-k_{t_{j}}+1)-(k_{t}-k_{t_{j}}+1+NM)}\right)\\ &=\bigoplus_{t_{j}\leq t<t_{j+1}}\operatorname{diag}\left(W(\Theta_{i}(y)_{k_{t},k_{t}}),1_{d_{t}}\right). \end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{diag}(V_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots,V_{i_{r}}(x_{r}))&=\bigoplus_{1\leq j\leq r}\bigoplus_{t_{j}\leq t<t_{j+1}}\operatorname{diag}\left(W(\Theta_{i}(y)_{k_{t},k_{t}}),1_{d_{t}}\right)\\ &=\bigoplus_{1\leq t\leq s}\operatorname{diag}\left(W(\Theta_{i}(y)_{k_{t},k_{t}}),1_{d_{t}}\right)\\ &=V_{i}(y), \end{aligned} $$ where the last equality follows by \autoref{Vi}. This shows that $V\in A$. The proof of \autoref{cross shift} is now complete.
nodes.statement_short: V_i(y) is the diagonal of the V_{i_j}(x_j), so V is in A

nodes.name: Block form of V_i(x)
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} V_{i}(x)&=\prod_{t=1}^{s}u_{k_{t}}(x)\\ &=\operatorname{diag}\left(W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{1},k_{1}}),1_{d_{1}},W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{2},k_{2}}),1_{d_{2}},\ldots,W(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k_{s},k_{s}}),1_{d_{s}}\right), \end{aligned}
nodes.label: Vi

nodes.name: Unitary making an element strictly lower triangular
nodes.statement: Suppose $A$ is a DSH algebra of length $ l $ and that $1\leq N<\mathfrak{s}(A)$. Suppose $f\in A$ is such that for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$, there is an open subset $U_{i,k}\subset X_{i}$ containing $B_{i,k}$ with the property that if $x\in U_{i,k}$, then $f_{i}(x)$ has zero crosses at indices $k,k+1,\ldots,k+N-1$, and such that $\mathfrak{r}(f_{i}(x))\leq N$ for all $x\in X_{i}$. Then, there is a unitary $V\in A$ such that for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $x\in X_{i}$, the matrix $(fV)_{i}(x)$ is strictly lower triangular.
assumptions: $A$ is a DSH algebra of length $ l $ and that $1\leq N<\mathfrak{s}(A)$

$f\in A$ is such that for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$, there is an open subset $U_{i,k}\subset X_{i}$ containing $B_{i,k}$ with the property that if $x\in U_{i,k}$, then $f_{i}(x)$ has zero crosses at indices $k,k+1,\ldots,k+N-1$, and such that $\mathfrak{r}(f_{i}(x))\leq N$ for all $x\in X_{i}$
conclusions: there is a unitary $V\in A$ such that for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $x\in X_{i}$, the matrix $(fV)_{i}(x)$ is strictly lower triangular
nodes.statement_short: With N consecutive zero crosses near each B_{i,k} and bandwidth at most N, right multiplication by a unitary makes f strictly lower triangular.
nodes.label: lower triangular

nodes.name: Proof of the lower triangular lemma
nodes.statement: Apply \autoref{indicators} with the natural number $N$, the index set $K=\{0\}$, and the closed sets $F_{i,k}:=X_{i}\setminus U_{i,k}$ for $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$. This yields a function $\Theta\in A$ with the following properties: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\Roman*)] \item for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $x\in X_{i}$, $\Theta_{i}(x)$ is a diagonal matrix with entries in $[0,1]$ whose final $N$ entries are all $0$ and such that at most one of every $N$ consecutive diagonal entries is non-zero; \item for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$, if $x\notin U_{i,k}$, then $\Theta_{i}(x)_{k,k}=0$; \item for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$, if $x\in B_{i,k}$, then $\Theta_{i}(x)_{k,k}=1$. \end{enumerate} Since $N<\mathfrak{s}(A)$, we may, for each $1\leq i\leq l $, define $W_{n_{i}}\in C([0,1]^{n_{i}},M_{n_{i}})$ as in \autoref{ltmatrix}. For $1\leq i\leq l$ and $x\in X_{i}$, define the unitary $V_{i}\in C(X_{i},M_{n_{i}})$ by $$ V_{i}(x):=W_{n_{i}}(\Theta_{i}(x)_{1,1},\ldots,\Theta_{i}(x)_{n_{i},n_{i}}) $$ and set $V:=(V_{1},\ldots,V_{\ell})$. Let us first argue that $(fV)_{i}(x)$ is strictly lower triangular for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $x\in X_{i}$, and then show that $V\in A$. Fix $1\leq i\leq l $ and $x\in X_{i}$. From \autoref{Wn}, we have \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} (fV)_{i}(x)&=f_{i}(x)W_{n_{i}}(\Theta_{i}(x)_{1,1},\ldots,\Theta_{i}(x)_{n_{i},n_{i}})\\ &=f_{i}(x)U[\gamma_{1,n_{i}}^{n_{i}}]^{N}\prod_{k=N}^{n_{i}-1}u^{n_{i}}_{k,n_{i}}(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k+1,k+1}). \end{aligned} \end{equation} If we write $f_{i}(x)=\big[\, C_{1}\, |\, \cdots\, |\, C_{n_{i}}\, \big]$, where $C_{j}$ is the $j$th column of $f_{i}(x)$, then $f_{i}(x)U[\gamma_{1,n_{i}}^{n_{i}}]^{N}=\big[C_{N+1}\, |\, \cdots\, |\, C_{n_{i}}\, |\, C_{1}\, |\, \cdots\, |\, C_{N}\, \big]$. By the assumption of the lemma, $\mathfrak{r}(f_{i}(x))\leq N$. Hence, all non-zero entries in the first $n_{i}-N$ columns of the matrix $f_{i}(x)U[\gamma_{1,n_{i}}^{n_{i}}]^{N}$ must lie strictly below the diagonal. But by \autoref{Bik}, $x\in B_{i,1}$ and, hence, by the assumptions of the lemma, $f_{i}(x)$ has zero crosses at indices $1,\ldots, N$. In particular, the columns $C_{1},\ldots,C_{N}$ consist entirely of zeros. Therefore, $f_{i}(x)U[\gamma_{1,n_{i}}^{n_{i}}]^{N}$ is strictly lower triangular. To show that $(fV)_{i}(x)$ is strictly lower triangular, we thus only need to verify that $(fV)_{i}(x)=f_{i}(x)U[\gamma_{1,n_{i}}^{n_{i}}]^{N}$. To do this, it is enough, by \autoref{fV}, to check that for each integer $N\leq k\leq n_{i}-1$, \begin{equation} f_{i}(x)U[\gamma_{1,n_{i}}^{n_{i}}]^{N}u^{n_{i}}_{k,n_{i}}(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k+1,k+1})=f_{i}(x)U[\gamma_{1,n_{i}}^{n_{i}}]^{N}. \end{equation} To this end, fix $N\leq k\leq n_{i}-1$. If $\Theta_{i}(x)_{k+1,k+1}=0$, then $u^{n_{i}}_{k,n_{i}}(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k+1,k+1})=1_{n_{i}}$ and there is nothing to show, and so we may assume $\Theta_{i}(x)_{k+1,k+1}>0$. Then, by (II) above, necessarily $x\in U_{i,k+1}$. Hence, by the assumption of the lemma, $f_{i}(x)$ has zero crosses at indices $k+1, \ldots,k+N$, from which it follows that the columns $C_{k+1},\ldots,C_{k+N}$ consist entirely of zeros. As noted above, these correspond to the columns of $f_{i}(x)U[\gamma_{1,n_{i}}^{n_{i}}]^{N}$ at indices $k+1-N,\ldots,k$. By \autoref{transposition prod}, the columns of $f_{i}(x)U[\gamma_{1,n_{i}}^{n_{i}}]^{N}u^{n_{i}}_{k,n_{i}}(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k+1,k+1})$ at indices $k-N+1,\ldots,k$ and $n_{i}-N+1,\ldots,n_{i}$ are linear combinations of the same set of columns of $f_{i}(x)U[\gamma_{1,n_{i}}^{n_{i}}]^{N}$ (i.e., of $C_{k+1},\ldots,C_{k+N},C_{1},\ldots,C_{N}$). But every column in this latter set consists entirely of zeros. Hence, since multiplying by the unitary $u^{n_{i}}_{k,n_{i}}(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k+1,k+1})$ on the right only alters columns at indices $k-N+1,\ldots,k$ and $n_{i}-N+1,\ldots,n_{i}$, \autoref{final} holds. Let us now ensure that $V\in A$. Suppose that $2\leq i\leq l $ and that $y\in Y_{i}$ decomposes into $x_{1}\in X_{i_{1}}\setminus Y_{i_{1}},\ldots,x_{s}\in X_{i_{s}}\setminus Y_{i_{s}}$. Then, $$ \begin{aligned} &(\Theta_{i}(y)_{1,1},\ldots,\Theta_{i}(y)_{n_{i},n_{i}})\\ =&(\Theta_{i_{1}}(x_{1})_{1,1},\ldots,\Theta_{i_{1}}(x_{1})_{n_{i_{1}},n_{i_{1}}},\ldots\ldots\ldots,\Theta_{i_{s}}(x_{s})_{1,1},\ldots,\Theta_{i_{s}}(x_{s})_{n_{i_{s}},n_{i_{s}}}). \end{aligned} $$ Define $B(y):=\{1\leq k\leq n_{i}:y\in B_{i,k}\}$. By \autoref{Bik}, $B(y)=\{1=k_{1}<\cdots<k_{s}\}$, where $k_{t}= 1+n_{i_{1}}+\cdots+n_{i_{t-1}}$ for $1\leq t\leq s$. Set $k_{s+1}:=n_{i}+1$ and note that $k_{t+1}-k_{t}=n_{i_{t}}$ for all $1\leq t\leq s$. By assumption $n_{i}\geq\mathfrak{s}(A)>N$, and so, in light of (I) and (III) above, we may apply \autoref{Wn reduction} with the vector $(\Theta_{i}(y)_{1,1},\ldots,\Theta_{i}(y)_{n_{i},n_{i}})$ and the set $B(y)$, to obtain $$ \begin{aligned} V_{i}(y)&=W_{n_{i}}(\Theta_{i}(y)_{1,1},\ldots,\Theta_{i}(y)_{n_{i},n_{i}})\\ &=\operatorname{diag}\left(W_{n_{i_{1}}}(\Theta_{i_{1}}(x_{1})_{1,1},\ldots,\Theta_{i_{1}}(x_{1})_{n_{i_{1}},n_{i_{1}}}),\ldots,W_{i_{s}}(\Theta_{i_{s}}(x_{s})_{1,1},\ldots,\Theta_{i_{s}}(x_{s})_{n_{i_{s}},n_{i_{s}}})\right)\\ &=\operatorname{diag}(V_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots,V_{i_{s}}(x_{s})). \end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $V\in A$. This completes the proof of \autoref{lower triangular}.
nodes.statement_short: Set V_i(x)=W_n(Theta_i(x)) with Theta from the indicator lemma; the cyclic shift makes f lower triangular and the block paths only mix zero columns; the W_n reduction gives V in A.

nodes.name: Indicator Theta
nodes.statement: Apply \autoref{indicators} with the natural number $N$, the index set $K=\{0\}$, and the closed sets $F_{i,k}:=X_{i}\setminus U_{i,k}$ for $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$. This yields a function $\Theta\in A$ with the following properties: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\Roman*)] \item for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $x\in X_{i}$, $\Theta_{i}(x)$ is a diagonal matrix with entries in $[0,1]$ whose final $N$ entries are all $0$ and such that at most one of every $N$ consecutive diagonal entries is non-zero; \item for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$, if $x\notin U_{i,k}$, then $\Theta_{i}(x)_{k,k}=0$; \item for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$, if $x\in B_{i,k}$, then $\Theta_{i}(x)_{k,k}=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the indicator lemma with K={0}

nodes.name: Apply the indicator lemma
nodes.statement: Apply \autoref{indicators} with the natural number $N$, the index set $K=\{0\}$, and the closed sets $F_{i,k}:=X_{i}\setminus U_{i,k}$ for $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$. This yields a function $\Theta\in A$ with the following properties:
nodes.statement_short: Get Theta in A with:

nodes.name: Property (I)
nodes.statement: for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $x\in X_{i}$, $\Theta_{i}(x)$ is a diagonal matrix with entries in $[0,1]$ whose final $N$ entries are all $0$ and such that at most one of every $N$ consecutive diagonal entries is non-zero;
nodes.statement_short: Sparse diagonal entries

nodes.name: Property (II)
nodes.statement: for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$, if $x\notin U_{i,k}$, then $\Theta_{i}(x)_{k,k}=0$;
nodes.statement_short: Theta vanishes off U_{i,k}

nodes.name: Property (III)
nodes.statement: for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$, if $x\in B_{i,k}$, then $\Theta_{i}(x)_{k,k}=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Theta equals 1 on B_{i,k}

nodes.name: Define V
nodes.statement: Since $N<\mathfrak{s}(A)$, we may, for each $1\leq i\leq l $, define $W_{n_{i}}\in C([0,1]^{n_{i}},M_{n_{i}})$ as in \autoref{ltmatrix}. For $1\leq i\leq l$ and $x\in X_{i}$, define the unitary $V_{i}\in C(X_{i},M_{n_{i}})$ by $$ V_{i}(x):=W_{n_{i}}(\Theta_{i}(x)_{1,1},\ldots,\Theta_{i}(x)_{n_{i},n_{i}}) $$ and set $V:=(V_{1},\ldots,V_{\ell})$. Let us first argue that $(fV)_{i}(x)$ is strictly lower triangular for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $x\in X_{i}$, and then show that $V\in A$.
nodes.statement_short: V_i(x)=W_{n_i}(Theta_i(x) diagonal)

nodes.name: Lower triangularity
nodes.statement: Fix $1\leq i\leq l $ and $x\in X_{i}$. From \autoref{Wn}, we have \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} (fV)_{i}(x)&=f_{i}(x)W_{n_{i}}(\Theta_{i}(x)_{1,1},\ldots,\Theta_{i}(x)_{n_{i},n_{i}})\\ &=f_{i}(x)U[\gamma_{1,n_{i}}^{n_{i}}]^{N}\prod_{k=N}^{n_{i}-1}u^{n_{i}}_{k,n_{i}}(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k+1,k+1}). \end{aligned} \end{equation} If we write $f_{i}(x)=\big[\, C_{1}\, |\, \cdots\, |\, C_{n_{i}}\, \big]$, where $C_{j}$ is the $j$th column of $f_{i}(x)$, then $f_{i}(x)U[\gamma_{1,n_{i}}^{n_{i}}]^{N}=\big[C_{N+1}\, |\, \cdots\, |\, C_{n_{i}}\, |\, C_{1}\, |\, \cdots\, |\, C_{N}\, \big]$. By the assumption of the lemma, $\mathfrak{r}(f_{i}(x))\leq N$. Hence, all non-zero entries in the first $n_{i}-N$ columns of the matrix $f_{i}(x)U[\gamma_{1,n_{i}}^{n_{i}}]^{N}$ must lie strictly below the diagonal. But by \autoref{Bik}, $x\in B_{i,1}$ and, hence, by the assumptions of the lemma, $f_{i}(x)$ has zero crosses at indices $1,\ldots, N$. In particular, the columns $C_{1},\ldots,C_{N}$ consist entirely of zeros. Therefore, $f_{i}(x)U[\gamma_{1,n_{i}}^{n_{i}}]^{N}$ is strictly lower triangular. To show that $(fV)_{i}(x)$ is strictly lower triangular, we thus only need to verify that $(fV)_{i}(x)=f_{i}(x)U[\gamma_{1,n_{i}}^{n_{i}}]^{N}$. To do this, it is enough, by \autoref{fV}, to check that for each integer $N\leq k\leq n_{i}-1$, \begin{equation} f_{i}(x)U[\gamma_{1,n_{i}}^{n_{i}}]^{N}u^{n_{i}}_{k,n_{i}}(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k+1,k+1})=f_{i}(x)U[\gamma_{1,n_{i}}^{n_{i}}]^{N}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to showing the block paths do not change f U[gamma]^N

nodes.name: Expand fV
nodes.statement: Fix $1\leq i\leq l $ and $x\in X_{i}$. From \autoref{Wn}, we have \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} (fV)_{i}(x)&=f_{i}(x)W_{n_{i}}(\Theta_{i}(x)_{1,1},\ldots,\Theta_{i}(x)_{n_{i},n_{i}})\\ &=f_{i}(x)U[\gamma_{1,n_{i}}^{n_{i}}]^{N}\prod_{k=N}^{n_{i}-1}u^{n_{i}}_{k,n_{i}}(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k+1,k+1}). \end{aligned} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Write (fV)_i(x) as f U[gamma]^N times block paths

nodes.name: Shifted matrix is strictly lower triangular
nodes.statement: If we write $f_{i}(x)=\big[\, C_{1}\, |\, \cdots\, |\, C_{n_{i}}\, \big]$, where $C_{j}$ is the $j$th column of $f_{i}(x)$, then $f_{i}(x)U[\gamma_{1,n_{i}}^{n_{i}}]^{N}=\big[C_{N+1}\, |\, \cdots\, |\, C_{n_{i}}\, |\, C_{1}\, |\, \cdots\, |\, C_{N}\, \big]$. By the assumption of the lemma, $\mathfrak{r}(f_{i}(x))\leq N$. Hence, all non-zero entries in the first $n_{i}-N$ columns of the matrix $f_{i}(x)U[\gamma_{1,n_{i}}^{n_{i}}]^{N}$ must lie strictly below the diagonal. But by \autoref{Bik}, $x\in B_{i,1}$ and, hence, by the assumptions of the lemma, $f_{i}(x)$ has zero crosses at indices $1,\ldots, N$. In particular, the columns $C_{1},\ldots,C_{N}$ consist entirely of zeros. Therefore, $f_{i}(x)U[\gamma_{1,n_{i}}^{n_{i}}]^{N}$ is strictly lower triangular.
nodes.statement_short: Bandwidth at most N and zero first N columns

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: To show that $(fV)_{i}(x)$ is strictly lower triangular, we thus only need to verify that $(fV)_{i}(x)=f_{i}(x)U[\gamma_{1,n_{i}}^{n_{i}}]^{N}$. To do this, it is enough, by \autoref{fV}, to check that for each integer $N\leq k\leq n_{i}-1$, \begin{equation} f_{i}(x)U[\gamma_{1,n_{i}}^{n_{i}}]^{N}u^{n_{i}}_{k,n_{i}}(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k+1,k+1})=f_{i}(x)U[\gamma_{1,n_{i}}^{n_{i}}]^{N}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Suffices: each block path fixes f U[gamma]^N

nodes.name: Block paths mix zero columns
nodes.statement: To this end, fix $N\leq k\leq n_{i}-1$. If $\Theta_{i}(x)_{k+1,k+1}=0$, then $u^{n_{i}}_{k,n_{i}}(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k+1,k+1})=1_{n_{i}}$ and there is nothing to show, and so we may assume $\Theta_{i}(x)_{k+1,k+1}>0$. Then, by (II) above, necessarily $x\in U_{i,k+1}$. Hence, by the assumption of the lemma, $f_{i}(x)$ has zero crosses at indices $k+1, \ldots,k+N$, from which it follows that the columns $C_{k+1},\ldots,C_{k+N}$ consist entirely of zeros. As noted above, these correspond to the columns of $f_{i}(x)U[\gamma_{1,n_{i}}^{n_{i}}]^{N}$ at indices $k+1-N,\ldots,k$. By \autoref{transposition prod}, the columns of $f_{i}(x)U[\gamma_{1,n_{i}}^{n_{i}}]^{N}u^{n_{i}}_{k,n_{i}}(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k+1,k+1})$ at indices $k-N+1,\ldots,k$ and $n_{i}-N+1,\ldots,n_{i}$ are linear combinations of the same set of columns of $f_{i}(x)U[\gamma_{1,n_{i}}^{n_{i}}]^{N}$ (i.e., of $C_{k+1},\ldots,C_{k+N},C_{1},\ldots,C_{N}$). But every column in this latter set consists entirely of zeros. Hence, since multiplying by the unitary $u^{n_{i}}_{k,n_{i}}(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k+1,k+1})$ on the right only alters columns at indices $k-N+1,\ldots,k$ and $n_{i}-N+1,\ldots,n_{i}$, \autoref{final} holds.
nodes.statement_short: When Theta_{k+1}>0, the columns mixed are zero columns

nodes.name: V lies in A
nodes.statement: Let us now ensure that $V\in A$. Suppose that $2\leq i\leq l $ and that $y\in Y_{i}$ decomposes into $x_{1}\in X_{i_{1}}\setminus Y_{i_{1}},\ldots,x_{s}\in X_{i_{s}}\setminus Y_{i_{s}}$. Then, $$ \begin{aligned} &(\Theta_{i}(y)_{1,1},\ldots,\Theta_{i}(y)_{n_{i},n_{i}})\\ =&(\Theta_{i_{1}}(x_{1})_{1,1},\ldots,\Theta_{i_{1}}(x_{1})_{n_{i_{1}},n_{i_{1}}},\ldots\ldots\ldots,\Theta_{i_{s}}(x_{s})_{1,1},\ldots,\Theta_{i_{s}}(x_{s})_{n_{i_{s}},n_{i_{s}}}). \end{aligned} $$ Define $B(y):=\{1\leq k\leq n_{i}:y\in B_{i,k}\}$. By \autoref{Bik}, $B(y)=\{1=k_{1}<\cdots<k_{s}\}$, where $k_{t}= 1+n_{i_{1}}+\cdots+n_{i_{t-1}}$ for $1\leq t\leq s$. Set $k_{s+1}:=n_{i}+1$ and note that $k_{t+1}-k_{t}=n_{i_{t}}$ for all $1\leq t\leq s$. By assumption $n_{i}\geq\mathfrak{s}(A)>N$, and so, in light of (I) and (III) above, we may apply \autoref{Wn reduction} with the vector $(\Theta_{i}(y)_{1,1},\ldots,\Theta_{i}(y)_{n_{i},n_{i}})$ and the set $B(y)$, to obtain $$ \begin{aligned} V_{i}(y)&=W_{n_{i}}(\Theta_{i}(y)_{1,1},\ldots,\Theta_{i}(y)_{n_{i},n_{i}})\\ &=\operatorname{diag}\left(W_{n_{i_{1}}}(\Theta_{i_{1}}(x_{1})_{1,1},\ldots,\Theta_{i_{1}}(x_{1})_{n_{i_{1}},n_{i_{1}}}),\ldots,W_{i_{s}}(\Theta_{i_{s}}(x_{s})_{1,1},\ldots,\Theta_{i_{s}}(x_{s})_{n_{i_{s}},n_{i_{s}}})\right)\\ &=\operatorname{diag}(V_{i_{1}}(x_{1}),\ldots,V_{i_{s}}(x_{s})). \end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $V\in A$. This completes the proof of \autoref{lower triangular}.
nodes.statement_short: W_n reduction lemma splits V_i(y) along the decomposition

nodes.name: Expansion of (fV)_i(x)
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} (fV)_{i}(x)&=f_{i}(x)W_{n_{i}}(\Theta_{i}(x)_{1,1},\ldots,\Theta_{i}(x)_{n_{i},n_{i}})\\ &=f_{i}(x)U[\gamma_{1,n_{i}}^{n_{i}}]^{N}\prod_{k=N}^{n_{i}-1}u^{n_{i}}_{k,n_{i}}(\Theta_{i}(x)_{k+1,k+1}). \end{aligned}
nodes.label: fV

nodes.name: Block paths fix the shifted matrix
nodes.label: final

nodes.name: Stable rank one for simple diagonal ASH algebras
nodes.statement: Suppose $$ A_{1}\overset{\psi_{1}}{\longrightarrow} A_{2}\overset{\psi_{2}}{\longrightarrow} A_{3}\overset{\psi_{3}}{\longrightarrow}\cdots\longrightarrow A:=\varinjlim A_{i} $$ is a simple inductive limit of DSH algebras with diagonal bonding maps. Then $A$ has stable rank one.
assumptions: is a simple inductive limit of DSH algebras with diagonal bonding maps
conclusions: $A$ has stable rank one
also_stated_at: every simple inductive limit of DSH algebra with diagonal bonding maps has stable rank one
every simple inductive limit of these algebras with diagonal bonding maps has stable rank one
nodes.label: main

nodes.name: Proof of the main theorem
nodes.statement: For $n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $\mu_{n}\colon A_{n}\to A$ denote the map in the construction of the inductive limit, which is unital (since the bonding maps are) and, by \autoref{injective} we may assume, injective. Furthermore, we may assume that the $A_{j}$'s are infinite-dimensional. Fix $\epsilon >0$ and $a\in A$. Our goal is to find an invertible element $a'\in A$ with $\|a-a'\|\leq\epsilon$. To start, choose $j\in\mathbb{N}$ and $f\in A_{j}$ such that $\|a-\mu_{j}(f)\|\leq\epsilon/4$. If $f$ is invertible in $A_{j}$, then $\mu_{j}(f)$ is invertible in $A$, in which case we are finished. Thus, we may assume that $f$ is not invertible in $A_{j}$. Since $A_{j}$ is infinite-dimensional, we may apply \autoref{far out} with $f$, $\epsilon/4$, and $N=\mathfrak{S}(A_{j})+M+1$, where $M$ is the natural number depending on $f$ and $\epsilon/4$, coming from the statement of \autoref{far out}. This yields a function $f'\in A_{j}$ with $\|f-f'\|\leq\epsilon/4$, a $j'>j$ such that $\mathfrak{s}(A_{j'})>NM$, and unitaries $V,V'\in A_{j'}$ with the following two properties (we adopt the same notation for the decomposition of $A_{j'}$ introduced just above \autoref{far out}): \begin{enumerate} \item for any $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$, there is a (possibly empty) open subset $U_{i,k}$ of $X_{i}$ containing $B_{i,k}$ such that $(V\psi_{j',j}(f')V')_{i}(x)$ has zero crosses at indices $k, k+M, k+2M,\ldots,k+(N-1)M$; \item for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $x\in X_{i}$, we have $\mathfrak{r}((V\psi_{j',j}(f')V')_{i}(x))\leq \mathfrak{S}(A_{j})+M-1$. \end{enumerate} Let $f'':=V\psi_{j',j}(f')V'\in A_{j'}$. Next, apply \autoref{block on set} with $A_{j'}$, $f''$, and $\epsilon/4$. This yields a function $g\in A_{j'}$ with $\|g-f''\|\leq \epsilon/4$ and, for $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$, open sets $\mathcal{O}_{i,k}\subset X_{i}$ containing $B_{i,k}$ on which $g_{i}$ always has a block point at index $k$; moreover, for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $x\in X_{i}$, the matrix $g_{i}(x)$ has a zero cross at every index that $f''_{i}(x)$ does, and $\mathfrak{r}(g_{i}(x))\leq\mathfrak{r}(f''_{i}(x))\leq\mathfrak{S}(A_{j})+M-1$. Thus, intersecting the $\mathcal{O}_{i,k}$'s with the $U_{i,k}$'s, we may assume that $g_{i}(x)$ has zero crosses at indices $k,k+M,\ldots,k+(N-1)M$ whenever $x\in \mathcal{O}_{i,k}$. Since $\mathfrak{s}(A_{j'})>NM$, we may now apply \autoref{cross shift} on $A_{j'}$ with $g$ and the $\mathcal{O}_{i,k}$'s above to obtain a unitary $W\in A_{j'}$ with the following properties: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\Roman*)] \item for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$, there are open sets $\mathcal{O}_{i,k}'\supset B_{i,k}$ in $X_{i}$ such that $W_{i}(x)g_{i}(x)W_{i}(x)^{*}$ has zero crosses at indices $k,k+1,\ldots,k+N-1$ whenever $x\in \mathcal{O}_{i,k}'$; \item $\mathfrak{r}(W_{i}(x)g_{i}(x)W_{i}(x)^{*})\leq \mathfrak{r}(g_{i}(x))+2\leq\mathfrak{S}(A_{j})+M+1=N$ for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $x\in X_{i}$. \end{enumerate} Let $g':=WgW^{*}\in A_{j'}$. Using these properties and the fact that $\mathfrak{s}(A_{j'})>NM\geq N$, we may apply \autoref{lower triangular} on $A_{j'}$ with $g'$ and the $\mathcal{O}_{i,k}'$'s to conclude that there is a unitary $W'\in A_{j'}$ such that for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $x\in X_{i}$, the matrix $(g'W')_{i}(x)$ is strictly lower triangular. Thus, $g'W'$ is a nilpotent element. As observed in Section 4 of \cite{Ror}, every nilpotent element of a unital $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra is arbitrarily close to an invertible element. Thus, there is an invertible element $h\in A_{j'}$ such that $\|g'W'-h\|\leq\epsilon/4$. Take $a':=\mu_{j'}(V^{*}W^{*}h(W')^{*}W(V')^{*})$ and observe that $a'$ is invertible in $A$. Then, since the $\mu_{n}$'s are injective, $$ \begin{aligned} \|\mu_{j}(f')-a'\|&=\|\psi_{j',j}(f')-V^{*}W^{*}h(W')^{*}W(V')^{*}\|\\ &=\|V^{*}W^{*}[WV\psi_{j',j}(f')V'W^{*}W'-h](W')^{*}W(V')^{*}\|\\ &\leq\|V^{*}W^{*}\|\|Wf''W^{*}W'-h\|\|(W')^{*}W(V')^{*}\|\\ &=\|Wf''W^{*}W'-h\|\\ &\leq\|Wf''W^{*}W'-WgW^{*}W'\|+\|WgW^{*}W'-h\|\\ &\leq\|W\|\|f''-g\|\|W^{*}W'\|+\|g'W'-h\|\\ &\leq\frac{\epsilon}{4}+\frac{\epsilon}{4}\\ &=\frac{\epsilon}{2}, \end{aligned} $$ and $$ \begin{aligned} \|a-\mu_{j}(f')\|&\leq\|a-\mu_{j}(f)\|+\|\mu_{j}(f)-\mu_{j}(f')\| \leq \frac{\epsilon}{4}+\|f-f'\| \leq\frac{\epsilon}{2}. \end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $$ \|a-a'\|\leq \|a-\mu_{j}(f')\|+\|\mu_{j}(f')-a'\|\leq\frac{\epsilon}{2}+\frac{\epsilon}{2}=\epsilon, $$ as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Approximate a by a non-invertible f in some A_j; via far-out, block-point, cross-shift and lower-triangular lemmas turn its image into a nilpotent, which is close to an invertible (Rørdam).

nodes.name: Normalize
nodes.statement: For $n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $\mu_{n}\colon A_{n}\to A$ denote the map in the construction of the inductive limit, which is unital (since the bonding maps are) and, by \autoref{injective} we may assume, injective. Furthermore, we may assume that the $A_{j}$'s are infinite-dimensional.
nodes.statement_short: Assume injective bonding maps and infinite-dimensional A_j

nodes.name: Reduce to a non-invertible f
nodes.statement: Fix $\epsilon >0$ and $a\in A$. Our goal is to find an invertible element $a'\in A$ with $\|a-a'\|\leq\epsilon$. To start, choose $j\in\mathbb{N}$ and $f\in A_{j}$ such that $\|a-\mu_{j}(f)\|\leq\epsilon/4$. If $f$ is invertible in $A_{j}$, then $\mu_{j}(f)$ is invertible in $A$, in which case we are finished. Thus, we may assume that $f$ is not invertible in $A_{j}$.
nodes.statement_short: Approximate a by mu_j(f) with f non-invertible

nodes.name: Apply the far-out lemma
nodes.statement: Since $A_{j}$ is infinite-dimensional, we may apply \autoref{far out} with $f$, $\epsilon/4$, and $N=\mathfrak{S}(A_{j})+M+1$, where $M$ is the natural number depending on $f$ and $\epsilon/4$, coming from the statement of \autoref{far out}. This yields a function $f'\in A_{j}$ with $\|f-f'\|\leq\epsilon/4$, a $j'>j$ such that $\mathfrak{s}(A_{j'})>NM$, and unitaries $V,V'\in A_{j'}$ with the following two properties (we adopt the same notation for the decomposition of $A_{j'}$ introduced just above \autoref{far out}): \begin{enumerate} \item for any $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$, there is a (possibly empty) open subset $U_{i,k}$ of $X_{i}$ containing $B_{i,k}$ such that $(V\psi_{j',j}(f')V')_{i}(x)$ has zero crosses at indices $k, k+M, k+2M,\ldots,k+(N-1)M$; \item for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $x\in X_{i}$, we have $\mathfrak{r}((V\psi_{j',j}(f')V')_{i}(x))\leq \mathfrak{S}(A_{j})+M-1$.
nodes.statement_short: Get f', j', V, V' with spaced zero crosses and bounded bandwidth

nodes.name: Choice of N
nodes.statement: Since $A_{j}$ is infinite-dimensional, we may apply \autoref{far out} with $f$, $\epsilon/4$, and $N=\mathfrak{S}(A_{j})+M+1$, where $M$ is the natural number depending on $f$ and $\epsilon/4$, coming from the statement of \autoref{far out}. This yields a function $f'\in A_{j}$ with $\|f-f'\|\leq\epsilon/4$, a $j'>j$ such that $\mathfrak{s}(A_{j'})>NM$, and unitaries $V,V'\in A_{j'}$ with the following two properties (we adopt the same notation for the decomposition of $A_{j'}$ introduced just above \autoref{far out}):
nodes.statement_short: Apply with N=S(A_j)+M+1, obtaining:

nodes.name: Property (1)
nodes.statement: for any $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$, there is a (possibly empty) open subset $U_{i,k}$ of $X_{i}$ containing $B_{i,k}$ such that $(V\psi_{j',j}(f')V')_{i}(x)$ has zero crosses at indices $k, k+M, k+2M,\ldots,k+(N-1)M$;
nodes.statement_short: Zero crosses at k, k+M, ...

nodes.name: Property (2)
nodes.statement: for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $x\in X_{i}$, we have $\mathfrak{r}((V\psi_{j',j}(f')V')_{i}(x))\leq \mathfrak{S}(A_{j})+M-1$.
nodes.statement_short: Bandwidth bound

nodes.name: Apply block-point approximation
nodes.statement: Let $f'':=V\psi_{j',j}(f')V'\in A_{j'}$. Next, apply \autoref{block on set} with $A_{j'}$, $f''$, and $\epsilon/4$. This yields a function $g\in A_{j'}$ with $\|g-f''\|\leq \epsilon/4$ and, for $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$, open sets $\mathcal{O}_{i,k}\subset X_{i}$ containing $B_{i,k}$ on which $g_{i}$ always has a block point at index $k$; moreover, for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $x\in X_{i}$, the matrix $g_{i}(x)$ has a zero cross at every index that $f''_{i}(x)$ does, and $\mathfrak{r}(g_{i}(x))\leq\mathfrak{r}(f''_{i}(x))\leq\mathfrak{S}(A_{j})+M-1$. Thus, intersecting the $\mathcal{O}_{i,k}$'s with the $U_{i,k}$'s, we may assume that $g_{i}(x)$ has zero crosses at indices $k,k+M,\ldots,k+(N-1)M$ whenever $x\in \mathcal{O}_{i,k}$.
nodes.statement_short: Approximate f'' by g with block points, keeping zero crosses

nodes.name: Apply the cross-shift lemma
nodes.statement: Since $\mathfrak{s}(A_{j'})>NM$, we may now apply \autoref{cross shift} on $A_{j'}$ with $g$ and the $\mathcal{O}_{i,k}$'s above to obtain a unitary $W\in A_{j'}$ with the following properties: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\Roman*)] \item for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$, there are open sets $\mathcal{O}_{i,k}'\supset B_{i,k}$ in $X_{i}$ such that $W_{i}(x)g_{i}(x)W_{i}(x)^{*}$ has zero crosses at indices $k,k+1,\ldots,k+N-1$ whenever $x\in \mathcal{O}_{i,k}'$; \item $\mathfrak{r}(W_{i}(x)g_{i}(x)W_{i}(x)^{*})\leq \mathfrak{r}(g_{i}(x))+2\leq\mathfrak{S}(A_{j})+M+1=N$ for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $x\in X_{i}$.
nodes.statement_short: Get W grouping zero crosses into N consecutive indices

nodes.name: Apply cross shift
nodes.statement: Since $\mathfrak{s}(A_{j'})>NM$, we may now apply \autoref{cross shift} on $A_{j'}$ with $g$ and the $\mathcal{O}_{i,k}$'s above to obtain a unitary $W\in A_{j'}$ with the following properties:
nodes.statement_short: Obtain W with:

nodes.name: Property (I)
nodes.statement: for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $1\leq k\leq n_{i}$, there are open sets $\mathcal{O}_{i,k}'\supset B_{i,k}$ in $X_{i}$ such that $W_{i}(x)g_{i}(x)W_{i}(x)^{*}$ has zero crosses at indices $k,k+1,\ldots,k+N-1$ whenever $x\in \mathcal{O}_{i,k}'$;
nodes.statement_short: N consecutive zero crosses near B_{i,k}

nodes.name: Property (II)
nodes.statement: $\mathfrak{r}(W_{i}(x)g_{i}(x)W_{i}(x)^{*})\leq \mathfrak{r}(g_{i}(x))+2\leq\mathfrak{S}(A_{j})+M+1=N$ for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $x\in X_{i}$.
nodes.statement_short: Bandwidth at most N

nodes.name: Lower triangular and nilpotent
nodes.statement: Let $g':=WgW^{*}\in A_{j'}$. Using these properties and the fact that $\mathfrak{s}(A_{j'})>NM\geq N$, we may apply \autoref{lower triangular} on $A_{j'}$ with $g'$ and the $\mathcal{O}_{i,k}'$'s to conclude that there is a unitary $W'\in A_{j'}$ such that for all $1\leq i\leq l $ and $x\in X_{i}$, the matrix $(g'W')_{i}(x)$ is strictly lower triangular. Thus, $g'W'$ is a nilpotent element. As observed in Section 4 of \cite{Ror}, every nilpotent element of a unital $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra is arbitrarily close to an invertible element. Thus, there is an invertible element $h\in A_{j'}$ such that $\|g'W'-h\|\leq\epsilon/4$.
nodes.statement_short: Lower-triangular lemma makes g'W' nilpotent; Rørdam gives a nearby invertible h

nodes.name: Estimate
nodes.statement: Take $a':=\mu_{j'}(V^{*}W^{*}h(W')^{*}W(V')^{*})$ and observe that $a'$ is invertible in $A$. Then, since the $\mu_{n}$'s are injective, $$ \begin{aligned} \|\mu_{j}(f')-a'\|&=\|\psi_{j',j}(f')-V^{*}W^{*}h(W')^{*}W(V')^{*}\|\\ &=\|V^{*}W^{*}[WV\psi_{j',j}(f')V'W^{*}W'-h](W')^{*}W(V')^{*}\|\\ &\leq\|V^{*}W^{*}\|\|Wf''W^{*}W'-h\|\|(W')^{*}W(V')^{*}\|\\ &=\|Wf''W^{*}W'-h\|\\ &\leq\|Wf''W^{*}W'-WgW^{*}W'\|+\|WgW^{*}W'-h\|\\ &\leq\|W\|\|f''-g\|\|W^{*}W'\|+\|g'W'-h\|\\ &\leq\frac{\epsilon}{4}+\frac{\epsilon}{4}\\ &=\frac{\epsilon}{2}, \end{aligned} $$ and $$ \begin{aligned} \|a-\mu_{j}(f')\|&\leq\|a-\mu_{j}(f)\|+\|\mu_{j}(f)-\mu_{j}(f')\| \leq \frac{\epsilon}{4}+\|f-f'\| \leq\frac{\epsilon}{2}. \end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $$ \|a-a'\|\leq \|a-\mu_{j}(f')\|+\|\mu_{j}(f')-a'\|\leq\frac{\epsilon}{2}+\frac{\epsilon}{2}=\epsilon, $$ as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Unpack the approximations: a' is invertible and within epsilon of a

nodes.name: Toms–Winter Conjecture
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a separable, unital, simple, non-elementary, nuclear $\mathrm{C}^{*}$-algebra. The following statements are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item $A$ has finite nuclear dimension. \item $A$ is $\mathcal{Z}$-stable; that is, $A\otimes \mathcal{Z}\cong A$. \item $A$ has strict comparison of positive elements. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: Let $A$ be a separable, unital, simple, non-elementary, nuclear $\mathrm{C}^{*}$-algebra
conclusions: The following statements are equivalent.
equivalent_conditions: $A$ has strict comparison of positive elements.
nodes.label: Toms-Winter

nodes.name: Rørdam: Z-stability implies strict comparison
nodes.statement: At the time, part of this conjecture had already been established by R\o rdam, who, in Theorem 4.5 and Corollary 4.6 of \cite{Ror2}, proved that \textit{(2)} implies \textit{(3)}.
conclusions: proved that \textit{(2)} implies \textit{(3)}

nodes.name: Winter: finite nuclear dimension implies Z-stability
nodes.statement: Winter showed in Corollary 7.3 of \cite{Win} that \textit{(1)} implies \textit{(2)}.
conclusions: \textit{(1)} implies \textit{(2)}

nodes.name: Castillejos–Evington–Tikuisis–White–Winter: Z-stability implies finite nuclear dimension
nodes.statement: The work of various hands established that \textit{(2)} implies \textit{(1)} in special cases, but very recently, in Theorem A of \cite{CETWW}, this implication was shown to hold in full generality.
nodes.origin_citation: Castillejos, Evington, Tikuisis, White, Winter 2021, Theorem A
conclusions: this implication was shown to hold in full generality

nodes.name: Automorphism sigma induced by h
nodes.statement: Let $\sigma\colon C(T)\to C(T)$ denote the automorphism arising from $h$ given by $\sigma(f):=f\circ h^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Implementing unitary u
nodes.statement: Let $u$ denote the unitary in the associated crossed product $A$ implementing the $\sigma$ action, i.e., $ufu^{*}=\sigma(f)$ for all $f\in C(T)$.

nodes.name: Orbit-breaking subalgebra A_S
nodes.statement: Given a closed set $S\subset T$ with non-empty interior, let $A_{S}$ denote the orbit-breaking sub-$\mathrm{C}^{*}$-algebra of $A$ associated to $S$, first introduced by Putnam in \cite{Put} for Cantor minimal systems and later by Q. Lin and Phillips for more general minimal systems (see \cite{Lin}, \cite{LP}, and \cite{LP2}); that is, $A_{S}$ is the $\mathrm{C}^{*}$-algebra generated by $\{f,ug:f\in C(T), g\in C_{0}(T\setminus S)\}$, where we adopt the shorthand $C_{0}(T\setminus S):=\{g\in C(T): g|_{S}\equiv 0\}$.
nodes.statement_short: A_S is the C*-subalgebra generated by C(T) and u C_0(T minus S).

nodes.name: Lin–Phillips: orbit-breaking subalgebras are DSH
nodes.statement: In \cite{Lin}, \cite{LP}, and \cite{LP2}, Q. Lin and Phillips showed that $A_{S}$ is a recursive subhomogeneous algebra, and in fact a DSH algebra.
conclusions: $A_{S}$ is a recursive subhomogeneous algebra, and in fact a DSH algebra
also_stated_at: It follows that $A_{S}$ is a DSH algebra.

nodes.name: First return time
nodes.statement: Given $s\in S$, let $\lambda_{S}(s):=\min\{n>0:h^{n}(s)\in S\}$ (the first return time of $s$ to $S$).

nodes.name: Return times n_i^S
nodes.statement: Thus there exist $1\leq n_{1}^{S}<n_{2}^{S}<\cdots<n_{ l (S)}^{S}$ such that $\{\lambda_{S}(s):s\in S\}=\{n_{i}^{S}:1\leq i\leq l (S)\}$.

nodes.name: Base spaces X_i^S and Y_i^S
nodes.statement: For $1\leq i\leq l (S)$, let $X_{i}^{S}:=\overline{\lambda_{S}^{-1}(n_{i}^{S})}$ and $Y_{i}^{S}:=X_{i}^{S}\setminus\lambda_{S}^{-1}(n_{i}^{S})$.

nodes.name: Return pattern of points in Y_i^S
nodes.statement: Then, for given $1\leq i \leq l (S)$ and $y\in Y_{i}^{S}$, there are indices $1\leq i_{1},\ldots,i_{p}< i$ with $y\in X_{i_{1}}^{S}\setminus Y_{i_{1}}^{S}$, such that $n_{i_{1}}^{S}+\cdots+n_{i_{p}}^{S}=n_{i}^{S}$ and such that $h^{k}(y)\in S$ if and only if $k=n_{i_{1}}^{S}+\cdots +n_{i_{j}}^{S}$ for some $1\leq j\leq p$.
assumptions: for given $1\leq i \leq l (S)$ and $y\in Y_{i}^{S}$
conclusions: there are indices $1\leq i_{1},\ldots,i_{p}< i$ with $y\in X_{i_{1}}^{S}\setminus Y_{i_{1}}^{S}$, such that $n_{i_{1}}^{S}+\cdots+n_{i_{p}}^{S}=n_{i}^{S}$

nodes.name: Intermediate returns lie in X minus Y
nodes.statement: Note, too, that $h^{n_{i_{1}}^{S}+\cdots +n_{i_{j-1}}^{S}}(y)\in X_{i_{j}}^{S}\setminus Y_{i_{j}}^{S}$ for all $2\leq j\leq p$.
conclusions: $h^{n_{i_{1}}^{S}+\cdots +n_{i_{j-1}}^{S}}(y)\in X_{i_{j}}^{S}\setminus Y_{i_{j}}^{S}$ for all $2\leq j\leq p$

nodes.name: Lin–Phillips recursive description of A_S
nodes.statement: Then, $A_{S}$ is isomorphic to a sub-$\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra of $\bigoplus_{i=1}^{ l (S)}C(X_{i}^{S},M_{n_{i}^{S}})$, where an element $(f_{1},\ldots,f_{ l (S)})$ of $\bigoplus_{i=1}^{ l (S)}C(X_{i}^{S},M_{n_{i}^{S}})$ is in $A_{S}$ if and only if, for given $1\leq i\leq l (S)$ and $y\in Y_{i}^{S}$, $$ f_{i}(y)=\operatorname{diag}\left(f_{i_{1}}(y),f_{i_{2}}(h^{n_{i_{1}}^{S}}(y)),\ldots,f_{i_{p}}(h^{n_{i_{1}}^{S}+\cdots +n_{i_{p-1}}^{S}}(y))\right), $$ where $i_{1},\ldots,i_{p}$ are as described above.
conclusions: $A_{S}$ is isomorphic to a sub-$\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra of $\bigoplus_{i=1}^{ l (S)}C(X_{i}^{S},M_{n_{i}^{S}})$
nodes.statement_short: A_S is the subalgebra of the direct sum of C(X_i^S, M_{n_i^S}) whose value at y in Y_i^S is the diagonal of values along the orbit's returns.

nodes.name: Return decomposition for nested sets R in S
nodes.statement: Suppose $R\subset S\subset T$. Let $1\leq i\leq l (R)$ and $x\in X_{i}^{R}\setminus Y_{i}^{R}=\lambda_{R}^{-1}(n_{i}^{R})$. Then, there are indices $1\leq i_{1},\ldots,i_{q}\leq l (S)$ such that: \begin{enumerate} \item $n_{i_{1}}^{S}+\cdots+n_{i_{q}}^{S}=n_{i}^{R}$; \item for all $1\leq k\leq n_{i}^{R}$, $h^{k}(x)\in S$ if and only if $k=n_{i_{1}}^{S}+\cdots+n_{i_{j}}^{S}$ for some $1\leq j\leq q$; \item $x\in X_{i_{1}}^{S}\setminus Y_{i_{1}}^{S}$ and, for all $2\leq j\leq q$, $h^{n_{i_{1}}^{S}+\cdots+n_{i_{j-1}}^{S}}(x)\in X_{i_{j}}^{S}\setminus Y_{i_{j}}^{S}$. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: $R\subset S\subset T$
$1\leq i\leq l (R)$ and $x\in X_{i}^{R}\setminus Y_{i}^{R}=\lambda_{R}^{-1}(n_{i}^{R})$
conclusions: there are indices $1\leq i_{1},\ldots,i_{q}\leq l (S)$ such that
nodes.label: returning

nodes.name: Proof of the return decomposition
nodes.statement: Since $R\subset S$ and the sets $X_{j}^{S}\setminus Y_{j}^{S}$ for $1\leq j\leq l (S)$ partition $S$, there is a unique $1\leq i_{1}\leq l (S)$ such that $x\in X_{i_{1}}^{S}\setminus Y_{i_{1}}^{S}$. Moreover, $n_{i_{1}}^{S}=\lambda_{S}(x)\leq \lambda_{R}(x)=n_{i}^{R}$. If $n_{i_{1}}^{S}=n_{i}^{R}$, then there is nothing to show. Otherwise, there is an $i_{2}$ such that $h^{n_{i_{1}}^{S}}(x)\in X_{i_{2}}^{S}\setminus Y_{i_{2}}^{S}$. Note that $n_{i_{2}}^{S}=\lambda_{S}(h^{n_{i_{1}}^{S}}(x))\leq n_{i}^{R}-n_{i_{1}}^{S}$. If $n_{i_{2}}^{S}=n_{i}^{R}-n_{i_{1}}^{S}$, the desired result follows. Otherwise, we let $i_{3}$ be such that $h^{n_{i_{1}}^{S}+n_{i_{2}}^{S}}(x)\in X_{i_{3}}^{S}\setminus Y_{i_{3}}^{S}$ and proceed as before. Eventually, this process terminates (when $n_{i_{1}}^{S}+\cdots+n_{i_{q}}^{S}=n_{i}^{R}$) and yields indices with the desired properties. This proves the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Follow the orbit of x, recording successive return times to S until the first return to R.

nodes.name: First return to S
nodes.statement: Since $R\subset S$ and the sets $X_{j}^{S}\setminus Y_{j}^{S}$ for $1\leq j\leq l (S)$ partition $S$, there is a unique $1\leq i_{1}\leq l (S)$ such that $x\in X_{i_{1}}^{S}\setminus Y_{i_{1}}^{S}$. Moreover, $n_{i_{1}}^{S}=\lambda_{S}(x)\leq \lambda_{R}(x)=n_{i}^{R}$. If $n_{i_{1}}^{S}=n_{i}^{R}$, then there is nothing to show.
nodes.statement_short: x lies in a unique piece X_{i_1}^S; its return time to S is at most that to R

nodes.name: Iterate returns
nodes.statement: Otherwise, there is an $i_{2}$ such that $h^{n_{i_{1}}^{S}}(x)\in X_{i_{2}}^{S}\setminus Y_{i_{2}}^{S}$. Note that $n_{i_{2}}^{S}=\lambda_{S}(h^{n_{i_{1}}^{S}}(x))\leq n_{i}^{R}-n_{i_{1}}^{S}$. If $n_{i_{2}}^{S}=n_{i}^{R}-n_{i_{1}}^{S}$, the desired result follows. Otherwise, we let $i_{3}$ be such that $h^{n_{i_{1}}^{S}+n_{i_{2}}^{S}}(x)\in X_{i_{3}}^{S}\setminus Y_{i_{3}}^{S}$ and proceed as before.
nodes.statement_short: Continue along the orbit to the next return to S

nodes.name: Termination
nodes.statement: Eventually, this process terminates (when $n_{i_{1}}^{S}+\cdots+n_{i_{q}}^{S}=n_{i}^{R}$) and yields indices with the desired properties. This proves the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: The process stops at the return time to R

nodes.name: Lin–Phillips homomorphism gamma_S
nodes.statement: By \cite{LP2}, Proposition 2.4, there is a unique homomorphism $\gamma_{S}\colon A_{S}\to \bigoplus_{i=1}^{ l (S)}C(X_{i}^{S},M_{n_{i}^{S}})$ with the property that for $f\in C(T)$ and $g\in C_{0}(T\setminus S)$, \begin{equation} \gamma_{S}(f)_{i}=\operatorname{diag}\left(f\circ h|_{X_{i}^{S}},f\circ h^{2}|_{X_{i}^{S}},\ldots,f\circ h^{n_{i}^{S}}|_{X_{i}^{S}}\right) \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \gamma_{S}(ug)_{i}= \begin{pmatrix} 0 & & & & \\ g\circ h|_{X_{i}^{S}} & 0 & & & \\ & g\circ h^{2}|_{X_{i}^{S}} & \ddots & &\\ & & \ddots & 0 &\\ & & & g\circ h^{n_{i}^{S}-1}|_{X_{i}^{S}} & 0 \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned} \end{equation} for $1\leq i\leq l (S)$.
conclusions: there is a unique homomorphism $\gamma_{S}\colon A_{S}\to \bigoplus_{i=1}^{ l (S)}C(X_{i}^{S},M_{n_{i}^{S}})$
nodes.statement_short: gamma_S sends f to the diagonal of f along the orbit and ug to the subdiagonal matrix of g along the orbit.

nodes.name: gamma_S on C(T)
nodes.statement: \gamma_{S}(f)_{i}=\operatorname{diag}\left(f\circ h|_{X_{i}^{S}},f\circ h^{2}|_{X_{i}^{S}},\ldots,f\circ h^{n_{i}^{S}}|_{X_{i}^{S}}\right)
nodes.label: function identification

nodes.name: gamma_S on uC_0(T minus S)
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} \gamma_{S}(ug)_{i}= \begin{pmatrix} 0 & & & & \\ g\circ h|_{X_{i}^{S}} & 0 & & & \\ & g\circ h^{2}|_{X_{i}^{S}} & \ddots & &\\ & & \ddots & 0 &\\ & & & g\circ h^{n_{i}^{S}-1}|_{X_{i}^{S}} & 0 \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned}
nodes.label: ufunction identification

nodes.name: A_S is contained in A_R
nodes.statement: Now, fix $R\subset S\subset T$. By examining the generating sets, it follows that $A_{S}$ is contained in $A_{R}$.
assumptions: fix $R\subset S\subset T$
conclusions: $A_{S}$ is contained in $A_{R}$

nodes.name: Inclusion map psi
nodes.statement: Let $\psi\colon A_{S}\to A_{R}$ denote the inclusion map.

nodes.name: Inclusions of orbit-breaking subalgebras are diagonal
nodes.statement: $\psi$ is a diagonal map (see \autoref{diagonal map}) between DSH algebras.
assumptions: fix $R\subset S\subset T$
conclusions: $\psi$ is a diagonal map (see \autoref{diagonal map}) between DSH algebras
nodes.label: diagonal inclusion

nodes.name: Proof that inclusions are diagonal
nodes.statement: Fix $1\leq i\leq l (R)$ and $x\in X_{i}^{R}\setminus Y_{i}^{R}=\lambda_{R}^{-1}(n_{i}^{R})$. By \autoref{returning}, there are indices $1\leq i_{1},\ldots,i_{q}\leq l (S)$ such that: \begin{enumerate} \item $n_{i_{1}}^{S}+\cdots+n_{i_{q}}^{S}=n_{i}^{R}$; \item for all $1\leq k\leq n_{i}^{R}$, $h^{k}(x)\in S$ if and only if $k=\beta_{j}$ for some $1\leq j\leq q$, where $\beta_{j}:=n_{i_{1}}^{S}+\cdots+n_{i_{j}}^{S}$; \item for all $1\leq j\leq q$, $h^{\beta_{j-1}}(x)\in X_{i_{j}}^{S}\setminus Y_{i_{j}}^{S}$ (here $\beta_{0}:=0$, so that $x\in X_{i_{1}}^{S}\setminus Y_{i_{1}}^{S}$). \end{enumerate} Let us show that $x$ decomposes into $h^{\beta_{0}}(x)=x,h^{\beta_{1}}(x),\ldots,h^{\beta_{q-1}}(x)$ under $\psi$. Suppose that $f\in C(T)$. Let us begin by verifying that \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \gamma_{R}(\psi(f))_{i}(x)=\operatorname{diag}\left(\gamma_{S}(f)_{i_{1}}(x),\gamma_{S}(f)_{i_{2}}(h^{\beta_{1}}(x)),\ldots,\gamma_{S}(f)_{i_{q}}(h^{\beta_{q-1}}(x))\right). \end{aligned} \end{equation} Fix $1\leq j\leq q$. By \autoref{function identification}, $$ \begin{aligned} \gamma_{S}(f)_{i_{j}}(h^{\beta_{j-1}}(x))&=\operatorname{diag}\left(f(h(h^{\beta_{j-1}}(x))),\ldots,f(h^{n_{i_{j}}^{S}}(h^{\beta_{j-1}}(x)))\right)\\ &=\operatorname{diag}\left(f(h^{\beta_{j-1}+1}(x)),\ldots,f(h^{\beta_{j}}(x))\right). \end{aligned} $$ Hence, $$ \begin{aligned} &\operatorname{diag}\left(\gamma_{S}(f)_{i_{1}}(x),\gamma_{S}(f)_{i_{2}}(h^{\beta_{1}}(x)),\ldots,\gamma_{S}(f)_{i_{q}}(h^{\beta_{q-1}}(x))\right)\\ =&\operatorname{diag}\left(f(h^{\beta_{0}+1}(x)),\ldots,f(h^{\beta_{1}}(x)),\ldots\ldots,f(h^{\beta_{q-1}+1}(x)),\ldots,f(h^{\beta_{q}}(x))\right)\\ =&\operatorname{diag}\left(f(h(x)),\ldots,f(h^{n_{i}^{R}}(x))\right)\\ =&\gamma_{R}(f)_{i}(x), \end{aligned} $$ which yields \autoref{diagonal f}. Next, suppose $g\in C_{0}(T\setminus S)$. Let us show that \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \gamma_{R}(\psi(ug))_{i}(x)=\operatorname{diag}\left(\gamma_{S}(ug)_{i_{1}}(x),\gamma_{S}(ug)_{i_{2}}(h^{\beta_{1}}(x)),\ldots,\gamma_{S}(ug)_{i_{q}}(h^{\beta_{q-1}}(x))\right). \end{aligned} \end{equation} By \autoref{ufunction identification}, $$ \begin{aligned} \gamma_{R}(ug)_{i}(x)= \begin{pmatrix} 0 & & & & \\ g(h(x)) & 0 & & & \\ & g(h^{2}(x)) & \ddots & &\\ & & \ddots & 0 &\\ & & & g(h^{n_{i}^{R}-1}(x)) & 0 \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned}. $$ For $1\leq j\leq q$, we have $h^{\beta_{j}}(x)\in S$ by property (2) above, so that $g(h^{\beta_{j}}(x))=0$. Hence, partitioning $\{1,2,\ldots,n_{i}^{R}\}$ into the sets $\{\beta_{j-1}+1,\ldots,\beta_{j}\}$ for $1\leq j\leq q$, we may view $\gamma_{R}(ug)_{i}(x)$ as a block-diagonal matrix $\operatorname{diag}(B_{1},\ldots,B_{q})$, where $$ \begin{aligned} B_{j}&:=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & & & & \\ g(h^{\beta_{j-1}+1}(x)) & 0 & & & \\ & g(h^{\beta_{j-1}+2}(x)) & \ddots & &\\ & & \ddots & 0 &\\ & & & g(h^{\beta_{j}-1}(x)) & 0 \end{pmatrix} =\gamma_{S}(ug)_{i_{j}}(h^{\beta_{j-1}}(x)), \end{aligned} $$ which yields \autoref{diagonal ug}. We have shown that $x$ decomposes into $h^{\beta_{0}}(x)=x,h^{\beta_{1}}(x),\ldots,h^{\beta_{q-1}}(x)$ under $\psi$ on the generators of $A_{S}$. Let us now use continuity to prove that this decomposition is maintained for all elements of $A_{S}$. Let $a\in A_{S}$ be arbitrary. By definition, we may write $a=\lim_{n\to\infty}w_{n}$, where for each $n\in\mathbb{N}$, $w_{n}$ is a word in $C(T)\cup uC_{0}(T\setminus S)\cup C_{0}(T\setminus S)u^{*}$. By \autoref{diagonal f} and \autoref{diagonal ug}, $$ \begin{aligned} \gamma_{R}(\psi(w_{n}))_{i}(x) =\operatorname{diag}\left(\gamma_{S}(w_{n})_{i_{1}}(x),\gamma_{S}(w_{n})_{i_{2}}(h^{\beta_{1}}(x)),\ldots,\gamma_{S}(w_{n})_{i_{q}}(h^{\beta_{q-1}}(x))\right) \end{aligned} $$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$.
